Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ [Al-Kahf: 15] ﴿And when you have separated from them and what they worship other than Allah, then take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread for you of His mercy and prepare for you from your affair a provision.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 16] ﴿And you would see the sun, when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it sets, passing them on the left, while they are in a spacious place within it. **Lexical notes**

*Bakhaʿa* (بَخَعَ) means to destroy oneself or to kill oneself from intensity of grief; its root sense is exertion. This is stated by al-Akhfash and al-Farra'. In a hadith of ʿĀʾisha, she mentioned ʿUmar and said: "He bakhaʿa the land," meaning he exerted it until he took what was in it of the wealth of kings. Al-Kisa'i said: "He bakhaʿa the land by cultivation," meaning he made it weak by continuously plowing it. Al-Layth said: "A man bakhaʿa himself," meaning he killed himself from intensity of his grief. He recited the verse of al-Farazdaq:

Ah, you who destroy yourself with grief
over a thing the decrees have pulled from his hands.

Meaning: "nahhatahu" with the ḥāʾ doubled, then lightened. Abu ʿUbayda said: Dhu al-Rumma used to recite "al-wajd" with a nominative ending. Al-Asmaʿi said: it is actually "al-wajda" with a fatḥa. End of quote. Thus its accusative would be as a *mafʿūl li-ajlihi* (object of purpose, an accusative of cause).

*Jaraza* (جَرَزَتِ): the land became barren from drought, locusts, or the like, its vegetation gone and nothing left in it. Barren lands are *ajrāz*. It is said: a year is *jurz*, and years are *ajrāz*, with no rain in them. The *juruz* of the land is locusts that consumed what was in it. A woman is *jarūz*, meaning a great eater. The poet said:

Indeed the old woman is a glutton, a devourer,
eating a qafīz every night.

*Al-kahf* is an open, wide cavity in a mountain; if it is not wide, it is a *ghār* (cave). Ibn al-Anbari said: the linguists reported that it is in the position of a *ghār* in a mountain.

*Al-raqīm* is a form of *raqama*, either in the sense of the passive participle or the active participle. The disagreement among the exegetes about its intended meaning will come, God willing. As for the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

There was nothing there but the *raqīm*, a neighbor,
and their hunting dog, while the people in the cave lay still.

Here it means their dog.

*Aḥṣā al-shayʾ* means he preserved it and mastered it. *Al-shaṭaṭ* means injustice, transgression of limits, and extremism. Al-Farra' said: "Ishtatta fī al-shu'm" means he exceeded the measure. *Shatta al-manzil* means it was far, *shuṭūṭan*. *Shatta al-rajul* and *ashatta* mean he was unjust. *Shattat al-jāriya* means the girl became tall.

*Tazāwaru* (تَزاوَرُ): it inclines and turns aside. Al-Akhfash said: *tazāwarru* means it contracts. End of quote. *Al-zawr* is inclination, and *al-azwar* is one who inclines with his eye to a side; this may also be used of other than the eye. Ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

And fear of the people made me incline away from her.

ʿAntara said:

It turned aside from the impact of the spears on its chest,
and complained to me with a tear and a neigh.

Bishr ibn Abi Hazim said:

The guides lead her toward the waters of a palm grove,
and in her there is a turning aside from exhausted camels.

From this comes *zārahu*, when he inclined toward him. *Al-zawr* is inclination away from truth.

*Qaraḍa al-shayʾ* means he cut it. The Arabs say: "She cut the place of such-and-such," meaning she passed by it. Dhu al-Rumma said:

Toward a caravan of women passing along the sides of a height,
on the left, and on their right are the horsemen.

The Kufans said: "Qaraḍat mawḍiʿ kadhā" means she brushed against it, and they related from the Arabs: "qaraḍathu qubulan wa duburan" (she passed it from the front and from the back).

*Al-fajwa* is the open space between the thighs; it comes from *al-fijāʾ*, which is the distance between the thighs. A man is *afjaʾ*, a woman is *fajwāʾ*, and the plural of *fajwa* is *fijāʾ*.

*Al-yaqiẓ* is one who is awake and alert; its plural is *ayqāẓ*, like *ʿaḍud* and *aʿḍād*, and *yiqāẓ*, like *rajul* and *rijāl*. A man is *yaqẓān* and a woman is *yaqẓā*.

*Al-ruqād* is well known, and it is used as a proper name.

*Al-waṣīd* is the courtyard. It is said: the threshold. It is said: the door. The poet said:

In a wide land whose *waṣīd* is not closed against me,
and my acquaintance there is not unknown.

*Al-warq* is silver, minted or unminted.

*Al-surādiq* (السُّرادِقُ): Abu Mansur al-Jawaliqi said: it is Persian, arabicized, and its origin is *sarādār*, which is the vestibule. Al-Farazdaq said:

I desired them until, when I met them,
I left for them before the strike the *surādiq*.

A *bayt musarduq* means one that has a *surādiq*.

*Al-muhl* is what is melted from the substances of the earth. It is said: the dregs of oil.

*Shawā al-laḥm* means he cooked the meat without broth.

*Al-siwār* is what is put on the arm of gold, silver, copper, or lead. It is pluralized as *asāwira* in the small number, like *khimār* and *akhmira*, and as *khumur*. In the large number, like *khimār* and *khumur*, except that its middle letter is pronounced with a sukūn, unless in poetry, where it is vocalized. *Asāwir* is the plural of *aswira*. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is the plural of *aswār*. It is said of all jewelry on the arm. From him and from Qutrub: it is by dropping the extra letter, and its original form is *asāwīr*. Ibn al-Anbari recited:

By God, were it not for young children, small,
whose faces are like moons,
whom the house of al-Fanīk gathers,
I fear that poverty may befall them,
or a striker who has no bracelets,
when a tyrant king saw me
at his door, when the day became clear.

*Al-sundus* is fine brocade, and *al-istabraq* is the thick kind of it. *Al-istabraq* is a Byzantine word arabicized; its origin is *istabarah*, and they replaced the *hāʾ* with *qāf*, as Ibn Qutayba said. It is said: it is named by a verb, from *al-barīq* (gleam), and its hamzat al-waṣl was cut off. It is said: *al-istabraq* is the name of silk. Al-Muraqqish said:

You see them sometimes wearing the coverings of the sanctuaries,
and at other times their garments are brocade and *istabraq*.

Ibn Bahr said: *al-istabraq* is that woven with gold.

*Al-arīka* is a couch in a canopy; if it is alone, it is not called *arīka*. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-arā'ik* are couches in the tents (*al-ḥijāl*).

**Lexical notes**

*Bakhaʿa* (بَخَعَ) means to destroy oneself or to kill oneself from intensity of grief; its root sense is exertion. This is stated by al-Akhfash and al-Farra'. In a hadith of ʿĀʾisha, she mentioned ʿUmar and said: "He bakhaʿa the land," meaning he exerted it until he took what was in it of the wealth of kings. Al-Kisa'i said: "He bakhaʿa the land by cultivation," meaning he made it weak by continuously plowing it. Al-Layth said: "A man bakhaʿa himself," meaning he killed himself from intensity of his grief. He recited the verse of al-Farazdaq:

Ah, you who destroy yourself with grief
over a thing the decrees have pulled from his hands.

Meaning: "nahhatahu" with the ḥāʾ doubled, then lightened. Abu ʿUbayda said: Dhu al-Rumma used to recite "al-wajd" with a nominative ending. Al-Asmaʿi said: it is actually "al-wajda" with a fatḥa. End of quote. Thus its accusative would be as a *mafʿūl li-ajlihi* (object of purpose, an accusative of cause).

*Jaraza* (جَرَزَتِ): the land became barren from drought, locusts, or the like, its vegetation gone and nothing left in it. Barren lands are *ajrāz*. It is said: a year is *jurz*, and years are *ajrāz*, with no rain in them. The *juruz* of the land is locusts that consumed what was in it. A woman is *jarūz*, meaning a great eater. The poet said:

Indeed the old woman is a glutton, a devourer,
eating a qafīz every night.

*Al-kahf* is an open, wide cavity in a mountain; if it is not wide, it is a *ghār* (cave). Ibn al-Anbari said: the linguists reported that it is in the position of a *ghār* in a mountain.

*Al-raqīm* is a form of *raqama*, either in the sense of the passive participle or the active participle. The disagreement among the exegetes about its intended meaning will come, God willing. As for the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

There was nothing there but the *raqīm*, a neighbor,
and their hunting dog, while the people in the cave lay still.

Here it means their dog.

*Aḥṣā al-shayʾ* means he preserved it and mastered it. *Al-shaṭaṭ* means injustice, transgression of limits, and extremism. Al-Farra' said: "Ishtatta fī al-shu'm" means he exceeded the measure. *Shatta al-manzil* means it was far, *shuṭūṭan*. *Shatta al-rajul* and *ashatta* mean he was unjust. *Shattat al-jāriya* means the girl became tall.

*Tazāwaru* (تَزاوَرُ): it inclines and turns aside. Al-Akhfash said: *tazāwarru* means it contracts. End of quote. *Al-zawr* is inclination, and *al-azwar* is one who inclines with his eye to a side; this may also be used of other than the eye. Ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

And fear of the people made me incline away from her.

ʿAntara said:

It turned aside from the impact of the spears on its chest,
and complained to me with a tear and a neigh.

Bishr ibn Abi Hazim said:

The guides lead her toward the waters of a palm grove,
and in her there is a turning aside from exhausted camels.

From this comes *zārahu*, when he inclined toward him. *Al-zawr* is inclination away from truth.

*Qaraḍa al-shayʾ* means he cut it. The Arabs say: "She cut the place of such-and-such," meaning she passed by it. Dhu al-Rumma said:

Toward a caravan of women passing along the sides of a height,
on the left, and on their right are the horsemen.

The Kufans said: "Qaraḍat mawḍiʿ kadhā" means she brushed against it, and they related from the Arabs: "qaraḍathu qubulan wa duburan" (she passed it from the front and from the back).

*Al-fajwa* is the open space between the thighs; it comes from *al-fijāʾ*, which is the distance between the thighs. A man is *afjaʾ*, a woman is *fajwāʾ*, and the plural of *fajwa* is *fijāʾ*.

*Al-yaqiẓ* is one who is awake and alert; its plural is *ayqāẓ*, like *ʿaḍud* and *aʿḍād*, and *yiqāẓ*, like *rajul* and *rijāl*. A man is *yaqẓān* and a woman is *yaqẓā*.

*Al-ruqād* is well known, and it is used as a proper name.

*Al-waṣīd* is the courtyard. It is said: the threshold. It is said: the door. The poet said:

In a wide land whose *waṣīd* is not closed against me,
and my acquaintance there is not unknown.

*Al-warq* is silver, minted or unminted.

*Al-surādiq* (السُّرادِقُ): Abu Mansur al-Jawaliqi said: it is Persian, arabicized, and its origin is *sarādār*, which is the vestibule. Al-Farazdaq said:

I desired them until, when I met them,
I left for them before the strike the *surādiq*.

A *bayt musarduq* means one that has a *surādiq*.

*Al-muhl* is what is melted from the substances of the earth. It is said: the dregs of oil.

*Shawā al-laḥm* means he cooked the meat without broth.

*Al-siwār* is what is put on the arm of gold, silver, copper, or lead. It is pluralized as *asāwira* in the small number, like *khimār* and *akhmira*, and as *khumur*. In the large number, like *khimār* and *khumur*, except that its middle letter is pronounced with a sukūn, unless in poetry, where it is vocalized. *Asāwir* is the plural of *aswira*. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is the plural of *aswār*. It is said of all jewelry on the arm. From him and from Qutrub: it is by dropping the extra letter, and its original form is *asāwīr*. Ibn al-Anbari recited:

By God, were it not for young children, small,
whose faces are like moons,
whom the house of al-Fanīk gathers,
I fear that poverty may befall them,
or a striker who has no bracelets,
when a tyrant king saw me
at his door, when the day became clear.

*Al-sundus* is fine brocade, and *al-istabraq* is the thick kind of it. *Al-istabraq* is a Byzantine word arabicized; its origin is *istabarah*, and they replaced the *hāʾ* with *qāf*, as Ibn Qutayba said. It is said: it is named by a verb, from *al-barīq* (gleam), and its hamzat al-waṣl was cut off. It is said: *al-istabraq* is the name of silk. Al-Muraqqish said:

You see them sometimes wearing the coverings of the sanctuaries,
and at other times their garments are brocade and *istabraq*.

Ibn Bahr said: *al-istabraq* is that woven with gold.

*Al-arīka* is a couch in a canopy; if it is alone, it is not called *arīka*. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-arā'ik* are couches in the tents (*al-ḥijāl*).

[p. 95] It is entirely Meccan, except for one opinion. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah reported that the exception is His saying, ﴿And keep yourself patient﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], and the verse following it, so that part is Medinan. Muqatil said: the exception is from its beginning to "barren [juruzan]," and from His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 30], the two verses that follow, so that part is Medinan.

The occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was that the Quraysh sent al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'it to the rabbis of the Jews in Medina. They said to them: "Ask them about Muhammad and describe his description to them, for they are the People of the First Book, and they have knowledge of the prophets that we do not have." The two set out until they reached Medina and asked them. The Jews said: "Ask him about three things. If he tells you them, then he is a sent prophet; but if he does not do so, then the man is a fabricator. Consider the matter well. Ask him about the youths who went forth in the earliest age, what their affair was, for they had a wondrous story. Ask him about the man who traveled round, who reached the easts and the wests of the earth, what was his story. And ask him about the Spirit." Al-Nadr and 'Uqbah then came back to Mecca and asked him. He said: "Tomorrow I will tell you," and he did not say, "If God wills." So revelation was withheld for fifteen days. The unbelievers of Quraysh spread rumors and said: "Muhammad has been abandoned by his companion who used to come to him from the jinn." Some of them said: "He has been unable to produce his lies." This grieved him greatly. When the period had passed, revelation came to him with the answers to the questions and to other matters.

It is also related concerning this occasion that the Jews said: "If he answers you about the three, then he is not a prophet; but if he answers about two and remains silent about the other, then he is a prophet." So God revealed the Surah of the People of the Cave, and after that He revealed, ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit﴾ [al-Isra: 85].

The connection (munasabah) between the beginning of this surah and the end of what precedes it is this: when He said, ﴿And with truth We have sent it down, and with truth it has descended﴾ [al-Isra: 105], and mentioned the believers in it who are people of knowledge, and that it increases them in humility, and that He, exalted is He, commanded that He be praised and that He has not taken a son, He commanded them to praise Him for sending down this Book, which is free from crookedness, which is a guardian over all the Books, which warns those who take a son, and which gives good news to the believers of a good reward. Then He digressed (istitrad) to the account of the unbelievers of Quraysh. He turned from address (khitab) in His saying, ﴿And magnify Him with magnification﴾ [al-Isra: 111], to the third person (ghaybah) in His saying, ﴿upon His servant﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], because of the honoring attribution contained in "His servant," which requires his exaltation. The construction did not come as "He sent down upon you."

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Qur'an. Crookedness in meanings is like crookedness in persons. "Iwajan" (crookedness) is indefinite so that it covers all its kinds, because it is an indefinite noun in a context of negation. The meaning is that it is in the utmost straightness: there is no contradiction and no disagreement in its meanings, and no harshness (hushiyyah) or incoherence ('iyy) in its structures and forms. "Qayyiman" (upright) is an emphasis establishing straightness, if its meaning is "straight"; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. It has been said: "qayyiman" means guardian over the interests of the servants, the laws of their religion, and the affairs of their livelihood and their hereafter. It has also been said: "qayyiman" means a guardian over the other Books by confirming them.

They differed regarding this negative clause. Al-Zamakhshari maintained that it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "anzala" (He sent down), so it falls within the relative clause (silah). On this basis he concluded that the best reading for the accusative of "qayyiman" is that it is governed by a hidden verb, and not made a circumstantial (hal) of "al-Kitab," because that would necessitate separating the circumstantial from its referent by part of the relative clause. He estimated the verb as "ja'alahu" (He made it) "qayyiman."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "qayyiman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial of "al-Kitab," so it means "preceded" but is later in wording: the meaning is "He sent down the Book, upright." The negative clause, ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], intervenes between the circumstantial and its referent. This was reported by al-Tabari from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also permissible that it be accusative governed by a hidden verb, whose estimate is "anzalahu" (He sent it down) or "ja'alahu" (He made it) "qayyiman." As for if we say that the negative clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh), then it is permissible, and the circumstantial may be separated from its referent by parenthetical clauses.

Al-'Askari said: there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, as if he said: "Praise God for sending down the Qur'an upright, without crookedness in it," and it is the habit of eloquent speakers to put first what is most important.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1] indicates that it is perfect in its essence, and His saying "qayyiman" indicates that it is perfected by other than itself. So it is established by rational proof that the correct order is the one God mentioned, and that what they mentioned of inversion and reversal is corrupt, and the intellect refuses to go to it.

Al-Karmani said: if you make it a circumstantial, which is the more apparent, then there is no inversion or reversal in it. The correct view is that the two are two circumstantials of "al-Kitab," the first being a clause and the second a single word. End of quotation. This is according to the view of those who permit two circumstantials to occur for one referent without a conjunction, while many of our companions prohibit that. End of quotation. Al-Isfahani preferred this and said: they are two consecutive circumstantials, and the estimate is "not making for it crookedness, upright [qayyiman]."

The author of Hall al-'Aqd (Solving the Knot) said: it is possible that His saying "qayyiman" is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], meaning: He made it straight, upright. End of quotation. This would be a substitution of a single word for a clause, as they said regarding "'arafta Zaydan abu man" (I knew Zayd, father of whom), that it is a substitution of a clause for a single word; and there is disagreement about this.

It has been said that "qayyiman" is a circumstantial of the pronoun ha' (his) in ﴿has not made for him﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], as an emphasis. It has also been said that it is a transitional (muntaqilah) circumstantial. The apparent view is that the pronoun in "lahu" (for it) refers to "al-Kitab," and on this basis the i'rab (grammatical) analyses mentioned above apply. Some people claimed that the pronoun in "lahu" refers to "'abdihi" (His servant), and the estimate is ﴿upon His servant﴾ [al-Kahf: 1] and He made him "qayyiman."

Hafs pauses briefly on His saying "iwajan" (crookedness), a light pause (sakta khafifah), and then says "qayyiman." In some of the codices of the Companions there is ﴿and has not made for him crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], but "ja'alahu qayyiman" (He made it upright). This is to be understood as an explanation of the meaning, not as a recitation (qira'ah).

"Anzara" (to warn) takes two objects, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ [al-Naba: 40]. Here the first object is omitted and the thing warned of is stated, because that is the purpose toward which the speech is directed, so it was restricted to it. Then the one who warns is stated in His saying, when He repeated the warning: ﴿and warn those who say, "God has taken a son"﴾ [al-Kahf: 4]. So the warner is omitted at first because the second indicates it, and the thing warned of is omitted because the first indicates it. This is of the wondrous omission and the sublime eloquence. And since He did not repeat the good news, He brought the one who gives good news and the thing good news is given of. The apparent view is that "li-yundhira" (so that he may warn) is connected to "anzala" (He sent down). Al-Hawfi said: it is connected to "qayyiman." The omitted object of "li-yundhira" was estimated by Ibn 'Atiyyah as "al-'alam" (the world), and by Abu al-Baqa' as "al-'ibad" (the servants) or "li-yundhirakum" (so that he may warn you). Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as specific, saying: its origin is "li-yundhira" (so that he may warn) "alladhina kafaru" (those who disbelieved) ﴿with severe punishment [ba'san shadidan]﴾ [al-Kahf: 2]. "Al-ba's" comes from His saying: ﴿with a wretched punishment [bi-'adhabin ba'is]﴾ [al-A'raf: 165], and the punishment became wretched, and the man became wretched, "ba's" and "ba'sah." End of quotation. It seems that in determining the omitted object he observed a correspondence with ﴿and gives good news to the believers who﴾ [al-Kahf: 2]. The severe "ba's" is the punishment of the Hereafter, and it is possible that the punishment of this world is included in it.

"Min ladunhu" (from Him) means "issuing from His presence." Abu Bakr read the dal with sukun and with ishmam (a slight rounding), the damm, and the nun with kasrah. The discussion of these was given earlier, at the beginning of Hud. It is also read ﴿wa-yubashshiru﴾ (and gives good news) with raf' (nominative), but the majority read it with nasb (accusative), coordinated with "li-yundhira." "Al-ajr al-hasan" (the goodly reward) is Paradise. When He alluded to Paradise by His saying ﴿a goodly reward﴾ [al-Kahf: 2], He said ﴿remaining therein﴾ [al-Kahf: 3], that is, dwelling in it, making it a container for their dwelling. And since staying does not necessarily entail eternity, He said "abadan" (forever), which is an adverb indicating an unlimited time. "Makithin" is accusative as a circumstantial, and its referent is the pronoun in "lahum" (for them). The ones who attributed a son to God, the Exalted, were some of the Jews concerning Uzayr, some of the Christians concerning the Messiah, and some of the Arabs concerning the angels. The apparent view is that the pronoun in "bihi" (about it) refers to the son they claimed. Al-Mahdawi said: then the clause is a description of the son. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is objectionable, because only the one who speaks would describe it, and they did not intend to describe it. In my view the correct reading is that it is a new negation (nafy mu'tanif), which God informed about their ignorance in this matter, and the clause has no place in the i'rab. It is also possible that it refers to God, the Exalted, and this interpretation is more condemnatory of them and more conclusive regarding their complete ignorance. This is the view of al-Tabari. End of quotation.

It has been said: the meaning is ﴿they have no knowledge [of it]﴾ concerning God, so that they might exalt Him above what is not befitting to Him. It is also possible that it refers to the saying understood from "qalu" (they said), meaning: they have no knowledge in their saying this, so the clause is in the position of a circumstantial: they said it ignorantly, without reflection, deliberation, or consideration of what is possible and what is impossible. It has also been said that it refers to the taking understood from "ittakhadha" (took), meaning: they have no knowledge of the wisdom of taking, since no one takes a son except one who is incapable and subdued, who needs a helper to strengthen his arm, and this is impossible for God.

Al-Zamakhshari said: God's taking a son in itself is impossible, so how is it said ﴿they have no knowledge of it﴾? I say: its meaning is that they have no knowledge of it, because it is not among things that can be known, due to its impossibility. The absence of knowledge of a thing is either due to ignorance of the way that leads to it, or because it is in itself impossible, so that the knowledge of it cannot properly relate to it. End of quotation.

"Wa-la li-abaihim" (nor to their fathers) is coordinated with "lahum" (for them). They are those of their predecessors who went to this flimsy statement. Rather, whoever said this only said it out of ignorance and blind imitation. He mentioned the fathers because they took that statement from them and received it from them.

Qara'a al-jumhur (the majority of reciters) ﴿kalimatan﴾ with the accusative, and the apparent reading is that it is in the accusative of specification (tamyiz). The subject of ﴿kaburat﴾ is an implied pronoun referring to the statement understood from His words ﴿They say: "God has taken a son."﴾ [18:4]. This carries the sense of wonder: how great is it as a word! The sentence following it is a description of it, conveying the enormity of their audacity in uttering it and bringing it out of their mouths. Many of the things that Satan whispers into hearts and that the soul speaks to itself cannot be uttered aloud; rather, one turns one's thoughts away from them. How then could one utter such a heinous thing? It is called ﴿kalimah﴾ (word) just as they call a qasidah (ode) a kalimah.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This statement, existing in the soul as a single meaning, may appropriately be called a kalimah." He also said: "The majority read the kalimah in the accusative, as you say: ni'ma rajulan Zayd (what an excellent man Zayd is). It is explained by the word kalimah and described by its coming out of their mouths." Some said: "Its accusative is that of explanation (tafsir), in the manner of the accusative in His words, ﴿and how evil a resting place﴾ [18:29]." A group said: "Its accusative is that of circumstance (hal), meaning: their slander is great," and similar. End of quotation.

According to his statement, "as you say: ni'ma rajulan Zayd," the one praised or blamed (al-makhsus bil-dhamm) would be omitted, because he made ﴿takhruju﴾ (comes out) a description of kalimah. The implied meaning is: ﴿kaburat kalimah﴾ (how great is a word) ﴿takhruju min afwahihim﴾ (coming out of their mouths), that statement which they uttered, namely their saying ﴿God has taken a son.﴾ The pronoun in ﴿kaburat﴾ does not refer to what precedes it; rather it is an implied pronoun explained by what follows it, which is the tamyiz according to the school of the Basrans. It is also permissible that the one blamed be omitted, with ﴿takhruju﴾ as its description, meaning: ﴿how great is a word﴾ (a word) ﴿coming out of their mouths.﴾

Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is in the accusative as an exclamation, meaning: "How great is it as a word!" Or, "from a word." It was also read ﴿kabrat﴾ with a sukun on the ba', and this is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Qawwas from Ibn Kathir read it in the nominative as the subject (fa'il), but the accusative is more eloquent and stronger in meaning. ﴿In﴾ here is negative, meaning: "they say nothing but," and ﴿kadhiban﴾ (a lie) is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: "a statement that is a lie."

﴿Fa-la'allaka bakhi'un nafsaka﴾ (Perhaps you would destroy yourself). La'alla is for hope regarding what is loved and for apprehension regarding what is feared. Al-'Askari said: "Here la'alla is used in the place of prohibition," meaning: do not destroy yourself. It was also said: it is used in the place of interrogation, its implied meaning being: "Are you about to destroy yourself?" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is an affirmation and a reproach, meaning: a denial of him, i.e., do not be like that. Al-Zamakhshari said: He likened him, and them, when they turned away from him and did not believe in him, and the grief and sorrow that overcame him over their turning away, to a man whose beloved and dear ones have departed from him; so he falls apart in sorrow after their traces and destroys himself out of grief for them and longing for their separation. End of quotation. La'alla serving as interrogation is a Kufan opinion. What appears evident is that it is for apprehension: he feared that the Messenger (ﷺ) would destroy himself because they did not believe.

His words ﴿'ala athharihim﴾ (after them) are an eloquent metaphor, since they have retreat, distance from faith and aversion from the Law. It is as if they, in the extremity of their retreat, have gone far away, and so he grieves over them in their retreat. The meaning of ﴿'ala athharihim﴾ is "after them," i.e., after your despair of their belief, or after their death in disbelief. It is said: "So-and-so died on the trail of so-and-so," meaning after him.

It was read ﴿bakhi'u nafsika﴾ with the genitive construction (idafah). The majority read ﴿bakhi'un﴾ with tanwin and ﴿nafsaka﴾ in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is according to the original rule," meaning that when the active participle fulfils the conditions for operating, the original rule is that it governs, and Sibawayh indicated this in his book. Al-Kisa'i said: working (governing) and the genitive construction are equal. We have held that the genitive construction is better than governing, for reasons we set out in what we composed in the science of grammar.

It was read ﴿in lam yu'minu﴾ with a kasrah and a fathah on the mim. As for the one who reads with a kasrah, al-Zamakhshari said: it refers, meaning the active participle, to the future; and whoever reads with a fathah, it refers to the past, meaning the state of the construction, i.e., because ﴿lam yu'minu﴾ (they did not believe) and the reference by ﴿hadha al-hadith﴾ (this discourse) is to the Qur'an. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿God has sent down the best discourse, a Book consistent in its parts﴾ [39:23].

﴿Asafan﴾ (grief). Mujahid said: "distress." Qatadah said: "anger," and also from him: "sorrow." Al-Suddi said: "regret and anguish." Al-Zajjaj said: "asaf is intensity in sorrow and anger." Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: "Asaf here means sorrow, because it is directed at one who does not possess or is not under the hand of the one grieving. If the asaf came from one powerful over one who is in his grasp and possession, it would be anger, as in His words: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took retribution from them﴾ [43:55], meaning: they angered Us." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "When you reflect on this in Arabic speech, it is consistent." End of quotation.

The accusative of ﴿asafan﴾ is either as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi) or as a verbal noun in the position of circumstance (hal). The connection of His words ﴿Indeed We have made﴾ (the verse) with what precedes it is by way of consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), because He, the Exalted, informed that He created what is upon the earth as adornment for the purpose of trial and testing: which of people is ﴿best in deed﴾ [18:7]. They are not of one pattern in uprightness and following the Messengers. Rather, there must be among them one who is best in deed and one who is worst in deed. So do not be distressed or grieved over those whom you have been given preference over, that they will be worse in deed; and even though they disbelieve in Me, I will not cut off from them the provisions of these blessings which I created.

﴿Ja'alna﴾ (We made) here means "created" (khalaqna). The apparent reading is that what is intended by ﴿ma﴾ is non-rational beings, and that it intends generality in what is non-rational. ﴿Zinah﴾ (adornment) is each thing according to its kind. It was said: this does not include what contains harm from animal, stone, or plant, since there is no adornment in it. Whoever holds to generality says that ﴿zinah﴾ is so in terms of its creation, craftsmanship and perfection. It was said: what is intended here is specifically non-rational beings. It was said: trees and rivers. It was said: plants, because of their variety and flowers. It was said: animals of differing forms, benefits and actions. It was said: gold, silver, copper, lead, rubies, chrysolite, pearls, coral, and similar precious stones.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ma 'ala al-ard﴾ (what is upon the earth) means what is fit to be ﴿adornment for it﴾ and for its people, of the ornaments of the world and what is considered beautiful in it. A group said: it intends bounties, garments, fruits, greenery and water. It was said: ﴿ma﴾ here is for rational beings; according to Mujahid, it means men, and Ibn Jubayr said this on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ikrimah transmitted that the adornment is the caliphs, scholars and rulers.

﴿Zinah﴾ is in the accusative as circumstance, or as an object of purpose if ﴿ja'alna﴾ means "created" and "brought into existence." If it means "made into," then it is in the accusative as a second object.

The lam in ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾ (that We may test them) is connected to ﴿ja'alna﴾. Al-ibtila' is testing and examination, and it is interpreted in relation to God, the Exalted. The pronoun in ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾, if ﴿ma﴾ is for rational beings, refers back to it according to meaning; and it may not refer to what is understood from the context of the speech, namely the inhabitants of the earth who are obligated. ﴿Ayyuhum﴾ (which of them) may be parsed with the pronoun in it being grammatically inflected, so that ﴿ayyuhum﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and ﴿ahsanu﴾ (best) is its predicate. The sentence is in the position of the object of ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾; and He has suspended ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾, treating it as the verb of knowledge, because testing and examination are a cause of knowledge, just as they suspended sal (ask) and unzur (look) in the visual sense, because these two are causes of knowledge. Al-Hawfi held that the sentence is interrogative, a subject and predicate. It is also possible that the dammah on it is a built form (binā') according to Sibawayh's school, because the condition for permitting indeclinability in ayyu is met, namely that it is annexed while the beginning of its complement has been omitted. So ﴿ahsanu﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, its implied meaning being "he is best," and ﴿ayyuhum﴾ is in the accusative position as an apposition to the pronoun in ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾. The one preferred over, the object of comparison, is omitted, its implied meaning being: "of those who are not ﴿best in deed﴾."

Al-Thawri said: "The best of them in deed is the most abstemious of them regarding it." Abu 'Asim al-'Asqalani said: "The one who most abandons it." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The goodness of deed is abstinence from it and not being deceived by it." Abu Bakr Ghalib ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The best deed is taking what is right with faith, performing the obligations, avoiding the forbidden, and increasing in what is recommended." Al-Kalbi said: "The best in obedience." Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: "Those upon it of prophets and scholars, to test those to whom the messenger is sent and the followers of the scholars: which of them is best in acceptance and response." Sahl said: "Best in trust in Us regarding it." It was said: "Purest in heart and best in demeanour." Ibn Ishaq said: "Which of them is most attentive to My command and most diligent in My obedience."

﴿Wa-inna lajā'iluna﴾ (And indeed We will make), i.e., We will turn into, ﴿ma 'alayha﴾ (what is upon it) of what was adornment for it, or ﴿ma 'alayha﴾ of what is more general than adornment and other things, into ﴿sa'idan juruzan﴾ (barren dust). This is an indication of making the world seem unattractive, turning away from it, and consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning what the hands of the affluent grasp of its adornment, since the end of all that is to annihilation and perishing.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ma 'alayha﴾ of this adornment ﴿sa'idan juruzan﴾, meaning like a white land with no vegetation, after having been green and luxuriant, in the removal of its radiance and the effacement of its beauty, and the nullification of what made it adornment, by causing animals to die, plants and trees to dry out, and the like. End of quotation.

It was said: the sa'id is what rises upon the surface of the earth. Mujahid said: "The land in which there is no vegetation." Al-Suddi said: "the smooth, level ground." It was said: "the road." In the hadith: "Beware of sitting on the sa'idat (roadsides)."

[p. 95] It is entirely Meccan, except for one opinion. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah reported that the exception is His saying, ﴿And keep yourself patient﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], and the verse following it, so that part is Medinan. Muqatil said: the exception is from its beginning to "barren [juruzan]," and from His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 30], the two verses that follow, so that part is Medinan.

The occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was that the Quraysh sent al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'it to the rabbis of the Jews in Medina. They said to them: "Ask them about Muhammad and describe his description to them, for they are the People of the First Book, and they have knowledge of the prophets that we do not have." The two set out until they reached Medina and asked them. The Jews said: "Ask him about three things. If he tells you them, then he is a sent prophet; but if he does not do so, then the man is a fabricator. Consider the matter well. Ask him about the youths who went forth in the earliest age, what their affair was, for they had a wondrous story. Ask him about the man who traveled round, who reached the easts and the wests of the earth, what was his story. And ask him about the Spirit." Al-Nadr and 'Uqbah then came back to Mecca and asked him. He said: "Tomorrow I will tell you," and he did not say, "If God wills." So revelation was withheld for fifteen days. The unbelievers of Quraysh spread rumors and said: "Muhammad has been abandoned by his companion who used to come to him from the jinn." Some of them said: "He has been unable to produce his lies." This grieved him greatly. When the period had passed, revelation came to him with the answers to the questions and to other matters.

It is also related concerning this occasion that the Jews said: "If he answers you about the three, then he is not a prophet; but if he answers about two and remains silent about the other, then he is a prophet." So God revealed the Surah of the People of the Cave, and after that He revealed, ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit﴾ [al-Isra: 85].

The connection (munasabah) between the beginning of this surah and the end of what precedes it is this: when He said, ﴿And with truth We have sent it down, and with truth it has descended﴾ [al-Isra: 105], and mentioned the believers in it who are people of knowledge, and that it increases them in humility, and that He, exalted is He, commanded that He be praised and that He has not taken a son, He commanded them to praise Him for sending down this Book, which is free from crookedness, which is a guardian over all the Books, which warns those who take a son, and which gives good news to the believers of a good reward. Then He digressed (istitrad) to the account of the unbelievers of Quraysh. He turned from address (khitab) in His saying, ﴿And magnify Him with magnification﴾ [al-Isra: 111], to the third person (ghaybah) in His saying, ﴿upon His servant﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], because of the honoring attribution contained in "His servant," which requires his exaltation. The construction did not come as "He sent down upon you."

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Qur'an. Crookedness in meanings is like crookedness in persons. "Iwajan" (crookedness) is indefinite so that it covers all its kinds, because it is an indefinite noun in a context of negation. The meaning is that it is in the utmost straightness: there is no contradiction and no disagreement in its meanings, and no harshness (hushiyyah) or incoherence ('iyy) in its structures and forms. "Qayyiman" (upright) is an emphasis establishing straightness, if its meaning is "straight"; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. It has been said: "qayyiman" means guardian over the interests of the servants, the laws of their religion, and the affairs of their livelihood and their hereafter. It has also been said: "qayyiman" means a guardian over the other Books by confirming them.

They differed regarding this negative clause. Al-Zamakhshari maintained that it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "anzala" (He sent down), so it falls within the relative clause (silah). On this basis he concluded that the best reading for the accusative of "qayyiman" is that it is governed by a hidden verb, and not made a circumstantial (hal) of "al-Kitab," because that would necessitate separating the circumstantial from its referent by part of the relative clause. He estimated the verb as "ja'alahu" (He made it) "qayyiman."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "qayyiman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial of "al-Kitab," so it means "preceded" but is later in wording: the meaning is "He sent down the Book, upright." The negative clause, ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], intervenes between the circumstantial and its referent. This was reported by al-Tabari from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also permissible that it be accusative governed by a hidden verb, whose estimate is "anzalahu" (He sent it down) or "ja'alahu" (He made it) "qayyiman." As for if we say that the negative clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh), then it is permissible, and the circumstantial may be separated from its referent by parenthetical clauses.

Al-'Askari said: there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, as if he said: "Praise God for sending down the Qur'an upright, without crookedness in it," and it is the habit of eloquent speakers to put first what is most important.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1] indicates that it is perfect in its essence, and His saying "qayyiman" indicates that it is perfected by other than itself. So it is established by rational proof that the correct order is the one God mentioned, and that what they mentioned of inversion and reversal is corrupt, and the intellect refuses to go to it.

Al-Karmani said: if you make it a circumstantial, which is the more apparent, then there is no inversion or reversal in it. The correct view is that the two are two circumstantials of "al-Kitab," the first being a clause and the second a single word. End of quotation. This is according to the view of those who permit two circumstantials to occur for one referent without a conjunction, while many of our companions prohibit that. End of quotation. Al-Isfahani preferred this and said: they are two consecutive circumstantials, and the estimate is "not making for it crookedness, upright [qayyiman]."

The author of Hall al-'Aqd (Solving the Knot) said: it is possible that His saying "qayyiman" is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], meaning: He made it straight, upright. End of quotation. This would be a substitution of a single word for a clause, as they said regarding "'arafta Zaydan abu man" (I knew Zayd, father of whom), that it is a substitution of a clause for a single word; and there is disagreement about this.

It has been said that "qayyiman" is a circumstantial of the pronoun ha' (his) in ﴿has not made for him﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], as an emphasis. It has also been said that it is a transitional (muntaqilah) circumstantial. The apparent view is that the pronoun in "lahu" (for it) refers to "al-Kitab," and on this basis the i'rab (grammatical) analyses mentioned above apply. Some people claimed that the pronoun in "lahu" refers to "'abdihi" (His servant), and the estimate is ﴿upon His servant﴾ [al-Kahf: 1] and He made him "qayyiman."

Hafs pauses briefly on His saying "iwajan" (crookedness), a light pause (sakta khafifah), and then says "qayyiman." In some of the codices of the Companions there is ﴿and has not made for him crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], but "ja'alahu qayyiman" (He made it upright). This is to be understood as an explanation of the meaning, not as a recitation (qira'ah).

"Anzara" (to warn) takes two objects, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ [al-Naba: 40]. Here the first object is omitted and the thing warned of is stated, because that is the purpose toward which the speech is directed, so it was restricted to it. Then the one who warns is stated in His saying, when He repeated the warning: ﴿and warn those who say, "God has taken a son"﴾ [al-Kahf: 4]. So the warner is omitted at first because the second indicates it, and the thing warned of is omitted because the first indicates it. This is of the wondrous omission and the sublime eloquence. And since He did not repeat the good news, He brought the one who gives good news and the thing good news is given of. The apparent view is that "li-yundhira" (so that he may warn) is connected to "anzala" (He sent down). Al-Hawfi said: it is connected to "qayyiman." The omitted object of "li-yundhira" was estimated by Ibn 'Atiyyah as "al-'alam" (the world), and by Abu al-Baqa' as "al-'ibad" (the servants) or "li-yundhirakum" (so that he may warn you). Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as specific, saying: its origin is "li-yundhira" (so that he may warn) "alladhina kafaru" (those who disbelieved) ﴿with severe punishment [ba'san shadidan]﴾ [al-Kahf: 2]. "Al-ba's" comes from His saying: ﴿with a wretched punishment [bi-'adhabin ba'is]﴾ [al-A'raf: 165], and the punishment became wretched, and the man became wretched, "ba's" and "ba'sah." End of quotation. It seems that in determining the omitted object he observed a correspondence with ﴿and gives good news to the believers who﴾ [al-Kahf: 2]. The severe "ba's" is the punishment of the Hereafter, and it is possible that the punishment of this world is included in it.

"Min ladunhu" (from Him) means "issuing from His presence." Abu Bakr read the dal with sukun and with ishmam (a slight rounding), the damm, and the nun with kasrah. The discussion of these was given earlier, at the beginning of Hud. It is also read ﴿wa-yubashshiru﴾ (and gives good news) with raf' (nominative), but the majority read it with nasb (accusative), coordinated with "li-yundhira." "Al-ajr al-hasan" (the goodly reward) is Paradise. When He alluded to Paradise by His saying ﴿a goodly reward﴾ [al-Kahf: 2], He said ﴿remaining therein﴾ [al-Kahf: 3], that is, dwelling in it, making it a container for their dwelling. And since staying does not necessarily entail eternity, He said "abadan" (forever), which is an adverb indicating an unlimited time. "Makithin" is accusative as a circumstantial, and its referent is the pronoun in "lahum" (for them). The ones who attributed a son to God, the Exalted, were some of the Jews concerning Uzayr, some of the Christians concerning the Messiah, and some of the Arabs concerning the angels. The apparent view is that the pronoun in "bihi" (about it) refers to the son they claimed. Al-Mahdawi said: then the clause is a description of the son. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is objectionable, because only the one who speaks would describe it, and they did not intend to describe it. In my view the correct reading is that it is a new negation (nafy mu'tanif), which God informed about their ignorance in this matter, and the clause has no place in the i'rab. It is also possible that it refers to God, the Exalted, and this interpretation is more condemnatory of them and more conclusive regarding their complete ignorance. This is the view of al-Tabari. End of quotation.

It has been said: the meaning is ﴿they have no knowledge [of it]﴾ concerning God, so that they might exalt Him above what is not befitting to Him. It is also possible that it refers to the saying understood from "qalu" (they said), meaning: they have no knowledge in their saying this, so the clause is in the position of a circumstantial: they said it ignorantly, without reflection, deliberation, or consideration of what is possible and what is impossible. It has also been said that it refers to the taking understood from "ittakhadha" (took), meaning: they have no knowledge of the wisdom of taking, since no one takes a son except one who is incapable and subdued, who needs a helper to strengthen his arm, and this is impossible for God.

Al-Zamakhshari said: God's taking a son in itself is impossible, so how is it said ﴿they have no knowledge of it﴾? I say: its meaning is that they have no knowledge of it, because it is not among things that can be known, due to its impossibility. The absence of knowledge of a thing is either due to ignorance of the way that leads to it, or because it is in itself impossible, so that the knowledge of it cannot properly relate to it. End of quotation.

"Wa-la li-abaihim" (nor to their fathers) is coordinated with "lahum" (for them). They are those of their predecessors who went to this flimsy statement. Rather, whoever said this only said it out of ignorance and blind imitation. He mentioned the fathers because they took that statement from them and received it from them.

Qara'a al-jumhur (the majority of reciters) ﴿kalimatan﴾ with the accusative, and the apparent reading is that it is in the accusative of specification (tamyiz). The subject of ﴿kaburat﴾ is an implied pronoun referring to the statement understood from His words ﴿They say: "God has taken a son."﴾ [18:4]. This carries the sense of wonder: how great is it as a word! The sentence following it is a description of it, conveying the enormity of their audacity in uttering it and bringing it out of their mouths. Many of the things that Satan whispers into hearts and that the soul speaks to itself cannot be uttered aloud; rather, one turns one's thoughts away from them. How then could one utter such a heinous thing? It is called ﴿kalimah﴾ (word) just as they call a qasidah (ode) a kalimah.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This statement, existing in the soul as a single meaning, may appropriately be called a kalimah." He also said: "The majority read the kalimah in the accusative, as you say: ni'ma rajulan Zayd (what an excellent man Zayd is). It is explained by the word kalimah and described by its coming out of their mouths." Some said: "Its accusative is that of explanation (tafsir), in the manner of the accusative in His words, ﴿and how evil a resting place﴾ [18:29]." A group said: "Its accusative is that of circumstance (hal), meaning: their slander is great," and similar. End of quotation.

According to his statement, "as you say: ni'ma rajulan Zayd," the one praised or blamed (al-makhsus bil-dhamm) would be omitted, because he made ﴿takhruju﴾ (comes out) a description of kalimah. The implied meaning is: ﴿kaburat kalimah﴾ (how great is a word) ﴿takhruju min afwahihim﴾ (coming out of their mouths), that statement which they uttered, namely their saying ﴿God has taken a son.﴾ The pronoun in ﴿kaburat﴾ does not refer to what precedes it; rather it is an implied pronoun explained by what follows it, which is the tamyiz according to the school of the Basrans. It is also permissible that the one blamed be omitted, with ﴿takhruju﴾ as its description, meaning: ﴿how great is a word﴾ (a word) ﴿coming out of their mouths.﴾

Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is in the accusative as an exclamation, meaning: "How great is it as a word!" Or, "from a word." It was also read ﴿kabrat﴾ with a sukun on the ba', and this is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Qawwas from Ibn Kathir read it in the nominative as the subject (fa'il), but the accusative is more eloquent and stronger in meaning. ﴿In﴾ here is negative, meaning: "they say nothing but," and ﴿kadhiban﴾ (a lie) is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: "a statement that is a lie."

﴿Fa-la'allaka bakhi'un nafsaka﴾ (Perhaps you would destroy yourself). La'alla is for hope regarding what is loved and for apprehension regarding what is feared. Al-'Askari said: "Here la'alla is used in the place of prohibition," meaning: do not destroy yourself. It was also said: it is used in the place of interrogation, its implied meaning being: "Are you about to destroy yourself?" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is an affirmation and a reproach, meaning: a denial of him, i.e., do not be like that. Al-Zamakhshari said: He likened him, and them, when they turned away from him and did not believe in him, and the grief and sorrow that overcame him over their turning away, to a man whose beloved and dear ones have departed from him; so he falls apart in sorrow after their traces and destroys himself out of grief for them and longing for their separation. End of quotation. La'alla serving as interrogation is a Kufan opinion. What appears evident is that it is for apprehension: he feared that the Messenger (ﷺ) would destroy himself because they did not believe.

His words ﴿'ala athharihim﴾ (after them) are an eloquent metaphor, since they have retreat, distance from faith and aversion from the Law. It is as if they, in the extremity of their retreat, have gone far away, and so he grieves over them in their retreat. The meaning of ﴿'ala athharihim﴾ is "after them," i.e., after your despair of their belief, or after their death in disbelief. It is said: "So-and-so died on the trail of so-and-so," meaning after him.

It was read ﴿bakhi'u nafsika﴾ with the genitive construction (idafah). The majority read ﴿bakhi'un﴾ with tanwin and ﴿nafsaka﴾ in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is according to the original rule," meaning that when the active participle fulfils the conditions for operating, the original rule is that it governs, and Sibawayh indicated this in his book. Al-Kisa'i said: working (governing) and the genitive construction are equal. We have held that the genitive construction is better than governing, for reasons we set out in what we composed in the science of grammar.

It was read ﴿in lam yu'minu﴾ with a kasrah and a fathah on the mim. As for the one who reads with a kasrah, al-Zamakhshari said: it refers, meaning the active participle, to the future; and whoever reads with a fathah, it refers to the past, meaning the state of the construction, i.e., because ﴿lam yu'minu﴾ (they did not believe) and the reference by ﴿hadha al-hadith﴾ (this discourse) is to the Qur'an. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿God has sent down the best discourse, a Book consistent in its parts﴾ [39:23].

﴿Asafan﴾ (grief). Mujahid said: "distress." Qatadah said: "anger," and also from him: "sorrow." Al-Suddi said: "regret and anguish." Al-Zajjaj said: "asaf is intensity in sorrow and anger." Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: "Asaf here means sorrow, because it is directed at one who does not possess or is not under the hand of the one grieving. If the asaf came from one powerful over one who is in his grasp and possession, it would be anger, as in His words: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took retribution from them﴾ [43:55], meaning: they angered Us." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "When you reflect on this in Arabic speech, it is consistent." End of quotation.

The accusative of ﴿asafan﴾ is either as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi) or as a verbal noun in the position of circumstance (hal). The connection of His words ﴿Indeed We have made﴾ (the verse) with what precedes it is by way of consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), because He, the Exalted, informed that He created what is upon the earth as adornment for the purpose of trial and testing: which of people is ﴿best in deed﴾ [18:7]. They are not of one pattern in uprightness and following the Messengers. Rather, there must be among them one who is best in deed and one who is worst in deed. So do not be distressed or grieved over those whom you have been given preference over, that they will be worse in deed; and even though they disbelieve in Me, I will not cut off from them the provisions of these blessings which I created.

﴿Ja'alna﴾ (We made) here means "created" (khalaqna). The apparent reading is that what is intended by ﴿ma﴾ is non-rational beings, and that it intends generality in what is non-rational. ﴿Zinah﴾ (adornment) is each thing according to its kind. It was said: this does not include what contains harm from animal, stone, or plant, since there is no adornment in it. Whoever holds to generality says that ﴿zinah﴾ is so in terms of its creation, craftsmanship and perfection. It was said: what is intended here is specifically non-rational beings. It was said: trees and rivers. It was said: plants, because of their variety and flowers. It was said: animals of differing forms, benefits and actions. It was said: gold, silver, copper, lead, rubies, chrysolite, pearls, coral, and similar precious stones.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ma 'ala al-ard﴾ (what is upon the earth) means what is fit to be ﴿adornment for it﴾ and for its people, of the ornaments of the world and what is considered beautiful in it. A group said: it intends bounties, garments, fruits, greenery and water. It was said: ﴿ma﴾ here is for rational beings; according to Mujahid, it means men, and Ibn Jubayr said this on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ikrimah transmitted that the adornment is the caliphs, scholars and rulers.

﴿Zinah﴾ is in the accusative as circumstance, or as an object of purpose if ﴿ja'alna﴾ means "created" and "brought into existence." If it means "made into," then it is in the accusative as a second object.

The lam in ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾ (that We may test them) is connected to ﴿ja'alna﴾. Al-ibtila' is testing and examination, and it is interpreted in relation to God, the Exalted. The pronoun in ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾, if ﴿ma﴾ is for rational beings, refers back to it according to meaning; and it may not refer to what is understood from the context of the speech, namely the inhabitants of the earth who are obligated. ﴿Ayyuhum﴾ (which of them) may be parsed with the pronoun in it being grammatically inflected, so that ﴿ayyuhum﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and ﴿ahsanu﴾ (best) is its predicate. The sentence is in the position of the object of ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾; and He has suspended ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾, treating it as the verb of knowledge, because testing and examination are a cause of knowledge, just as they suspended sal (ask) and unzur (look) in the visual sense, because these two are causes of knowledge. Al-Hawfi held that the sentence is interrogative, a subject and predicate. It is also possible that the dammah on it is a built form (binā') according to Sibawayh's school, because the condition for permitting indeclinability in ayyu is met, namely that it is annexed while the beginning of its complement has been omitted. So ﴿ahsanu﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, its implied meaning being "he is best," and ﴿ayyuhum﴾ is in the accusative position as an apposition to the pronoun in ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾. The one preferred over, the object of comparison, is omitted, its implied meaning being: "of those who are not ﴿best in deed﴾."

Al-Thawri said: "The best of them in deed is the most abstemious of them regarding it." Abu 'Asim al-'Asqalani said: "The one who most abandons it." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The goodness of deed is abstinence from it and not being deceived by it." Abu Bakr Ghalib ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The best deed is taking what is right with faith, performing the obligations, avoiding the forbidden, and increasing in what is recommended." Al-Kalbi said: "The best in obedience." Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: "Those upon it of prophets and scholars, to test those to whom the messenger is sent and the followers of the scholars: which of them is best in acceptance and response." Sahl said: "Best in trust in Us regarding it." It was said: "Purest in heart and best in demeanour." Ibn Ishaq said: "Which of them is most attentive to My command and most diligent in My obedience."

﴿Wa-inna lajā'iluna﴾ (And indeed We will make), i.e., We will turn into, ﴿ma 'alayha﴾ (what is upon it) of what was adornment for it, or ﴿ma 'alayha﴾ of what is more general than adornment and other things, into ﴿sa'idan juruzan﴾ (barren dust). This is an indication of making the world seem unattractive, turning away from it, and consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning what the hands of the affluent grasp of its adornment, since the end of all that is to annihilation and perishing.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ma 'alayha﴾ of this adornment ﴿sa'idan juruzan﴾, meaning like a white land with no vegetation, after having been green and luxuriant, in the removal of its radiance and the effacement of its beauty, and the nullification of what made it adornment, by causing animals to die, plants and trees to dry out, and the like. End of quotation.

It was said: the sa'id is what rises upon the surface of the earth. Mujahid said: "The land in which there is no vegetation." Al-Suddi said: "the smooth, level ground." It was said: "the road." In the hadith: "Beware of sitting on the sa'idat (roadsides)."

[p. 95] It is entirely Meccan, except for one opinion. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah reported that the exception is His saying, ﴿And keep yourself patient﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], and the verse following it, so that part is Medinan. Muqatil said: the exception is from its beginning to "barren [juruzan]," and from His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 30], the two verses that follow, so that part is Medinan.

The occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was that the Quraysh sent al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'it to the rabbis of the Jews in Medina. They said to them: "Ask them about Muhammad and describe his description to them, for they are the People of the First Book, and they have knowledge of the prophets that we do not have." The two set out until they reached Medina and asked them. The Jews said: "Ask him about three things. If he tells you them, then he is a sent prophet; but if he does not do so, then the man is a fabricator. Consider the matter well. Ask him about the youths who went forth in the earliest age, what their affair was, for they had a wondrous story. Ask him about the man who traveled round, who reached the easts and the wests of the earth, what was his story. And ask him about the Spirit." Al-Nadr and 'Uqbah then came back to Mecca and asked him. He said: "Tomorrow I will tell you," and he did not say, "If God wills." So revelation was withheld for fifteen days. The unbelievers of Quraysh spread rumors and said: "Muhammad has been abandoned by his companion who used to come to him from the jinn." Some of them said: "He has been unable to produce his lies." This grieved him greatly. When the period had passed, revelation came to him with the answers to the questions and to other matters.

It is also related concerning this occasion that the Jews said: "If he answers you about the three, then he is not a prophet; but if he answers about two and remains silent about the other, then he is a prophet." So God revealed the Surah of the People of the Cave, and after that He revealed, ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit﴾ [al-Isra: 85].

The connection (munasabah) between the beginning of this surah and the end of what precedes it is this: when He said, ﴿And with truth We have sent it down, and with truth it has descended﴾ [al-Isra: 105], and mentioned the believers in it who are people of knowledge, and that it increases them in humility, and that He, exalted is He, commanded that He be praised and that He has not taken a son, He commanded them to praise Him for sending down this Book, which is free from crookedness, which is a guardian over all the Books, which warns those who take a son, and which gives good news to the believers of a good reward. Then He digressed (istitrad) to the account of the unbelievers of Quraysh. He turned from address (khitab) in His saying, ﴿And magnify Him with magnification﴾ [al-Isra: 111], to the third person (ghaybah) in His saying, ﴿upon His servant﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], because of the honoring attribution contained in "His servant," which requires his exaltation. The construction did not come as "He sent down upon you."

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Qur'an. Crookedness in meanings is like crookedness in persons. "Iwajan" (crookedness) is indefinite so that it covers all its kinds, because it is an indefinite noun in a context of negation. The meaning is that it is in the utmost straightness: there is no contradiction and no disagreement in its meanings, and no harshness (hushiyyah) or incoherence ('iyy) in its structures and forms. "Qayyiman" (upright) is an emphasis establishing straightness, if its meaning is "straight"; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. It has been said: "qayyiman" means guardian over the interests of the servants, the laws of their religion, and the affairs of their livelihood and their hereafter. It has also been said: "qayyiman" means a guardian over the other Books by confirming them.

They differed regarding this negative clause. Al-Zamakhshari maintained that it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "anzala" (He sent down), so it falls within the relative clause (silah). On this basis he concluded that the best reading for the accusative of "qayyiman" is that it is governed by a hidden verb, and not made a circumstantial (hal) of "al-Kitab," because that would necessitate separating the circumstantial from its referent by part of the relative clause. He estimated the verb as "ja'alahu" (He made it) "qayyiman."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "qayyiman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial of "al-Kitab," so it means "preceded" but is later in wording: the meaning is "He sent down the Book, upright." The negative clause, ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], intervenes between the circumstantial and its referent. This was reported by al-Tabari from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also permissible that it be accusative governed by a hidden verb, whose estimate is "anzalahu" (He sent it down) or "ja'alahu" (He made it) "qayyiman." As for if we say that the negative clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh), then it is permissible, and the circumstantial may be separated from its referent by parenthetical clauses.

Al-'Askari said: there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, as if he said: "Praise God for sending down the Qur'an upright, without crookedness in it," and it is the habit of eloquent speakers to put first what is most important.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1] indicates that it is perfect in its essence, and His saying "qayyiman" indicates that it is perfected by other than itself. So it is established by rational proof that the correct order is the one God mentioned, and that what they mentioned of inversion and reversal is corrupt, and the intellect refuses to go to it.

Al-Karmani said: if you make it a circumstantial, which is the more apparent, then there is no inversion or reversal in it. The correct view is that the two are two circumstantials of "al-Kitab," the first being a clause and the second a single word. End of quotation. This is according to the view of those who permit two circumstantials to occur for one referent without a conjunction, while many of our companions prohibit that. End of quotation. Al-Isfahani preferred this and said: they are two consecutive circumstantials, and the estimate is "not making for it crookedness, upright [qayyiman]."

The author of Hall al-'Aqd (Solving the Knot) said: it is possible that His saying "qayyiman" is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], meaning: He made it straight, upright. End of quotation. This would be a substitution of a single word for a clause, as they said regarding "'arafta Zaydan abu man" (I knew Zayd, father of whom), that it is a substitution of a clause for a single word; and there is disagreement about this.

It has been said that "qayyiman" is a circumstantial of the pronoun ha' (his) in ﴿has not made for him﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], as an emphasis. It has also been said that it is a transitional (muntaqilah) circumstantial. The apparent view is that the pronoun in "lahu" (for it) refers to "al-Kitab," and on this basis the i'rab (grammatical) analyses mentioned above apply. Some people claimed that the pronoun in "lahu" refers to "'abdihi" (His servant), and the estimate is ﴿upon His servant﴾ [al-Kahf: 1] and He made him "qayyiman."

Hafs pauses briefly on His saying "iwajan" (crookedness), a light pause (sakta khafifah), and then says "qayyiman." In some of the codices of the Companions there is ﴿and has not made for him crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], but "ja'alahu qayyiman" (He made it upright). This is to be understood as an explanation of the meaning, not as a recitation (qira'ah).

"Anzara" (to warn) takes two objects, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ [al-Naba: 40]. Here the first object is omitted and the thing warned of is stated, because that is the purpose toward which the speech is directed, so it was restricted to it. Then the one who warns is stated in His saying, when He repeated the warning: ﴿and warn those who say, "God has taken a son"﴾ [al-Kahf: 4]. So the warner is omitted at first because the second indicates it, and the thing warned of is omitted because the first indicates it. This is of the wondrous omission and the sublime eloquence. And since He did not repeat the good news, He brought the one who gives good news and the thing good news is given of. The apparent view is that "li-yundhira" (so that he may warn) is connected to "anzala" (He sent down). Al-Hawfi said: it is connected to "qayyiman." The omitted object of "li-yundhira" was estimated by Ibn 'Atiyyah as "al-'alam" (the world), and by Abu al-Baqa' as "al-'ibad" (the servants) or "li-yundhirakum" (so that he may warn you). Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as specific, saying: its origin is "li-yundhira" (so that he may warn) "alladhina kafaru" (those who disbelieved) ﴿with severe punishment [ba'san shadidan]﴾ [al-Kahf: 2]. "Al-ba's" comes from His saying: ﴿with a wretched punishment [bi-'adhabin ba'is]﴾ [al-A'raf: 165], and the punishment became wretched, and the man became wretched, "ba's" and "ba'sah." End of quotation. It seems that in determining the omitted object he observed a correspondence with ﴿and gives good news to the believers who﴾ [al-Kahf: 2]. The severe "ba's" is the punishment of the Hereafter, and it is possible that the punishment of this world is included in it.

"Min ladunhu" (from Him) means "issuing from His presence." Abu Bakr read the dal with sukun and with ishmam (a slight rounding), the damm, and the nun with kasrah. The discussion of these was given earlier, at the beginning of Hud. It is also read ﴿wa-yubashshiru﴾ (and gives good news) with raf' (nominative), but the majority read it with nasb (accusative), coordinated with "li-yundhira." "Al-ajr al-hasan" (the goodly reward) is Paradise. When He alluded to Paradise by His saying ﴿a goodly reward﴾ [al-Kahf: 2], He said ﴿remaining therein﴾ [al-Kahf: 3], that is, dwelling in it, making it a container for their dwelling. And since staying does not necessarily entail eternity, He said "abadan" (forever), which is an adverb indicating an unlimited time. "Makithin" is accusative as a circumstantial, and its referent is the pronoun in "lahum" (for them). The ones who attributed a son to God, the Exalted, were some of the Jews concerning Uzayr, some of the Christians concerning the Messiah, and some of the Arabs concerning the angels. The apparent view is that the pronoun in "bihi" (about it) refers to the son they claimed. Al-Mahdawi said: then the clause is a description of the son. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is objectionable, because only the one who speaks would describe it, and they did not intend to describe it. In my view the correct reading is that it is a new negation (nafy mu'tanif), which God informed about their ignorance in this matter, and the clause has no place in the i'rab. It is also possible that it refers to God, the Exalted, and this interpretation is more condemnatory of them and more conclusive regarding their complete ignorance. This is the view of al-Tabari. End of quotation.

It has been said: the meaning is ﴿they have no knowledge [of it]﴾ concerning God, so that they might exalt Him above what is not befitting to Him. It is also possible that it refers to the saying understood from "qalu" (they said), meaning: they have no knowledge in their saying this, so the clause is in the position of a circumstantial: they said it ignorantly, without reflection, deliberation, or consideration of what is possible and what is impossible. It has also been said that it refers to the taking understood from "ittakhadha" (took), meaning: they have no knowledge of the wisdom of taking, since no one takes a son except one who is incapable and subdued, who needs a helper to strengthen his arm, and this is impossible for God.

Al-Zamakhshari said: God's taking a son in itself is impossible, so how is it said ﴿they have no knowledge of it﴾? I say: its meaning is that they have no knowledge of it, because it is not among things that can be known, due to its impossibility. The absence of knowledge of a thing is either due to ignorance of the way that leads to it, or because it is in itself impossible, so that the knowledge of it cannot properly relate to it. End of quotation.

"Wa-la li-abaihim" (nor to their fathers) is coordinated with "lahum" (for them). They are those of their predecessors who went to this flimsy statement. Rather, whoever said this only said it out of ignorance and blind imitation. He mentioned the fathers because they took that statement from them and received it from them.

Qara'a al-jumhur (the majority of reciters) ﴿kalimatan﴾ with the accusative, and the apparent reading is that it is in the accusative of specification (tamyiz). The subject of ﴿kaburat﴾ is an implied pronoun referring to the statement understood from His words ﴿They say: "God has taken a son."﴾ [18:4]. This carries the sense of wonder: how great is it as a word! The sentence following it is a description of it, conveying the enormity of their audacity in uttering it and bringing it out of their mouths. Many of the things that Satan whispers into hearts and that the soul speaks to itself cannot be uttered aloud; rather, one turns one's thoughts away from them. How then could one utter such a heinous thing? It is called ﴿kalimah﴾ (word) just as they call a qasidah (ode) a kalimah.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This statement, existing in the soul as a single meaning, may appropriately be called a kalimah." He also said: "The majority read the kalimah in the accusative, as you say: ni'ma rajulan Zayd (what an excellent man Zayd is). It is explained by the word kalimah and described by its coming out of their mouths." Some said: "Its accusative is that of explanation (tafsir), in the manner of the accusative in His words, ﴿and how evil a resting place﴾ [18:29]." A group said: "Its accusative is that of circumstance (hal), meaning: their slander is great," and similar. End of quotation.

According to his statement, "as you say: ni'ma rajulan Zayd," the one praised or blamed (al-makhsus bil-dhamm) would be omitted, because he made ﴿takhruju﴾ (comes out) a description of kalimah. The implied meaning is: ﴿kaburat kalimah﴾ (how great is a word) ﴿takhruju min afwahihim﴾ (coming out of their mouths), that statement which they uttered, namely their saying ﴿God has taken a son.﴾ The pronoun in ﴿kaburat﴾ does not refer to what precedes it; rather it is an implied pronoun explained by what follows it, which is the tamyiz according to the school of the Basrans. It is also permissible that the one blamed be omitted, with ﴿takhruju﴾ as its description, meaning: ﴿how great is a word﴾ (a word) ﴿coming out of their mouths.﴾

Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is in the accusative as an exclamation, meaning: "How great is it as a word!" Or, "from a word." It was also read ﴿kabrat﴾ with a sukun on the ba', and this is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Qawwas from Ibn Kathir read it in the nominative as the subject (fa'il), but the accusative is more eloquent and stronger in meaning. ﴿In﴾ here is negative, meaning: "they say nothing but," and ﴿kadhiban﴾ (a lie) is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: "a statement that is a lie."

﴿Fa-la'allaka bakhi'un nafsaka﴾ (Perhaps you would destroy yourself). La'alla is for hope regarding what is loved and for apprehension regarding what is feared. Al-'Askari said: "Here la'alla is used in the place of prohibition," meaning: do not destroy yourself. It was also said: it is used in the place of interrogation, its implied meaning being: "Are you about to destroy yourself?" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is an affirmation and a reproach, meaning: a denial of him, i.e., do not be like that. Al-Zamakhshari said: He likened him, and them, when they turned away from him and did not believe in him, and the grief and sorrow that overcame him over their turning away, to a man whose beloved and dear ones have departed from him; so he falls apart in sorrow after their traces and destroys himself out of grief for them and longing for their separation. End of quotation. La'alla serving as interrogation is a Kufan opinion. What appears evident is that it is for apprehension: he feared that the Messenger (ﷺ) would destroy himself because they did not believe.

His words ﴿'ala athharihim﴾ (after them) are an eloquent metaphor, since they have retreat, distance from faith and aversion from the Law. It is as if they, in the extremity of their retreat, have gone far away, and so he grieves over them in their retreat. The meaning of ﴿'ala athharihim﴾ is "after them," i.e., after your despair of their belief, or after their death in disbelief. It is said: "So-and-so died on the trail of so-and-so," meaning after him.

It was read ﴿bakhi'u nafsika﴾ with the genitive construction (idafah). The majority read ﴿bakhi'un﴾ with tanwin and ﴿nafsaka﴾ in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is according to the original rule," meaning that when the active participle fulfils the conditions for operating, the original rule is that it governs, and Sibawayh indicated this in his book. Al-Kisa'i said: working (governing) and the genitive construction are equal. We have held that the genitive construction is better than governing, for reasons we set out in what we composed in the science of grammar.

It was read ﴿in lam yu'minu﴾ with a kasrah and a fathah on the mim. As for the one who reads with a kasrah, al-Zamakhshari said: it refers, meaning the active participle, to the future; and whoever reads with a fathah, it refers to the past, meaning the state of the construction, i.e., because ﴿lam yu'minu﴾ (they did not believe) and the reference by ﴿hadha al-hadith﴾ (this discourse) is to the Qur'an. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿God has sent down the best discourse, a Book consistent in its parts﴾ [39:23].
