Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ma 'alayha﴾ of this adornment ﴿sa'idan juruzan﴾, meaning like a white land with no vegetation, after having been green and luxuriant, in the removal of its radiance and the effacement of its beauty, and the nullification of what made it adornment, by causing animals to die, plants and trees to dry out, and the like. End of quotation.

It was said: the sa'id is what rises upon the surface of the earth. Mujahid said: "The land in which there is no vegetation." Al-Suddi said: "the smooth, level ground." It was said: "the road." In the hadith: "Beware of sitting on the sa'idat (roadsides)."

[p. 95] It is entirely Meccan, except for one opinion. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah reported that the exception is His saying, ﴿And keep yourself patient﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], and the verse following it, so that part is Medinan. Muqatil said: the exception is from its beginning to "barren [juruzan]," and from His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 30], the two verses that follow, so that part is Medinan.

The occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was that the Quraysh sent al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'it to the rabbis of the Jews in Medina. They said to them: "Ask them about Muhammad and describe his description to them, for they are the People of the First Book, and they have knowledge of the prophets that we do not have." The two set out until they reached Medina and asked them. The Jews said: "Ask him about three things. If he tells you them, then he is a sent prophet; but if he does not do so, then the man is a fabricator. Consider the matter well. Ask him about the youths who went forth in the earliest age, what their affair was, for they had a wondrous story. Ask him about the man who traveled round, who reached the easts and the wests of the earth, what was his story. And ask him about the Spirit." Al-Nadr and 'Uqbah then came back to Mecca and asked him. He said: "Tomorrow I will tell you," and he did not say, "If God wills." So revelation was withheld for fifteen days. The unbelievers of Quraysh spread rumors and said: "Muhammad has been abandoned by his companion who used to come to him from the jinn." Some of them said: "He has been unable to produce his lies." This grieved him greatly. When the period had passed, revelation came to him with the answers to the questions and to other matters.

It is also related concerning this occasion that the Jews said: "If he answers you about the three, then he is not a prophet; but if he answers about two and remains silent about the other, then he is a prophet." So God revealed the Surah of the People of the Cave, and after that He revealed, ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit﴾ [al-Isra: 85].

The connection (munasabah) between the beginning of this surah and the end of what precedes it is this: when He said, ﴿And with truth We have sent it down, and with truth it has descended﴾ [al-Isra: 105], and mentioned the believers in it who are people of knowledge, and that it increases them in humility, and that He, exalted is He, commanded that He be praised and that He has not taken a son, He commanded them to praise Him for sending down this Book, which is free from crookedness, which is a guardian over all the Books, which warns those who take a son, and which gives good news to the believers of a good reward. Then He digressed (istitrad) to the account of the unbelievers of Quraysh. He turned from address (khitab) in His saying, ﴿And magnify Him with magnification﴾ [al-Isra: 111], to the third person (ghaybah) in His saying, ﴿upon His servant﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], because of the honoring attribution contained in "His servant," which requires his exaltation. The construction did not come as "He sent down upon you."

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Qur'an. Crookedness in meanings is like crookedness in persons. "Iwajan" (crookedness) is indefinite so that it covers all its kinds, because it is an indefinite noun in a context of negation. The meaning is that it is in the utmost straightness: there is no contradiction and no disagreement in its meanings, and no harshness (hushiyyah) or incoherence ('iyy) in its structures and forms. "Qayyiman" (upright) is an emphasis establishing straightness, if its meaning is "straight"; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. It has been said: "qayyiman" means guardian over the interests of the servants, the laws of their religion, and the affairs of their livelihood and their hereafter. It has also been said: "qayyiman" means a guardian over the other Books by confirming them.

They differed regarding this negative clause. Al-Zamakhshari maintained that it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "anzala" (He sent down), so it falls within the relative clause (silah). On this basis he concluded that the best reading for the accusative of "qayyiman" is that it is governed by a hidden verb, and not made a circumstantial (hal) of "al-Kitab," because that would necessitate separating the circumstantial from its referent by part of the relative clause. He estimated the verb as "ja'alahu" (He made it) "qayyiman."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "qayyiman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial of "al-Kitab," so it means "preceded" but is later in wording: the meaning is "He sent down the Book, upright." The negative clause, ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], intervenes between the circumstantial and its referent. This was reported by al-Tabari from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also permissible that it be accusative governed by a hidden verb, whose estimate is "anzalahu" (He sent it down) or "ja'alahu" (He made it) "qayyiman." As for if we say that the negative clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh), then it is permissible, and the circumstantial may be separated from its referent by parenthetical clauses.

Al-'Askari said: there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, as if he said: "Praise God for sending down the Qur'an upright, without crookedness in it," and it is the habit of eloquent speakers to put first what is most important.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1] indicates that it is perfect in its essence, and His saying "qayyiman" indicates that it is perfected by other than itself. So it is established by rational proof that the correct order is the one God mentioned, and that what they mentioned of inversion and reversal is corrupt, and the intellect refuses to go to it.

Al-Karmani said: if you make it a circumstantial, which is the more apparent, then there is no inversion or reversal in it. The correct view is that the two are two circumstantials of "al-Kitab," the first being a clause and the second a single word. End of quotation. This is according to the view of those who permit two circumstantials to occur for one referent without a conjunction, while many of our companions prohibit that. End of quotation. Al-Isfahani preferred this and said: they are two consecutive circumstantials, and the estimate is "not making for it crookedness, upright [qayyiman]."

The author of Hall al-'Aqd (Solving the Knot) said: it is possible that His saying "qayyiman" is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿and has not made for it any crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], meaning: He made it straight, upright. End of quotation. This would be a substitution of a single word for a clause, as they said regarding "'arafta Zaydan abu man" (I knew Zayd, father of whom), that it is a substitution of a clause for a single word; and there is disagreement about this.

It has been said that "qayyiman" is a circumstantial of the pronoun ha' (his) in ﴿has not made for him﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], as an emphasis. It has also been said that it is a transitional (muntaqilah) circumstantial. The apparent view is that the pronoun in "lahu" (for it) refers to "al-Kitab," and on this basis the i'rab (grammatical) analyses mentioned above apply. Some people claimed that the pronoun in "lahu" refers to "'abdihi" (His servant), and the estimate is ﴿upon His servant﴾ [al-Kahf: 1] and He made him "qayyiman."

Hafs pauses briefly on His saying "iwajan" (crookedness), a light pause (sakta khafifah), and then says "qayyiman." In some of the codices of the Companions there is ﴿and has not made for him crookedness﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], but "ja'alahu qayyiman" (He made it upright). This is to be understood as an explanation of the meaning, not as a recitation (qira'ah).

"Anzara" (to warn) takes two objects, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ [al-Naba: 40]. Here the first object is omitted and the thing warned of is stated, because that is the purpose toward which the speech is directed, so it was restricted to it. Then the one who warns is stated in His saying, when He repeated the warning: ﴿and warn those who say, "God has taken a son"﴾ [al-Kahf: 4]. So the warner is omitted at first because the second indicates it, and the thing warned of is omitted because the first indicates it. This is of the wondrous omission and the sublime eloquence. And since He did not repeat the good news, He brought the one who gives good news and the thing good news is given of. The apparent view is that "li-yundhira" (so that he may warn) is connected to "anzala" (He sent down). Al-Hawfi said: it is connected to "qayyiman." The omitted object of "li-yundhira" was estimated by Ibn 'Atiyyah as "al-'alam" (the world), and by Abu al-Baqa' as "al-'ibad" (the servants) or "li-yundhirakum" (so that he may warn you). Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as specific, saying: its origin is "li-yundhira" (so that he may warn) "alladhina kafaru" (those who disbelieved) ﴿with severe punishment [ba'san shadidan]﴾ [al-Kahf: 2]. "Al-ba's" comes from His saying: ﴿with a wretched punishment [bi-'adhabin ba'is]﴾ [al-A'raf: 165], and the punishment became wretched, and the man became wretched, "ba's" and "ba'sah." End of quotation. It seems that in determining the omitted object he observed a correspondence with ﴿and gives good news to the believers who﴾ [al-Kahf: 2]. The severe "ba's" is the punishment of the Hereafter, and it is possible that the punishment of this world is included in it.

"Min ladunhu" (from Him) means "issuing from His presence." Abu Bakr read the dal with sukun and with ishmam (a slight rounding), the damm, and the nun with kasrah. The discussion of these was given earlier, at the beginning of Hud. It is also read ﴿wa-yubashshiru﴾ (and gives good news) with raf' (nominative), but the majority read it with nasb (accusative), coordinated with "li-yundhira." "Al-ajr al-hasan" (the goodly reward) is Paradise. When He alluded to Paradise by His saying ﴿a goodly reward﴾ [al-Kahf: 2], He said ﴿remaining therein﴾ [al-Kahf: 3], that is, dwelling in it, making it a container for their dwelling. And since staying does not necessarily entail eternity, He said "abadan" (forever), which is an adverb indicating an unlimited time. "Makithin" is accusative as a circumstantial, and its referent is the pronoun in "lahum" (for them). The ones who attributed a son to God, the Exalted, were some of the Jews concerning Uzayr, some of the Christians concerning the Messiah, and some of the Arabs concerning the angels. The apparent view is that the pronoun in "bihi" (about it) refers to the son they claimed. Al-Mahdawi said: then the clause is a description of the son. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is objectionable, because only the one who speaks would describe it, and they did not intend to describe it. In my view the correct reading is that it is a new negation (nafy mu'tanif), which God informed about their ignorance in this matter, and the clause has no place in the i'rab. It is also possible that it refers to God, the Exalted, and this interpretation is more condemnatory of them and more conclusive regarding their complete ignorance. This is the view of al-Tabari. End of quotation.

It has been said: the meaning is ﴿they have no knowledge [of it]﴾ concerning God, so that they might exalt Him above what is not befitting to Him. It is also possible that it refers to the saying understood from "qalu" (they said), meaning: they have no knowledge in their saying this, so the clause is in the position of a circumstantial: they said it ignorantly, without reflection, deliberation, or consideration of what is possible and what is impossible. It has also been said that it refers to the taking understood from "ittakhadha" (took), meaning: they have no knowledge of the wisdom of taking, since no one takes a son except one who is incapable and subdued, who needs a helper to strengthen his arm, and this is impossible for God.

Al-Zamakhshari said: God's taking a son in itself is impossible, so how is it said ﴿they have no knowledge of it﴾? I say: its meaning is that they have no knowledge of it, because it is not among things that can be known, due to its impossibility. The absence of knowledge of a thing is either due to ignorance of the way that leads to it, or because it is in itself impossible, so that the knowledge of it cannot properly relate to it. End of quotation.

"Wa-la li-abaihim" (nor to their fathers) is coordinated with "lahum" (for them). They are those of their predecessors who went to this flimsy statement. Rather, whoever said this only said it out of ignorance and blind imitation. He mentioned the fathers because they took that statement from them and received it from them.

Qara'a al-jumhur (the majority of reciters) ﴿kalimatan﴾ with the accusative, and the apparent reading is that it is in the accusative of specification (tamyiz). The subject of ﴿kaburat﴾ is an implied pronoun referring to the statement understood from His words ﴿They say: "God has taken a son."﴾ [18:4]. This carries the sense of wonder: how great is it as a word! The sentence following it is a description of it, conveying the enormity of their audacity in uttering it and bringing it out of their mouths. Many of the things that Satan whispers into hearts and that the soul speaks to itself cannot be uttered aloud; rather, one turns one's thoughts away from them. How then could one utter such a heinous thing? It is called ﴿kalimah﴾ (word) just as they call a qasidah (ode) a kalimah.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This statement, existing in the soul as a single meaning, may appropriately be called a kalimah." He also said: "The majority read the kalimah in the accusative, as you say: ni'ma rajulan Zayd (what an excellent man Zayd is). It is explained by the word kalimah and described by its coming out of their mouths." Some said: "Its accusative is that of explanation (tafsir), in the manner of the accusative in His words, ﴿and how evil a resting place﴾ [18:29]." A group said: "Its accusative is that of circumstance (hal), meaning: their slander is great," and similar. End of quotation.

According to his statement, "as you say: ni'ma rajulan Zayd," the one praised or blamed (al-makhsus bil-dhamm) would be omitted, because he made ﴿takhruju﴾ (comes out) a description of kalimah. The implied meaning is: ﴿kaburat kalimah﴾ (how great is a word) ﴿takhruju min afwahihim﴾ (coming out of their mouths), that statement which they uttered, namely their saying ﴿God has taken a son.﴾ The pronoun in ﴿kaburat﴾ does not refer to what precedes it; rather it is an implied pronoun explained by what follows it, which is the tamyiz according to the school of the Basrans. It is also permissible that the one blamed be omitted, with ﴿takhruju﴾ as its description, meaning: ﴿how great is a word﴾ (a word) ﴿coming out of their mouths.﴾

Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is in the accusative as an exclamation, meaning: "How great is it as a word!" Or, "from a word." It was also read ﴿kabrat﴾ with a sukun on the ba', and this is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Qawwas from Ibn Kathir read it in the nominative as the subject (fa'il), but the accusative is more eloquent and stronger in meaning. ﴿In﴾ here is negative, meaning: "they say nothing but," and ﴿kadhiban﴾ (a lie) is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: "a statement that is a lie."

﴿Fa-la'allaka bakhi'un nafsaka﴾ (Perhaps you would destroy yourself). La'alla is for hope regarding what is loved and for apprehension regarding what is feared. Al-'Askari said: "Here la'alla is used in the place of prohibition," meaning: do not destroy yourself. It was also said: it is used in the place of interrogation, its implied meaning being: "Are you about to destroy yourself?" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is an affirmation and a reproach, meaning: a denial of him, i.e., do not be like that. Al-Zamakhshari said: He likened him, and them, when they turned away from him and did not believe in him, and the grief and sorrow that overcame him over their turning away, to a man whose beloved and dear ones have departed from him; so he falls apart in sorrow after their traces and destroys himself out of grief for them and longing for their separation. End of quotation. La'alla serving as interrogation is a Kufan opinion. What appears evident is that it is for apprehension: he feared that the Messenger (ﷺ) would destroy himself because they did not believe.

His words ﴿'ala athharihim﴾ (after them) are an eloquent metaphor, since they have retreat, distance from faith and aversion from the Law. It is as if they, in the extremity of their retreat, have gone far away, and so he grieves over them in their retreat. The meaning of ﴿'ala athharihim﴾ is "after them," i.e., after your despair of their belief, or after their death in disbelief. It is said: "So-and-so died on the trail of so-and-so," meaning after him.

It was read ﴿bakhi'u nafsika﴾ with the genitive construction (idafah). The majority read ﴿bakhi'un﴾ with tanwin and ﴿nafsaka﴾ in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is according to the original rule," meaning that when the active participle fulfils the conditions for operating, the original rule is that it governs, and Sibawayh indicated this in his book. Al-Kisa'i said: working (governing) and the genitive construction are equal. We have held that the genitive construction is better than governing, for reasons we set out in what we composed in the science of grammar.

It was read ﴿in lam yu'minu﴾ with a kasrah and a fathah on the mim. As for the one who reads with a kasrah, al-Zamakhshari said: it refers, meaning the active participle, to the future; and whoever reads with a fathah, it refers to the past, meaning the state of the construction, i.e., because ﴿lam yu'minu﴾ (they did not believe) and the reference by ﴿hadha al-hadith﴾ (this discourse) is to the Qur'an. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿God has sent down the best discourse, a Book consistent in its parts﴾ [39:23].

﴿Asafan﴾ (grief). Mujahid said: "distress." Qatadah said: "anger," and also from him: "sorrow." Al-Suddi said: "regret and anguish." Al-Zajjaj said: "asaf is intensity in sorrow and anger." Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: "Asaf here means sorrow, because it is directed at one who does not possess or is not under the hand of the one grieving. If the asaf came from one powerful over one who is in his grasp and possession, it would be anger, as in His words: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took retribution from them﴾ [43:55], meaning: they angered Us." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "When you reflect on this in Arabic speech, it is consistent." End of quotation.

The accusative of ﴿asafan﴾ is either as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi) or as a verbal noun in the position of circumstance (hal). The connection of His words ﴿Indeed We have made﴾ (the verse) with what precedes it is by way of consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), because He, the Exalted, informed that He created what is upon the earth as adornment for the purpose of trial and testing: which of people is ﴿best in deed﴾ [18:7]. They are not of one pattern in uprightness and following the Messengers. Rather, there must be among them one who is best in deed and one who is worst in deed. So do not be distressed or grieved over those whom you have been given preference over, that they will be worse in deed; and even though they disbelieve in Me, I will not cut off from them the provisions of these blessings which I created.

﴿Ja'alna﴾ (We made) here means "created" (khalaqna). The apparent reading is that what is intended by ﴿ma﴾ is non-rational beings, and that it intends generality in what is non-rational. ﴿Zinah﴾ (adornment) is each thing according to its kind. It was said: this does not include what contains harm from animal, stone, or plant, since there is no adornment in it. Whoever holds to generality says that ﴿zinah﴾ is so in terms of its creation, craftsmanship and perfection. It was said: what is intended here is specifically non-rational beings. It was said: trees and rivers. It was said: plants, because of their variety and flowers. It was said: animals of differing forms, benefits and actions. It was said: gold, silver, copper, lead, rubies, chrysolite, pearls, coral, and similar precious stones.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ma 'ala al-ard﴾ (what is upon the earth) means what is fit to be ﴿adornment for it﴾ and for its people, of the ornaments of the world and what is considered beautiful in it. A group said: it intends bounties, garments, fruits, greenery and water. It was said: ﴿ma﴾ here is for rational beings; according to Mujahid, it means men, and Ibn Jubayr said this on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ikrimah transmitted that the adornment is the caliphs, scholars and rulers.

﴿Zinah﴾ is in the accusative as circumstance, or as an object of purpose if ﴿ja'alna﴾ means "created" and "brought into existence." If it means "made into," then it is in the accusative as a second object.

The lam in ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾ (that We may test them) is connected to ﴿ja'alna﴾. Al-ibtila' is testing and examination, and it is interpreted in relation to God, the Exalted. The pronoun in ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾, if ﴿ma﴾ is for rational beings, refers back to it according to meaning; and it may not refer to what is understood from the context of the speech, namely the inhabitants of the earth who are obligated. ﴿Ayyuhum﴾ (which of them) may be parsed with the pronoun in it being grammatically inflected, so that ﴿ayyuhum﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and ﴿ahsanu﴾ (best) is its predicate. The sentence is in the position of the object of ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾; and He has suspended ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾, treating it as the verb of knowledge, because testing and examination are a cause of knowledge, just as they suspended sal (ask) and unzur (look) in the visual sense, because these two are causes of knowledge. Al-Hawfi held that the sentence is interrogative, a subject and predicate. It is also possible that the dammah on it is a built form (binā') according to Sibawayh's school, because the condition for permitting indeclinability in ayyu is met, namely that it is annexed while the beginning of its complement has been omitted. So ﴿ahsanu﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, its implied meaning being "he is best," and ﴿ayyuhum﴾ is in the accusative position as an apposition to the pronoun in ﴿li-nabluwahum﴾. The one preferred over, the object of comparison, is omitted, its implied meaning being: "of those who are not ﴿best in deed﴾."

Al-Thawri said: "The best of them in deed is the most abstemious of them regarding it." Abu 'Asim al-'Asqalani said: "The one who most abandons it." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The goodness of deed is abstinence from it and not being deceived by it." Abu Bakr Ghalib ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The best deed is taking what is right with faith, performing the obligations, avoiding the forbidden, and increasing in what is recommended." Al-Kalbi said: "The best in obedience." Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: "Those upon it of prophets and scholars, to test those to whom the messenger is sent and the followers of the scholars: which of them is best in acceptance and response." Sahl said: "Best in trust in Us regarding it." It was said: "Purest in heart and best in demeanour." Ibn Ishaq said: "Which of them is most attentive to My command and most diligent in My obedience."

﴿Wa-inna lajā'iluna﴾ (And indeed We will make), i.e., We will turn into, ﴿ma 'alayha﴾ (what is upon it) of what was adornment for it, or ﴿ma 'alayha﴾ of what is more general than adornment and other things, into ﴿sa'idan juruzan﴾ (barren dust). This is an indication of making the world seem unattractive, turning away from it, and consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning what the hands of the affluent grasp of its adornment, since the end of all that is to annihilation and perishing.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ma 'alayha﴾ of this adornment ﴿sa'idan juruzan﴾, meaning like a white land with no vegetation, after having been green and luxuriant, in the removal of its radiance and the effacement of its beauty, and the nullification of what made it adornment, by causing animals to die, plants and trees to dry out, and the like. End of quotation.

It was said: the sa'id is what rises upon the surface of the earth. Mujahid said: "The land in which there is no vegetation." Al-Suddi said: "the smooth, level ground." It was said: "the road." In the hadith: "Beware of sitting on the sa'idat (roadsides)."

(p. 100) Here *am* is the disjunctive (*munqati'a*) particle, so it is to be read as equivalent to *bal* ("rather") together with the interrogative *hamza*. It is said that it signals a transition (*idrab*) from one statement to another, in the sense of moving on to a different topic rather than cancelling the first. The *hamza* is the interrogative particle. Some grammarians claimed that *am* here means only the *hamza*. Apparently, in ﴿Or did you think﴾ [al-Kahf: 9], the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ). Mujahid said: "He did not forbid him from wondering, but He meant that all of Our signs are like that." Qatadah said: "He should not be amazed by them, for the wonders in the creation of the heavens and the earth are greater."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They asked you about this so that they could make your answer a sign of your truthfulness or falsehood. The rest of the Qur'an's signs are more eloquent, more wondrous, and more indicative of your truthfulness."

Al-Tabari said: "This is a confirmation to him (peace be upon him) of his supposition that the companions of the Cave were a wonder, in the sense of rejecting that he should not magnify it as the disbelieving questioners magnified it for you, since all of God's other signs are greater than their story." He said: "This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq."

Al-Zahrawi said: "It may carry another meaning, which is that it is an interrogation to him: does he know that the companions of the Cave were a wonder, in the sense of affirming that they were a wonder? The purpose of this confirmation is to prepare himself for the matter, because his answer would be, 'I did not suppose it, nor did I know it,' and then it would be said to him: describe them at that point. The metaphor in this interpretation lies in the word *hasibta* (you supposed)." End of his quotation. Others said: its meaning is "Did you know?", i.e., you did not know it until We informed you.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He mentioned among the universal signs the adornment of the earth with what He created upon it of kinds that cannot be counted, and the removal of all of that as though it had never been. Then He said, *Or did you think* [al-Kahf: 9], meaning that this is part of the story of the People of the Cave and of their preservation alive for a long period." End of his quotation. It was also said: meaning "Or do you know," that is, "Know then that they were a wonder," just as you say, "Do you know that so-and-so did such-and-such?", meaning "He has done it, so know it." It was also said: the address is to the listener, and what is meant is the polytheists, that is: say to them, "Or do you suppose..." etc. *Zann* (supposition) may be used in place of *'ilm* (knowledge), so *hasibta* is in the sense of *'alimta*. As for *al-kahf* (the cave), its explanation has already been given in the vocabulary section (*al-mufradat*). From Anas: *al-kahf* is the mountain. The judge (al-Qadi) said: "This is not well known in the language." Mujahid said: it is a split between two mountains.

The apparent meaning of ﴿that the companions of the Cave and the Inscription﴾ [al-Kahf: 9] is that they are the young men mentioned here. From Ibn al-Musayyib: they were a people whose condition was like that of the companions of the Cave. Al-Dahhak said: "*al-Raqim* is a town in the lands of the Romans, in which there is a cave containing twenty-one souls, all dead, all asleep in the same state as the companions of the Cave." It was also said: they are the companions of the cave-shelter. There is a hadith from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that he heard the Messenger (ﷺ) mention the *Raqim*, saying: "Three men were caught by rain, so they took shelter in a cave, and a rock came down from the mountain and sealed the mouth of the cave." He mentioned the hadith, which is the hadith of the hired man, the chaste man, and the one who was dutiful to his parents, and in what he transmitted there are additional words beyond what is in the *Sahih*. As for those who said they were two groups, they said: God told us about the companions of the Cave and did not tell us anything about the companions of the Inscription. As for those who said they were one group, they disagreed about the explanation of *al-Raqim*. From Ibn 'Abbas: he did not know what *al-Raqim* was, whether it was a book or a building. Also from him: it was a book that they had, containing the law to which they held from the religion of the Messiah (peace be upon him). It was also said: it is from a religion before 'Isa. From Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb: it is the name of their town. It was said: a plate of gold under the wall, which al-Khidr (peace be upon him) set up. It was said: he wrote on it their names, their story, and the cause of their departure. It was said: a plate of lead on which the affair of the young men was written, placed in a copper chest at the mouth of the cave. It was said: a rock on which their names were written, placed in the city wall. It was said: it is the name of their dog, and the verse of Umayya was mentioned before, said by Anas, al-Sha'bi and Ibn Jubayr. From al-Hasan: it is the mountain on which the cave is. From 'Ikrimah: it is the name of the inkwell in Roman. It was said: it is the name of the valley in which the cave is. It was said: people wrote down their story by engraving it on the mountain.

﴿Wonder﴾ (*'ajaban*) is in the accusative because it is an adjective of an omitted noun indicated by what precedes it. Its estimated sense is "a sign that is wonderful," described by the verbal noun (*masdar*), or it is in the sense of "a thing possessing wonder." As for the names of the young men of the Cave, they are non-Arabic and cannot be fixed by vowel-marks or dots, and the chain of transmission for knowing them is weak. The narrators differ on their stories, on how they gathered and how they went out. No authentic hadith has described how this happened, nor does the Qur'an contain anything except what God related to us of their stories. Whoever wishes to seek that should consult the books of tafsir.

It is narrated that the name of the disbelieving king in whose days they left his religion was Diqyanus. It is also narrated that they were in the lands of the Romans. It was said: in Syria, and that in Syria there is a cave containing dead bodies, and its neighbours claim that they are the companions of the Cave, and there is a mosque and a building over them called al-Raqim, and with them is a dog, a dry bone. In al-Andalus, in the area of Granada near a village called Lusha, there is a cave containing dead bodies, and with them is a dog, a dry bone, and most of them have had their flesh stripped away and some are still intact. Centuries have passed, and we have not found anyone who knows their condition, and some people claim that they are the companions of the Cave. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "I entered among them and saw them four hundred and fifty years ago, and they were in this state. Over them is a mosque, and near them is a Roman building called al-Raqim, as if it were a carved palace of which some walls remain. It is in a wasteland in a ruined area, and above the city of Granada, on the side facing the qibla, are traces of an ancient city called the city of Diqyus, and in its ruins we found strange things, such as graves and the like. I only found it easy to mention this despite its distance, because it is a wonder whose mention will remain, God willing." End of quotation. When we were in al-Andalus, people used to visit this cave and say that they made mistakes when counting them, and that there was a dog with them, and people would travel to Lusha to visit them. As for what I mentioned about the city of Diqyus that is before me, Granada, I have passed by it many times, uncountable, and I have seen large stones there. It is more likely that the people of the Cave were in al-Andalus, because Christianity is widespread there, to the point that it was the land of their great kingdom, and because reports about what is in the farthest place from the land of the Hijaz are stranger, and it is more remote that anyone should know it except by revelation from God, exalted is He.

The governing element (*al-'amil*) of ﴿when﴾ (*idh*) is said to be an implied "remember." It was also said: it is *'ajaban* (wonder). The meaning of ﴿took refuge﴾ (*awa*) is that they made the cave a shelter for themselves and a place of protection. Then they called upon God, exalted is He, to grant them mercy from Himself, and the exegetes explained this mercy as provision. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is forgiveness, provision, and safety from enemies. *Al-fityah* (the young men) is a broken plural of *fata*, a plural of paucity, and likewise they were few. According to Ibn al-Sarraj, it is a collective noun, not a broken plural. The word *al-fityah* indicates that they were young, and it is also narrated that they were young men from the sons of the nobles and the great, adorned with gold necklaces and gold bracelets, with long locks, and they were from the Romans, who followed the religion of 'Isa (peace be upon him). It was also said that they were before 'Isa. Our fellow Andalusians often use in their speech and poetry, and in addressing the common people, the name "Romans" for the Christians of al-Andalus, saying, "We fought the Romans," "The Romans came to us." Few say the word "Christians." When they called for the bestowal of mercy, which includes provision and other things, they called upon God to prepare for them, from their affair, which had led them to leave the religion of their people and to affirm the oneness of God, right guidance (*rashad*), which is being rightly guided and being steadfast upon it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Make our whole affair right guidance, as you would say: 'I saw from you a lion.'" Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-Zuhri read *wa-hayyi'* and *yuhayyi* with two *ya's* without *hamza*, meaning that they replaced the quiescent *hamza* with *ya'*. In Ibn Khalawayh's book, al-A'sha reported from Abu Bakr from 'Asim: *wa-hayyi lana* and *yuhayyi lakum*, without *hamza*. End of quotation. This may mean that he replaced the *hamza* with *ya'*, or that he deleted it. The first is a regular substitution (*ibdal qiyasi*), and the second is disputed, since deleting the letter substituted for *hamza* in the imperative or the imperfect in jussive form is a recognized analogical process. Abu Raja' read *rushdun* with a *damma* on the *ra'* and a sukun on the *shin*. The majority read *rashadan* with a *fatha* on both. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is more preferred because it resembles the verse endings before and after it. This supplication from them concerned the affairs of their worldly life, and its wording implies that. They were confident of the right guidance and mercy of the Hereafter, and every believer should make his supplication for his worldly affairs this verse, for it is sufficient. The word *mercy* may also be understood to mean matters of the Hereafter." End of quotation.

﴿So We struck upon their ears﴾ [al-Kahf: 11] is a striking metaphor for a heavy sleep in which one can hardly hear. He used the verb *darb* (striking) to indicate strength of contact, adherence and permanence, as in ﴿Humiliation was struck upon them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 112], and the imposing of the poll-tax (*darb al-jizyah*), and the sending forth (*darb al-ba'th*). Al-Farazdaq said:

*The spider has spun its web over you,*
*and the revealed Book has decreed against you what it has decreed.*

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

*And among the calamities, may you have no father, that the earth has been struck against me with barriers.*

Another said:

*Indeed, manliness, generosity and open-handedness*
*are in a dome struck over the son of al-Hashraj.*

It is borrowed to express the permanence of these qualities for this praised man. He mentioned the organ that is the ears, since hearing comes through them, because sleep does not become firm except when hearing is disabled. In a hadith: "That is a man on whose ear Satan has urinated," meaning that his sleep was extremely heavy, so that he would not rise during the night. The object of *darabna* (We struck) is omitted, meaning "a veil from hearing," as one says, "He built over his wife," meaning he built the dome over her. *Sinin* (years) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and its governing verb is *fa-darabna*. *'Adadan* (a number) is a verbal noun described by it, or it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "after counting," and in the sense of the passive participle, like *al-qabd* (the grasp) and *al-naft* (the shaking). *Sinin* is described by it, meaning "years that were counted." The apparent sense of His saying *'adadan* indicates abundance, since one needs to count only what is numerous, not what is little.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that it means few, because the many is little in His sight, as in His saying: ﴿They did not remain but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]." End of quotation. This is a distortion in the comparison, because the wording of that verse is as if: on the day they see what they are promised, they will have remained only an hour of a day, which is a comparison to the swiftness of the passing of the life they lived in this world when they see the punishment, as the poet said:

*As though the youth had never been bare when he is clothed,*
*and had not been poor when he became rich.*

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verse 12–14 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Then We roused them﴾, i.e., We woke them from their sleep. Al-ba'th (raising, sending forth) is moving something from stillness, either regarding the person or regarding the matter in which he is roused, even if the thing in which he is roused is itself moving. And ﴿li-na'lam﴾, i.e., so that We might make manifest to them what We already knew of their affair. The discussion of its like has already occurred in His saying: ﴿so that We may know who follows the Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. In al-Tahrir it is said: the majority read ﴿li-na'lam﴾ with the nun, and al-Zuhri read it with the ya'. In Ibn Khalawayh's book it is li-ya'lama ﴿ayyu al-hizbayn﴾, related by al-Akhfash. In al-Kashshaf: "It is read li-ya'lama, and it is mu'allaq ('suspended') from it, because its being raised is by the inchoative (mubtada'), not by attributing 'ya'lamu' to it, and the agent of ya'lamu is the content of the sentence, just as the object of ya'lamu is." End of quotation. As for the reading li-na'lam, it appears that this is an iltifat (shift) from the first-person speaker to the third-person, so its meaning and the meaning of li-na'lam with the nun are the same. As for li-ya'lama, it appears that the first object is omitted, as the meaning indicates, and the estimate is: "so that God might make people know ﴿which of the two parties﴾". The sentence of the inchoative and its predicate is in the position of the second and third objects of yu'lim, and li-ya'lama is mu'allaq. As for what is in al-Kashshaf, it is not permissible according to the school of the Basrans, because the sentence in that case would be in the position of the object that is not named as its agent, standing in for the agent. Just as that sentence and other sentences do not stand in for the agent, so it does not stand in for what it replaces. The Kufans have two positions: One: that attribution to a verbal sentence is permissible absolutely. Two: that it is not permissible except if it is of that which can be suspended.

The apparent meaning is that the two parties are both from among them, due to His saying: ﴿And thus We roused them so that they might question one another. A speaker among them said﴾ [al-Kahf: 19], etc. It seems that those who said ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you remained﴾ knew that their stay had been long. This is supported by the fact that He began with their story, not abbreviated from His saying ﴿Did you think...﴾ [al-Kahf: 9] up to His saying ﴿a term﴾, and then He related it at length and in detail from His saying ﴿We relate﴾ up to His saying ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained﴾ [al-Kahf: 26].

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The apparent meaning of the verse is that the one party is ﴿the youths﴾, i.e., they thought their stay was short, and the second party are the people of the city among whom the youths were raised, at the time when history of the youths was known to them. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. End of quotation. A group said: they are two disbelieving parties who disagreed about the period the People of the Cave remained in the Cave. Al-Suddi said: they are from the Jews and Christians who taught Quraysh to ask about the People of the Cave, about al-Khidr, and about the Spirit, and they had disagreed about the length of the People of the Cave's stay in the Cave. Mujahid said: among the people of the People of the Cave there were believers and disbelievers, and they disagreed about the length of their stay. It was said: they are two parties of believers in the time of the Companions of the Cave who disagreed about the length of their stay; this was said by al-Farra'. Ibn 'Abbas said: the kings who successively ruled the city are one party, and the People of the Cave are a party. Ibn Bahr said: the two parties are God and the creation, like His saying ﴿Are you more knowing, or God?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 140]. All these views are disordered. Ibn Qatadah said: neither party had knowledge of their stay, neither believer nor disbeliever, by the evidence of His saying ﴿God knows best how long they remained﴾ [al-Kahf: 26]. Muqatil said: once they were raised, doubt was removed and the reality of the stay became known.

﴿Ahsa﴾: al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a past-tense verb, with ma being a verbal-noun particle and ﴿amadan﴾ being the object; and that it be the elative form (af'al of preference), with ﴿amadan﴾ as a specifier (tamyiz). al-Zajjaj and al-Tibrizi chose that it be the elative form of preference. al-Farisi and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah chose that it be a past-tense verb, and they preferred this because when ahsa is for intensification it is formed from a non-triliteral root, and in their view "ma a'taahu" and "ma awlahu" (for the subject) and "a'da min al-jaraba" are anomalous and not to be analogized. Abu Ishaq says: it has become frequent from the quadriliteral, so it is permissible. Ibn 'Atiyyah confused matters, citing among what is formed from the quadriliteral: "a'taahu" for wealth, "atahu" for good, "hiya aswadu min al-qar" (it is blacker than pitch), and "maa'uhu abyadu min al-laban" (its water is whiter than milk). He said: all these are af'al from the quadriliteral. End of quotation. But "aswad" and "abyad" are not formed from the quadriliteral. On the formation of af'al for exclamation and for preference there are three positions: one, it is formed from it absolutely, which is the apparent sense of Sibawayh's words, and words have come from it; two, it is not formed from it absolutely, and what came is treated as anomalous; three, a distinction: if the hamza is for transitivity (naql), it is not permitted, but if it is not for transitivity, as in "ashkala al-amr" (the matter became unclear) and "adhlama al-layl" (the night became dark), then one may say "ma ashkala hadhihi al-mas'alah" and "ma adhlama hadha al-layl." This is the choice of Ibn 'Usfur among our companions. The proofs of these positions are mentioned in the books of grammar. When we say that ahsa is a noun of preference, it is permissible that ﴿ayyu al-hizbayn﴾ be a relative (mawsul) built according to Sibawayh's school, because the condition for permissibility of building is present in it, namely that ayyu is attached (mudafa) with its initial element of the relative clause omitted; the estimate being: "so that the party which is 'ahsa' (most accurate) ﴿for what they remained, a term﴾ from those who did not count might be known." But if it is a past-tense verb this is impossible, because then the initial element of its clause is not omitted, the verb being itself the relative clause if ayyu is taken as a relative; so its building is not permitted, because the condition of its completion has failed, namely that the initial element of its clause is omitted.

He said: If you say: what do you say about the one who made it an elative of preference? I say: it is not the sound view, because its formation from a non-triliteral unaugmented root is not by analogy, and like "a'da min al-jaraba" and "aflasa min Ibn al-Mudhalliq," it is anomalous, and analogizing on the anomalous outside the Qur'an is impermissible, how much more so within it. Also, ﴿amadan﴾ either is governed by ahsa, but then af'al does not govern; or it is governed by labithu, but then the meaning is not sound. If you claim I govern it by an implied verb indicated by ahsa, as in the line:

"And I strike from us with swords the crowns (qawanis)"

with an implied "yadrib al-qawanis," you have gone far from the immediate construction, though it is near, since you refused that ahsa be a verb and then were compelled to return to estimating and implying it.

End of quotation. As for his claim of anomaly, that is the view of Abu 'Ali, and we have mentioned that the apparent view of Sibawayh is permissibility of forming it from af'al absolutely, that this is the view of Abu Ishaq, and that the distinction is the choice of Ibn 'Usfur and the view of others. The hamza in ahsa is not for transitivity. As for his statement "af'al does not govern," this is not correct, for it governs in the specifier (tamyiz), and ﴿amadan﴾ is a specifier, and thus did the one who held ahsa to be an elative of preference parse it, as you say: "Zaydan aqta'u al-nas sayfan" and "Zayd aqta'u lil-haam sayfan," and he did not parse it as an object. As for his statement "or it is governed by labithu, but then the meaning is not sound," i.e., it is not correct, al-Tabari went to governing ﴿amadan﴾ by labithu. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is not tenable. It may be tenable in that amad is the endpoint, and it is an expression for the period, inasmuch as a period has an endpoint in the actual sense of its term; and ma is in the sense of "alladhi," and ﴿amadan﴾ is put in the accusative by dropping the preposition, its estimate being "li-ma labithu min amadin," i.e., of a period, and "min amad" becomes an explanation of what is in the words "ma labithu," like His saying ﴿whatever verse We abrogate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106] and ﴿whatever mercy God opens to people﴾ [Fatir: 2]; and when the preposition dropped, the verb reached it. As for his statement "if you claim" to its end, one says: there is no need for this claim, because the one who says it may take the path of the Kufans, that the elative of preference governs a direct object; so "al-qawanis" is in their view governed by "adrib" as a direct object, and interpreting it as "striking the crowns" is the view of the Basrans. For this reason some grammarians held that His saying ﴿who strays﴾ [al-An'am: 117] "man" is governed by "a'lamu" as a direct object. Had the like of the line "And I strike from us with swords the crowns" been frequent, we would analogize it, and its meaning would be sound, because the elative of preference carries the sense of the verbal noun, so it governs by that implicit transfer; do you not see that the meaning is that our striking with swords the crowns exceeds the striking of others?

When He mentioned ﴿li-ya'lama﴾, indicating a difference in their affair, He followed it by stating that He is the One who relates their story to His Messenger ﷺ bit by bit, ﴿with truth﴾, i.e., in the manner of truthfulness. The phrase ﴿We relate﴾ came parallel to His saying ﴿li-na'lam﴾.

Then He said: ﴿They believed in their Lord﴾, and in it is the attribution of "Lord," who is the Master and the one who oversees the welfare of His servants. The construction did not come as "amanu" (passive-style) in order to convey that rank, that they are those cared for and owned by Him. Then He said: ﴿And We increased them in guidance﴾. The construction did not come as "wa-zadahum" because of the greatness and majesty in the word "Nā" (We). His increasing them in ﴿guidance﴾ is His facilitating for them righteous action, devotion to Him, distancing from people, and asceticism toward the world; and this is an increase in the faith that had come to them. In al-Tahrir: "We increased them" in the fruits of guidance, or in certainty, are two opinions; and what the increase was accomplished by is compliance with the command and abandonment of the prohibited, or the dog's speaking to them that it is upon what they are upon of faith, or the sending down of an angel upon them with glad tidings and strengthening, and informing them of the emergence of a Prophet from the Arabs by whom the religion will be entirely for God, so they believed in him before his mission. These are summarized views from al-Tahrir.

﴿And We fortified their hearts﴾: We made them firm and strengthened them to endure patiently the leaving of homeland and comfort, and fleeing with their religion to a cave in a desolate place with no companion, no water, and no food. Since fear and dread of the soul resemble, by association, loosening, it is fitting that in the strength of the soul and firmness of resolve it be likened to binding; from this comes "fulanun rabitu al-ja'sh" (so-and-so is steady of heart) when his soul does not scatter at fear and war. God the Exalted said: ﴿Had We not fortified her heart, she would almost have disclosed it﴾ [al-Qasas: 10]. The governing element of ﴿idh rabatna﴾ is: "We fortified when they stood up." The standing may be their standing before the disbelieving king Decius (Diqyanus), for it was a station needing fortification of the heart, where they were crucified (?) for him, abandoned his religion, and rejected, for the sake of God, his awe. It may also be a figure of speech for their rising with resolve to flee to God and separate from the people, as one says: "so-and-so stood up to such-and-such" when he resolved upon it with utmost earnestness.

Al-Karmani said: "They stood" upon their feet. It was said: "They stood" calling people secretly. 'Ata' said: "They stood" when they rose from sleep and said. It was said: "They stood" upon their faith. The author of al-Ghunyan said: ﴿when they stood﴾ before the king, and a cat moved, or it was said a mouse, so Decius was startled; and some looked at one another and could not restrain themselves from saying: ﴿Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾. Their people were worshippers of idols, and how excellent was their monotheism, that their Lord is the originator of the heavens and earth, who disposes them as He wills. Then they reinforced this monotheism with disavowal of any other god, with a negation that encompasses the eternity of time, according to one view. The lam in ﴿la-qad﴾ is the lam of emphasis, and ﴿idhan﴾ is a particle of response and consequence, i.e., ﴿We have indeed said: we shall never call upon any god other than Him, [for then] we would have uttered an excess﴾ [al-Kahf: 14]. ﴿Shatatan﴾ means: possessing excess, which is transgression and injustice; so ﴿shatatan﴾ is an adjective of an elided verbal noun, either by elision as we estimated, or by description with it by way of intensification. It was said: it is an object of ﴿qulna﴾. Qatadah said: ﴿shatatan﴾ means a lie. Abu Zayd said: an error.

(p. 100) Here *am* is the disjunctive (*munqati'a*) particle, so it is to be read as equivalent to *bal* ("rather") together with the interrogative *hamza*. It is said that it signals a transition (*idrab*) from one statement to another, in the sense of moving on to a different topic rather than cancelling the first. The *hamza* is the interrogative particle. Some grammarians claimed that *am* here means only the *hamza*. Apparently, in ﴿Or did you think﴾ [al-Kahf: 9], the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ). Mujahid said: "He did not forbid him from wondering, but He meant that all of Our signs are like that." Qatadah said: "He should not be amazed by them, for the wonders in the creation of the heavens and the earth are greater."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They asked you about this so that they could make your answer a sign of your truthfulness or falsehood. The rest of the Qur'an's signs are more eloquent, more wondrous, and more indicative of your truthfulness."

Al-Tabari said: "This is a confirmation to him (peace be upon him) of his supposition that the companions of the Cave were a wonder, in the sense of rejecting that he should not magnify it as the disbelieving questioners magnified it for you, since all of God's other signs are greater than their story." He said: "This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq."

Al-Zahrawi said: "It may carry another meaning, which is that it is an interrogation to him: does he know that the companions of the Cave were a wonder, in the sense of affirming that they were a wonder? The purpose of this confirmation is to prepare himself for the matter, because his answer would be, 'I did not suppose it, nor did I know it,' and then it would be said to him: describe them at that point. The metaphor in this interpretation lies in the word *hasibta* (you supposed)." End of his quotation. Others said: its meaning is "Did you know?", i.e., you did not know it until We informed you.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He mentioned among the universal signs the adornment of the earth with what He created upon it of kinds that cannot be counted, and the removal of all of that as though it had never been. Then He said, *Or did you think* [al-Kahf: 9], meaning that this is part of the story of the People of the Cave and of their preservation alive for a long period." End of his quotation. It was also said: meaning "Or do you know," that is, "Know then that they were a wonder," just as you say, "Do you know that so-and-so did such-and-such?", meaning "He has done it, so know it." It was also said: the address is to the listener, and what is meant is the polytheists, that is: say to them, "Or do you suppose..." etc. *Zann* (supposition) may be used in place of *'ilm* (knowledge), so *hasibta* is in the sense of *'alimta*. As for *al-kahf* (the cave), its explanation has already been given in the vocabulary section (*al-mufradat*). From Anas: *al-kahf* is the mountain. The judge (al-Qadi) said: "This is not well known in the language." Mujahid said: it is a split between two mountains.

The apparent meaning of ﴿that the companions of the Cave and the Inscription﴾ [al-Kahf: 9] is that they are the young men mentioned here. From Ibn al-Musayyib: they were a people whose condition was like that of the companions of the Cave. Al-Dahhak said: "*al-Raqim* is a town in the lands of the Romans, in which there is a cave containing twenty-one souls, all dead, all asleep in the same state as the companions of the Cave." It was also said: they are the companions of the cave-shelter. There is a hadith from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that he heard the Messenger (ﷺ) mention the *Raqim*, saying: "Three men were caught by rain, so they took shelter in a cave, and a rock came down from the mountain and sealed the mouth of the cave." He mentioned the hadith, which is the hadith of the hired man, the chaste man, and the one who was dutiful to his parents, and in what he transmitted there are additional words beyond what is in the *Sahih*. As for those who said they were two groups, they said: God told us about the companions of the Cave and did not tell us anything about the companions of the Inscription. As for those who said they were one group, they disagreed about the explanation of *al-Raqim*. From Ibn 'Abbas: he did not know what *al-Raqim* was, whether it was a book or a building. Also from him: it was a book that they had, containing the law to which they held from the religion of the Messiah (peace be upon him). It was also said: it is from a religion before 'Isa. From Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb: it is the name of their town. It was said: a plate of gold under the wall, which al-Khidr (peace be upon him) set up. It was said: he wrote on it their names, their story, and the cause of their departure. It was said: a plate of lead on which the affair of the young men was written, placed in a copper chest at the mouth of the cave. It was said: a rock on which their names were written, placed in the city wall. It was said: it is the name of their dog, and the verse of Umayya was mentioned before, said by Anas, al-Sha'bi and Ibn Jubayr. From al-Hasan: it is the mountain on which the cave is. From 'Ikrimah: it is the name of the inkwell in Roman. It was said: it is the name of the valley in which the cave is. It was said: people wrote down their story by engraving it on the mountain.

﴿Wonder﴾ (*'ajaban*) is in the accusative because it is an adjective of an omitted noun indicated by what precedes it. Its estimated sense is "a sign that is wonderful," described by the verbal noun (*masdar*), or it is in the sense of "a thing possessing wonder." As for the names of the young men of the Cave, they are non-Arabic and cannot be fixed by vowel-marks or dots, and the chain of transmission for knowing them is weak. The narrators differ on their stories, on how they gathered and how they went out. No authentic hadith has described how this happened, nor does the Qur'an contain anything except what God related to us of their stories. Whoever wishes to seek that should consult the books of tafsir.

It is narrated that the name of the disbelieving king in whose days they left his religion was Diqyanus. It is also narrated that they were in the lands of the Romans. It was said: in Syria, and that in Syria there is a cave containing dead bodies, and its neighbours claim that they are the companions of the Cave, and there is a mosque and a building over them called al-Raqim, and with them is a dog, a dry bone. In al-Andalus, in the area of Granada near a village called Lusha, there is a cave containing dead bodies, and with them is a dog, a dry bone, and most of them have had their flesh stripped away and some are still intact. Centuries have passed, and we have not found anyone who knows their condition, and some people claim that they are the companions of the Cave. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "I entered among them and saw them four hundred and fifty years ago, and they were in this state. Over them is a mosque, and near them is a Roman building called al-Raqim, as if it were a carved palace of which some walls remain. It is in a wasteland in a ruined area, and above the city of Granada, on the side facing the qibla, are traces of an ancient city called the city of Diqyus, and in its ruins we found strange things, such as graves and the like. I only found it easy to mention this despite its distance, because it is a wonder whose mention will remain, God willing." End of quotation. When we were in al-Andalus, people used to visit this cave and say that they made mistakes when counting them, and that there was a dog with them, and people would travel to Lusha to visit them. As for what I mentioned about the city of Diqyus that is before me, Granada, I have passed by it many times, uncountable, and I have seen large stones there. It is more likely that the people of the Cave were in al-Andalus, because Christianity is widespread there, to the point that it was the land of their great kingdom, and because reports about what is in the farthest place from the land of the Hijaz are stranger, and it is more remote that anyone should know it except by revelation from God, exalted is He.

The governing element (*al-'amil*) of ﴿when﴾ (*idh*) is said to be an implied "remember." It was also said: it is *'ajaban* (wonder). The meaning of ﴿took refuge﴾ (*awa*) is that they made the cave a shelter for themselves and a place of protection. Then they called upon God, exalted is He, to grant them mercy from Himself, and the exegetes explained this mercy as provision. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is forgiveness, provision, and safety from enemies. *Al-fityah* (the young men) is a broken plural of *fata*, a plural of paucity, and likewise they were few. According to Ibn al-Sarraj, it is a collective noun, not a broken plural. The word *al-fityah* indicates that they were young, and it is also narrated that they were young men from the sons of the nobles and the great, adorned with gold necklaces and gold bracelets, with long locks, and they were from the Romans, who followed the religion of 'Isa (peace be upon him). It was also said that they were before 'Isa. Our fellow Andalusians often use in their speech and poetry, and in addressing the common people, the name "Romans" for the Christians of al-Andalus, saying, "We fought the Romans," "The Romans came to us." Few say the word "Christians." When they called for the bestowal of mercy, which includes provision and other things, they called upon God to prepare for them, from their affair, which had led them to leave the religion of their people and to affirm the oneness of God, right guidance (*rashad*), which is being rightly guided and being steadfast upon it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Make our whole affair right guidance, as you would say: 'I saw from you a lion.'" Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-Zuhri read *wa-hayyi'* and *yuhayyi* with two *ya's* without *hamza*, meaning that they replaced the quiescent *hamza* with *ya'*. In Ibn Khalawayh's book, al-A'sha reported from Abu Bakr from 'Asim: *wa-hayyi lana* and *yuhayyi lakum*, without *hamza*. End of quotation. This may mean that he replaced the *hamza* with *ya'*, or that he deleted it. The first is a regular substitution (*ibdal qiyasi*), and the second is disputed, since deleting the letter substituted for *hamza* in the imperative or the imperfect in jussive form is a recognized analogical process. Abu Raja' read *rushdun* with a *damma* on the *ra'* and a sukun on the *shin*. The majority read *rashadan* with a *fatha* on both. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is more preferred because it resembles the verse endings before and after it. This supplication from them concerned the affairs of their worldly life, and its wording implies that. They were confident of the right guidance and mercy of the Hereafter, and every believer should make his supplication for his worldly affairs this verse, for it is sufficient. The word *mercy* may also be understood to mean matters of the Hereafter." End of quotation.

﴿So We struck upon their ears﴾ [al-Kahf: 11] is a striking metaphor for a heavy sleep in which one can hardly hear. He used the verb *darb* (striking) to indicate strength of contact, adherence and permanence, as in ﴿Humiliation was struck upon them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 112], and the imposing of the poll-tax (*darb al-jizyah*), and the sending forth (*darb al-ba'th*). Al-Farazdaq said:

*The spider has spun its web over you,*
*and the revealed Book has decreed against you what it has decreed.*

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

*And among the calamities, may you have no father, that the earth has been struck against me with barriers.*

Another said:

*Indeed, manliness, generosity and open-handedness*
*are in a dome struck over the son of al-Hashraj.*

It is borrowed to express the permanence of these qualities for this praised man. He mentioned the organ that is the ears, since hearing comes through them, because sleep does not become firm except when hearing is disabled. In a hadith: "That is a man on whose ear Satan has urinated," meaning that his sleep was extremely heavy, so that he would not rise during the night. The object of *darabna* (We struck) is omitted, meaning "a veil from hearing," as one says, "He built over his wife," meaning he built the dome over her. *Sinin* (years) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and its governing verb is *fa-darabna*. *'Adadan* (a number) is a verbal noun described by it, or it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "after counting," and in the sense of the passive participle, like *al-qabd* (the grasp) and *al-naft* (the shaking). *Sinin* is described by it, meaning "years that were counted." The apparent sense of His saying *'adadan* indicates abundance, since one needs to count only what is numerous, not what is little.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that it means few, because the many is little in His sight, as in His saying: ﴿They did not remain but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]." End of quotation. This is a distortion in the comparison, because the wording of that verse is as if: on the day they see what they are promised, they will have remained only an hour of a day, which is a comparison to the swiftness of the passing of the life they lived in this world when they see the punishment, as the poet said:

*As though the youth had never been bare when he is clothed,*
*and had not been poor when he became rich.*

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verse 12–14 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Then We roused them﴾, i.e., We woke them from their sleep. Al-ba'th (raising, sending forth) is moving something from stillness, either regarding the person or regarding the matter in which he is roused, even if the thing in which he is roused is itself moving. And ﴿li-na'lam﴾, i.e., so that We might make manifest to them what We already knew of their affair. The discussion of its like has already occurred in His saying: ﴿so that We may know who follows the Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. In al-Tahrir it is said: the majority read ﴿li-na'lam﴾ with the nun, and al-Zuhri read it with the ya'. In Ibn Khalawayh's book it is li-ya'lama ﴿ayyu al-hizbayn﴾, related by al-Akhfash. In al-Kashshaf: "It is read li-ya'lama, and it is mu'allaq ('suspended') from it, because its being raised is by the inchoative (mubtada'), not by attributing 'ya'lamu' to it, and the agent of ya'lamu is the content of the sentence, just as the object of ya'lamu is." End of quotation. As for the reading li-na'lam, it appears that this is an iltifat (shift) from the first-person speaker to the third-person, so its meaning and the meaning of li-na'lam with the nun are the same. As for li-ya'lama, it appears that the first object is omitted, as the meaning indicates, and the estimate is: "so that God might make people know ﴿which of the two parties﴾". The sentence of the inchoative and its predicate is in the position of the second and third objects of yu'lim, and li-ya'lama is mu'allaq. As for what is in al-Kashshaf, it is not permissible according to the school of the Basrans, because the sentence in that case would be in the position of the object that is not named as its agent, standing in for the agent. Just as that sentence and other sentences do not stand in for the agent, so it does not stand in for what it replaces. The Kufans have two positions: One: that attribution to a verbal sentence is permissible absolutely. Two: that it is not permissible except if it is of that which can be suspended.

The apparent meaning is that the two parties are both from among them, due to His saying: ﴿And thus We roused them so that they might question one another. A speaker among them said﴾ [al-Kahf: 19], etc. It seems that those who said ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you remained﴾ knew that their stay had been long. This is supported by the fact that He began with their story, not abbreviated from His saying ﴿Did you think...﴾ [al-Kahf: 9] up to His saying ﴿a term﴾, and then He related it at length and in detail from His saying ﴿We relate﴾ up to His saying ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained﴾ [al-Kahf: 26].

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The apparent meaning of the verse is that the one party is ﴿the youths﴾, i.e., they thought their stay was short, and the second party are the people of the city among whom the youths were raised, at the time when history of the youths was known to them. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. End of quotation. A group said: they are two disbelieving parties who disagreed about the period the People of the Cave remained in the Cave. Al-Suddi said: they are from the Jews and Christians who taught Quraysh to ask about the People of the Cave, about al-Khidr, and about the Spirit, and they had disagreed about the length of the People of the Cave's stay in the Cave. Mujahid said: among the people of the People of the Cave there were believers and disbelievers, and they disagreed about the length of their stay. It was said: they are two parties of believers in the time of the Companions of the Cave who disagreed about the length of their stay; this was said by al-Farra'. Ibn 'Abbas said: the kings who successively ruled the city are one party, and the People of the Cave are a party. Ibn Bahr said: the two parties are God and the creation, like His saying ﴿Are you more knowing, or God?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 140]. All these views are disordered. Ibn Qatadah said: neither party had knowledge of their stay, neither believer nor disbeliever, by the evidence of His saying ﴿God knows best how long they remained﴾ [al-Kahf: 26]. Muqatil said: once they were raised, doubt was removed and the reality of the stay became known.

﴿Ahsa﴾: al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a past-tense verb, with ma being a verbal-noun particle and ﴿amadan﴾ being the object; and that it be the elative form (af'al of preference), with ﴿amadan﴾ as a specifier (tamyiz). al-Zajjaj and al-Tibrizi chose that it be the elative form of preference. al-Farisi and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah chose that it be a past-tense verb, and they preferred this because when ahsa is for intensification it is formed from a non-triliteral root, and in their view "ma a'taahu" and "ma awlahu" (for the subject) and "a'da min al-jaraba" are anomalous and not to be analogized. Abu Ishaq says: it has become frequent from the quadriliteral, so it is permissible. Ibn 'Atiyyah confused matters, citing among what is formed from the quadriliteral: "a'taahu" for wealth, "atahu" for good, "hiya aswadu min al-qar" (it is blacker than pitch), and "maa'uhu abyadu min al-laban" (its water is whiter than milk). He said: all these are af'al from the quadriliteral. End of quotation. But "aswad" and "abyad" are not formed from the quadriliteral. On the formation of af'al for exclamation and for preference there are three positions: one, it is formed from it absolutely, which is the apparent sense of Sibawayh's words, and words have come from it; two, it is not formed from it absolutely, and what came is treated as anomalous; three, a distinction: if the hamza is for transitivity (naql), it is not permitted, but if it is not for transitivity, as in "ashkala al-amr" (the matter became unclear) and "adhlama al-layl" (the night became dark), then one may say "ma ashkala hadhihi al-mas'alah" and "ma adhlama hadha al-layl." This is the choice of Ibn 'Usfur among our companions. The proofs of these positions are mentioned in the books of grammar. When we say that ahsa is a noun of preference, it is permissible that ﴿ayyu al-hizbayn﴾ be a relative (mawsul) built according to Sibawayh's school, because the condition for permissibility of building is present in it, namely that ayyu is attached (mudafa) with its initial element of the relative clause omitted; the estimate being: "so that the party which is 'ahsa' (most accurate) ﴿for what they remained, a term﴾ from those who did not count might be known." But if it is a past-tense verb this is impossible, because then the initial element of its clause is not omitted, the verb being itself the relative clause if ayyu is taken as a relative; so its building is not permitted, because the condition of its completion has failed, namely that the initial element of its clause is omitted.

He said: If you say: what do you say about the one who made it an elative of preference? I say: it is not the sound view, because its formation from a non-triliteral unaugmented root is not by analogy, and like "a'da min al-jaraba" and "aflasa min Ibn al-Mudhalliq," it is anomalous, and analogizing on the anomalous outside the Qur'an is impermissible, how much more so within it. Also, ﴿amadan﴾ either is governed by ahsa, but then af'al does not govern; or it is governed by labithu, but then the meaning is not sound. If you claim I govern it by an implied verb indicated by ahsa, as in the line:

"And I strike from us with swords the crowns (qawanis)"

with an implied "yadrib al-qawanis," you have gone far from the immediate construction, though it is near, since you refused that ahsa be a verb and then were compelled to return to estimating and implying it.

End of quotation. As for his claim of anomaly, that is the view of Abu 'Ali, and we have mentioned that the apparent view of Sibawayh is permissibility of forming it from af'al absolutely, that this is the view of Abu Ishaq, and that the distinction is the choice of Ibn 'Usfur and the view of others. The hamza in ahsa is not for transitivity. As for his statement "af'al does not govern," this is not correct, for it governs in the specifier (tamyiz), and ﴿amadan﴾ is a specifier, and thus did the one who held ahsa to be an elative of preference parse it, as you say: "Zaydan aqta'u al-nas sayfan" and "Zayd aqta'u lil-haam sayfan," and he did not parse it as an object. As for his statement "or it is governed by labithu, but then the meaning is not sound," i.e., it is not correct, al-Tabari went to governing ﴿amadan﴾ by labithu. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is not tenable. It may be tenable in that amad is the endpoint, and it is an expression for the period, inasmuch as a period has an endpoint in the actual sense of its term; and ma is in the sense of "alladhi," and ﴿amadan﴾ is put in the accusative by dropping the preposition, its estimate being "li-ma labithu min amadin," i.e., of a period, and "min amad" becomes an explanation of what is in the words "ma labithu," like His saying ﴿whatever verse We abrogate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106] and ﴿whatever mercy God opens to people﴾ [Fatir: 2]; and when the preposition dropped, the verb reached it. As for his statement "if you claim" to its end, one says: there is no need for this claim, because the one who says it may take the path of the Kufans, that the elative of preference governs a direct object; so "al-qawanis" is in their view governed by "adrib" as a direct object, and interpreting it as "striking the crowns" is the view of the Basrans. For this reason some grammarians held that His saying ﴿who strays﴾ [al-An'am: 117] "man" is governed by "a'lamu" as a direct object. Had the like of the line "And I strike from us with swords the crowns" been frequent, we would analogize it, and its meaning would be sound, because the elative of preference carries the sense of the verbal noun, so it governs by that implicit transfer; do you not see that the meaning is that our striking with swords the crowns exceeds the striking of others?

When He mentioned ﴿li-ya'lama﴾, indicating a difference in their affair, He followed it by stating that He is the One who relates their story to His Messenger ﷺ bit by bit, ﴿with truth﴾, i.e., in the manner of truthfulness. The phrase ﴿We relate﴾ came parallel to His saying ﴿li-na'lam﴾.

Then He said: ﴿They believed in their Lord﴾, and in it is the attribution of "Lord," who is the Master and the one who oversees the welfare of His servants. The construction did not come as "amanu" (passive-style) in order to convey that rank, that they are those cared for and owned by Him. Then He said: ﴿And We increased them in guidance﴾. The construction did not come as "wa-zadahum" because of the greatness and majesty in the word "Nā" (We). His increasing them in ﴿guidance﴾ is His facilitating for them righteous action, devotion to Him, distancing from people, and asceticism toward the world; and this is an increase in the faith that had come to them. In al-Tahrir: "We increased them" in the fruits of guidance, or in certainty, are two opinions; and what the increase was accomplished by is compliance with the command and abandonment of the prohibited, or the dog's speaking to them that it is upon what they are upon of faith, or the sending down of an angel upon them with glad tidings and strengthening, and informing them of the emergence of a Prophet from the Arabs by whom the religion will be entirely for God, so they believed in him before his mission. These are summarized views from al-Tahrir.

﴿And We fortified their hearts﴾: We made them firm and strengthened them to endure patiently the leaving of homeland and comfort, and fleeing with their religion to a cave in a desolate place with no companion, no water, and no food. Since fear and dread of the soul resemble, by association, loosening, it is fitting that in the strength of the soul and firmness of resolve it be likened to binding; from this comes "fulanun rabitu al-ja'sh" (so-and-so is steady of heart) when his soul does not scatter at fear and war. God the Exalted said: ﴿Had We not fortified her heart, she would almost have disclosed it﴾ [al-Qasas: 10]. The governing element of ﴿idh rabatna﴾ is: "We fortified when they stood up." The standing may be their standing before the disbelieving king Decius (Diqyanus), for it was a station needing fortification of the heart, where they were crucified (?) for him, abandoned his religion, and rejected, for the sake of God, his awe. It may also be a figure of speech for their rising with resolve to flee to God and separate from the people, as one says: "so-and-so stood up to such-and-such" when he resolved upon it with utmost earnestness.

Al-Karmani said: "They stood" upon their feet. It was said: "They stood" calling people secretly. 'Ata' said: "They stood" when they rose from sleep and said. It was said: "They stood" upon their faith. The author of al-Ghunyan said: ﴿when they stood﴾ before the king, and a cat moved, or it was said a mouse, so Decius was startled; and some looked at one another and could not restrain themselves from saying: ﴿Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾. Their people were worshippers of idols, and how excellent was their monotheism, that their Lord is the originator of the heavens and earth, who disposes them as He wills. Then they reinforced this monotheism with disavowal of any other god, with a negation that encompasses the eternity of time, according to one view.
