The lam in ﴿la-qad﴾ is the lam of emphasis, and ﴿idhan﴾ is a particle of response and consequence, i.e., ﴿We have indeed said: we shall never call upon any god other than Him, [for then] we would have uttered an excess﴾ [al-Kahf: 14]. ﴿Shatatan﴾ means: possessing excess, which is transgression and injustice; so ﴿shatatan﴾ is an adjective of an elided verbal noun, either by elision as we estimated, or by description with it by way of intensification. It was said: it is an object of ﴿qulna﴾. Qatadah said: ﴿shatatan﴾ means a lie. Abu Zayd said: an error.

(p. 100) Here *am* is the disjunctive (*munqati'a*) particle, so it is to be read as equivalent to *bal* ("rather") together with the interrogative *hamza*. It is said that it signals a transition (*idrab*) from one statement to another, in the sense of moving on to a different topic rather than cancelling the first. The *hamza* is the interrogative particle. Some grammarians claimed that *am* here means only the *hamza*. Apparently, in ﴿Or did you think﴾ [al-Kahf: 9], the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ). Mujahid said: "He did not forbid him from wondering, but He meant that all of Our signs are like that." Qatadah said: "He should not be amazed by them, for the wonders in the creation of the heavens and the earth are greater."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They asked you about this so that they could make your answer a sign of your truthfulness or falsehood. The rest of the Qur'an's signs are more eloquent, more wondrous, and more indicative of your truthfulness."

Al-Tabari said: "This is a confirmation to him (peace be upon him) of his supposition that the companions of the Cave were a wonder, in the sense of rejecting that he should not magnify it as the disbelieving questioners magnified it for you, since all of God's other signs are greater than their story." He said: "This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq."

Al-Zahrawi said: "It may carry another meaning, which is that it is an interrogation to him: does he know that the companions of the Cave were a wonder, in the sense of affirming that they were a wonder? The purpose of this confirmation is to prepare himself for the matter, because his answer would be, 'I did not suppose it, nor did I know it,' and then it would be said to him: describe them at that point. The metaphor in this interpretation lies in the word *hasibta* (you supposed)." End of his quotation. Others said: its meaning is "Did you know?", i.e., you did not know it until We informed you.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He mentioned among the universal signs the adornment of the earth with what He created upon it of kinds that cannot be counted, and the removal of all of that as though it had never been. Then He said, *Or did you think* [al-Kahf: 9], meaning that this is part of the story of the People of the Cave and of their preservation alive for a long period." End of his quotation. It was also said: meaning "Or do you know," that is, "Know then that they were a wonder," just as you say, "Do you know that so-and-so did such-and-such?", meaning "He has done it, so know it." It was also said: the address is to the listener, and what is meant is the polytheists, that is: say to them, "Or do you suppose..." etc. *Zann* (supposition) may be used in place of *'ilm* (knowledge), so *hasibta* is in the sense of *'alimta*. As for *al-kahf* (the cave), its explanation has already been given in the vocabulary section (*al-mufradat*). From Anas: *al-kahf* is the mountain. The judge (al-Qadi) said: "This is not well known in the language." Mujahid said: it is a split between two mountains.

The apparent meaning of ﴿that the companions of the Cave and the Inscription﴾ [al-Kahf: 9] is that they are the young men mentioned here. From Ibn al-Musayyib: they were a people whose condition was like that of the companions of the Cave. Al-Dahhak said: "*al-Raqim* is a town in the lands of the Romans, in which there is a cave containing twenty-one souls, all dead, all asleep in the same state as the companions of the Cave." It was also said: they are the companions of the cave-shelter. There is a hadith from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that he heard the Messenger (ﷺ) mention the *Raqim*, saying: "Three men were caught by rain, so they took shelter in a cave, and a rock came down from the mountain and sealed the mouth of the cave." He mentioned the hadith, which is the hadith of the hired man, the chaste man, and the one who was dutiful to his parents, and in what he transmitted there are additional words beyond what is in the *Sahih*. As for those who said they were two groups, they said: God told us about the companions of the Cave and did not tell us anything about the companions of the Inscription. As for those who said they were one group, they disagreed about the explanation of *al-Raqim*. From Ibn 'Abbas: he did not know what *al-Raqim* was, whether it was a book or a building. Also from him: it was a book that they had, containing the law to which they held from the religion of the Messiah (peace be upon him). It was also said: it is from a religion before 'Isa. From Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb: it is the name of their town. It was said: a plate of gold under the wall, which al-Khidr (peace be upon him) set up. It was said: he wrote on it their names, their story, and the cause of their departure. It was said: a plate of lead on which the affair of the young men was written, placed in a copper chest at the mouth of the cave. It was said: a rock on which their names were written, placed in the city wall. It was said: it is the name of their dog, and the verse of Umayya was mentioned before, said by Anas, al-Sha'bi and Ibn Jubayr. From al-Hasan: it is the mountain on which the cave is. From 'Ikrimah: it is the name of the inkwell in Roman. It was said: it is the name of the valley in which the cave is. It was said: people wrote down their story by engraving it on the mountain.

﴿Wonder﴾ (*'ajaban*) is in the accusative because it is an adjective of an omitted noun indicated by what precedes it. Its estimated sense is "a sign that is wonderful," described by the verbal noun (*masdar*), or it is in the sense of "a thing possessing wonder." As for the names of the young men of the Cave, they are non-Arabic and cannot be fixed by vowel-marks or dots, and the chain of transmission for knowing them is weak. The narrators differ on their stories, on how they gathered and how they went out. No authentic hadith has described how this happened, nor does the Qur'an contain anything except what God related to us of their stories. Whoever wishes to seek that should consult the books of tafsir.

It is narrated that the name of the disbelieving king in whose days they left his religion was Diqyanus. It is also narrated that they were in the lands of the Romans. It was said: in Syria, and that in Syria there is a cave containing dead bodies, and its neighbours claim that they are the companions of the Cave, and there is a mosque and a building over them called al-Raqim, and with them is a dog, a dry bone. In al-Andalus, in the area of Granada near a village called Lusha, there is a cave containing dead bodies, and with them is a dog, a dry bone, and most of them have had their flesh stripped away and some are still intact. Centuries have passed, and we have not found anyone who knows their condition, and some people claim that they are the companions of the Cave. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "I entered among them and saw them four hundred and fifty years ago, and they were in this state. Over them is a mosque, and near them is a Roman building called al-Raqim, as if it were a carved palace of which some walls remain. It is in a wasteland in a ruined area, and above the city of Granada, on the side facing the qibla, are traces of an ancient city called the city of Diqyus, and in its ruins we found strange things, such as graves and the like. I only found it easy to mention this despite its distance, because it is a wonder whose mention will remain, God willing." End of quotation. When we were in al-Andalus, people used to visit this cave and say that they made mistakes when counting them, and that there was a dog with them, and people would travel to Lusha to visit them. As for what I mentioned about the city of Diqyus that is before me, Granada, I have passed by it many times, uncountable, and I have seen large stones there. It is more likely that the people of the Cave were in al-Andalus, because Christianity is widespread there, to the point that it was the land of their great kingdom, and because reports about what is in the farthest place from the land of the Hijaz are stranger, and it is more remote that anyone should know it except by revelation from God, exalted is He.

The governing element (*al-'amil*) of ﴿when﴾ (*idh*) is said to be an implied "remember." It was also said: it is *'ajaban* (wonder). The meaning of ﴿took refuge﴾ (*awa*) is that they made the cave a shelter for themselves and a place of protection. Then they called upon God, exalted is He, to grant them mercy from Himself, and the exegetes explained this mercy as provision. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is forgiveness, provision, and safety from enemies. *Al-fityah* (the young men) is a broken plural of *fata*, a plural of paucity, and likewise they were few. According to Ibn al-Sarraj, it is a collective noun, not a broken plural. The word *al-fityah* indicates that they were young, and it is also narrated that they were young men from the sons of the nobles and the great, adorned with gold necklaces and gold bracelets, with long locks, and they were from the Romans, who followed the religion of 'Isa (peace be upon him). It was also said that they were before 'Isa. Our fellow Andalusians often use in their speech and poetry, and in addressing the common people, the name "Romans" for the Christians of al-Andalus, saying, "We fought the Romans," "The Romans came to us." Few say the word "Christians." When they called for the bestowal of mercy, which includes provision and other things, they called upon God to prepare for them, from their affair, which had led them to leave the religion of their people and to affirm the oneness of God, right guidance (*rashad*), which is being rightly guided and being steadfast upon it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Make our whole affair right guidance, as you would say: 'I saw from you a lion.'" Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-Zuhri read *wa-hayyi'* and *yuhayyi* with two *ya's* without *hamza*, meaning that they replaced the quiescent *hamza* with *ya'*. In Ibn Khalawayh's book, al-A'sha reported from Abu Bakr from 'Asim: *wa-hayyi lana* and *yuhayyi lakum*, without *hamza*. End of quotation. This may mean that he replaced the *hamza* with *ya'*, or that he deleted it. The first is a regular substitution (*ibdal qiyasi*), and the second is disputed, since deleting the letter substituted for *hamza* in the imperative or the imperfect in jussive form is a recognized analogical process. Abu Raja' read *rushdun* with a *damma* on the *ra'* and a sukun on the *shin*. The majority read *rashadan* with a *fatha* on both. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is more preferred because it resembles the verse endings before and after it. This supplication from them concerned the affairs of their worldly life, and its wording implies that. They were confident of the right guidance and mercy of the Hereafter, and every believer should make his supplication for his worldly affairs this verse, for it is sufficient. The word *mercy* may also be understood to mean matters of the Hereafter." End of quotation.

﴿So We struck upon their ears﴾ [al-Kahf: 11] is a striking metaphor for a heavy sleep in which one can hardly hear. He used the verb *darb* (striking) to indicate strength of contact, adherence and permanence, as in ﴿Humiliation was struck upon them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 112], and the imposing of the poll-tax (*darb al-jizyah*), and the sending forth (*darb al-ba'th*). Al-Farazdaq said:

*The spider has spun its web over you,*
*and the revealed Book has decreed against you what it has decreed.*

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

*And among the calamities, may you have no father, that the earth has been struck against me with barriers.*

Another said:

*Indeed, manliness, generosity and open-handedness*
*are in a dome struck over the son of al-Hashraj.*

It is borrowed to express the permanence of these qualities for this praised man. He mentioned the organ that is the ears, since hearing comes through them, because sleep does not become firm except when hearing is disabled. In a hadith: "That is a man on whose ear Satan has urinated," meaning that his sleep was extremely heavy, so that he would not rise during the night. The object of *darabna* (We struck) is omitted, meaning "a veil from hearing," as one says, "He built over his wife," meaning he built the dome over her. *Sinin* (years) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and its governing verb is *fa-darabna*. *'Adadan* (a number) is a verbal noun described by it, or it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "after counting," and in the sense of the passive participle, like *al-qabd* (the grasp) and *al-naft* (the shaking). *Sinin* is described by it, meaning "years that were counted." The apparent sense of His saying *'adadan* indicates abundance, since one needs to count only what is numerous, not what is little.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that it means few, because the many is little in His sight, as in His saying: ﴿They did not remain but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]." End of quotation. This is a distortion in the comparison, because the wording of that verse is as if: on the day they see what they are promised, they will have remained only an hour of a day, which is a comparison to the swiftness of the passing of the life they lived in this world when they see the punishment, as the poet said:

*As though the youth had never been bare when he is clothed,*
*and had not been poor when he became rich.*

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verse 12–14 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Then We roused them﴾, i.e., We woke them from their sleep. Al-ba'th (raising, sending forth) is moving something from stillness, either regarding the person or regarding the matter in which he is roused, even if the thing in which he is roused is itself moving. And ﴿li-na'lam﴾, i.e., so that We might make manifest to them what We already knew of their affair. The discussion of its like has already occurred in His saying: ﴿so that We may know who follows the Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. In al-Tahrir it is said: the majority read ﴿li-na'lam﴾ with the nun, and al-Zuhri read it with the ya'. In Ibn Khalawayh's book it is li-ya'lama ﴿ayyu al-hizbayn﴾, related by al-Akhfash. In al-Kashshaf: "It is read li-ya'lama, and it is mu'allaq ('suspended') from it, because its being raised is by the inchoative (mubtada'), not by attributing 'ya'lamu' to it, and the agent of ya'lamu is the content of the sentence, just as the object of ya'lamu is." End of quotation. As for the reading li-na'lam, it appears that this is an iltifat (shift) from the first-person speaker to the third-person, so its meaning and the meaning of li-na'lam with the nun are the same. As for li-ya'lama, it appears that the first object is omitted, as the meaning indicates, and the estimate is: "so that God might make people know ﴿which of the two parties﴾". The sentence of the inchoative and its predicate is in the position of the second and third objects of yu'lim, and li-ya'lama is mu'allaq. As for what is in al-Kashshaf, it is not permissible according to the school of the Basrans, because the sentence in that case would be in the position of the object that is not named as its agent, standing in for the agent. Just as that sentence and other sentences do not stand in for the agent, so it does not stand in for what it replaces. The Kufans have two positions: One: that attribution to a verbal sentence is permissible absolutely. Two: that it is not permissible except if it is of that which can be suspended.

The apparent meaning is that the two parties are both from among them, due to His saying: ﴿And thus We roused them so that they might question one another. A speaker among them said﴾ [al-Kahf: 19], etc. It seems that those who said ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you remained﴾ knew that their stay had been long. This is supported by the fact that He began with their story, not abbreviated from His saying ﴿Did you think...﴾ [al-Kahf: 9] up to His saying ﴿a term﴾, and then He related it at length and in detail from His saying ﴿We relate﴾ up to His saying ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained﴾ [al-Kahf: 26].

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The apparent meaning of the verse is that the one party is ﴿the youths﴾, i.e., they thought their stay was short, and the second party are the people of the city among whom the youths were raised, at the time when history of the youths was known to them. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. End of quotation. A group said: they are two disbelieving parties who disagreed about the period the People of the Cave remained in the Cave. Al-Suddi said: they are from the Jews and Christians who taught Quraysh to ask about the People of the Cave, about al-Khidr, and about the Spirit, and they had disagreed about the length of the People of the Cave's stay in the Cave. Mujahid said: among the people of the People of the Cave there were believers and disbelievers, and they disagreed about the length of their stay. It was said: they are two parties of believers in the time of the Companions of the Cave who disagreed about the length of their stay; this was said by al-Farra'. Ibn 'Abbas said: the kings who successively ruled the city are one party, and the People of the Cave are a party. Ibn Bahr said: the two parties are God and the creation, like His saying ﴿Are you more knowing, or God?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 140]. All these views are disordered. Ibn Qatadah said: neither party had knowledge of their stay, neither believer nor disbeliever, by the evidence of His saying ﴿God knows best how long they remained﴾ [al-Kahf: 26]. Muqatil said: once they were raised, doubt was removed and the reality of the stay became known.

﴿Ahsa﴾: al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a past-tense verb, with ma being a verbal-noun particle and ﴿amadan﴾ being the object; and that it be the elative form (af'al of preference), with ﴿amadan﴾ as a specifier (tamyiz). al-Zajjaj and al-Tibrizi chose that it be the elative form of preference. al-Farisi and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah chose that it be a past-tense verb, and they preferred this because when ahsa is for intensification it is formed from a non-triliteral root, and in their view "ma a'taahu" and "ma awlahu" (for the subject) and "a'da min al-jaraba" are anomalous and not to be analogized. Abu Ishaq says: it has become frequent from the quadriliteral, so it is permissible. Ibn 'Atiyyah confused matters, citing among what is formed from the quadriliteral: "a'taahu" for wealth, "atahu" for good, "hiya aswadu min al-qar" (it is blacker than pitch), and "maa'uhu abyadu min al-laban" (its water is whiter than milk). He said: all these are af'al from the quadriliteral. End of quotation. But "aswad" and "abyad" are not formed from the quadriliteral. On the formation of af'al for exclamation and for preference there are three positions: one, it is formed from it absolutely, which is the apparent sense of Sibawayh's words, and words have come from it; two, it is not formed from it absolutely, and what came is treated as anomalous; three, a distinction: if the hamza is for transitivity (naql), it is not permitted, but if it is not for transitivity, as in "ashkala al-amr" (the matter became unclear) and "adhlama al-layl" (the night became dark), then one may say "ma ashkala hadhihi al-mas'alah" and "ma adhlama hadha al-layl." This is the choice of Ibn 'Usfur among our companions. The proofs of these positions are mentioned in the books of grammar. When we say that ahsa is a noun of preference, it is permissible that ﴿ayyu al-hizbayn﴾ be a relative (mawsul) built according to Sibawayh's school, because the condition for permissibility of building is present in it, namely that ayyu is attached (mudafa) with its initial element of the relative clause omitted; the estimate being: "so that the party which is 'ahsa' (most accurate) ﴿for what they remained, a term﴾ from those who did not count might be known." But if it is a past-tense verb this is impossible, because then the initial element of its clause is not omitted, the verb being itself the relative clause if ayyu is taken as a relative; so its building is not permitted, because the condition of its completion has failed, namely that the initial element of its clause is omitted.

He said: If you say: what do you say about the one who made it an elative of preference? I say: it is not the sound view, because its formation from a non-triliteral unaugmented root is not by analogy, and like "a'da min al-jaraba" and "aflasa min Ibn al-Mudhalliq," it is anomalous, and analogizing on the anomalous outside the Qur'an is impermissible, how much more so within it. Also, ﴿amadan﴾ either is governed by ahsa, but then af'al does not govern; or it is governed by labithu, but then the meaning is not sound. If you claim I govern it by an implied verb indicated by ahsa, as in the line:

"And I strike from us with swords the crowns (qawanis)"

with an implied "yadrib al-qawanis," you have gone far from the immediate construction, though it is near, since you refused that ahsa be a verb and then were compelled to return to estimating and implying it.

End of quotation. As for his claim of anomaly, that is the view of Abu 'Ali, and we have mentioned that the apparent view of Sibawayh is permissibility of forming it from af'al absolutely, that this is the view of Abu Ishaq, and that the distinction is the choice of Ibn 'Usfur and the view of others. The hamza in ahsa is not for transitivity. As for his statement "af'al does not govern," this is not correct, for it governs in the specifier (tamyiz), and ﴿amadan﴾ is a specifier, and thus did the one who held ahsa to be an elative of preference parse it, as you say: "Zaydan aqta'u al-nas sayfan" and "Zayd aqta'u lil-haam sayfan," and he did not parse it as an object. As for his statement "or it is governed by labithu, but then the meaning is not sound," i.e., it is not correct, al-Tabari went to governing ﴿amadan﴾ by labithu. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is not tenable. It may be tenable in that amad is the endpoint, and it is an expression for the period, inasmuch as a period has an endpoint in the actual sense of its term; and ma is in the sense of "alladhi," and ﴿amadan﴾ is put in the accusative by dropping the preposition, its estimate being "li-ma labithu min amadin," i.e., of a period, and "min amad" becomes an explanation of what is in the words "ma labithu," like His saying ﴿whatever verse We abrogate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106] and ﴿whatever mercy God opens to people﴾ [Fatir: 2]; and when the preposition dropped, the verb reached it. As for his statement "if you claim" to its end, one says: there is no need for this claim, because the one who says it may take the path of the Kufans, that the elative of preference governs a direct object; so "al-qawanis" is in their view governed by "adrib" as a direct object, and interpreting it as "striking the crowns" is the view of the Basrans. For this reason some grammarians held that His saying ﴿who strays﴾ [al-An'am: 117] "man" is governed by "a'lamu" as a direct object. Had the like of the line "And I strike from us with swords the crowns" been frequent, we would analogize it, and its meaning would be sound, because the elative of preference carries the sense of the verbal noun, so it governs by that implicit transfer; do you not see that the meaning is that our striking with swords the crowns exceeds the striking of others?

When He mentioned ﴿li-ya'lama﴾, indicating a difference in their affair, He followed it by stating that He is the One who relates their story to His Messenger ﷺ bit by bit, ﴿with truth﴾, i.e., in the manner of truthfulness. The phrase ﴿We relate﴾ came parallel to His saying ﴿li-na'lam﴾.

Then He said: ﴿They believed in their Lord﴾, and in it is the attribution of "Lord," who is the Master and the one who oversees the welfare of His servants. The construction did not come as "amanu" (passive-style) in order to convey that rank, that they are those cared for and owned by Him. Then He said: ﴿And We increased them in guidance﴾. The construction did not come as "wa-zadahum" because of the greatness and majesty in the word "Nā" (We). His increasing them in ﴿guidance﴾ is His facilitating for them righteous action, devotion to Him, distancing from people, and asceticism toward the world; and this is an increase in the faith that had come to them. In al-Tahrir: "We increased them" in the fruits of guidance, or in certainty, are two opinions; and what the increase was accomplished by is compliance with the command and abandonment of the prohibited, or the dog's speaking to them that it is upon what they are upon of faith, or the sending down of an angel upon them with glad tidings and strengthening, and informing them of the emergence of a Prophet from the Arabs by whom the religion will be entirely for God, so they believed in him before his mission. These are summarized views from al-Tahrir.

﴿And We fortified their hearts﴾: We made them firm and strengthened them to endure patiently the leaving of homeland and comfort, and fleeing with their religion to a cave in a desolate place with no companion, no water, and no food. Since fear and dread of the soul resemble, by association, loosening, it is fitting that in the strength of the soul and firmness of resolve it be likened to binding; from this comes "fulanun rabitu al-ja'sh" (so-and-so is steady of heart) when his soul does not scatter at fear and war. God the Exalted said: ﴿Had We not fortified her heart, she would almost have disclosed it﴾ [al-Qasas: 10]. The governing element of ﴿idh rabatna﴾ is: "We fortified when they stood up." The standing may be their standing before the disbelieving king Decius (Diqyanus), for it was a station needing fortification of the heart, where they were crucified (?) for him, abandoned his religion, and rejected, for the sake of God, his awe. It may also be a figure of speech for their rising with resolve to flee to God and separate from the people, as one says: "so-and-so stood up to such-and-such" when he resolved upon it with utmost earnestness.

Al-Karmani said: "They stood" upon their feet. It was said: "They stood" calling people secretly. 'Ata' said: "They stood" when they rose from sleep and said. It was said: "They stood" upon their faith. The author of al-Ghunyan said: ﴿when they stood﴾ before the king, and a cat moved, or it was said a mouse, so Decius was startled; and some looked at one another and could not restrain themselves from saying: ﴿Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾. Their people were worshippers of idols, and how excellent was their monotheism, that their Lord is the originator of the heavens and earth, who disposes them as He wills. Then they reinforced this monotheism with disavowal of any other god, with a negation that encompasses the eternity of time, according to one view. The lam in ﴿la-qad﴾ is the lam of emphasis, and ﴿idhan﴾ is a particle of response and consequence, i.e., ﴿We have indeed said: we shall never call upon any god other than Him, [for then] we would have uttered an excess﴾ [al-Kahf: 14]. ﴿Shatatan﴾ means: possessing excess, which is transgression and injustice; so ﴿shatatan﴾ is an adjective of an elided verbal noun, either by elision as we estimated, or by description with it by way of intensification. It was said: it is an object of ﴿qulna﴾. Qatadah said: ﴿shatatan﴾ means a lie. Abu Zayd said: an error.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 15–16:

﴿These our people have taken gods besides Him. Why do they not bring a clear authority concerning them? Who then is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ ﴿And when you have withdrawn from them and what they worship other than Allah, then take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread for you of His mercy and will prepare for you of your affair a means of ease.﴾

When they had affirmed the oneness of Allah the Exalted and rejected what is worshipped besides Him of gods, they proceeded to censure their people and their evil conduct, and [affirmed] that they have no proof for worshipping other than Allah. Then they magnified the crime of one who fabricates a lie against Allah. This statement may have been made by them in their station before the king, as a denunciation of what he and his people were upon, and that is more eloquent in disavowing the worship of idols, and more weakening to the king's resolve when they dared to censure what he is upon. It is also possible that they said this when they stood up for the matter they had resolved upon. And (hā'ulā'i) is a subject (mubtada').

As for (qawmunā), al-Ḥawfī said: it is a predicate (khabar), and (ittakhadhū) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Al-Zamakhsharī said, and Abu al-Baqā' followed him: (qawmunā) is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān), and (ittakhadhū) is in the position of the predicate. The pronoun in ﴿min dūnihi﴾ [al-Kahf: 14] refers to Allah. (Lawlā) here is a request (taḥḍīḍ) accompanied by denunciation, since it is impossible for a clear authority to exist for that; therefore the pure urging is not possible in it, so they urged them to it in the manner of challenging them to produce it (taʿjīz). The meaning of (ʿalayhim) is "concerning their taking of gods." (Ittakhadhū) here may be understood to mean "made" (ʿamilū), because they are idols they carved, and it may be understood to mean "made into" (ṣayyarū). In what they mentioned is evidence that religion is not taken except by proof; claims without valid evidence are wrong, and they are injustice, fabrication against Allah, and a lie through attributing partners to Allah.

﴿And when you have withdrawn from them﴾ is an address from some of them to others. Withdrawal (iʿtizāl) includes separating from the homelands of their people and their beliefs, so it is both physical and spiritual withdrawal. And (mā) is conjoined to the object in (iʿtazaltumūhum), meaning: and you have withdrawn from what they worship. (Illā Allāh) is an exceptive construction (istithnāʾ muttaṣil) if their people worshipped Allah along with their gods, since the word of majesty (Allah) is included in His saying: ﴿and they do not worship except Allah﴾.

Abu Nuʿaym al-Ḥāfiẓ mentioned from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī that they used to worship Allah and worship other gods along with Him, so the youths withdrew from worshipping those gods but did not withdraw from worshipping Allah. al-Farrāʾ also said this. It is a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ) if they did not know Allah nor worship Him, since He is not included in what they worshipped. In the codex of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿūd) is: ﴿wa-mā yaʿbudūna min dūnanā﴾ ("and what they worship besides us"). The end. What is in the codex of ʿAbd Allah, as Hārūn mentioned, was only intended as an explanation of the meaning, and that these youths withdrew from their people and from what they worship besides Allah; but that is not a Qur'an, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the codex; and because what is widely transmitted from ʿAbd Allah, indeed what is mutawatir, is what is established in the text, which is (mā yaʿbudūna illā Allāh). It has also been said: ﴿wa-mā yaʿbudūna illā Allāh﴾ is a parenthetical statement, an informative statement from Allah the Exalted about the youths that they did not worship other than Allah the Exalted. In this case (mā) in it and (illā) is a deficient exceptive construction (istithnāʾ mufarragh), with the governing element removed.

﴿Then take refuge in the cave﴾, i.e., make it a shelter for yourselves in which you remain and to which you retreat. His saying (yanshur) contains what they were upon of trust in Allah (tawakkul), in that they took refuge in a cave, and they connected to their refuge there the spreading of Allah's mercy upon them and the preparation of His gentleness toward them; for whoever brings someone out of the darkness of disbelief into the light of faith will not waste him. The meaning is that He the Exalted will extend His mercy over us and will prepare for us what we may use to ease our livelihood.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: ﴿and will prepare for you﴾ will make easy for you what you fear from the king and his oppression, and will bring you ease, gentleness and kindness. Ibn al-Anbārī said: the meaning of ﴿and will prepare for you﴾ is, in place of your difficult affair, (mirfaqan) ["a means of ease"]. The poet said:

*So would that for us from the water of Zamzam a cool draught were there, that has spent the night on Ṭahyān.*

That is: in place of the water of Zamzam. Al-Zamakhsharī said: either they say this out of confidence in Allah's bounty and strength in their hope, because of their trust in Him and the purity of their certainty; or a prophet of their era informed them of it; or some of them were prophets.

Abu Jaʿfar, al-Aʿraj, Shayba, Ḥumayd, Ibn Saʿdān, Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Bakr in the narration of al-Aʿshā, al-Burjī and al-Juʿfī from him, and Abū ʿAmr in the narration of Hārūn, read (mirfaqan) with a fatḥa on the mīm and a kasra on the fāʾ. Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Ṭalḥa, al-Aʿmash and the rest of the Seven read it with a kasra on the mīm and a fatḥa on the fāʾ (mirfaqan), because both apply to the matter by which one is aided and to the limb (the elbow); al-Zajjāj and Thaʿlab related this. Makkī related from al-Farrāʾ that he said: I know of no form other than the kasra of the mīm for "the matter," "the hand," and everything. al-Kisāʾī denied that the mirfaq could be the limb except with a fatḥa on the mīm and a kasra on the fāʾ, and Abū Ḥātim disagreed with him, saying: mirfaq with a fatḥa on the mīm is a place, like masjid. Abū Zayd said: it is a verbal noun like al-rifq, of the pattern mifʿal. It has also been said: they are two dialects for what one is aided by; and if it is from the limb, then it is with a kasra on the mīm and a fatḥa on the fāʾ only. From al-Farrāʾ: the people of the Ḥijāz say (mirfaqan) with a fatḥa on the mīm and a kasra on the fāʾ for what you are aided by, and they say with a kasra the elbow of a person; and the Arabs may use a kasra on the mīm in both. The end. Muʿādh permitted a fatḥa on both the mīm and the fāʾ.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 15–16:

﴿These our people have taken gods besides Him. Why do they not bring a clear authority concerning them? Who then is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ ﴿And when you have withdrawn from them and what they worship other than Allah, then take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread for you of His mercy and will prepare for you of your affair a means of ease.﴾

When they had affirmed the oneness of Allah the Exalted and rejected what is worshipped besides Him of gods, they proceeded to censure their people and their evil conduct, and [affirmed] that they have no proof for worshipping other than Allah. Then they magnified the crime of one who fabricates a lie against Allah. This statement may have been made by them in their station before the king, as a denunciation of what he and his people were upon, and that is more eloquent in disavowing the worship of idols, and more weakening to the king's resolve when they dared to censure what he is upon. It is also possible that they said this when they stood up for the matter they had resolved upon. And (hā'ulā'i) is a subject (mubtada').

As for (qawmunā), al-Ḥawfī said: it is a predicate (khabar), and (ittakhadhū) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Al-Zamakhsharī said, and Abu al-Baqā' followed him: (qawmunā) is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān), and (ittakhadhū) is in the position of the predicate. The pronoun in ﴿min dūnihi﴾ [al-Kahf: 14] refers to Allah. (Lawlā) here is a request (taḥḍīḍ) accompanied by denunciation, since it is impossible for a clear authority to exist for that; therefore the pure urging is not possible in it, so they urged them to it in the manner of challenging them to produce it (taʿjīz). The meaning of (ʿalayhim) is "concerning their taking of gods." (Ittakhadhū) here may be understood to mean "made" (ʿamilū), because they are idols they carved, and it may be understood to mean "made into" (ṣayyarū). In what they mentioned is evidence that religion is not taken except by proof; claims without valid evidence are wrong, and they are injustice, fabrication against Allah, and a lie through attributing partners to Allah.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 17–18:

﴿And you would see the sun, when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it sets, passing them on the left, while they were in a spacious place within it. That is among the signs of Allah. Whomever Allah guides is the one rightly guided, and whomever He sends astray, you will not find for him a guiding ally.﴾ ﴿And you would think them awake while they were asleep, and We turned them to the right and to the left, and their dog stretched out its forelegs at the threshold. Had you looked upon them, you would have turned away from them in flight and been filled with dread of them.﴾

Here there are omitted clauses, indicated by what preceded them. The implied meaning is: ﴿So take refuge in the cave﴾ [al-Kahf: 16], so Allah cast sleep upon them, answered their supplication, and provided them with things within the cave.

The two Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Abu 'Amr read (tazzawaru) with the assimilation of tatazawaru into the zay. The Kufans, al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Manadhir, Khalaf, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Sa'dan, Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani, and Ahmad ibn Jubayr al-Antaki read it with a light zay, dropping the ta'. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn 'Amir, Qatada, Humayd, and Ya'qub from al-'Umari read (tazwarru) on the pattern of (tahmarru). Al-Jahdari, Abu Raja', Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Ibn Abi 'Ablah (p-108) and Jabir read it, and it is reported from Ayyub as (tazwarru) on the pattern of (tahmaru). Ibn Mas'ud and Abu al-Mutawakkil read (tazwa'irru), with a hamza before the ra', on the basis of their saying (adhha'amma) and (ash'alla), to avoid meeting two sakins; the meaning is "it swerves and inclines."

(Dhat al-yamin), "the side of the right," means the direction of the right of the cave, its literal meaning being the side called the right, i.e., the right of one entering the cave or the right of the youths. (Taqriduhum) means "does not approach them," from the sense of severance. (Wahum fi fajwatin minhu) means: in a spacious area of the cave. The majority read (taqriduhum) with a ta'. A group read it with a ya', meaning "the cave cuts them off." Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning is that the sun never touched them at all. Another group said: in the evening the sun would reach them with what its contact contained of benefit for their bodies. This description regarding the sun implies that they had a screen from the direction of the south and a screen from the direction of the east wind, and they were in a corner. 'Abdullah ibn Muslim said: the door of the cave faced the Bananat Na'sh, and on this view the top of the cave was covered from rain. Ibn 'Atiyya said: their cave faced the Bananat Na'sh, the sun did not enter it at rising or at setting; Allah chose for them a spacious resting place in a recess that the sun did not enter to harm them, and it removed from them the distress and grief of the cave. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is that they were in shade throughout their entire day, the sun not touching them at its rising or its setting, although they were in a wide, open place exposed to the sun's reach were it not that Allah veils it from them. End. This is an elaboration of the saying of al-Zajjaj.

Al-Zajjaj said: the action of the sun is a sign ﴿from the signs of Allah﴾, without the cave's door being toward a direction that would necessitate this. Abu 'Ali said: the meaning of (taqriduhum) is that it gives them some of its light and then quickly departs, like a loan that is repaid. His meaning is that the sun inclines in the morning and touches them in the evening with a light touch. End. But if it were from the loan that is given and then retrieved, the verb would be quadrilateral and would be (tuqridhuhum) with a ta' and a damma; rather it is from cutting off, and the implied meaning is (tuqridu lahum), that is, it cuts off for them some of its light. It is said: if the sun did not reach their place at all, its air would become foul and what is in it would rot, and they would perish. The meaning is that He, exalted, arranged their affair and placed them in a dwelling where the sun does not fall so often as to scorch them, nor is it absent from them in a permanent absence so that they would decay. The indication of (dhalika) refers to what He, exalted, did for them, namely the sun's inclining and its cutting off of them when rising and setting, which is a sign of His signs; that is, what lies in that direction is touched by the sun while it does not touch them, as a particular honor for them. Whoever said that it faced the Bananat Na'sh such that they had a screen from the sun takes the indication to be that their story is ﴿from the signs of Allah﴾, namely His guidance of them to His oneness, their removal from among the idol-worshippers, their being sheltered in that cave, their protection from their enemy, the casting of awe upon them, the turning of the sun away from them to the right and left so that their bodies would not decay, their being made to sleep this long duration, the preservation of them from decay, and the preservation of their garments from tearing.

That it is an indication of guidance is shown by His saying: (whomever Allah guides is the one rightly guided), which is a general statement that includes those whose story has preceded, namely the People of the Cave; (and whomever He sends astray) is likewise general, like Diqyanus the unbeliever and his companions. The address in (and you would think them) and in ﴿and you would see the sun﴾ is to whoever is destined to look upon them. It is said: their eyes were open while they slept, so the observer would think them awake. Abu Muhammad ibn 'Atiyya said: it is also possible that the observer thinks this because of the intensity of the protection that was upon them and the scarcity of change; for it is generally the case with sleepers that they have slackness and postures that indicate sleep, so the observer takes them to be awake even if their eyes are closed. Had the opening of their eyes been established by a chain that eliminates excuse, it would have been clearer in making the observer think them wakeful. The apparent meaning is that His saying (and you would think them awake) is a new, independent statement and not a conditional clause. It is also said: there is an elision in the speech, its implied meaning being: had you seen them, you would have thought them (awake).

The apparent meaning is that His saying (and We turned them) is a new independent statement. It is also said: the impression of their being awake arose only from their turning, especially when it was from right to left and from left to right. In the recitation of the majority, (wa-nuqallibuhum) with a nun, there is an added emphasis of Allah's care for them, in attributing the turning to Him, exalted, and that He is the one (p-109) doing that. Al-Zamakhshari reports that it was read (wa-yuqallibuhum) with a ya' and a shadda, meaning Allah turns them. Al-Hasan, as reported by al-Ahwazi in al-Iqna', read (wa-yaqlibuhum) with an open ya', a sukun on the qaf, and a light lam. Al-Hasan, as reported by Ibn Jinni, read (wa-taqallaba-hum) as a verbal noun of taqallaba in the accusative, and said: this is governed by an implied verb, as if he said: "and you see or witness their turning." Also from him, he read likewise but with a damma on the ya', making it a verbal noun in the nominative as a subject, as said by Abu Hatim; Ibn Khalawayh mentioned this reading from al-Yamani. He mentioned that Ikrima read (wa-taqlibuhum) with a ta' above, the present of qalaba in light form. It is said: the benefit of turning them in both directions is so that the earth would not wear out their garments and eat their flesh, and so that people would think they had died. This is weak, for He who was able to keep them alive for that long period is able to preserve their bodies and garments.

From Ibn 'Abbas: had the sun touched them, it would have burned them, and had there been no turning, the earth would have consumed them. End. (Dhat) here is in the sense of "possessor of," i.e., a direction: (dhat al-yamin), the right side. The exegetes transmitted disagreement regarding the times of their turning and the number of turnings from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayra, Qatada, Mujahid, and Ibn 'Iyad, with contradictory and conflicting sayings, which we set aside without citing. Likewise we have not addressed the name of their dog, or whether it was the dog of a shepherd or of someone else; for things like the number, description, and naming cannot be known by reason, but only by revelation, and revelation in such matters can come only from the prophets or the divine books, and it is impossible that such disagreement would come from them. The apparent meaning of (wa-kalbuhum) is that it refers to the well-known animal. Those who said it was a lion are further off, and further still are those who said it was a cook-servant who followed them, or one of them who sat at the door as a watchman. Abu 'Amr al-Zahid, the client of Tha'lab, reported that it was read (wa-kali'uhum) as an active participle of kala'a, "to guard," so it should be understood as the dog, for its guarding of humans. It is said: it is possible that by the kali' is meant a man, as narrated, since spreading the forearms, lying flat on the ground with the face raised for watching is the posture of one who hides himself from view. Abu Ja'far al-Sadiq read (wa-kalibuhum) with a single ba', meaning "the owner of their dog," as you say labin and tamir, meaning "owner of milk and dates."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (basitun dhira'ayhi) is a narration of a past state, since the active participle does not govern when it has the meaning of the past, and its annexation, when it is annexed in actual fact to a definite noun like "the boy of Zayd," is only when you intend the narration of a past state. End. His statement "the active participle does not govern when it has the meaning of the past" is not a consensus; al-Kisa'i and Hisham, and among our companions Abu Ja'far ibn Mudaʼ, held that it may govern. The arguments of both sides are mentioned in the science of grammar.

As for (al-wasid): Ibn 'Abbas said it is the door; also from him, and from Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr, it is the courtyard; from Qatada, the surface and dust; it was also said it is the threshold. Also from Ibn Jubayr: the dust.

The address in (law iṭṭala'ta) is to the one addressed in (and you would see) and (and you would think them). Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read (law uṭṭala'ta) with a damma on the waw when connected. The majority read it with a kasra; its damma is also reported from Shayba, Abu Ja'far, and Nafi'. The overwhelming fear is due to the awe and majesty that Allah cast upon them; whoever intends to look upon them is overtaken by that awe.

The meaning of (la-wallayta minhum) is: you would turn your face away from them. (Awlaytahum kashhaka) means you turned your side toward them. (Firaran) is in the accusative as a verbal noun, either with an implied verb (la-farartа), or (wallayta) since it has the sense of (la-farartа), or as an object of purpose. (Ru'ban) is in the accusative as a second object. Those who said it is a specification transferred from the object, like His saying: ﴿and We caused the earth to gush forth with springs﴾ [al-Qamar: 12], according to the opinion of those who permit transferring the specification from the object, are further off; for if you imposed the verb upon it, it would not transitively reach it as a direct object does, unlike ﴿and We caused the earth to gush forth with springs﴾. It was also said: the cause of the dread was the length of their hair and nails, the yellowness of their faces, and the change of their clothing. It was also said: because of the darkness of the place and its desolation. These two sayings are worthless, for had they been in that state, they would have been unaware of their condition and would not have said ﴿We have stayed a day or part of a day﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]; and because the one who was sent to the city denied only the world and the building, not his own state in himself; and because they were in such a good condition that the observer could not distinguish them from the wakeful, ﴿and they were in a spacious place﴾, which the winds pass through, and a place in this form is not desolate.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Amir... [sic] — read (wa-lumli'ta) with a shadda on the lam and the hamza; the remaining seven read with a light lam and hamza. Abu Ja'far and Shayba read with a shadda on the lam and replacing the hamza with ya'. Al-Zuhri read with a light lam and replacement. The disagreement regarding (ru'ban) was mentioned in Al 'Imran. Here Abu Ja'far and 'Isa read it with a damma on the 'ayn.

The meaning is that He, exalted, arranged their affair and placed them in a dwelling where the sun does not fall so often as to scorch them, nor is it absent from them in a permanent absence so that they would decay. The indication of (dhalika) refers to what He, exalted, did for them, namely the sun's inclining and its cutting off of them when rising and setting, which is a sign of His signs; that is, what lies in that direction is touched by the sun while it does not touch them, as a particular honor for them. Whoever said that it faced the Bananat Na'sh such that they had a screen from the sun takes the indication to be that their story is ﴿from the signs of Allah﴾, namely His guidance of them to His oneness, their removal from among the idol-worshippers, their being sheltered in that cave, their protection from their enemy, the casting of awe upon them, the turning of the sun away from them to the right and left so that their bodies would not decay, their being made to sleep this long duration, the preservation of them from decay, and the preservation of their garments from tearing.

That it is an indication of guidance is shown by His saying: (whomever Allah guides is the one rightly guided), which is a general statement that includes those whose story has preceded, namely the People of the Cave; (and whomever He sends astray) is likewise general, like Diqyanus the unbeliever and his companions. The address in (and you would think them) and in ﴿and you would see the sun﴾ is to whoever is destined to look upon them. It is said: their eyes were open while they slept, so the observer would think them awake. Abu Muhammad ibn 'Atiyya said: it is also possible that the observer thinks this because of the intensity of the protection that was upon them and the scarcity of change; for it is generally the case with sleepers that they have slackness and postures that indicate sleep, so the observer takes them to be awake even if their eyes are closed. Had the opening of their eyes been established by a chain that eliminates excuse, it would have been clearer in making the observer think them wakeful. The apparent meaning is that His saying (and you would think them awake) is a new, independent statement and not a conditional clause. It is also said: there is an elision in the speech, its implied meaning being: had you seen them, you would have thought them (awake).

The apparent meaning is that His saying (and We turned them) is a new independent statement. It is also said: the impression of their being awake arose only from their turning, especially when it was from right to left and from left to right. In the recitation of the majority, (wa-nuqallibuhum) with a nun, there is an added emphasis of Allah's care for them, in attributing the turning to Him, exalted, and that He is the one (p-109) doing that. Al-Zamakhshari reports that it was read (wa-yuqallibuhum) with a ya' and a shadda, meaning Allah turns them. Al-Hasan, as reported by al-Ahwazi in al-Iqna', read (wa-yaqlibuhum) with an open ya', a sukun on the qaf, and a light lam. Al-Hasan, as reported by Ibn Jinni, read (wa-taqallaba-hum) as a verbal noun of taqallaba in the accusative, and said: this is governed by an implied verb, as if he said: "and you see or witness their turning." Also from him, he read likewise but with a damma on the ya', making it a verbal noun in the nominative as a subject, as said by Abu Hatim; Ibn Khalawayh mentioned this reading from al-Yamani. He mentioned that Ikrima read (wa-taqlibuhum) with a ta' above, the present of qalaba in light form. It is said: the benefit of turning them in both directions is so that the earth would not wear out their garments and eat their flesh, and so that people would think they had died. This is weak, for He who was able to keep them alive for that long period is able to preserve their bodies and garments.

From Ibn 'Abbas: had the sun touched them, it would have burned them, and had there been no turning, the earth would have consumed them. End. (Dhat) here is in the sense of "possessor of," i.e., a direction: (dhat al-yamin), the right side. The exegetes transmitted disagreement regarding the times of their turning and the number of turnings from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayra, Qatada, Mujahid, and Ibn 'Iyad, with contradictory and conflicting sayings, which we set aside without citing. Likewise we have not addressed the name of their dog, or whether it was the dog of a shepherd or of someone else; for things like the number, description, and naming cannot be known by reason, but only by revelation, and revelation in such matters can come only from the prophets or the divine books, and it is impossible that such disagreement would come from them. The apparent meaning of (wa-kalbuhum) is that it refers to the well-known animal. Those who said it was a lion are further off, and further still are those who said it was a cook-servant who followed them, or one of them who sat at the door as a watchman. Abu 'Amr al-Zahid, the client of Tha'lab, reported that it was read (wa-kali'uhum) as an active participle of kala'a, "to guard," so it should be understood as the dog, for its guarding of humans. It is said: it is possible that by the kali' is meant a man, as narrated, since spreading the forearms, lying flat on the ground with the face raised for watching is the posture of one who hides himself from view. Abu Ja'far al-Sadiq read (wa-kalibuhum) with a single ba', meaning "the owner of their dog," as you say labin and tamir, meaning "owner of milk and dates."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (basitun dhira'ayhi) is a narration of a past state, since the active participle does not govern when it has the meaning of the past, and its annexation, when it is annexed in actual fact to a definite noun like "the boy of Zayd," is only when you intend the narration of a past state. End. His statement "the active participle does not govern when it has the meaning of the past" is not a consensus; al-Kisa'i and Hisham, and among our companions Abu Ja'far ibn Mudaʼ, held that it may govern. The arguments of both sides are mentioned in the science of grammar.

As for (al-wasid): Ibn 'Abbas said it is the door; also from him, and from Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr, it is the courtyard; from Qatada, the surface and dust; it was also said it is the threshold. Also from Ibn Jubayr: the dust.

The address in (law iṭṭala'ta) is to the one addressed in (and you would see) and (and you would think them). Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read (law uṭṭala'ta) with a damma on the waw when connected. The majority read it with a kasra; its damma is also reported from Shayba, Abu Ja'far, and Nafi'. The overwhelming fear is due to the awe and majesty that Allah cast upon them; whoever intends to look upon them is overtaken by that awe.

The meaning of (la-wallayta minhum) is: you would turn your face away from them. (Awlaytahum kashhaka) means you turned your side toward them. (Firaran) is in the accusative as a verbal noun, either with an implied verb (la-farartа), or (wallayta) since it has the sense of (la-farartа), or as an object of purpose. (Ru'ban) is in the accusative as a second object. Those who said it is a specification transferred from the object, like His saying: ﴿and We caused the earth to gush forth with springs﴾ [al-Qamar: 12], according to the opinion of those who permit transferring the specification from the object, are further off; for if you imposed the verb upon it, it would not transitively reach it as a direct object does, unlike ﴿and We caused the earth to gush forth with springs﴾. It was also said: the cause of the dread was the length of their hair and nails, the yellowness of their faces, and the change of their clothing. It was also said: because of the darkness of the place and its desolation. These two sayings are worthless, for had they been in that state, they would have been unaware of their condition and would not have said ﴿We have stayed a day or part of a day﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]; and because the one who was sent to the city denied only the world and the building, not his own state in himself; and because they were in such a good condition that the observer could not distinguish them from the wakeful, ﴿and they were in a spacious place﴾, which the winds pass through, and a place in this form is not desolate.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Amir... [sic] — read (wa-lumli'ta) with a shadda on the lam and the hamza; the remaining seven read with a light lam and hamza. Abu Ja'far and Shayba read with a shadda on the lam and replacing the hamza with ya'. Al-Zuhri read with a light lam and replacement. The disagreement regarding (ru'ban) was mentioned in Al 'Imran. Here Abu Ja'far and 'Isa read it with a damma on the 'ayn.

Thus did We raise them up that they might question one another. A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?" They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day." They said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained. So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city, and let him see which of them has the purest food, and bring you provision from it, and let him be gentle and let him not make anyone aware of you. Indeed, if they gain the upper hand over you, they will stone you or return you to their religion, and then you will never succeed."

The kaf is for comparison (tashbih), and the demonstrative is bi-dhalika (thus). It is said that it refers to the verbal noun implied in ﴿فَضَرَبْنا عَلى آذانِهِمْ﴾ [al-Kahf: 11], meaning: as We made their sleep this long period a sign, We made their awakening a sign. This was said by al-Zajjaj, and al-Zamakhshari approved it, saying: "Just as We put them to that sleep, (thus We raised them up) as a reminder of His power over causing death and raising to life alike, so that some of them would question others and learn their own condition and what God had done with them, so that they would take heed and draw inference from the greatness of God's power, increase in certainty, and give thanks for what God bestowed upon them and with which they were honoured." End of quote. This comparison suits His words, exalted is He, when He first related their story briefly: ﴿فَضَرَبْنا عَلى آذانِهِمْ في الكَهْفِ سِنِينَ عَدَدًا ثُمَّ بَعَثْناهُمْ﴾ [al-Kahf: 11].

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the demonstrative bi-dhalika refers to the matter which God mentioned concerning them and the lesson which He made of them. The lam in (li-yatasa'alu) is the lam of consequence (lam al-sayrura), because their raising was not for the sake of their questioning itself. End of quote. The speaker: it is said he was their eldest, Maksalmina. It is also said he was the one who held their expenses, Tamlikha. The kam (how many) is a question about the number, and the meaning is: how many days did you remain asleep? The apparent view is that the doubt came from those being asked. It is said that (aw) is for detailing: some of them said, ﴿لَبِثْنا يَوْمًا﴾ ("we remained a day"), and some said, ﴿بَعْضَ يَوْمٍ﴾ ("part of a day"). The questioner sensed in his mind the length of their sleep, and for that reason he asked. It is said they slept at the beginning of the day and awoke at the end of the day. Their answer was based on a preponderant assumption (ghalabat al-zann), and speaking on a prevailing assumption is not considered a lie. When doubt arose for them regarding the report, they referred the knowledge of their stay to God, exalted is He.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿قالُوا رَبُّكم أعْلَمُ بِما لَبِثْتُمْ﴾ is a rebuke directed at them by some of their number, and that God, exalted is He, knows best the duration of their stay. These men had known, through evidences or by inspiration from God, that the period was lengthy, and that its exact amount is unknown and known only to God. End of quote. When they awoke from their sleep, they were seized by what overtakes anyone who has slept a long time: need for food. (Fa-ib'athu) is connected to the discussion of questioning, as if they had said: "Attend to what concerns you, and leave the knowledge of that to God." The one sent is said to be Tamlikha. They had taken with them, when they fled, dirhams for their expenses, and these were present with them, which is why they pointed to them with their words "this" (hadhihi).

Abu 'Amr, Hamza, Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, al-A'mash, al-Yazidi, Ya'qub in one narration, Khalaf, Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn Sa'dan read (bi-warqikum) with a sukun on the ra'. The rest of the seven, and Zayd ibn 'Ali, read it with a kasra on it. Abu Raja' read with a kasra on the waw, sukun on the ra', and idgham of the qaf into the kaf; likewise Isma'il reported from Ibn Muhaysin. Also from Ibn Muhaysin (p-111) similarly, except that he kasra'd the ra' so that the idgham would be valid. Al-Zamakhshari said: Ibn Kathir read (bi-wariqikum) with a kasra on the ra' and idgham of the qaf into the kaf. End of quote, and this contradicts what people have transmitted from him. Al-Zajjaj related a reading with a kasra on the waw and sukun on the ra' without idgham. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib read (bawariqikum) on the pattern fawa'il, treating it as a collective noun, like baqir and ja'il.

(Al-Madina) is their city from which they went out. It is said it is now called Tarsus, and its name at the time of their departure was Afsus. (Fa-l-yanzur) may be from seeing with the eye, or from seeing with the heart. The clause is in the position of an object of fa-l-yanzur, the verb being suspended from it. (Ayyuha) is an interrogative, a subject (mubtada'), and (azka) is its predicate. It may also be that (ayyuha) is a relative pronoun, built, as an object of yanzura, according to the view of Sibawayh, with (azka) as the predicate of an omitted subject. As for (azka), Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' said: the most lawful slaughtered meat and the purest. For most of their town were disbelievers who slaughtered for idols. Ibn Jubayr said: the most lawful food. al-Dahhak said: most of their wealth was usurped. Mujahid said: they told him, do not buy food in which there is injustice. 'Ikrima said: the most abundant. Qatada said: the best quality. Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil said: the best. Yaman ibn Rayyan said: the cheapest. It is said: the most blessed in yield. It is said: it is rice. It is said: dates. It is said: raisins. It is said: there is an omission in the speech, meaning: the people of it, (azka ta'aman), so that the feminine pronoun refers to (al-madina). If there is no omission, its referent is what is understood from the context of the speech, as if it were said: which of the foods.

In His words ﴿فابْعَثُوا أحَدَكم بِوَرِقِكُمْ﴾ there is evidence that carrying provisions and what is suitable for the traveller is the course of those who rely upon God, not of those who rely upon provisions and upon what is in people's bags. Some scholars said: nothing is needed for this journey, meaning the Hajj journey, except two things: tying the money-belt, and trust in the All-Merciful. (Wa-l-yatalattaf) means in his concealment and his stratagem, in entering and leaving. Al-Zamakhshari said: let him exert himself in gentleness and discretion in what he undertakes of the transaction, so that he is not cheated, or in the matter of concealment, so that he is not recognised. End of quote. The second meaning is the apparent one. Al-Hasan read (wa-liyatalattaf) with a kasra on the imperative lam, and Qutayba al-Mayyal read (wa-lyutalattaf) with a damma on the ya', in the passive. (Wa-la yush'iranna) means: he should not do what would lead, without intending it, to their awareness of us; this is called making them aware because he is the cause of it. Abu Salih, Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' and Qutayba read ﴿ولا يُشْعِرَنَّ بِكُمْ﴾ aḥadun with the verb built for the active and aḥadun in the nominative.

The pronoun in (innahum) refers to what the meaning indicates, namely the disbelievers of that city. It is said it may also refer to (aḥadan), because its wording is general, so the pronoun may be plural, as in His words ﴿فَما مِنكم مِن أحَدٍ عَنْهُ حاجِزِينَ﴾ [al-Haqqa: 47], where in ḥājizīn there is a plural pronoun referring to aḥad.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the pronoun in (innahum) refers to the people presupposed in (ayyuha), and "zuhur" (overcoming) here means gaining knowledge of them and of their whereabouts. It is said it means high position and dominance. Zayd ibn 'Ali read (yuzhharu) with a damma on the ya', in the passive. The apparent meaning is stoning with stones, and the king was resolved to kill them had he gained control over them. Stoning was a customary punishment in earlier times for those among the people who opposed, since it is more severe and they share in it. Hajjaj said: its meaning is by speech, meaning abuse, and Ibn Jubayr said the same. ﴿أوْ يُعِيدُوكُمْ﴾ means they will make you return to it, against your will. Returning to a thing does not necessarily imply having been involved in it before, since the term is used to mean becoming. ﴿ولَنْ تُفْلِحُوا﴾ means if you enter their religion. (Idhan) is a particle of condition and response, and its discussion has been mentioned before; often the presumption of a condition and a response becomes clear.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verse 24–27 (part 1 of 3):

(p-112) ﴿And thus We caused them to be found, that they might know that the promise of Allah is true and that the Hour, there is no doubt about it, when they disputed among themselves over their affair and said, "Build over them a structure; their Lord knows best about them." Those who prevailed over their affair said, "We will surely take over them a place of worship."﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] ﴿They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them being their dog," and they will say, "They were five, the sixth of them being their dog," guessing at the unseen; and they will say, "They were seven, and the eighth of them was their dog." Say, "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few. So do not argue concerning them except with an apparent argument, and do not inquire about them from any of them."﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," except [when adding], "If Allah wills." And remember your Lord when you forget, and say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this to right guidance."﴾ [al-Kahf: 23].

Before this statement there are omitted clauses; the implied sense is: "So they sent one of them, and he looked to see which of them was purest in food, and he acted discreetly, and he did not let anyone become aware of them. Then Allah made the people of the city aware of their condition." The story of his going to the city, what happened to him with its people, his being brought to the king, their claim against him that he had found much of the treasure of the ancients, and the king's and his companions' coming to them, is mentioned in the exegetical works, in more detail than what has passed, and Allah knows best the details of that.

It is said: "I came upon (ʿathartu ʿalā) the matter" when I became aware of it, and "another caused me to come upon it (aʿthanī)" when he made me aware of it. The discussion of this root has already passed in His saying: ﴿So if it is discovered that they had deserved sin﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 107]. The object of (aʿtharnā) is omitted; its implied sense is ﴿We caused them to be found﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] — the people of their city. The kaf in (wa-kadhālika) is for comparison, and the implied sense is: "And as We put them to sleep, We raised them, for the wisdom in that, We made them known to people." The pronoun in (liyaʿlamū) refers to the object of (aʿtharnā), and this is the view taken by al-Tabari.

And ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] is the resurrection, because their state in sleep and in waking after the long period is like the state of one who dies and then is raised. Then ﴿there is no doubt﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] about it, that is: there is no doubt and no uncertainty about the Hour and the recompense in it. Those who were made aware of the People of the Cave had been seized by a trial concerning the matter of the gathering and the raising of bodies from graves; some people doubted this and considered it unlikely, and said: "Only the spirits will be gathered." This distressed their king, and he remained perplexed, not knowing how to clarify the matter to them, until he put on sackcloth, sat on ashes, and humbled himself before Allah, seeking proof and clarification. So Allah made the People of the Cave known, and when Allah raised them and people became clear about their affair, the king was delighted, and those who had doubted the matter of the resurrection of bodies returned to certainty. To this the statement points: ﴿when they disputed among themselves over their affair﴾ [al-Kahf: 21]. And (idh) is governed either by (aʿtharnā) or by (liyaʿlamū).

(p-113) It has been said: it is possible that the pronoun in ﴿liyaʿlamū﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] refers to the People of the Cave, meaning: Allah made their affair a sign for them, indicating the raising of bodies from graves. According to this view, the statement ﴿when they disputed﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] begins a report about the people who were raised in their time, and the dispute at that time concerned the building and the place of worship, not the matter of the Resurrection.

It has also been said: the dispute was only about whether they had been made known to people. Some said: "They are dead," and some said: "They are alive." It is narrated that the king and the people of the city went out with Tamlikha to the Cave and saw them. Then the youths said to the king: "We entrust you to Allah and seek refuge with Him for you from the evil of jinn and men," and then they returned to their resting places, and Allah took their souls. The king cast his garments over them and ordered that a coffin of gold be made for each one; but he saw them in a dream disliking gold, so he made them of teak, and it was built over the entrance of the Cave. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿their Lord knows best about them﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] is part of the speech of the disputants, falling under "they said," that is: they ordered the building and reported the content of this clause; as if they were recalling their affair and exchanging words about their lineages, their conditions, and the length of their stay, and when they could not reach the truth of that, they said: ﴿their Lord knows best about them﴾ [al-Kahf: 21]. It has also been said: it is possible that it is part of Allah's speech, a rejection of the words of those who plunged into discussing them, from among those disputants, or from those who disputed about it in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from among the People of the Book. And ﴿those who prevailed﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] — Qatadah said: they were the rulers. It is narrated that one group wished to seal the Cave over them and leave them hidden within it, while the dominant group said: ﴿We will surely take over them a place of worship﴾ [al-Kahf: 21], and so they took it.

It is also narrated that the one who called for the building was an unbeliever who wanted to build a church or a place of worship for their disbelief, but the believers prevented them and built over them a place of worship. Al-Hasan and ʿIsa al-Thaqafi read (ghulibū) with a damma on the ghayn and a kasra on the lam. The meaning is that the group that wanted the place of worship wanted nothing to be built over them and no one to approach their place; and it is narrated that another group, of believers, wanted the Cave not to be sealed. When the first group was overcome in that something had to be built, they said: "Let it be a place of worship (masjid)," and it became so. It is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that Allah concealed their affair from the people and kept them from knowing it, and that this was the call to building a structure so that it might be a landmark for them.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (sayaqūlūna) refers to those previously mentioned, namely those who disputed about their account before their being made known; so Allah informed His Prophet of what had happened of disagreement among their people about their number. That the pronoun refers to what we have said was mentioned by al-Mawardi. It has also been said: it refers to the Christians of Najran who debated with the Messenger (ﷺ) about their number. The Melkites said the first statement, the Jacobites the second, and the Nestorians the third; this is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. In al-Kashshaf it is stated that al-Sayyid said the first statement and he was a Jacobite; al-ʿAqib said the second and he was a Nestorian; and the Muslims said the third and were correct, and they knew this through the Messenger's report from Gabriel, peace be upon them both. Thus the pronouns in (sayaqūlūna) and (wa-yaqūlūna) would refer partly to the Christians of Najran and partly to the believers. It is narrated from ʿAli: they were seven men, whose names were Tamlikha, Maksalbina and Mashlabina — these were the companions of the king's right hand; on his left was Marnush, Dabarnush and Shadhanush, who consulted these six in his affair; and the seventh was the shepherd who agreed with them. They fled from their king Diqyanus, and the name of their city was Afsus, and the name of their dog was Qitmir. End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the pronoun in His saying (sayaqūlūna) is intended to refer to the People of the Torah among the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ), because they differed over the number of the People of the Cave, this explicit disagreement. End of quotation. It has been said: the future particle sin (sa-) was used because there is in the speech a folding and insertion; the implied sense is: "When you answer them concerning their question and relate to them the story of the People of the Cave, then ask them about their number, for when you ask them, they will say (sayaqūlūna)." Ibn Muhaysin read (thalātha) with the thā assimilated into the tā, and this is good because their places of articulation are close and both are voiceless; and because the quiescent letter before the thā is a soft letter (ḥurūf al-līn). The verb (yaqūlūna) has no sin either in it or after it, because it is conjoined to the future, so it falls within the future sense, or because the meaning of the future that it is fit for is intended. Shibl ibn ʿAbbad from Ibn Kathir read the mīm of (khamsa) with a fatha, which is a dialect like (ʿashara). Ibn Muhaysin read with a kasra on the kha and the mīm, and assimilated the tā into the sīn; and from him also the assimilation of the tanwin into the sīn without ghunna.

﴿Rajman bil-ghayb﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] means: casting at a hidden thing concealed from them, or guessing. It is borrowed from stoning (rajm), as if a person throws at an unknown place by his conjecture time after time, hoping to hit it; and from it come (turjumān) "interpreter" and (tarjamat al-kitāb) "translation of a book." And the verse of Zuhayr:

"War is nothing but what you know and have tasted, and he is not one who speaks of it with a stoned (guessed) tale."

That is, a conjectured one. This is placed after what preceded to show that the speakers of those two statements did not say that from knowledge, but only by way of estimation and guesswork; while the third statement came free of this restriction, indicating that it is the true statement, as was mentioned above from ʿAli, and from the Messenger of Allah, from Gabriel, peace be upon them both. (Rajman) is in the accusative either as a verbal noun of an implied verb, meaning "they stone with that," or as an implied verb in (sayaqūlūna) and (yaqūlūna) carrying the sense of "they stone," or as an object of purpose, meaning: they said that because of their casting at the hidden report, or because of their conjecture; that is, what moved them to this statement is the stoning in the unseen.

(Thalātha) is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause after it is a qualifier; that is: they are three persons. We estimated "persons" because (rābiʿuhum) is an active participle joined to a pronoun, and its sense is that He made them fourth, that is, made them four and brought them to this number. Had (thalātha) been estimated as "men," it would be impossible for three men to become four, because of the difference in the two kinds. The wāw in (wa-thāminuhum) is for conjunction with the preceding clause; that is: they say, "They are seven, and the eighth of them is their dog." They first reported seven men with certainty, then they reported a second time that "the eighth of them is their dog," unlike the two preceding statements, for each of them was a single clause describing the subject with an attribute, without conjoining a clause to it. It is mentioned from Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash and Ibn Khalawayh that it is the wāw of eight, and that when Quraysh speak they say "six, seven, and eight, nine," and they insert the wāw at eight. That the two are clauses, one conjoined to the other, indicates affirmation in the report, unlike what preceded, for they reported something described by something without that description being postponed after the report; and for this reason ﴿rajman bil-ghayb﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] is absent from it, and nothing in these two clauses undermines them. It is read (wa-thāminuhum kālibuhum), meaning: the companion of their dog; and some held that they were eight men, and this reading and the first phrase "and their dog" were taken as evidence for an omitted genitive, meaning: "and the companion of their dog." Some exegetes held that His saying (wa-thāminuhum) is not included in their saying, but in His saying ﴿and they say, "seven"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], then Allah reported this by way of a fresh statement; and if it is a fresh statement from Allah, it indicates that they were eight, with the dog. As for ﴿their fourth is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] and ﴿their sixth is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], they are part of what is related from their saying, because each of the two clauses is a qualifier.
