The majority recited (﴿ولا يُشْرِكُ﴾) with the yā' as a negation. Mujahid recited it with the yā' and the jazm (apocope). Yaʿqub said: I do not know its justification. Ibn ʿAmir, al-Hasan, Abu Rajaʾ, Qatada, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, Zayd, Humayd ibn al-Wazir on the authority of Yaʿqub, al-Juʿfi, and al-Lu'lu'i on the authority of Abu Bakr recited (ولا تُشْرِكْ) with the tā' and the jazm, as a prohibition.

When He revealed to him what He revealed of the account of the People of the Cave, He commanded him to relate it and recite to his contemporaries what was revealed to him by God Most High from His Book concerning the story of the People of the Cave and others, and that what He revealed to him (لا مُبَدِّلَ) has no changer. (لا مُبَدِّلَ) is general, and (لِكَلِماتِهِ) is also general. The specification is either in (لا مُبَدِّلَ), meaning: there is no changer of it besides Him; do you not see His saying: ﴿وإذا بَدَّلْنا آيَةً مَكانَ آيَةٍ﴾ [an-Nahl: 101]? Or it is in (كَلِماتِهِ), meaning His words that contain information, because what contained other than information was subject to abrogation in part of it. In His command to recite what was revealed to him, and in His informing that there is no changer of (لِكَلِماتِهِ), there is an allusion to the alteration by those who disputed about the People of the Cave and the distortion of their reports. (p-118) The (مُلْتَحَدٌ) is the refuge to which one inclines and turns.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verse 24–27 (part 1 of 3):

(p-112) ﴿And thus We caused them to be found, that they might know that the promise of Allah is true and that the Hour, there is no doubt about it, when they disputed among themselves over their affair and said, "Build over them a structure; their Lord knows best about them." Those who prevailed over their affair said, "We will surely take over them a place of worship."﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] ﴿They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them being their dog," and they will say, "They were five, the sixth of them being their dog," guessing at the unseen; and they will say, "They were seven, and the eighth of them was their dog." Say, "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few. So do not argue concerning them except with an apparent argument, and do not inquire about them from any of them."﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," except [when adding], "If Allah wills." And remember your Lord when you forget, and say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this to right guidance."﴾ [al-Kahf: 23].

Before this statement there are omitted clauses; the implied sense is: "So they sent one of them, and he looked to see which of them was purest in food, and he acted discreetly, and he did not let anyone become aware of them. Then Allah made the people of the city aware of their condition." The story of his going to the city, what happened to him with its people, his being brought to the king, their claim against him that he had found much of the treasure of the ancients, and the king's and his companions' coming to them, is mentioned in the exegetical works, in more detail than what has passed, and Allah knows best the details of that.

It is said: "I came upon (ʿathartu ʿalā) the matter" when I became aware of it, and "another caused me to come upon it (aʿthanī)" when he made me aware of it. The discussion of this root has already passed in His saying: ﴿So if it is discovered that they had deserved sin﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 107]. The object of (aʿtharnā) is omitted; its implied sense is ﴿We caused them to be found﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] — the people of their city. The kaf in (wa-kadhālika) is for comparison, and the implied sense is: "And as We put them to sleep, We raised them, for the wisdom in that, We made them known to people." The pronoun in (liyaʿlamū) refers to the object of (aʿtharnā), and this is the view taken by al-Tabari.

And ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] is the resurrection, because their state in sleep and in waking after the long period is like the state of one who dies and then is raised. Then ﴿there is no doubt﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] about it, that is: there is no doubt and no uncertainty about the Hour and the recompense in it. Those who were made aware of the People of the Cave had been seized by a trial concerning the matter of the gathering and the raising of bodies from graves; some people doubted this and considered it unlikely, and said: "Only the spirits will be gathered." This distressed their king, and he remained perplexed, not knowing how to clarify the matter to them, until he put on sackcloth, sat on ashes, and humbled himself before Allah, seeking proof and clarification. So Allah made the People of the Cave known, and when Allah raised them and people became clear about their affair, the king was delighted, and those who had doubted the matter of the resurrection of bodies returned to certainty. To this the statement points: ﴿when they disputed among themselves over their affair﴾ [al-Kahf: 21]. And (idh) is governed either by (aʿtharnā) or by (liyaʿlamū).

(p-113) It has been said: it is possible that the pronoun in ﴿liyaʿlamū﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] refers to the People of the Cave, meaning: Allah made their affair a sign for them, indicating the raising of bodies from graves. According to this view, the statement ﴿when they disputed﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] begins a report about the people who were raised in their time, and the dispute at that time concerned the building and the place of worship, not the matter of the Resurrection.

It has also been said: the dispute was only about whether they had been made known to people. Some said: "They are dead," and some said: "They are alive." It is narrated that the king and the people of the city went out with Tamlikha to the Cave and saw them. Then the youths said to the king: "We entrust you to Allah and seek refuge with Him for you from the evil of jinn and men," and then they returned to their resting places, and Allah took their souls. The king cast his garments over them and ordered that a coffin of gold be made for each one; but he saw them in a dream disliking gold, so he made them of teak, and it was built over the entrance of the Cave. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿their Lord knows best about them﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] is part of the speech of the disputants, falling under "they said," that is: they ordered the building and reported the content of this clause; as if they were recalling their affair and exchanging words about their lineages, their conditions, and the length of their stay, and when they could not reach the truth of that, they said: ﴿their Lord knows best about them﴾ [al-Kahf: 21]. It has also been said: it is possible that it is part of Allah's speech, a rejection of the words of those who plunged into discussing them, from among those disputants, or from those who disputed about it in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from among the People of the Book. And ﴿those who prevailed﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] — Qatadah said: they were the rulers. It is narrated that one group wished to seal the Cave over them and leave them hidden within it, while the dominant group said: ﴿We will surely take over them a place of worship﴾ [al-Kahf: 21], and so they took it.

It is also narrated that the one who called for the building was an unbeliever who wanted to build a church or a place of worship for their disbelief, but the believers prevented them and built over them a place of worship. Al-Hasan and ʿIsa al-Thaqafi read (ghulibū) with a damma on the ghayn and a kasra on the lam. The meaning is that the group that wanted the place of worship wanted nothing to be built over them and no one to approach their place; and it is narrated that another group, of believers, wanted the Cave not to be sealed. When the first group was overcome in that something had to be built, they said: "Let it be a place of worship (masjid)," and it became so. It is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that Allah concealed their affair from the people and kept them from knowing it, and that this was the call to building a structure so that it might be a landmark for them.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (sayaqūlūna) refers to those previously mentioned, namely those who disputed about their account before their being made known; so Allah informed His Prophet of what had happened of disagreement among their people about their number. That the pronoun refers to what we have said was mentioned by al-Mawardi. It has also been said: it refers to the Christians of Najran who debated with the Messenger (ﷺ) about their number. The Melkites said the first statement, the Jacobites the second, and the Nestorians the third; this is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. In al-Kashshaf it is stated that al-Sayyid said the first statement and he was a Jacobite; al-ʿAqib said the second and he was a Nestorian; and the Muslims said the third and were correct, and they knew this through the Messenger's report from Gabriel, peace be upon them both. Thus the pronouns in (sayaqūlūna) and (wa-yaqūlūna) would refer partly to the Christians of Najran and partly to the believers. It is narrated from ʿAli: they were seven men, whose names were Tamlikha, Maksalbina and Mashlabina — these were the companions of the king's right hand; on his left was Marnush, Dabarnush and Shadhanush, who consulted these six in his affair; and the seventh was the shepherd who agreed with them. They fled from their king Diqyanus, and the name of their city was Afsus, and the name of their dog was Qitmir. End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the pronoun in His saying (sayaqūlūna) is intended to refer to the People of the Torah among the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ), because they differed over the number of the People of the Cave, this explicit disagreement. End of quotation. It has been said: the future particle sin (sa-) was used because there is in the speech a folding and insertion; the implied sense is: "When you answer them concerning their question and relate to them the story of the People of the Cave, then ask them about their number, for when you ask them, they will say (sayaqūlūna)." Ibn Muhaysin read (thalātha) with the thā assimilated into the tā, and this is good because their places of articulation are close and both are voiceless; and because the quiescent letter before the thā is a soft letter (ḥurūf al-līn). The verb (yaqūlūna) has no sin either in it or after it, because it is conjoined to the future, so it falls within the future sense, or because the meaning of the future that it is fit for is intended. Shibl ibn ʿAbbad from Ibn Kathir read the mīm of (khamsa) with a fatha, which is a dialect like (ʿashara). Ibn Muhaysin read with a kasra on the kha and the mīm, and assimilated the tā into the sīn; and from him also the assimilation of the tanwin into the sīn without ghunna.

﴿Rajman bil-ghayb﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] means: casting at a hidden thing concealed from them, or guessing. It is borrowed from stoning (rajm), as if a person throws at an unknown place by his conjecture time after time, hoping to hit it; and from it come (turjumān) "interpreter" and (tarjamat al-kitāb) "translation of a book." And the verse of Zuhayr:

"War is nothing but what you know and have tasted, and he is not one who speaks of it with a stoned (guessed) tale."

That is, a conjectured one. This is placed after what preceded to show that the speakers of those two statements did not say that from knowledge, but only by way of estimation and guesswork; while the third statement came free of this restriction, indicating that it is the true statement, as was mentioned above from ʿAli, and from the Messenger of Allah, from Gabriel, peace be upon them both. (Rajman) is in the accusative either as a verbal noun of an implied verb, meaning "they stone with that," or as an implied verb in (sayaqūlūna) and (yaqūlūna) carrying the sense of "they stone," or as an object of purpose, meaning: they said that because of their casting at the hidden report, or because of their conjecture; that is, what moved them to this statement is the stoning in the unseen.

(Thalātha) is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause after it is a qualifier; that is: they are three persons. We estimated "persons" because (rābiʿuhum) is an active participle joined to a pronoun, and its sense is that He made them fourth, that is, made them four and brought them to this number. Had (thalātha) been estimated as "men," it would be impossible for three men to become four, because of the difference in the two kinds. The wāw in (wa-thāminuhum) is for conjunction with the preceding clause; that is: they say, "They are seven, and the eighth of them is their dog." They first reported seven men with certainty, then they reported a second time that "the eighth of them is their dog," unlike the two preceding statements, for each of them was a single clause describing the subject with an attribute, without conjoining a clause to it. It is mentioned from Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash and Ibn Khalawayh that it is the wāw of eight, and that when Quraysh speak they say "six, seven, and eight, nine," and they insert the wāw at eight. That the two are clauses, one conjoined to the other, indicates affirmation in the report, unlike what preceded, for they reported something described by something without that description being postponed after the report; and for this reason ﴿rajman bil-ghayb﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] is absent from it, and nothing in these two clauses undermines them. It is read (wa-thāminuhum kālibuhum), meaning: the companion of their dog; and some held that they were eight men, and this reading and the first phrase "and their dog" were taken as evidence for an omitted genitive, meaning: "and the companion of their dog." Some exegetes held that His saying (wa-thāminuhum) is not included in their saying, but in His saying ﴿and they say, "seven"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], then Allah reported this by way of a fresh statement; and if it is a fresh statement from Allah, it indicates that they were eight, with the dog. As for ﴿their fourth is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] and ﴿their sixth is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], they are part of what is related from their saying, because each of the two clauses is a qualifier. The majority of the Companions, the Successors, and the leading exegetes held that the number was eight including the dog.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is this wāw that enters the third clause, and why did it enter it rather than the first two?" I say: it is the wāw that enters a clause that is a qualifier of an indefinite noun, as it enters a clause that is a circumstantial state of a definite noun, as in your saying: "A man came to me and with him another," and "I passed by Zayd and in his hand was a sword." From it is His, the Mighty and Exalted, saying: ﴿And We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree﴾ [al-Hijr: 4]. Its benefit is to affirm the adherence of the qualifier to the qualified, and the indication that the attribution is a fixed, established matter; and it is the wāw which signals that those who said ﴿seven, and the eighth of them is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] said it from firm knowledge and tranquil soul, and did not guess by conjecture as others did. End of quotation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verse 24–27 (part 2 of 3):

That the waw (wa, "and") enters upon a clause (jumla) that stands as a qualifier (sifa), indicating that the qualifier is attached to the qualified noun and that its connection to it is firmly established, is something the grammarians do not recognize. Rather, they have established that one does not conjoin a qualifier that is not a clause to another qualifier unless the meanings differ, so that the conjunction indicates difference. If the meanings do not differ, conjoining is not permitted. This applies to single nouns; as for clauses that serve as qualifiers, they are even further from being permitted to be conjoined in this way. They have refuted those who held that the words of Sibawayh, "As for what came for a meaning and is neither a noun nor a verb," are a qualifier of his statement "for a meaning," and that the waw entered the clause because that is not from the speech of the Arabs: "I passed by a man and he eats," taken as a qualifier. As for the words of the Exalted, ﴿except that there was for it﴾ [al-Hijr: 4], the clause is circumstantial (hali), and it suffices as a refutation of the statement of al-Zamakhshari: "We do not know of any of the scholars of grammar who went to that."

When the Exalted related their saying and their disagreement about their number, He commanded him to say: ﴿Say: My Lord knows best their number﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], meaning: none informs of their number except one who knows them in truth, and that is God the Exalted. ﴿None knows them except a few﴾ [al-Kahf: 22]. What is affirmed for God the Exalted is the superiority of knowledge (al-a'lamiyya), and for the few the mere having knowledge (al-'alamiyya), so there is no contradiction. It was said: they are from the angels; it was said: from the scholars. The knowledge of the few is only through the informing of God.

Ibn Abbas said: "I am among the few." Then He forbade him from disputing about them, that is, about their number, and from contention (miraʾ). He called his reviewing of them "contention" by way of counterpart to the People of the Book's contending with him about that. He restricted it by His saying "apparent" (zahiran), meaning: not probing deeply into it, and it is that you narrate to them what has been revealed to you, and no more, without ignorance-attributing or rebuke, as He said: ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Nahl: 125]. Ibn Zayd said: ﴿apparent contention﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] is your saying to them: "It is not as you know." Al-Mawardi related: "except with a clear proof." Ibn al-Anbari said: "except a debate of one certain, knowing the reality of the report, and God the Exalted has cast to you what no falsehood can touch." Ibn Bahr said: "apparent" means "witnessed by the people." Al-Tabrizi said: "apparent" means "going away with the opponent's argument," and he recited:

"And that is a complaint whose shame has gone away from you"

meaning: it has departed.

Then He forbade him to ask any of the People of the Book about their story, not as a seeking of difficulty (mu'annit), since that contradicts what I commanded you concerning argument in the best manner; nor as a seeking of guidance (mustarshid), since He the Exalted has already guided you by revealing their story to you. Then He forbade him to inform that he will do something in the future without attaching it to the will of God the Exalted.

It has been mentioned in the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) that when Quraysh asked him about the People of the Cave, al-Khidr and the Spirit, he said, peace be upon him: "Tomorrow I will inform you," and he did not say "if God wills," so the revelation was delayed for a period. It was said: fifteen days; it was said: forty. And ﴿except that God wills﴾ is an exception that cannot be taken in its outward sense, because it would then fall under the saying, and thus be part of what is said. God does not forbid him to say: "I will do that tomorrow, unless God wills," since that is a sound statement in itself and it is not possible to forbid it. Hence, to interpret this outward meaning, a supposition (taqdir) is needed.

Ibn Atiyya said: there is an ellipsis in the speech which the outward meaning requires and which brevity embellishes; its supposition is: "except that you say: ﴿except that God wills﴾," or "except that you say: if God wills." So the meaning is: except that you mention the will of God, and then ﴿except that God wills﴾ is not part of the saying that He forbade.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿except that God wills﴾ is connected to the prohibition, not to the words ﴿I will do﴾ [al-Kahf: 23], because if he said: ﴿I will do﴾ [al-Kahf: 23] such-and-such ﴿except that God wills﴾, its meaning would be: except that the will of God intervenes between him and his act, and that has no place in the prohibition. Its connection to the prohibition is in two ways:

The first: "And do not say that saying except that God wills that you say it," with that being in it.

The second: "And do not say it except by God's willing," that is: except by His will, and it is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), meaning: except being bound by God's will, saying "if God wills."

There is a third way as well, which is that "except that God wills" has the meaning of a second word, as if it were said: "And do not say it ever," and similar to it: ﴿It is not for us to return to it except that our Lord wills﴾ [al-A'raf: 89], because their returning to their creed is something God will not will. This is a prohibition of discipline from God to His Prophet when he said: "Come to me tomorrow and I will inform you," and did not make an exception. End.

Ibn Atiyya said: a group said it is an exception from His saying ﴿and do not say﴾ [al-Kahf: 23]. Al-Tabari related it and refuted it, and it is among the corruptions, since what is obligatory is that it not be related. End. The al-Zamakhshari's derivation has already been mentioned, that it is connected to the prohibition. The exegetes spoke about this verse concerning the exception in oaths, though the verse is not about oaths. The apparent meaning is His command to remember God when forgetfulness overtakes you, and the object of forgetting is not the object of remembering. It was said: the sense is ﴿and remember your Lord﴾ when you abandon some of what He commanded you. It was said: remember Him when forgetfulness seizes you, so that He reminds you of what was forgotten. Qatada took that to mean the performance of a forgotten prayer when it is recalled. It was said: ﴿and remember your Lord﴾ with glorification and seeking forgiveness ﴿when you forget﴾ the word of exception, as an emphasis on urging attention to it. It was said: (and remember) the will of (your Lord) when there occurs from you forgetfulness of that, that is, when you forget the word of exception and then you become aware of it, and you make up for it by remembering, said by Ibn Jubayr. He said: even after a day or a month or a year. Ibn al-Anbari said: after the forgetfulness has passed, as you say: "Mention to Abdullah when your companion has prayed," meaning: when he has finished the prayer.

The reference in His saying "for something nearer than this" to the forgotten matter means: remember your Lord at the time of forgetting it by saying: ﴿It may be that my Lord guides me﴾ to something else in place of this forgotten thing, nearer than it in ﴿right guidance﴾ (rashadan), and nearer in good or benefit. Perhaps the forgetting was a choice, as in His saying: ﴿Or We cause it to be forgotten, We bring one better than it﴾ [al-Baqara: 106]. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a reference to the building of the People of the Cave, and its meaning is: perhaps God will give me, from the clear signs and proofs that I am a truthful prophet, what is greater in indication and nearer in guidance than the building of the Companions of the Cave. He did so, for He gave him narratives of the prophets and reports of the unseen greater than that and more indicative. End. Al-Zajjaj had preceded him to this, saying: the meaning is: "it may be" that God makes easy for me proofs of my prophethood nearer than the proof of the Companions of the Cave. Ibn al-Anbari said: "it may be" that He informs me of the answer to your questions before the time I set for you, and hastens for me from Him right guidance. Muhammad al-Kufi the exegete said: these words are among those commanded to be said by everyone who did not make the exception, and that they are an expiation for forgetting the exception.

* *

﴿And thus We made them known to them, that they might know that the promise of God is true and that the Hour, there is no doubt in it, when they disputed among themselves about their affair, and said: Build over them a building; their Lord knows best about them. Those who prevailed over their affair said: We will surely take over them a place of worship﴾ [al-Kahf: 21] ﴿They will say: they were three, the fourth of them their dog; and they will say: five, the sixth of them their dog, guessing blindly; and they will say: seven, and the eighth of them their dog. Say: My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few. So do not dispute about them except with apparent argument, and do not ask any of them about them﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] ﴿And do not say of anything: I will surely do that tomorrow﴾ [al-Kahf: 23] ﴿except that God wills. And remember your Lord when you forget, and say: It may be that my Lord guides me to something nearer than this in right guidance﴾ ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine﴾ ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained; to Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How clearly He sees and hears. They have no protector besides Him, and He does not share His rule with anyone﴾ ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord; none can alter His words, and you will find no refuge besides Him﴾.

The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿And they remained﴾ up to the end of the verse is a report from God the Exalted about the period of their sleeping in the cave until God made them known to people. Mujahid said: it is an explanation of the general statement of His saying: ﴿So We struck upon their ears in the cave for a counted number of years﴾ [al-Kahf: 11]. When this number was fixed by a report from God the Exalted, He commanded His Prophet to say: ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained﴾. So this report of His is the truth and the sincerity into which doubt does not enter, because He knows ﴿the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿how long they remained﴾ is that it refers to the period previously mentioned. Some said: ﴿how long they remained﴾ refers to the period after their being made known until the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him. It was said: when He said ﴿and added nine﴾, the nine were indefinite: they could be hours, days, months, or years, and the Children of Israel differed according to this; so He commanded him to refer knowledge of it to Him, meaning regarding the nine. This is far-fetched, because when a specified number precedes and something unspecified is conjoined to it, its specification is taken to refer to the preceding one. Al-Naqqash related that they were three hundred solar years, and since the address was to the Arabs, the nine were added, since the Arab reckoning is by the moon, so that the two reckonings agree. Qatada and Matar al-Warraq said: "they remained" is a report from the Children of Israel, and they argued by what is in the codex of Abdullah, and they said: "they remained." According to a reading other than Abdullah's, it is conjoined to what was related by His saying "they will say."

Then God commanded His Prophet to refer knowledge to Him ﴿how long they remained﴾ as a refutation of them and a demolition of their saying. It was said: it is from the saying of those disputing about their affair, and this is the correct view according to the context of the verse; it is supported by ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained﴾, which makes that among the unseen matters that He alone is specialized in. Al-Jumhur read: "three hundred" with tanwin. Ibn Atiyya said: in apposition (badal or ʿatf al-bayan). It was said: as a specification (tafsir) and a tamyiz. Al-Zamakhshari said: ʿatf al-bayan to "three hundred." Abu al-Baqa related that some permitted it to be a badal of "hundred," since "hundred" means "hundreds." As for ʿatf al-bayan, it is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans; and as for putting it in the accusative as a tamyiz, the well-known transmitted usage of the Arabs is that "hundred" is only specified by a singular genitive noun, and that the saying "when a youth reaches two hundred years" is among the necessities of poetry, especially since "years" here is a plural. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Talha, Yahya, al-A'mash, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Layla, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn Isa al-Isfahani, and Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki read "hundred" without tanwin, in construct with "years," placing the plural in the position of the singular. Abu Hatim criticized this reading, but it is not permitted for him to do so. Abu Ali said: this is in the well-known usage construed with the singular, and it is sometimes construed with the plural. Ubayy read "a year" (sanatan), and likewise in the codex of Abdullah. Al-Dahhak read "sunun" with waw, as if supposing "they are sunun." Al-Hasan and Abu Amr, in the transmission of al-Lu'lu'i from him, read "tisʿan" with a fatha on the ta', as they say "ʿashra."

Then he mentioned His exclusive knowledge of what is unseen in the heavens and the earth, and what is hidden in them of the conditions of their inhabitants. He brought what indicates wonder at His perception of things heard and things seen, to show that His perception is beyond the limit of what the hearers and the seers are capable of; for He perceives the most subtle and smallest things just as He perceives the largest in bulk and the densest in body, and He perceives the inward just as He perceives the outward.

The pronoun in (بِهِ) refers to God Most High. Is it in a nominative or accusative position? And are (أسْمِعْ) and (أبْصِرْ) truly imperatives, or are they imperatives only in form? Their meaning is the expression of wonder. This is a well-established point of disagreement in grammar.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that the meaning is "See (أبْصِرْ) by the religion of God, and hear (﴿وأسْمِعْ﴾)," that is: "Make sight by the guidance of God and make hearing," so the pronoun refers either to the guidance or to God. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

ʿIsa recited "Asmi‘ bihi wa-abṣir" as a declarative past-tense verb, not as an expression of wonder, meaning: He makes His servants see through knowledge of Him and makes them hear, and the pronoun is a reference to God Most High.

The pronoun in His saying (ما لَهم) — al-Zamakhshari said: for the people of the heavens and the earth there is no (وَلِيٌّ) protector who manages their affairs, and (ولا يُشْرِكُ) He does not make anyone a partner in His judgment (أحَدًا) among them. It was said: it is possible that it refers to the People of the Cave, meaning: this is His power alone, and He did not take any other as a protector for them; He is gentle with them, and He did not associate anyone with Him in this ruling. It is possible that it refers to the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger ﷺ and his opponents, and the verse would be an interjected threat, as Ibn ʿAtiyya said. It was also said: it is possible that it refers to the believers among the people of the heavens and the earth, meaning: He will never take anyone other than Him as a protector. It was said: it refers to those who differ about the length of their stay, meaning: they have no one other than God to manage their affairs, so how could they know more than Him? Or how could they know without His informing them?

The majority recited (﴿ولا يُشْرِكُ﴾) with the yā' as a negation. Mujahid recited it with the yā' and the jazm (apocope). Yaʿqub said: I do not know its justification. Ibn ʿAmir, al-Hasan, Abu Rajaʾ, Qatada, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, Zayd, Humayd ibn al-Wazir on the authority of Yaʿqub, al-Juʿfi, and al-Lu'lu'i on the authority of Abu Bakr recited (ولا تُشْرِكْ) with the tā' and the jazm, as a prohibition.

When He revealed to him what He revealed of the account of the People of the Cave, He commanded him to relate it and recite to his contemporaries what was revealed to him by God Most High from His Book concerning the story of the People of the Cave and others, and that what He revealed to him (لا مُبَدِّلَ) has no changer. (لا مُبَدِّلَ) is general, and (لِكَلِماتِهِ) is also general. The specification is either in (لا مُبَدِّلَ), meaning: there is no changer of it besides Him; do you not see His saying: ﴿وإذا بَدَّلْنا آيَةً مَكانَ آيَةٍ﴾ [an-Nahl: 101]? Or it is in (كَلِماتِهِ), meaning His words that contain information, because what contained other than information was subject to abrogation in part of it. In His command to recite what was revealed to him, and in His informing that there is no changer of (لِكَلِماتِهِ), there is an allusion to the alteration by those who disputed about the People of the Cave and the distortion of their reports. (p-118) The (مُلْتَحَدٌ) is the refuge to which one inclines and turns.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 28–29:

﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. Do not let your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life. And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his own desire and whose affair has become excess.﴾ ﴿And say: The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve. Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose enclosure surrounds them. If they ask for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal that scalds the faces. Wretched is the drink, and evil is the resting place.﴾

The disbelievers of Quraysh said: "If you were to push these people away from yourself, we would sit with you and keep your company." They meant ʿAmmar, Suhayb, Salman, Ibn Masʿud, Bilal and others like them from among the poor. They also said: "The smell of their garments harms us." So the verse ﴿And keep yourself patient﴾ was revealed. It is related from Salman that the one who said this was ʿUyayna ibn Hisn, al-Aqraʿ and their kinsmen from among the Muallafa (those whose hearts were being won over), and so the verse was revealed. According to this, the verse is Madani. But the first view is more sound, because the surah is Makki, and the Muallafa did the same as Quraysh, so the verse answered them.

﴿Keep yourself patient﴾, i.e., restrain it and steady it. Abu Dhuʾayb said:

*So she endured, knowing of that, a free woman who stays firm when the soul of the coward rises up in alarm.*

In the hadith there is a prohibition against *sabr al-hayawan* (the "patience" of animals), i.e., confining an animal in order to shoot it. The particle *maʿa* ("with") implies companionship, accompaniment and agreement. The command to be patient here shows great concern for these people, with whom he was commanded to restrain himself. This is more emphatic than the expression in al-Anʿam: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-Anʿam: 52], and so on. Ibn ʿUmar, Mujahid and Ibrahim said: ﴿morning and evening﴾ refers to the five prayers. Qatada said: it refers to the Fajr and ʿAsr prayers. It may also be said that it is meant in a general sense, i.e., they call upon their Lord constantly (p-119), like the saying: "Zayd was struck on the back and the belly," meaning his whole body, not the specific meaning of the literal wording. The discussion of ﴿morning and evening﴾, regarding its recitation and its grammatical analysis (iʿrab), has already been given in al-Anʿam.

﴿And do not let pass﴾, i.e., do not turn ﴿your eyes﴾ away from them, away from the Gaze toward the sons of this world. *ʿAda* is transitive: you say "ʿada Fulan tawrahu" (Fulan overstepped his bounds) and "jāʾa al-qawmu ʿadā Zaydan" (the people came, excluding Zayd). Therefore we have considered the object to be omitted, so that the verb remains in its original transitivity. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is made transitive with ʿan because *ʿada* is used in the sense of *nabā* and *ʿalā* in your saying: "nabat ʿanhu ʿaynuhu" and "ʿalat ʿanhu ʿaynuhu," when you rush at something and do not cling to it. If you say: what is the purpose of this implicit meaning? Why not say: "wa-lā taʿdūhum ʿaynāka" or "wa-lā taʿdu ʿaynāka ʿanhum"? I say: the purpose is to give the combined meaning of two senses, and that is stronger than giving a single meaning. Do you not see how the meaning returns to your saying: "and let not your eyes break in upon them, passing beyond them to others"? It is like His saying: ﴿and do not consume their wealth along with your wealth﴾ [al-Nisa: 2], i.e., do not add it to yours, consuming it. End of quote. What he mentioned about implicit meaning (tadmin) is not analogical according to the Basrans; it is resorted to only in cases of necessity. But when the word can be applied to its literal meaning, that is preferable.

al-Hasan recited: ﴿wa-lā tuʿdi﴾ from *aʿdā*, and this is also reported from him, and from ʿIsa and al-Aʿmash: ﴿wa-lā taʿdu﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: [this is] transferred by the hamza and by the doubling of the middle radical, and of this is his saying:

*So turn away from what you see, since there is no reclaiming it.*

Because its meaning is: "turn your concern away from what you see." End of quote. Ibn Jinni's companion of al-Lawaʾih said likewise, saying: "This is one I have made transitive by doubling, as it was in the first by hamza." What they both said is not good. Rather, the hamza and the intensive form in this word are not for transitivity, but for matching the pattern *afʿala* and *fuʿila* to the bare verb. We say this because the bare form is transitive, and al-Zamakhshari himself acknowledged this, for he said: "ʿadāhu" is used when you pass beyond it. Then he said: "ʿan" is used with it by implicit meaning, and what is used in implicit meaning is metaphorical, and they do not extend it when they imply it, so they make it transitive by hamza or doubling. If it were transitive by both, it would take two objects, and in this reading it governs only one object, which shows that it is not made transitive by both.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿tuʿridu zinata al-hayati al-dunya﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). End of quote. The companion of the circumstantial clause said: if ﴿ʿaynāka﴾ is taken as the subject, the construction would have been "turidani" (they both desire). If the pronoun *kaf* (you) is taken as the referent, then a circumstantial clause coming from a genitive governed by an annexation (idafa) has a problem in this, because the governing element of the circumstantial clause and of the one it describes differs. Some have permitted this when the annexed noun is a part or like a part. What makes this acceptable here is that the Prophet ﷺ was forbidden to turn away from them and incline toward others. The phrase ﴿ʿaynāka﴾ was used although the intended object is the person himself, because it is by means of the eyes that one attends to a person and looks toward him. So the meaning is: ﴿do not let pass﴾ (you) ﴿from them﴾ your gaze toward others.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿man aghfalnā qalbahu﴾ means: whoever We have made to have a heart heedless of remembrance through abandonment (khidhlan), or whom We found heedless of it, as in your saying: "ajbantuhu" (I found him a coward), "afhamtuhu" (I found him dumbfounded), and "abkhaltuhu" (I found him stingy), when you found him to be so. Or it derives from *aghfala ibilahu*, when one leaves his camels without a mark, i.e., We did not mark him with remembrance, and We did not make them among those whose faith We wrote in their hearts. God has refuted the delusion of the Jabriyya (determinists) by His saying: ﴿and followed his desire﴾. End of quote. This is according to the doctrine of the Muʿtazila. The other interpretation is that of al-Rummani, who was a Muʿtazili; he said: "We did not mark him with what We mark the hearts of believers with, by which their success is made clear," as in: "kataba fi qulubihim al-iman" (He wrote faith in their hearts), from the phrase "biʿir ghufl" (a camel with no mark), and "kitab ghufl" (a book with no pointing). As for the People of the Sunna, they say: God Most High truly made him heedless, and He is the creator of misguidance in him and of heedlessness. Al-Mufaddal said: "We left him empty of the remembrance," which is the Qur'an. Ibn Jurayj said: "We occupied his heart with disbelief and with the overwhelming of wretchedness." The apparent meaning of ﴿man aghfalnā﴾ is the disbelievers of Quraysh. It was also said: ʿUyayna and al-Aqraʿ. The first is better, because the verse is Makki.

ʿUmar ibn Faʾid, Musa al-Aswari, and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd recited ﴿aghfalanā﴾ with a fatha on the *lam*, and *qalbuhu* with a damma on the *ba*, ascribing the verbs to the heart. Ibn Jinni said: "whom we thought heedless of him." Al-Zamakhshari said: "We considered his heart heedless, from *aghfaltuhu*, when I found him heedless." End of quote.

﴿and followed his desire﴾ in seeking lusts. ﴿and whose affair has become excess﴾. Qatada and Mujahid said: lost, wasted. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: extravagance. al-Farraʾ said: abandoned. al-Akhfash said: exceeding the limit. It was said: this is the saying of ʿUtba: "If we become Muslims, the people will become Muslims." Ibn Bahr said: *al-farat* is that which is hasty and swift, as He said: ﴿and man was ever hasty﴾ [al-Isra: 11]. It was also said: regret. It was said: falsehood. Ibn Zayd said: opposing the truth. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: *al-farat* may mean neglect and waste, i.e., his affair which must be upheld, and it may mean excess and extravagance, i.e., his affair and his desire which he is pursuing. End of quote.

The word ﴿al-haqq﴾ may be the predicate of an omitted subject. Ibn ʿAtiyya estimated it as: "This is the truth," i.e., this Qur'an, or this turning away from you, the abandonment of obedience to you, and the patience of the soul with the believers. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿al-haqq﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the meaning is: "The truth has come and the pretexts have been removed, so nothing remains except your choosing for yourselves whatever you wish, of taking the path of salvation or the path of destruction." The imperative and the option are used because, since he has been empowered to choose whichever he wills, it is as though he is given the choice and commanded to choose whatever he wills from the two paths. End of quote. This is according to the Muʿtazila. It is also possible that it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿from your Lord﴾. Al-Dahhak said: it is monotheism. Muqatil said: it is the Qur'an. Makki said: that is, guidance and success and abandonment are from God; He guides whom He wills, so He grants him success and he believes, and He leads astray whom He wills, so He abandons him and he disbelieves; none of that is in my hands. al-Kirmani said: that is, Islam and the Qur'an. This command, whose wording is that of an imperative, has the meaning of threat and warning, and for this reason it is followed by ﴿Indeed We have prepared for the wrongdoers﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said likewise. al-Suddi said: it is abrogated by His saying: ﴿and you do not will except that God wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30]. This is a weak view. The apparent meaning is that the subject of *shaʾa* refers back to *man* ("whoever").

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Whoever God wills faith for, believes; and whoever He does not, does not." End of quote. Ibn ʿAtiyya reported from a group that the pronoun in *shaʾa* refers to God Most High, and it seems that since faith and disbelief follow God's will, He used the form of command, as if its occurrence were certain and it were something commanded and required of him. Abu al-Samal Qunbul recited ﴿Qula al-haqqa﴾ with a fatha on the *lam* wherever it occurs. Abu Hatim said: "That is poor in Arabic." End of quote. It is also reported from him that he used a damma on the *lam* wherever it occurs, as if following the vowel of the *qaf*. He also recited ﴿al-haqqa﴾ in the accusative. The companion of al-Lawaʾih said: it is in the manner of a verbal noun understood, because the verb indicates its verbal noun even if it is not mentioned, so it governs it as a definite noun just as it governs it as an indefinite noun, and its estimated form is: "Say the saying, the truth." The attachment of *min* to an implied element on that basis is like "huwa irjaʾ" (it is postponement). God knows best. al-Hasan and ʿIsa al-Thaqafi recited the *lam* of the imperative with a kasra.

Since faith and disbelief were mentioned, He followed with what was prepared for each of them. He mentioned what was prepared for the disbelievers immediately after His saying ﴿fa-l-yakfur﴾ ("let him disbelieve"), and after that He mentioned what was prepared for the believers. Since the discourse was with the disbelievers, and in the context of what they had asked of the Messenger ﷺ, beginning with what was prepared for them was more important and more emphatic. These are two methods of the Arabs: this method, and the other in which the first item in the division corresponds to the first in mention, and the second to the second.

*Surradiq* (the enclosure): Ibn ʿAbbas said: a wall of fire surrounding them (p-121). Al-Qadi al-Akbar al-Mawardi reported that it is the ocean encircling the world. al-Kalbi reported that it is a neck coming out of the Fire which encircles the disbelievers. It was also said: it is smoke.

﴿And if they ask for relief﴾, i.e., they seek relief from what has befallen them of the Fire, the intensity of its burning, and the severity of their thirst, ﴿they will be relieved﴾ by way of counterpart; otherwise it is not truly relief. It is related in a hadith that it is like the dregs of oil: when it comes near him, the skin of his face falls off into it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is a thick water like the sediment of oil. It is reported from Mujahid that it is pus and black blood. It is reported from Ibn Jubayr: every molten thing whose heat has reached its extreme. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned that it is pus. It is reported from al-Hasan that it is the ash which blisters when it comes out of the oven. It was also said: a kind of tar.

﴿yashwi﴾ ("scalds") is in the position of a descriptive clause for *maʾ* (water), or in the position of a circumstantial clause from it; since it has been described, it is good for a circumstantial clause to come from it. The faces are specifically mentioned because when they drink, its heat comes near their faces. It was also said: the faces are mentioned to represent their whole bodies, and the meaning is that all their skins are cooked by it, like His saying: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted﴾ [al-Nisa: 56]. The object of blame is omitted, its estimated form being ﴿wretched is the drink﴾, i.e., the water with which they are relieved. The pronoun in *sa'at* (evil is) refers back to the Fire. *Murtafaq* (resting place): Ibn ʿAbbas said: the dwelling; ʿAta said: the place of rest; al-Qutabi said: the sitting place; Mujahid said: the gathering place. al-Tabari denied that a meaning could be known for Mujahid's view, but that is not so: Mujahid went to the sense of companionship, from which comes *rufqa* (company). Abu ʿUbayda said: the reclining place. al-Zajjaj said: the reclining upon the elbow. al-Zamakhshari took this and said: a reclining place from the elbow (*mirfaq*), and this is for the sake of rhyming with His saying ﴿and good is it as a resting place﴾ [al-Kahf: 31]; otherwise there is no resting or reclining for the people of the Fire. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is "evil as a place sought for ease," because whoever seeks ease from Hell will not find it. Ibn ʿAtiyya said, close to the view of Ibn al-Anbari, and said: "The more apparent to me is that *murtafaq* means the thing whose ease is sought by reclining and other things." Abu ʿAbdullah al-Razi said: the meaning is "wretched are these companions, and wretched is the place of companionship, the Fire."

*So turn away from what you see, since there is no reclaiming it.*

Because its meaning is: "turn your concern away from what you see." End of quote. Ibn Jinni's companion of al-Lawaʾih said likewise, saying: "This is one I have made transitive by doubling, as it was in the first by hamza." What they both said is not good. Rather, the hamza and the intensive form in this word are not for transitivity, but for matching the pattern *afʿala* and *fuʿila* to the bare verb. We say this because the bare form is transitive, and al-Zamakhshari himself acknowledged this, for he said: "ʿadāhu" is used when you pass beyond it. Then he said: "ʿan" is used with it by implicit meaning, and what is used in implicit meaning is metaphorical, and they do not extend it when they imply it, so they make it transitive by hamza or doubling. If it were transitive by both, it would take two objects, and in this reading it governs only one object, which shows that it is not made transitive by both.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿tuʿridu zinata al-hayati al-dunya﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). End of quote. The companion of the circumstantial clause said: if ﴿ʿaynāka﴾ is taken as the subject, the construction would have been "turidani" (they both desire). If the pronoun *kaf* (you) is taken as the referent, then a circumstantial clause coming from a genitive governed by an annexation (idafa) has a problem in this, because the governing element of the circumstantial clause and of the one it describes differs. Some have permitted this when the annexed noun is a part or like a part. What makes this acceptable here is that the Prophet ﷺ was forbidden to turn away from them and incline toward others. The phrase ﴿ʿaynāka﴾ was used although the intended object is the person himself, because it is by means of the eyes that one attends to a person and looks toward him. So the meaning is: ﴿do not let pass﴾ (you) ﴿from them﴾ your gaze toward others.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿man aghfalnā qalbahu﴾ means: whoever We have made to have a heart heedless of remembrance through abandonment (khidhlan), or whom We found heedless of it, as in your saying: "ajbantuhu" (I found him a coward), "afhamtuhu" (I found him dumbfounded), and "abkhaltuhu" (I found him stingy), when you found him to be so. Or it derives from *aghfala ibilahu*, when one leaves his camels without a mark, i.e., We did not mark him with remembrance, and We did not make them among those whose faith We wrote in their hearts. God has refuted the delusion of the Jabriyya (determinists) by His saying: ﴿and followed his desire﴾. End of quote. This is according to the doctrine of the Muʿtazila. The other interpretation is that of al-Rummani, who was a Muʿtazili; he said: "We did not mark him with what We mark the hearts of believers with, by which their success is made clear," as in: "kataba fi qulubihim al-iman" (He wrote faith in their hearts), from the phrase "biʿir ghufl" (a camel with no mark), and "kitab ghufl" (a book with no pointing). As for the People of the Sunna, they say: God Most High truly made him heedless, and He is the creator of misguidance in him and of heedlessness. Al-Mufaddal said: "We left him empty of the remembrance," which is the Qur'an. Ibn Jurayj said: "We occupied his heart with disbelief and with the overwhelming of wretchedness." The apparent meaning of ﴿man aghfalnā﴾ is the disbelievers of Quraysh. It was also said: ʿUyayna and al-Aqraʿ. The first is better, because the verse is Makki.

ʿUmar ibn Faʾid, Musa al-Aswari, and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd recited ﴿aghfalanā﴾ with a fatha on the *lam*, and *qalbuhu* with a damma on the *ba*, ascribing the verbs to the heart. Ibn Jinni said: "whom we thought heedless of him." Al-Zamakhshari said: "We considered his heart heedless, from *aghfaltuhu*, when I found him heedless." End of quote.

﴿and followed his desire﴾ in seeking lusts. ﴿and whose affair has become excess﴾. Qatada and Mujahid said: lost, wasted. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: extravagance. al-Farraʾ said: abandoned. al-Akhfash said: exceeding the limit. It was said: this is the saying of ʿUtba: "If we become Muslims, the people will become Muslims." Ibn Bahr said: *al-farat* is that which is hasty and swift, as He said: ﴿and man was ever hasty﴾ [al-Isra: 11]. It was also said: regret. It was said: falsehood. Ibn Zayd said: opposing the truth. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: *al-farat* may mean neglect and waste, i.e., his affair which must be upheld, and it may mean excess and extravagance, i.e., his affair and his desire which he is pursuing. End of quote.

The word ﴿al-haqq﴾ may be the predicate of an omitted subject. Ibn ʿAtiyya estimated it as: "This is the truth," i.e., this Qur'an, or this turning away from you, the abandonment of obedience to you, and the patience of the soul with the believers. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿al-haqq﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the meaning is: "The truth has come and the pretexts have been removed, so nothing remains except your choosing for yourselves whatever you wish, of taking the path of salvation or the path of destruction." The imperative and the option are used because, since he has been empowered to choose whichever he wills, it is as though he is given the choice and commanded to choose whatever he wills from the two paths. End of quote. This is according to the Muʿtazila. It is also possible that it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿from your Lord﴾. Al-Dahhak said: it is monotheism. Muqatil said: it is the Qur'an. Makki said: that is, guidance and success and abandonment are from God; He guides whom He wills, so He grants him success and he believes, and He leads astray whom He wills, so He abandons him and he disbelieves; none of that is in my hands. al-Kirmani said: that is, Islam and the Qur'an. This command, whose wording is that of an imperative, has the meaning of threat and warning, and for this reason it is followed by ﴿Indeed We have prepared for the wrongdoers﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said likewise. al-Suddi said: it is abrogated by His saying: ﴿and you do not will except that God wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30]. This is a weak view. The apparent meaning is that the subject of *shaʾa* refers back to *man* ("whoever").

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Whoever God wills faith for, believes; and whoever He does not, does not." End of quote. Ibn ʿAtiyya reported from a group that the pronoun in *shaʾa* refers to God Most High, and it seems that since faith and disbelief follow God's will, He used the form of command, as if its occurrence were certain and it were something commanded and required of him. Abu al-Samal Qunbul recited ﴿Qula al-haqqa﴾ with a fatha on the *lam* wherever it occurs. Abu Hatim said: "That is poor in Arabic." End of quote. It is also reported from him that he used a damma on the *lam* wherever it occurs, as if following the vowel of the *qaf*. He also recited ﴿al-haqqa﴾ in the accusative. The companion of al-Lawaʾih said: it is in the manner of a verbal noun understood, because the verb indicates its verbal noun even if it is not mentioned, so it governs it as a definite noun just as it governs it as an indefinite noun, and its estimated form is: "Say the saying, the truth." The attachment of *min* to an implied element on that basis is like "huwa irjaʾ" (it is postponement). God knows best. al-Hasan and ʿIsa al-Thaqafi recited the *lam* of the imperative with a kasra.

Since faith and disbelief were mentioned, He followed with what was prepared for each of them. He mentioned what was prepared for the disbelievers immediately after His saying ﴿fa-l-yakfur﴾ ("let him disbelieve"), and after that He mentioned what was prepared for the believers. Since the discourse was with the disbelievers, and in the context of what they had asked of the Messenger ﷺ, beginning with what was prepared for them was more important and more emphatic. These are two methods of the Arabs: this method, and the other in which the first item in the division corresponds to the first in mention, and the second to the second.

*Surradiq* (the enclosure): Ibn ʿAbbas said: a wall of fire surrounding them (p-121). Al-Qadi al-Akbar al-Mawardi reported that it is the ocean encircling the world. al-Kalbi reported that it is a neck coming out of the Fire which encircles the disbelievers. It was also said: it is smoke.

﴿And if they ask for relief﴾, i.e., they seek relief from what has befallen them of the Fire, the intensity of its burning, and the severity of their thirst, ﴿they will be relieved﴾ by way of counterpart; otherwise it is not truly relief. It is related in a hadith that it is like the dregs of oil: when it comes near him, the skin of his face falls off into it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is a thick water like the sediment of oil. It is reported from Mujahid that it is pus and black blood. It is reported from Ibn Jubayr: every molten thing whose heat has reached its extreme. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned that it is pus. It is reported from al-Hasan that it is the ash which blisters when it comes out of the oven. It was also said: a kind of tar.

﴿yashwi﴾ ("scalds") is in the position of a descriptive clause for *maʾ* (water), or in the position of a circumstantial clause from it; since it has been described, it is good for a circumstantial clause to come from it. The faces are specifically mentioned because when they drink, its heat comes near their faces. It was also said: the faces are mentioned to represent their whole bodies, and the meaning is that all their skins are cooked by it, like His saying: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted﴾ [al-Nisa: 56]. The object of blame is omitted, its estimated form being ﴿wretched is the drink﴾, i.e., the water with which they are relieved. The pronoun in *sa'at* (evil is) refers back to the Fire. *Murtafaq* (resting place): Ibn ʿAbbas said: the dwelling; ʿAta said: the place of rest; al-Qutabi said: the sitting place; Mujahid said: the gathering place. al-Tabari denied that a meaning could be known for Mujahid's view, but that is not so: Mujahid went to the sense of companionship, from which comes *rufqa* (company). Abu ʿUbayda said: the reclining place. al-Zajjaj said: the reclining upon the elbow. al-Zamakhshari took this and said: a reclining place from the elbow (*mirfaq*), and this is for the sake of rhyming with His saying ﴿and good is it as a resting place﴾ [al-Kahf: 31]; otherwise there is no resting or reclining for the people of the Fire. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is "evil as a place sought for ease," because whoever seeks ease from Hell will not find it. Ibn ʿAtiyya said, close to the view of Ibn al-Anbari, and said: "The more apparent to me is that *murtafaq* means the thing whose ease is sought by reclining and other things." Abu ʿAbdullah al-Razi said: the meaning is "wretched are these companions, and wretched is the place of companionship, the Fire."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 30–31:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not waste the reward of one who does good in deed.﴾ ﴿For them are Gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and they will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade, reclining therein upon couches. How excellent the reward, and how good a resting place.﴾

When Exalted God mentioned the state of the people of disbelief and what He has prepared for them in the Fire, He mentioned the state of the people of faith and what He has prepared for them in Paradise. The predicate (khabar) of inna may be the clause "for them" (ula'ika lahum). The statement "indeed We do not waste" is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "Similar to this kind of parenthesis is the saying of the poet:

*Indeed the Caliph, indeed God has clothed him
In the mantle of kingship, by which the outcomes are hoped for.*

End of quotation. In his words "indeed God has clothed him," it is not necessary that it be a parenthesis. The subject of inna and its predicate, which is "by which the outcomes are hoped for," may be the case; it is possible that "indeed God has clothed him" is the predicate. It is also possible that the predicate is His saying ﴿indeed We do not waste the reward of﴾, with the returning pronoun omitted, its estimated form being ﴿one who does good in deed﴾ [among them], or it is His saying ﴿one who does good in deed﴾ according to the view of al-Akhfash regarding linking the clause to the noun when it is the subject in meaning, because ﴿one who does good in deed﴾ are ﴿those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. So it is as if he said: "Indeed We do not waste their reward." It is also possible that the two clauses are two predicates, according to the view of those who allow the subject to have two or more predicates without the condition that they be such, or that they be in the meaning of one predicate.

If the predicate of inna is His saying ﴿indeed We do not waste﴾, then His saying "ula'ika" (those) is a resumptive informative statement (isti'naf) clarifying what was left vague in His saying ﴿indeed We do not waste﴾ regarding the vague reward.

ʿĪsā al-Thaqafī read (lā nuḍayyiʿu) from ḍayyaʿa, making it transitive by gemination, while the majority read from aḍāʿa, making it transitive by the hamza. When He mentioned the place of the people of disbelief, which is the Fire, He mentioned the place of the people of faith, which is ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ [al-Tawba: 72]. When He mentioned there what they are relieved with, which is water like molten brass, He mentioned here what is specific to the people of Paradise: the rivers flowing beneath them. Then He mentioned the favors He bestowed upon them of adornment and clothing, which are an outward adornment.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: each one will be adorned with three bracelets: a bracelet of gold, a bracelet of silver, and a bracelet of pearls and rubies.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The first "min" (from) is for the starting point (ibtidaʾ), and the second is for explanation (tabyin), and the indefinite form of "bracelets" is for vagueness regarding the excellence of their quality. End of quotation. It is possible that the "min" in His saying ﴿of gold﴾ is partitive (tabʿiḍ), not explanatory.

Abān on the authority of ʿĀṣim read (min asāwira min) without an alif, with an added hāʾ, and it is the plural of siwār (bracelet). Abān also transmitted on the authority of ʿĀṣim, and Ibn Abī Ḥammād on the authority of Abū Bakr, the reading (wa-yalbisūna) with a kasra on the bāʾ.

Ibn Muḥayṣin read (wa-istabraqa) with a connecting hamza and a fatḥa on the qāf wherever it occurs, making it a past-tense verb on the pattern istafʿala, from al-bariq (glitter). In this case istafʿala would be equivalent to the bare form which is barraqa, just as you say qarra and istaqarra with a fatḥa on the qāf. Al-Ahwazī mentioned this in al-Iqnaʿ on the authority of Ibn Muḥayṣin. Ibn Muḥayṣin alone said: (wa-istabraq) with a connecting hamza and a fatḥa on the qāf wherever it does not take tanwīn. End of quotation. Its apparent meaning is that it is not a past-tense verb, but a noun prevented from taking tanwīn (ism mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf). Ibn Khālawayh said: Ibn Muḥayṣin made it istafʿala from al-bariq, so its apparent meaning is that it is a past-tense verb. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ disagreed with both of them. Ibn Muḥayṣin said: (wa-istabraq) with a connecting hamza throughout the Qur'an. It is possible that he dropped the hamza for lightness, contrary to analogy. It is also possible that he made it Arabic from barraqa yabruqu, buruq (to glitter), which is when a garment shines because of its newness and freshness. Its pattern would then be istafʿala from that, and when it became a proper name he treated it as a verb regarding the connecting of the hamza, and as one of the fully declinable nouns regarding diptotic prohibition and tanwīn. Most of the exegetes hold that it is Arabic and not an arabized foreign word that entered their speech and they inflected it.

It is possible that the two statements are two narrations from him: a fatḥa on the qāf with tanwīn, and the form with diptosis.

Abu al-Fath Ibn Jinnī mentioned the reading with a fatḥa on the qāf and said: "This is a slip, or like a slip." End of quotation. He said that because making it a noun and prohibiting its tanwīn is not permissible, since it is not a proper name, while it is possible to make it a past-tense verb, so this reading is not a slip.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The plural of (sundus), which is the thinnest of silk brocade, and (istabraq), which is the thick kind, combines the two kinds. The adornment is mentioned before the clothing, because jewelry is greater in the soul, dearer to the heart, more valuable in price, and sweeter to the eye. The verb's form is passive, the subject unnamed, to indicate that they are honored with this, and do not take it upon themselves, as the poet said:

*Maidens in seclusion, in protection and in comfort,
They are adorned with rubies and fine pearls, scattered.*

He attributed the clothing to them because a person takes that upon himself, especially if he was exposed in his nakedness. He described the garments as green because it is the best of colors, and the soul is more delighted by it than by others. A report has been transmitted regarding this that it increases the brightness of sight. Some of the men of letters said:

*Four things dispel every worry and grief:
Water, greenery, a garden, and a beautiful face.*

He specified reclining because it is the posture of the pampered and of kings on their couches. Ibn Muḥayṣin read ﴿upon the couches﴾ by transferring the hamza to the definite article lām and assimilating the lām into (fīhā), so the alif of (ʿalā) is dropped, owing to the supposed quiescence of the lām of the definite article, and it is pronounced (ʿalarāʾik). Similar to this is the saying of the poet:

*So no soul has risen upon the earth, a pure one,
Nor any other except Sulaymān, who knows its affairs.*

He means (ʿalā al-arḍ, upon the earth). The object of praise is omitted, meaning: "How excellent is the reward, what they were promised." The pronoun in ﴿and how good﴾ [al-Furqān: 76] refers to the Gardens.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 32–36 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Set forth for them the parable of two men. For one of them We had made two gardens of grapevines, and We surrounded them with date palms, and We placed between them fields of crops.﴾ ﴿Both gardens yielded their produce and did not fall short in anything, and We caused a river to gush forth between them.﴾ ﴿He had fruit, so he said to his companion while arguing with him: "I have more wealth than you and greater support in men."﴾ ﴿He entered his garden while wronging himself, and said: "I do not think this will ever perish.﴾ ﴿Nor do I think the Hour will come. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a final destination."﴾ ﴿His companion said to him, while arguing with him: "Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then fashioned you as a man?"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 37] ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I do not associate anyone with my Lord.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 38] ﴿Why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "What Allah wills [has come to pass]; there is no power except through Allah"? If you see me as less than you in wealth and children,﴾ [Al-Kahf: 39] ﴿then perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden, and send upon it a calamity from the sky, so that it becomes barren land, slippery [with mud].﴾ [Al-Kahf: 40] ﴿Or its water will sink into the earth, and you will never be able to seek it.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 41]

*Ḥaffahu* (حَفَّهُ): he circled it, going around it from its sides. The poet said:

Muqatil said: his name was Tamlikha, and he is the one mentioned in al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿One of them said, "Indeed, I had a companion"﴾ [Al-Saffat: 51]. And from Ibn 'Abbas: they were two sons of a king from the Children of Israel; one of them spent his wealth in the way of Allah, and the other disbelieved and occupied himself with the adornment of the world and the growing of his wealth. And from Makki: they were two men from the Children of Israel who partnered in the wealth of a disbeliever, six thousand, and divided it. It was also narrated that they were two blacksmiths who earned wealth. It was narrated that they inherited eight thousand dinars from their father. The disbeliever bought land for a thousand, built a house for a thousand, married a woman for a thousand, and bought servants and goods for a thousand. The believer bought land in Paradise for a thousand and gave it in charity; he set aside a thousand as a dowry for the houris and gave it in charity; and he bought the eternal youths (al-wildan al-mukhalladun) for a thousand and gave it in charity. Then he was afflicted by need, so he sat on his brother's road, and when he passed by with his retinue, he approached him, but he drove him away and rebuked him for giving away his wealth in charity.

The pronoun in (*lahum*) refers to the arrogant ones who asked the Messenger (ﷺ) to drive away the weak believers. So the disbelieving man corresponds to the arrogant ones, and the believing man corresponds to the weak among the believers. The connection between this verse and the one before it becomes apparent by setting forth this parable, since the one who associates partners [with Allah] boasted of his wealth and supporters, and this can pass away, so that the rich becomes poor. Rather, true pride lies in obedience to Allah. The estimated meaning of ﴿Set forth for them a parable﴾ is the story of "two men." The clause *ja'alnā* (and *ja'alnā*) is an explanation of the parable, so it has no place in grammatical analysis (i'rab). It is permissible for it to have a place in the accusative as a qualifier (na't) of "two men."

The subject is left vague in His saying ﴿We had made for one of them﴾, and it is clarified that he is the disbeliever who doubted the resurrection. He, exalted is He, left vague the place of the two gardens, since specifying it has no great benefit. Ibrahim ibn al-Qasim the scribe mentioned in his book *Fī ʿAjāʾib al-Bilād* (On the Wonders of the Lands) that the lake of Tinnis was these two gardens, and that they belonged to two brothers. One of them sold his share to the other and spent it in obedience to Allah, until the other reproached him, and this dialogue took place between them. He said: Allah drowned them in a single night, and it is these two whom He meant by this verse. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Consider this state which Allah described, for a person can hardly imagine anything more splendid among the means of livelihood of people: two grape gardens surrounded by date palms, with an open space between them that is cultivated with all kinds of grains, and abundant flowing water, all of it irrigated from the river.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿two gardens of grapevines﴾: orchards of vineyards. ﴿And We surrounded them﴾ ﴿with date palms, and We made﴾ the palms surround the two gardens. This is something landowners (al-dahāqīn) prefer for their vineyards: to make them enclosed by fruit-bearing trees. End of quote.

The majority read ﴿Both gardens﴾ (*kilta al-jannatayni*). In the codex of 'Abd Allah it is *kilā al-jannatayni*, with the masculine form, because the feminine of "the two gardens" is metaphorical (majāzī). Then he read ﴿yielded﴾ (*ātat*) with the feminine, because it is a feminine pronoun, so it became like the expression: "the sun rose and shone" (*ṭala'a al-shamsu wa ashraqat*). Al-Zamakhshari said: He made it a land comprising foodstuffs and fruits, and described the cultivation as continuous and interlaced, with nothing in between to cut it off or separate them, along with a good appearance and an elegant arrangement. Then he described the essence of goodness and its source in the matter of irrigation, making it the best of what is watered with, which is irrigation by a flowing river within them. Al-A'mash, Abu Raja', and Abu 'Amr read with a *sukūn* on the *mīm* in both, as a lightening, or as the plural of *thamarah* like *badanah* and *budun*. According to this meaning, he had many possessions of gold, silver, and other things besides the two gardens, so he was able to cultivate the two gardens. As for the one who read with the *fatḥah*, there is no difficulty that it refers to the fruit of the trees. The apparent reading is that the one in the state is the speaker, meaning he was disputing with him in his denial of the resurrection and in his associating others with Allah. It is also said that it is a state of the companion, meaning the Muslim, who was arguing with him through admonition and calling him to Allah and to belief in the resurrection. The apparent reading is that *afʿal* is comparative, and that his companion had wealth and men, and was not poor as the historians mentioned, and that he came asking him for help. This is supported by the fact that he answered him with His saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾ [Al-Kahf: 39]. This is in the manner of disbelievers in boasting of abundant wealth, the might of their clan, arrogance, and deception by what they attained of the rubbish of the world. His saying to his companion corresponds to the saying of 'Uyayna and al-Aqra' to the Messenger (ﷺ): "We are the masters of the Arabs and the people of the tents and the cities, so push away from us Salman and his fellows." He meant by *nafar* his supporters and retinue. It is said: sons who are males, because they go out with him (*yanfirūna maʿahu*) and not females. It was used as evidence that he was not his brother by His saying ﴿and more powerful in men﴾, since if he were his brother, his men and clan would be the men of his brother and clan. According to the two previous interpretations, this objection does not arise. As for the one who interprets *nafar* as the clan that they share in common, the objection does arise. The singular "garden" in His saying ﴿and he entered his garden﴾ is also in terms of existence, since he could not enter both at one time.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: why did he use the singular "garden" after the dual? I say: its meaning is "he entered what was his garden, the thing he had, having no garden other than it." He means that he has no share in the garden promised to the God-fearing, so what he owned in this world is his garden and nothing else. He did not intend the two gardens nor either one of them. End of quote.

What he said is not conceivable, because His saying "and he entered his garden" is a report from Allah, exalted is He, of that disbeliever's entering his garden. So in the report it must be intended that he entered one of his two gardens, since it is impossible for him to enter both together at one time. The meaning of ﴿and he entered his garden﴾ is that he showed his companion what it had of splendor, freshness, and beauty.

﴿While he was wronging himself﴾ is a circumstantial clause, meaning: he was a disbeliever in the blessing of his Lord, deceived by what he possessed, doubting the ending of what He had bestowed upon him, and doubting the resurrection about which his companion argued with him. The apparent reading is that the demonstrative in His saying "this" (*hādhihi*) refers to the garden he entered. By "the eternity" he meant the eternity of his life, because of the length of his hope and the persistence of his heedlessness, and because of his good management of it with the wealth and servants he had been given. So it would remain for the duration of his life in its state of beauty and freshness. Sense perception requires that all the conditions of this world are not lasting, or else one would have to hold the eternity of the world, and that whatever this garden contained, the individual fruits perish, and other individuals replace them, and so on always. The statement of one who said that the demonstrative "this" may refer to the form of the heavens and the earth and kinds of created beings is far-fetched. His words indicate that the dialogue that took place between them concerned the annihilation of this world, of which this garden is a part, and the resurrection in the Hereafter, which his companion had established for him as two matters he doubted.

Then he swore that if he were returned to his Lord, on the assumption and supposition, analogizing the Hereafter to this world, and as his companion claims, he would surely find something better than his garden in this world. This is out of covetousness and wishful desire regarding God, and a claim to His honor toward him and his station with Him, and that what He granted him the two gardens in this world was only because of his deserving it, and that he would have this deservedness wherever he turned, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, for me with Him is the best [reward]﴾ [Fussilat: 50].

As for what God Exalted related of what al-As ibn Wa'il said, "I will surely be given wealth and children" (Maryam: 77), it is not on the same footing as the statement of this man to his companion, because the sinner intended mockery while being firmly set in denial, whereas this man said in substance: if there is a return, then my condition will be such-and-such.

Ibn al-Zubayr, Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Bahriyya, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Ibn Munadhir, Nafi' and Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir read ﴿minhuma﴾ in the dual, with the pronoun referring back to the two gardens; and likewise it is in the codices of Makkah, Madinah and Syria. The Kufans and Abu Amr read ﴿minha﴾ in the singular, with the pronoun referring back to the garden that was entered; and likewise it is in the codices of Kufa and Basra. The meaning of ﴿munqalaban﴾ is "return" and "outcome," i.e., the return of the Hereafter, because its permanence makes it better than the return of this world because of its passing away. ﴿Munqalaban﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) transferred from the subject (mubtada').
