Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-wilāyah* with a fatha means help (*al-nuṣrah*), and *al-tawallī*, with a kasra, means authority and dominion (*al-sulṭān wa-l-mulk*). It has been read with both. The meaning is: there, that is, in that station and that state, help belongs to God alone; no one else possesses it, and no one other than Him is able to provide it, confirming His saying: ﴿and he had no party to help him apart from God﴾. Or *hunālika* means: authority and dominion belong to God; He cannot be overcome, and He is not prevented from anything. Or: in such a severe state, God is the one to whom every person in distress turns and believes. That is, his saying, ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord﴾, is a word he was compelled to utter, and he said it in terror because of the ill omen of his unbelief; had it not been for that, he would not have said it. It is also possible that the meaning is: ﴿there guardianship belongs to God﴾, He helps His friends, the believers, against the unbelievers, avenges them, and heals their hearts from their enemies. That is, He helped the believer, his brother, by what He did to the unbeliever, and confirmed his statement, ﴿Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden and will send upon it a bolt from heaven﴾. This is supported by His saying: ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome﴾, that is, for His friends. End of quote.

The two grammarians (Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisai, i.e. "the two Naḥwīs" as Abu Hayyan designates them, the Kufan and Basran pair), Ḥumayd, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Munadhir, al-Yazidi and Ibn ʿIsa al-Isbahani read *al-ḥaqq* (الحَقُّ) with a damma on the qaf, as an adjective of *al-wilāyah*. The rest of the seven read it with a kasra on the qaf, as an adjective of God, exalted is He. Ubayy read *hunālika al-wilāyatu al-ḥaqqu lillāh* with *al-ḥaqq* in the nominative as an adjective of *al-wilāyah*, and placed it before *lillāh*. Abu Haywah, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, Abu al-Sammal and Yaʿqub, on the authority of ʿIṣmah from Abu ʿAmr, read *lillāh al-ḥaqqa* with a fatha on the qaf. Al-Zamakhshari said: as an emphatic (*taʾkīd*), like your saying, "This is the servant of God, the truth, not falsehood." It is a fine and eloquent reading. ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, may God have mercy on him and be pleased with him, was one of the most eloquent and sincere of people. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari had said: "ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, may God have mercy on him," end of quote. Thus he (Abu Hayyan's source) invoked mercy upon him and expressed approval of him, because he is among the earliest great shaykhs of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), and he was in the highest degree of asceticism and worship, and there are reports about that. However, the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) criticize him and his followers. On this, Abu ʿAmr al-Dani says in his poem called *al-Munabbihah*:

Ibn ʿUbayd is the shaykh of i'tizal (Mu'tazilism),
and the initiator of innovation and misguidance.

The Hasan, al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read *ʿuqban* (عُقْبًا) with a sukun on the qaf and tanwin. On the authority of ʿĀṣim, it is read *ʿuqbā* (عُقْبى) with the feminine *alif* of the restricted (maqṣūrah) pattern on the form *rujʿā*. The majority read it with a damma on the qaf and tanwin. All three readings have the same meaning: the outcome (*al-ʿāqibah*).

﴿His companion said to him while he was disputing with him: "Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then fashioned you as a man?"﴾ ﴿"But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I associate none with my Lord."﴾ ﴿"And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: 'What Allah wills [has come to pass]; there is no power except through Allah'? If you see me as less than you in wealth and children—﴾ ﴿perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden and will send upon it a calamity from heaven, so that it becomes barren, slippery earth,﴾ ﴿or its water sinks into the ground, and you will not be able to find it."﴾ ﴿And his fruit was encompassed [by ruin], so he began to wring his hands over what he had spent on it, while it lay in ruins upon its trellises, and he said: "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord!"﴾ ﴿And he had no group to help him against Allah, nor was he one who could defend himself.﴾ ﴿There, guardianship belongs to Allah, the Truth. He is best in reward and best in outcome.﴾

(p-127) ﴿وهُوَ يُحاوِرُهُ﴾ ["while he was disputing with him" (18:34)] is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject, and the "companion" here is the believer. Ubayy read وهو يُخاصِمُهُ ("while he was quarrelling with him"). This is a recitation of interpretation (qirā'at tafsīr), not a recitation of transmission (qirā'at riwāya), because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf and because what is transmitted by mass transmission (tawātur) is (هو يُحاوِرُهُ), not يُخاصِمُهُ. ﴿أكَفَرْتَ﴾ ["Do you disbelieve"] is an interrogative of denial and rebuke, since he associated others with Allah. Thābit al-Bunānī recited: ويلَكَ ﴿أكَفَرْتَ﴾ ("Woe to you! Do you disbelieve?"). This is an explanation of the sense of rebuke and denial, not a recitation established from the Messenger ﷺ. Then he (the believer) alerted him to the origin of his creation and his coming into existence after non-existence, and that this is evidence for the possibility of resurrection from the graves. Then this was confirmed by the report of the truthful ones, who are the messengers, upon them be peace. His saying ﴿خَلَقَكَ مِن تُرابٍ﴾ ["created you from dust"] may mean either: the creation of your origin from dust, namely Adam, peace be upon him, and the creation of his origin is a cause of his creation, so creating him is creating [the man] himself; or it may mean that a man's semen is generated from nourishment that returns to the dust. Thus he alerted him first to that from which his father's semen was generated, then secondly to the drop (nuṭfa), which is his father's semen. As for what is reported, that an angel is entrusted with the drop and casts a little dust into it before it enters the womb, this requires authentic transmission.

Then he alerted him to His making him a man (تَسْوِيَتِهِ رَجُلًا), which is creating him balanced, with sound limbs. It is said of a boy when his youth is complete: "he has become balanced" (قَدِ اسْتَوى). It was also said: he reminded him of Allah's blessing upon him in being a man and not created as a female. By these transitions he alerted him to the perfection of His power and that nothing can overpower Him. Al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿سَوّاكَ﴾ ["fashioned you"] means He made you proportionate and completed you as a human, a male who reached the stage of men, and that made him a disbeliever in Allah, a denier of His blessings, because of his doubt about resurrection, just as one who denies the Messenger is a disbeliever. End of quote. (رَجُلًا) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Al-Ḥawfī said: (رَجُلًا) is governed by سَوّى, meaning: He made you (a man). Its apparent meaning is that sawwā is transitive to two objects. Since the interrogative is not one of seeking information but of denial and rebuke, it is in reality an affirmation of his disbelief and a report about it, because its meaning is: "You have disbelieved in the One who..." Then he (the believer) added, reporting about himself: ﴿لَكِنّا هو اللَّهُ رَبِّي﴾ ["But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord"], an affirmation of the oneness of Allah and that he does not associate anyone with Him.

The Kufans, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Kathīr, and Nāfiʿ in the transmission of Warsh and Qālūn read لَكِنَّ with a doubled nūn without an alif in pause (waṣl), and with an alif in stopping (waqf). Its original form is وَلَكِنْ أنا: the hamza's vowel was transferred to the nūn of lākin and the hamza was dropped, so two identical consonants met and one was assimilated into the other. It was also said: the hamza of anā was dropped contrary to analogy, so the nūn of lākin, which is sukūn, met the nūn of anā and was assimilated into it. As for stopping, he retained the alif of anā, which is the well-known form at stopping on anā; while in connected speech the well-known form is to omit it. Abū ʿAmr replaced it with an alif in stopping; and in one transmission he stopped on لَكِنَّهُ, which Ibn Khālawayh mentioned. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: Hārūn related from Abū ʿAmr: لَكِنَّهُ ﴿هُوَ اللَّهُ رَبِّي﴾ with a pronoun attached to lākin.

Ibn ʿĀmir, Nāfiʿ in the transmission of al-Musayyabī, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī, Abū Bahriyya, Yaʿqūb in one transmission, and Abū ʿUmar, and in another transmission Kardam, Warsh in one transmission, and Abū Jaʿfar read it with the alif retained both in pause and connected speech. In pause it is clear; in connection, the Banū Tamīm retain it in speech, while others retain it only under poetic necessity; so it came in the dialect of Banū Tamīm. From Abū Jaʿfar, the alif was omitted both in connection and in pause, and this is from the transmission of al-Hāshimī. The retention of the alif in connection also indicates that the original form of this is لَكِنِ أنا.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: What made this good, i.e., retaining the alif in connection, is that the alif came as a substitute for the omitted hamza. End of quote. What also supports this is the recitation of a group: لَكِنَنا, with the hamza omitted and the two nūns lightened. Al-Zamakhsharī also said, and similar to it—i.e., similar to the assimilation of the nūn of lākin into the nūn of anā after the hamza is dropped—is the saying of a poet:

*And you shoot me with your glance—you are the guilty one—and you shun me. But, as for you, I do not shun you.*

I.e., lākin anā lā aqlīki ("but I do not shun you"). End of quote. What he said about the verse is not necessarily the only possibility, since it may be that the original is لَكِنَّنِي, and the subject of lākinna was elided; scholars mention that its elision is eloquent when the context indicates it, and they cite as evidence the saying of a poet:

*Had you been a Ḍabbī, you would have known my kinship, but you are a Zanjī with great lips.*

I.e., but you are a Zanjī. Abū ʿAlī (al-Fārisī) allowed that lākin may have been attached to the nūn of plurality found in kharajnā and ḍarabnā, and the assimilation occurred because of the meeting of identical letters; then he used the singular in rabbī according to meaning; had he followed the wording, he would have said rabbanā. End of quote. This is a distant interpretation. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: What is possible for lākinnā is that it be the well-known one among the sisters of inna, meaning: "but my saying is: He is Allah, my Lord"; however, I do not know anyone who reads it so, either in connection or in pause. End of quote. Abū al-Qāsim Yūsuf ibn ʿAlī ibn Jubāra al-Hudhalī mentioned in his book al-Kāmil fī al-Qirāʾāt the following text: with the omission of the alif in both states—i.e., connection and pause—the Ḥimṣī, Ibn ʿUtba, Qutayba other than al-Thaqafī, and Yūnus from Abū ʿUmar. By "Ḥimṣī" he means Ibn Abī ʿAbla, Abū Ḥaywa, and Abū Bahriyya. Ubayy and al-Ḥasan read لَكِنِ أنا هو اللَّهُ ("but I, He is Allah") with separation, with the hamza unassimilated and fully pronounced; Ibn ʿAṭiyya related this from Ibn Masʿūd. ʿĪsā al-Thaqafī read لَكِنَّ هو اللَّهُ without أنا; Ibn Khālawayh related it from Ibn Masʿūd, and al-Ahwāzī related it from al-Ḥasan. As for the one who affirms (هو), it is the pronoun of the matter and affair (ḍamīr al-amr wa-al-shaʾn), and there is an elided saying: "but I say: He is Allah, my Lord." It may also refer back to the one who "created you from dust," i.e., "I say: He—that is, your Creator—is Allah, my Lord." (رَبِّي) is an attribute (naʿt), or an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān), or a substitution (badal). It is also possible not to posit an elided "I say," so that anā is the subject; (هو) is the second subject, the pronoun of the matter; (اللَّهُ) is the third subject; (رَبِّي) is its predicate; the third is a predicate of the second; and the second with its predicate is a predicate of anā; the link back to it is the yāʾ in rabbī. The structure becomes like: Hind, he is Zayd, the one who strikes her. On the transmission of Hārūn, it is possible that (هو) is an emphasis of the object pronoun in lākinnahu, which refers back to "the One who created you"; it is also possible that it is a separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl), since it occurs between two definites; but it cannot be the pronoun of the matter, because there is no link back to the subject of lākinna from the sentence that occurs as its predicate.

In His saying ﴿ولا أُشْرِكُ بِرَبِّي أحَدًا﴾ ["and I associate none with my Lord"] there is an allusion to the association of his companion, and that he opposes him in this; his companion himself made this explicit in his saying: "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord!" It was also said: he meant by it that he sees wealth and poverty only as coming from Him, the Exalted; He makes poor whom He wills and makes rich whom He wills. It was also said: I will not limit His power over returning [creatures], so that I equate Him with another, which would be association, as you did.

When the believer rebuked the disbeliever, he presented to him advice. He urged him to say, when he entered his garden: ﴿"What Allah wills [has come to pass]; there is no power except through Allah"﴾, meaning: things are determined by the will of Allah; if He wills, He impoverishes, and if He wills, He enriches; if He wills, He grants victory, and if He wills, He forsakes. It may be that ما ("what") is conditional, governed by شاءَ ("willed"), and the response is elided, meaning: whatever Allah wills occurs. It may also be relative, meaning "that which," in the nominative as subject: "that which Allah willed is what occurs"; or as predicate: "the matter is what Allah willed." (وَلَوْلا) is hortatory (taḥḍīḍiyya, "why not"), and the verb was separated from it by the adverbial phrase, which is governed by the verb (قُلْتَ) ("you said"). Then he advised him to disown power regarding what he attempts and undertakes, and to ascribe all power to Allah, the Exalted.

In a ḥadīth, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Abū Hurayra: "Shall I direct you to a word from the treasure of Paradise?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "There is no power except through Allah; when the servant says it, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: 'My servant has submitted and surrendered.'" A similar report is from the ḥadīth of Abū Mūsā, and in it: "There is no power or might except through Allah, the Most High, the Mighty."

Then he followed that advice with a hope from Allah, expecting that He would reverse what he and his companion possessed of poverty and wealth. So he said: ﴿"If you see me as less than you in wealth and children—"﴾, meaning: I hope from the workings and kindness of Allah, the Exalted, that He will grant me a garden better than your garden because of my faith in Him, and that He will remove His blessing from you because of your disbelief in Him and destroy your orchard. The majority read (أقَلَّ) ["less"] in the accusative as a second object of تَرَنِي ["you see me"]; it is of the knowledge type (ʿilmiyya), not the sight type (baṣariyya), because (أنا) occurs as a separating pronoun. It may be a corroborative of the object pronoun in tarani. It may also be of the sight type, with anā as a corroborative of the object pronoun in tarani, so that (أقَلَّ) is a circumstantial clause. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read (أقَلُّ) ["less"] in the nominative, with anā as the subject and (أقَلُّ) as its predicate; the clause then stands in the position of the second object of tarani if it is of the knowledge type, and in the position of a circumstantial clause if it is of the sight type.

His saying (وَوَلَدًا) ["and children"] indicates that his companion's saying ﴿"and more powerful in followers"﴾ (18:34) meant children, if he matched the abundance of wealth with few [followers], and the power of followers with the few children and the lack of sons. Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda said: ﴿ḥusbān﴾ ["a calamity"] means punishment. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: hail. al-Kalbī said: fire. Ibn Zayd said: decree. al-Akhfash said: arrows shot in a course, which rarely miss. It was also said: a spear; it was also said: thunderbolts; it was also said: a destroying blight. al-Zajjāj said: a punishment of ḥusbān, and that ḥusbān is the reckoning of what your hands have earned. This hope, if it means that He grants him in this world, is more painful to the disbeliever and more afflicting, since he sees his state of wealth having passed to his companion; and if it means that He grants him in the Hereafter, that is more honorable and more lasting, along with goodness and righteousness. ﴿"So it becomes [a bare] ṣaʿīd"﴾, i.e., white earth in which there is no growth, neither vine nor palm nor crop; all of that has been uprooted, and it remains a barren desolate waste, slippery because of its smoothness. A "zalaq" is a place in which no foot can stand; its plantings and buildings have gone, and its benefits have been stripped away, even the benefit of walking upon it. It is mud in which nothing grows and no foot is firm. al-Ḥasan said: "zalaq" is a road on which nothing grows. It was also said: ruin. Mujāhid said: a vast sand heap. It was also said: "zalaq" is saline ground. The believer's hope for the garden of this disbeliever is a heavenly blight from above or a terrestrial blight from below, which is the sinking of its water, so that everything in it of trees and crops is destroyed. ghawr ("sinking") is a verbal noun serving as the predicate of aṣbaḥa ("becomes") by way of intensification. ﴿"or its water becomes sunken"﴾ is conjoined to his saying (يُرْسِلَ) ["send"], because the sinking of water does not follow from a heavenly blight unless by ḥusbān one means the divine decree; in that case the morning of the garden becoming ṣaʿīdan zalaqan follows from it, or the morning of its water becoming ghawran.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 37–44 (part 2 of 2)**

The majority of reciters read *ghawran* (غَوْرًا) with a fatha on the ghayn. Al-Burjumi read *ghuwran* (غُورًا) with a damma on the ghayn. A group read it with a damma on the ghayn and a hamza on the waw, meaning *ghu'uran* (غُئُورًا) with a waw after the hamza, as in the verbal noun of *ghārat ʿaynuhu ghu'uran* (his eye sank). The pronoun in *lahu* (لَهُ) refers to the water, meaning: he will not be able to seek it, because it is not within his power to bring back what God has caused to sink. Al-Mawardi reported that its meaning is: you will not be able to seek anything else in its place. God fulfilled what the believer hoped for, namely the destruction and annihilation of what was in the hand of his companion the unbeliever, contrary to what he thought when he said, ﴿I do not think this will ever perish﴾. God then said that his fruit was ﴿encompassed﴾ (*uhīṭa bi-thamarihi*), which is an expression for destruction. Its origin is from the enemy encircling someone (*aḥāṭa bihi al-ʿaduww*), meaning surrounding him from all sides. When it encircles him, it takes possession of him and seizes him. Then it was used for every kind of destruction, and from this is ﴿unless you are encompassed﴾ [Yusuf: 66]. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "The encompassing is a kināyah (allusion/metonymy) for the generality of punishment and corruption." End of quote.

It is apparent that the encompassing took place at night, because of His saying, ﴿and he woke up﴾ (*fa-aṣbaḥa*). However, it is possible that the meaning of *fa-aṣbaḥa* is "he became," so it does not restrict the report to the morning.

The turning of his two palms: its apparent meaning is that he ﴿turns his palms﴾ back to front, which is that he shows the inside of his palm and then turns his hand until its back appears. This is the action of one who regrets and grieves over something that has passed him by, and who is sorrowful over losing it, just as clenching the hand and "falling into the hand" (*al-suqūṭ fī al-yad*) are used as allusions. It has been said that he claps one hand against the other, and ﴿turns his palms﴾ back to front. It has also been said that he places the inside of one of them on the back of the other. Since this act is an allusion to regret, it is given the construction of the verb of regret, so He says: ﴿over what he had spent on it﴾, as if He had said: he woke up regretting the loss of what he had spent on the cultivation of that garden, ﴿while it lay in ruins upon its trellises﴾. The discussion of this sentence has already been given at the end of al-Baqarah.

As for his wish that he had not associated anyone with his Lord: it is apparent that this was said by him in the life of this world, in the manner of repentance after the calamity had struck. In this there is a warning to the unbelievers of Quraysh and others, lest a state should come upon them in which they believe after punishments have descended upon them. It has been said that God sent a fire upon it, and it consumed it, so he recalled the admonition of his brother and knew that he had been afflicted because of his polytheism and transgression, so he wished that he had not been a polytheist. Some exegetes said: this is a report of the unbeliever's statement in the Hereafter. When he boasted of the abundance of his wealth and the might of his group, God informed that ﴿he had no party﴾ (*fi'ah*), that is, a group to help him, nor was he able to defend himself. The pronoun in *yanṣurūnahu* (يَنْصُرُونَهُ) is made plural according to meaning, just as it is made singular according to wording in His saying: ﴿a party fighting in the cause of God﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 13]. The negation may be understood as applying to the condition only, meaning: he has a party, but he is unable to help him. Or it may apply to the condition, and what is meant is the negation of the thing itself, because of the negation of what is a description of it, meaning: there is no party, therefore no help, and he was not one who could defend himself by strength against God's retribution.

Al-Akhawan (ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah), Mujahid, Ibn Thabit, al-Aʿmash, Talhah, Ayyub, Khalaf, Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn Saʿdan, Ibn ʿIsa al-Isbahani and Ibn Jarir read *yakun* with a *yāʾ* (ya), because the feminine gender of *fiʾah* is figurative (*majāz*). The rest of the seven and al-Hasan, Abu Jaʿfar and Shaybah read it with a *tāʾ* (ta). Ibn Abi ʿAblah read *fiʾatin* (فِئَةٍ) with the wording and literal sense, *tanṣuruhu* (تَنْصُرُهُ).

As for *hunālika* (هُنالِكَ) in the sense of place, it is an adverb of place used for distance. Apparently it refers to the abode of the Hereafter, meaning: in that abode, guardianship belongs to God, as in His saying: ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾ [Ghafir: 16]. It has been said: when He denied him a helping party in this world, He denied him the ability to defend himself in the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿and he was not one who could defend himself there﴾, that is, in the abode of the Hereafter. In that case *hunālika* is governed by *muntaṣiran* (مُنْتَصِرًا). Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, he was not one who could defend himself in that state. On this view, ﴿guardianship belongs to God﴾ is a subject and predicate. It has also been said that ﴿there guardianship belongs to God﴾ is a subject and predicate, and the pause is on *muntaṣiran*.

Al-Akhawan, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Thabit, Shaybah, Ibn Ghazwan on the authority of Talhah, Khalaf, Ibn Saʿdan, Ibn ʿIsa al-Isbahani and Ibn Jarir read *al-wilāyah* (الوِلايَةُ) with a kasra on the waw, meaning leadership and guardianship (*al-riʾāsah wa-l-riʿāyah*). The rest of the seven read it with a fatha, meaning allegiance and connection (*al-muwālāh wa-l-ṣilah*). It is reported from Abu ʿAmr and al-Asmaʿi that the kasra on the waw here is a solecism (*laḥn*), because the pattern *faʿālah* occurs only for crafts or for a meaning that is assumed as an office, and there is no assumption of administration here. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-wilāyah* with a fatha means help (*al-nuṣrah*), and *al-tawallī*, with a kasra, means authority and dominion (*al-sulṭān wa-l-mulk*). It has been read with both. The meaning is: there, that is, in that station and that state, help belongs to God alone; no one else possesses it, and no one other than Him is able to provide it, confirming His saying: ﴿and he had no party to help him apart from God﴾. Or *hunālika* means: authority and dominion belong to God; He cannot be overcome, and He is not prevented from anything. Or: in such a severe state, God is the one to whom every person in distress turns and believes. That is, his saying, ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord﴾, is a word he was compelled to utter, and he said it in terror because of the ill omen of his unbelief; had it not been for that, he would not have said it. It is also possible that the meaning is: ﴿there guardianship belongs to God﴾, He helps His friends, the believers, against the unbelievers, avenges them, and heals their hearts from their enemies. That is, He helped the believer, his brother, by what He did to the unbeliever, and confirmed his statement, ﴿Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden and will send upon it a bolt from heaven﴾. This is supported by His saying: ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome﴾, that is, for His friends. End of quote.

The two grammarians (Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisai, i.e. "the two Naḥwīs" as Abu Hayyan designates them, the Kufan and Basran pair), Ḥumayd, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Munadhir, al-Yazidi and Ibn ʿIsa al-Isbahani read *al-ḥaqq* (الحَقُّ) with a damma on the qaf, as an adjective of *al-wilāyah*. The rest of the seven read it with a kasra on the qaf, as an adjective of God, exalted is He. Ubayy read *hunālika al-wilāyatu al-ḥaqqu lillāh* with *al-ḥaqq* in the nominative as an adjective of *al-wilāyah*, and placed it before *lillāh*. Abu Haywah, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, Abu al-Sammal and Yaʿqub, on the authority of ʿIṣmah from Abu ʿAmr, read *lillāh al-ḥaqqa* with a fatha on the qaf. Al-Zamakhshari said: as an emphatic (*taʾkīd*), like your saying, "This is the servant of God, the truth, not falsehood." It is a fine and eloquent reading. ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, may God have mercy on him and be pleased with him, was one of the most eloquent and sincere of people. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari had said: "ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, may God have mercy on him," end of quote. Thus he (Abu Hayyan's source) invoked mercy upon him and expressed approval of him, because he is among the earliest great shaykhs of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), and he was in the highest degree of asceticism and worship, and there are reports about that. However, the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) criticize him and his followers. On this, Abu ʿAmr al-Dani says in his poem called *al-Munabbihah*:

Ibn ʿUbayd is the shaykh of i'tizal (Mu'tazilism),
and the initiator of innovation and misguidance.

The Hasan, al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read *ʿuqban* (عُقْبًا) with a sukun on the qaf and tanwin. On the authority of ʿĀṣim, it is read *ʿuqbā* (عُقْبى) with the feminine *alif* of the restricted (maqṣūrah) pattern on the form *rujʿā*. The majority read it with a damma on the qaf and tanwin. All three readings have the same meaning: the outcome (*al-ʿāqibah*).

﴿His companion said to him while he was disputing with him: "Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then fashioned you as a man?"﴾ ﴿"But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I associate none with my Lord."﴾ ﴿"And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: 'What Allah wills [has come to pass]; there is no power except through Allah'? If you see me as less than you in wealth and children—﴾ ﴿perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden and will send upon it a calamity from heaven, so that it becomes barren, slippery earth,﴾ ﴿or its water sinks into the ground, and you will not be able to find it."﴾ ﴿And his fruit was encompassed [by ruin], so he began to wring his hands over what he had spent on it, while it lay in ruins upon its trellises, and he said: "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord!"﴾ ﴿And he had no group to help him against Allah, nor was he one who could defend himself.﴾ ﴿There, guardianship belongs to Allah, the Truth. He is best in reward and best in outcome.﴾

(p-127) ﴿وهُوَ يُحاوِرُهُ﴾ ["while he was disputing with him" (18:34)] is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject, and the "companion" here is the believer. Ubayy read وهو يُخاصِمُهُ ("while he was quarrelling with him"). This is a recitation of interpretation (qirā'at tafsīr), not a recitation of transmission (qirā'at riwāya), because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf and because what is transmitted by mass transmission (tawātur) is (هو يُحاوِرُهُ), not يُخاصِمُهُ. ﴿أكَفَرْتَ﴾ ["Do you disbelieve"] is an interrogative of denial and rebuke, since he associated others with Allah. Thābit al-Bunānī recited: ويلَكَ ﴿أكَفَرْتَ﴾ ("Woe to you! Do you disbelieve?"). This is an explanation of the sense of rebuke and denial, not a recitation established from the Messenger ﷺ. Then he (the believer) alerted him to the origin of his creation and his coming into existence after non-existence, and that this is evidence for the possibility of resurrection from the graves. Then this was confirmed by the report of the truthful ones, who are the messengers, upon them be peace. His saying ﴿خَلَقَكَ مِن تُرابٍ﴾ ["created you from dust"] may mean either: the creation of your origin from dust, namely Adam, peace be upon him, and the creation of his origin is a cause of his creation, so creating him is creating [the man] himself; or it may mean that a man's semen is generated from nourishment that returns to the dust. Thus he alerted him first to that from which his father's semen was generated, then secondly to the drop (nuṭfa), which is his father's semen. As for what is reported, that an angel is entrusted with the drop and casts a little dust into it before it enters the womb, this requires authentic transmission.

Then he alerted him to His making him a man (تَسْوِيَتِهِ رَجُلًا), which is creating him balanced, with sound limbs. It is said of a boy when his youth is complete: "he has become balanced" (قَدِ اسْتَوى). It was also said: he reminded him of Allah's blessing upon him in being a man and not created as a female. By these transitions he alerted him to the perfection of His power and that nothing can overpower Him. Al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿سَوّاكَ﴾ ["fashioned you"] means He made you proportionate and completed you as a human, a male who reached the stage of men, and that made him a disbeliever in Allah, a denier of His blessings, because of his doubt about resurrection, just as one who denies the Messenger is a disbeliever. End of quote. (رَجُلًا) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Al-Ḥawfī said: (رَجُلًا) is governed by سَوّى, meaning: He made you (a man). Its apparent meaning is that sawwā is transitive to two objects. Since the interrogative is not one of seeking information but of denial and rebuke, it is in reality an affirmation of his disbelief and a report about it, because its meaning is: "You have disbelieved in the One who..." Then he (the believer) added, reporting about himself: ﴿لَكِنّا هو اللَّهُ رَبِّي﴾ ["But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord"], an affirmation of the oneness of Allah and that he does not associate anyone with Him.

The Kufans, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Kathīr, and Nāfiʿ in the transmission of Warsh and Qālūn read لَكِنَّ with a doubled nūn without an alif in pause (waṣl), and with an alif in stopping (waqf). Its original form is وَلَكِنْ أنا: the hamza's vowel was transferred to the nūn of lākin and the hamza was dropped, so two identical consonants met and one was assimilated into the other. It was also said: the hamza of anā was dropped contrary to analogy, so the nūn of lākin, which is sukūn, met the nūn of anā and was assimilated into it. As for stopping, he retained the alif of anā, which is the well-known form at stopping on anā; while in connected speech the well-known form is to omit it. Abū ʿAmr replaced it with an alif in stopping; and in one transmission he stopped on لَكِنَّهُ, which Ibn Khālawayh mentioned. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: Hārūn related from Abū ʿAmr: لَكِنَّهُ ﴿هُوَ اللَّهُ رَبِّي﴾ with a pronoun attached to lākin.

Ibn ʿĀmir, Nāfiʿ in the transmission of al-Musayyabī, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī, Abū Bahriyya, Yaʿqūb in one transmission, and Abū ʿUmar, and in another transmission Kardam, Warsh in one transmission, and Abū Jaʿfar read it with the alif retained both in pause and connected speech. In pause it is clear; in connection, the Banū Tamīm retain it in speech, while others retain it only under poetic necessity; so it came in the dialect of Banū Tamīm. From Abū Jaʿfar, the alif was omitted both in connection and in pause, and this is from the transmission of al-Hāshimī. The retention of the alif in connection also indicates that the original form of this is لَكِنِ أنا.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: What made this good, i.e., retaining the alif in connection, is that the alif came as a substitute for the omitted hamza. End of quote. What also supports this is the recitation of a group: لَكِنَنا, with the hamza omitted and the two nūns lightened. Al-Zamakhsharī also said, and similar to it—i.e., similar to the assimilation of the nūn of lākin into the nūn of anā after the hamza is dropped—is the saying of a poet:

*And you shoot me with your glance—you are the guilty one—and you shun me. But, as for you, I do not shun you.*

I.e., lākin anā lā aqlīki ("but I do not shun you"). End of quote. What he said about the verse is not necessarily the only possibility, since it may be that the original is لَكِنَّنِي, and the subject of lākinna was elided; scholars mention that its elision is eloquent when the context indicates it, and they cite as evidence the saying of a poet:

*Had you been a Ḍabbī, you would have known my kinship, but you are a Zanjī with great lips.*

I.e., but you are a Zanjī. Abū ʿAlī (al-Fārisī) allowed that lākin may have been attached to the nūn of plurality found in kharajnā and ḍarabnā, and the assimilation occurred because of the meeting of identical letters; then he used the singular in rabbī according to meaning; had he followed the wording, he would have said rabbanā. End of quote. This is a distant interpretation. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: What is possible for lākinnā is that it be the well-known one among the sisters of inna, meaning: "but my saying is: He is Allah, my Lord"; however, I do not know anyone who reads it so, either in connection or in pause. End of quote. Abū al-Qāsim Yūsuf ibn ʿAlī ibn Jubāra al-Hudhalī mentioned in his book al-Kāmil fī al-Qirāʾāt the following text: with the omission of the alif in both states—i.e., connection and pause—the Ḥimṣī, Ibn ʿUtba, Qutayba other than al-Thaqafī, and Yūnus from Abū ʿUmar. By "Ḥimṣī" he means Ibn Abī ʿAbla, Abū Ḥaywa, and Abū Bahriyya. Ubayy and al-Ḥasan read لَكِنِ أنا هو اللَّهُ ("but I, He is Allah") with separation, with the hamza unassimilated and fully pronounced; Ibn ʿAṭiyya related this from Ibn Masʿūd. ʿĪsā al-Thaqafī read لَكِنَّ هو اللَّهُ without أنا; Ibn Khālawayh related it from Ibn Masʿūd, and al-Ahwāzī related it from al-Ḥasan. As for the one who affirms (هو), it is the pronoun of the matter and affair (ḍamīr al-amr wa-al-shaʾn), and there is an elided saying: "but I say: He is Allah, my Lord." It may also refer back to the one who "created you from dust," i.e., "I say: He—that is, your Creator—is Allah, my Lord." (رَبِّي) is an attribute (naʿt), or an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān), or a substitution (badal). It is also possible not to posit an elided "I say," so that anā is the subject; (هو) is the second subject, the pronoun of the matter; (اللَّهُ) is the third subject; (رَبِّي) is its predicate; the third is a predicate of the second; and the second with its predicate is a predicate of anā; the link back to it is the yāʾ in rabbī. The structure becomes like: Hind, he is Zayd, the one who strikes her. On the transmission of Hārūn, it is possible that (هو) is an emphasis of the object pronoun in lākinnahu, which refers back to "the One who created you"; it is also possible that it is a separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl), since it occurs between two definites; but it cannot be the pronoun of the matter, because there is no link back to the subject of lākinna from the sentence that occurs as its predicate.

In His saying ﴿ولا أُشْرِكُ بِرَبِّي أحَدًا﴾ ["and I associate none with my Lord"] there is an allusion to the association of his companion, and that he opposes him in this; his companion himself made this explicit in his saying: "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord!" It was also said: he meant by it that he sees wealth and poverty only as coming from Him, the Exalted; He makes poor whom He wills and makes rich whom He wills. It was also said: I will not limit His power over returning [creatures], so that I equate Him with another, which would be association, as you did.

When the believer rebuked the disbeliever, he presented to him advice. He urged him to say, when he entered his garden: ﴿"What Allah wills [has come to pass]; there is no power except through Allah"﴾, meaning: things are determined by the will of Allah; if He wills, He impoverishes, and if He wills, He enriches; if He wills, He grants victory, and if He wills, He forsakes. It may be that ما ("what") is conditional, governed by شاءَ ("willed"), and the response is elided, meaning: whatever Allah wills occurs. It may also be relative, meaning "that which," in the nominative as subject: "that which Allah willed is what occurs"; or as predicate: "the matter is what Allah willed." (وَلَوْلا) is hortatory (taḥḍīḍiyya, "why not"), and the verb was separated from it by the adverbial phrase, which is governed by the verb (قُلْتَ) ("you said"). Then he advised him to disown power regarding what he attempts and undertakes, and to ascribe all power to Allah, the Exalted.

In a ḥadīth, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Abū Hurayra: "Shall I direct you to a word from the treasure of Paradise?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "There is no power except through Allah; when the servant says it, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: 'My servant has submitted and surrendered.'" A similar report is from the ḥadīth of Abū Mūsā, and in it: "There is no power or might except through Allah, the Most High, the Mighty."

Then he followed that advice with a hope from Allah, expecting that He would reverse what he and his companion possessed of poverty and wealth. So he said: ﴿"If you see me as less than you in wealth and children—"﴾, meaning: I hope from the workings and kindness of Allah, the Exalted, that He will grant me a garden better than your garden because of my faith in Him, and that He will remove His blessing from you because of your disbelief in Him and destroy your orchard. The majority read (أقَلَّ) ["less"] in the accusative as a second object of تَرَنِي ["you see me"]; it is of the knowledge type (ʿilmiyya), not the sight type (baṣariyya), because (أنا) occurs as a separating pronoun. It may be a corroborative of the object pronoun in tarani. It may also be of the sight type, with anā as a corroborative of the object pronoun in tarani, so that (أقَلَّ) is a circumstantial clause. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read (أقَلُّ) ["less"] in the nominative, with anā as the subject and (أقَلُّ) as its predicate; the clause then stands in the position of the second object of tarani if it is of the knowledge type, and in the position of a circumstantial clause if it is of the sight type.

His saying (وَوَلَدًا) ["and children"] indicates that his companion's saying ﴿"and more powerful in followers"﴾ (18:34) meant children, if he matched the abundance of wealth with few [followers], and the power of followers with the few children and the lack of sons. Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda said: ﴿ḥusbān﴾ ["a calamity"] means punishment. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: hail. al-Kalbī said: fire. Ibn Zayd said: decree. al-Akhfash said: arrows shot in a course, which rarely miss. It was also said: a spear; it was also said: thunderbolts; it was also said: a destroying blight. al-Zajjāj said: a punishment of ḥusbān, and that ḥusbān is the reckoning of what your hands have earned. This hope, if it means that He grants him in this world, is more painful to the disbeliever and more afflicting, since he sees his state of wealth having passed to his companion; and if it means that He grants him in the Hereafter, that is more honorable and more lasting, along with goodness and righteousness. ﴿"So it becomes [a bare] ṣaʿīd"﴾, i.e., white earth in which there is no growth, neither vine nor palm nor crop; all of that has been uprooted, and it remains a barren desolate waste, slippery because of its smoothness. A "zalaq" is a place in which no foot can stand; its plantings and buildings have gone, and its benefits have been stripped away, even the benefit of walking upon it. It is mud in which nothing grows and no foot is firm. al-Ḥasan said: "zalaq" is a road on which nothing grows. It was also said: ruin. Mujāhid said: a vast sand heap. It was also said: "zalaq" is saline ground. The believer's hope for the garden of this disbeliever is a heavenly blight from above or a terrestrial blight from below, which is the sinking of its water, so that everything in it of trees and crops is destroyed. ghawr ("sinking") is a verbal noun serving as the predicate of aṣbaḥa ("becomes") by way of intensification. ﴿"or its water becomes sunken"﴾ is conjoined to his saying (يُرْسِلَ) ["send"], because the sinking of water does not follow from a heavenly blight unless by ḥusbān one means the divine decree; in that case the morning of the garden becoming ṣaʿīdan zalaqan follows from it, or the morning of its water becoming ghawran.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 37–44 (part 2 of 2)**

The majority of reciters read *ghawran* (غَوْرًا) with a fatha on the ghayn. Al-Burjumi read *ghuwran* (غُورًا) with a damma on the ghayn. A group read it with a damma on the ghayn and a hamza on the waw, meaning *ghu'uran* (غُئُورًا) with a waw after the hamza, as in the verbal noun of *ghārat ʿaynuhu ghu'uran* (his eye sank). The pronoun in *lahu* (لَهُ) refers to the water, meaning: he will not be able to seek it, because it is not within his power to bring back what God has caused to sink. Al-Mawardi reported that its meaning is: you will not be able to seek anything else in its place. God fulfilled what the believer hoped for, namely the destruction and annihilation of what was in the hand of his companion the unbeliever, contrary to what he thought when he said, ﴿I do not think this will ever perish﴾. God then said that his fruit was ﴿encompassed﴾ (*uhīṭa bi-thamarihi*), which is an expression for destruction. Its origin is from the enemy encircling someone (*aḥāṭa bihi al-ʿaduww*), meaning surrounding him from all sides. When it encircles him, it takes possession of him and seizes him. Then it was used for every kind of destruction, and from this is ﴿unless you are encompassed﴾ [Yusuf: 66]. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "The encompassing is a kināyah (allusion/metonymy) for the generality of punishment and corruption." End of quote.

It is apparent that the encompassing took place at night, because of His saying, ﴿and he woke up﴾ (*fa-aṣbaḥa*). However, it is possible that the meaning of *fa-aṣbaḥa* is "he became," so it does not restrict the report to the morning.

The turning of his two palms: its apparent meaning is that he ﴿turns his palms﴾ back to front, which is that he shows the inside of his palm and then turns his hand until its back appears. This is the action of one who regrets and grieves over something that has passed him by, and who is sorrowful over losing it, just as clenching the hand and "falling into the hand" (*al-suqūṭ fī al-yad*) are used as allusions. It has been said that he claps one hand against the other, and ﴿turns his palms﴾ back to front. It has also been said that he places the inside of one of them on the back of the other. Since this act is an allusion to regret, it is given the construction of the verb of regret, so He says: ﴿over what he had spent on it﴾, as if He had said: he woke up regretting the loss of what he had spent on the cultivation of that garden, ﴿while it lay in ruins upon its trellises﴾. The discussion of this sentence has already been given at the end of al-Baqarah.

As for his wish that he had not associated anyone with his Lord: it is apparent that this was said by him in the life of this world, in the manner of repentance after the calamity had struck. In this there is a warning to the unbelievers of Quraysh and others, lest a state should come upon them in which they believe after punishments have descended upon them. It has been said that God sent a fire upon it, and it consumed it, so he recalled the admonition of his brother and knew that he had been afflicted because of his polytheism and transgression, so he wished that he had not been a polytheist. Some exegetes said: this is a report of the unbeliever's statement in the Hereafter. When he boasted of the abundance of his wealth and the might of his group, God informed that ﴿he had no party﴾ (*fi'ah*), that is, a group to help him, nor was he able to defend himself. The pronoun in *yanṣurūnahu* (يَنْصُرُونَهُ) is made plural according to meaning, just as it is made singular according to wording in His saying: ﴿a party fighting in the cause of God﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 13]. The negation may be understood as applying to the condition only, meaning: he has a party, but he is unable to help him. Or it may apply to the condition, and what is meant is the negation of the thing itself, because of the negation of what is a description of it, meaning: there is no party, therefore no help, and he was not one who could defend himself by strength against God's retribution.

Al-Akhawan (ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah), Mujahid, Ibn Thabit, al-Aʿmash, Talhah, Ayyub, Khalaf, Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn Saʿdan, Ibn ʿIsa al-Isbahani and Ibn Jarir read *yakun* with a *yāʾ* (ya), because the feminine gender of *fiʾah* is figurative (*majāz*). The rest of the seven and al-Hasan, Abu Jaʿfar and Shaybah read it with a *tāʾ* (ta). Ibn Abi ʿAblah read *fiʾatin* (فِئَةٍ) with the wording and literal sense, *tanṣuruhu* (تَنْصُرُهُ).

As for *hunālika* (هُنالِكَ) in the sense of place, it is an adverb of place used for distance. Apparently it refers to the abode of the Hereafter, meaning: in that abode, guardianship belongs to God, as in His saying: ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾ [Ghafir: 16]. It has been said: when He denied him a helping party in this world, He denied him the ability to defend himself in the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿and he was not one who could defend himself there﴾, that is, in the abode of the Hereafter. In that case *hunālika* is governed by *muntaṣiran* (مُنْتَصِرًا). Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, he was not one who could defend himself in that state. On this view, ﴿guardianship belongs to God﴾ is a subject and predicate. It has also been said that ﴿there guardianship belongs to God﴾ is a subject and predicate, and the pause is on *muntaṣiran*.

Al-Akhawan, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Thabit, Shaybah, Ibn Ghazwan on the authority of Talhah, Khalaf, Ibn Saʿdan, Ibn ʿIsa al-Isbahani and Ibn Jarir read *al-wilāyah* (الوِلايَةُ) with a kasra on the waw, meaning leadership and guardianship (*al-riʾāsah wa-l-riʿāyah*). The rest of the seven read it with a fatha, meaning allegiance and connection (*al-muwālāh wa-l-ṣilah*). It is reported from Abu ʿAmr and al-Asmaʿi that the kasra on the waw here is a solecism (*laḥn*), because the pattern *faʿālah* occurs only for crafts or for a meaning that is assumed as an office, and there is no assumption of administration here. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-wilāyah* with a fatha means help (*al-nuṣrah*), and *al-tawallī*, with a kasra, means authority and dominion (*al-sulṭān wa-l-mulk*). It has been read with both. The meaning is: there, that is, in that station and that state, help belongs to God alone; no one else possesses it, and no one other than Him is able to provide it, confirming His saying: ﴿and he had no party to help him apart from God﴾. Or *hunālika* means: authority and dominion belong to God; He cannot be overcome, and He is not prevented from anything. Or: in such a severe state, God is the one to whom every person in distress turns and believes. That is, his saying, ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord﴾, is a word he was compelled to utter, and he said it in terror because of the ill omen of his unbelief; had it not been for that, he would not have said it. It is also possible that the meaning is: ﴿there guardianship belongs to God﴾, He helps His friends, the believers, against the unbelievers, avenges them, and heals their hearts from their enemies. That is, He helped the believer, his brother, by what He did to the unbeliever, and confirmed his statement, ﴿Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden and will send upon it a bolt from heaven﴾. This is supported by His saying: ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome﴾, that is, for His friends. End of quote.

The two grammarians (Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisai, i.e. "the two Naḥwīs" as Abu Hayyan designates them, the Kufan and Basran pair), Ḥumayd, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Munadhir, al-Yazidi and Ibn ʿIsa al-Isbahani read *al-ḥaqq* (الحَقُّ) with a damma on the qaf, as an adjective of *al-wilāyah*. The rest of the seven read it with a kasra on the qaf, as an adjective of God, exalted is He. Ubayy read *hunālika al-wilāyatu al-ḥaqqu lillāh* with *al-ḥaqq* in the nominative as an adjective of *al-wilāyah*, and placed it before *lillāh*. Abu Haywah, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, Abu al-Sammal and Yaʿqub, on the authority of ʿIṣmah from Abu ʿAmr, read *lillāh al-ḥaqqa* with a fatha on the qaf. Al-Zamakhshari said: as an emphatic (*taʾkīd*), like your saying, "This is the servant of God, the truth, not falsehood." It is a fine and eloquent reading. ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, may God have mercy on him and be pleased with him, was one of the most eloquent and sincere of people. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari had said: "ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, may God have mercy on him," end of quote. Thus he (Abu Hayyan's source) invoked mercy upon him and expressed approval of him, because he is among the earliest great shaykhs of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), and he was in the highest degree of asceticism and worship, and there are reports about that. However, the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) criticize him and his followers. On this, Abu ʿAmr al-Dani says in his poem called *al-Munabbihah*:

Ibn ʿUbayd is the shaykh of i'tizal (Mu'tazilism),
and the initiator of innovation and misguidance.

The Hasan, al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read *ʿuqban* (عُقْبًا) with a sukun on the qaf and tanwin. On the authority of ʿĀṣim, it is read *ʿuqbā* (عُقْبى) with the feminine *alif* of the restricted (maqṣūrah) pattern on the form *rujʿā*. The majority read it with a damma on the qaf and tanwin. All three readings have the same meaning: the outcome (*al-ʿāqibah*).

(p. 132)

﴿And set forth for them the example of the life of this world: it is like water which We sent down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingled with it, then it becomes dry stubble which the winds scatter. And Allah is capable of everything.﴾ ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world, but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope.﴾ ﴿And the Day We set the mountains moving, and you see the earth laid bare, and We gather them and leave none of them behind.﴾

The Hashish (dry stubble) is dried-up plant matter. Al-Farra' said this, and its singular is hashīsha. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba said: anything that was moist and then dried, such as the brushwood of a hedge-builder (kahashīm al-muhtazir) and the crumbs of crushed bread (hashīm al-tharīd). The root meaning of hashīm is what has crumbled from dry grass. Dhara and adhra are two dialects, meaning "to scatter," as Abu 'Ubayda said. Ibn Kaysan said: tadhruhu means it carries it away and goes with it. Al-Akhfash said: it lifts it.

Ghādara means to leave behind, and it derives from ghadr, which is the abandonment of loyalty. From the same root comes ghadīr, which is what the flood leaves behind. Al-Saff is a person standing opposite another up to their end, whether standing, sitting, or in some other state, lengthwise or in a circle. From it one says ṣaffa yaṣuffu, and the plural is ṣufūf. Al-'Adud is a limb of a human or other creature, and it is known. It has two dialects: 'adud with the 'ayn open and the ḍād either pronounced or with a sukūn, and 'uḍud with the 'ayn and ḍād both vowelled. It is also used for help and a supporter. Al-Zajjaj said: al-i'ḍād means to strengthen and seek assistance. One says "I'taḍadtu bi-fulān," meaning I sought help from him. Al-Mawbiq is the place of destruction. One says wabaqa yawbaqu wabaqan, and wabaqa yabiqu wabūqan, meaning he perished, so he is wābiq. His sins destroyed him (awbaqathu dhunūbuhu), meaning they ruined him.

Adḥaḍa al-ḥaqq means it overwhelmed him. Tha'lab said this, and its origin is from idḥāḍ al-qadam, which is causing the foot to slip. A poet said:

I came, and al-Yashkurī's caution saved him, and he swerved as a camel swerves from the slippery ground.

Another said:

Abū Mundhir, you wished for loyalty and dreaded it, and you swerved as a camel swerves from the slippery ground.

Al-daḥḍ is the mud in which one slips. Al-mawʾil: al-Farra' said it means refuge. One says "walat nafs fulān," meaning the person's soul escaped. Al-A'sha said:

I might steal from the master of the house his carelessness, though he might guard against me, where there is no escape.

That is, where there is no escape. Ibn Qutayba said: it means a place of refuge. One says "wa'ala fulān ilā kadhā," meaning he sought refuge, ya'ilu, wa'lan and wu'ūlan.

﴿And set forth for them the example of the life of this world: it is like water which We sent down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingled with it, then it becomes dry stubble which the winds scatter. And Allah is capable of everything.﴾ ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world, but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope.﴾ ﴿And the Day We set the mountains moving, and you see the earth laid bare, and We gather them and leave none of them behind.﴾

(p. 133) When Allah, exalted is He, explained in the first parable the condition of the disbeliever and the believer, and what the disbeliever's pride in destruction led to, He explained in this parable the condition of "the life of this world" (al-ḥayāt al-dunyā) [18:28], its dissolution, and the fate of its luxuries and comforts, which is destruction. The phrase "like water" (ka-mā'in) is parsed by Ibn 'Aṭiyya as the predicate (khabar, the complement of the subject) of a deleted subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), meaning: it, that is, the life of this world, is like water. Al-Ḥawfī said the kāf is connected to the meaning of the verbal noun, meaning: a striking like "water which We sent down." I say that "like water" is in the position of the second object of the verb "strike" (waḍrib), meaning: make for them the example of the life of this world, that is, its description, a semblance of water. The explanation of a similar sentence has already been given in His words: "The likeness of the life of this world is only like water which We sent down from the sky, so the vegetation of the earth mingled with it of what men and cattle eat" [10:24], in Surah Yunus.

"Then it became" (fa-aṣbaḥa): that is, became. It does not restrict the statement to the morning. It is like the poet's words:

I have become one who carries no weapon, and does not own the head of a camel if it bolts.

It was also said that it indicates restriction to the morning, because heavenly calamities most often strike at night, so it is like His words: "So he began turning his hands" [18:42].

Ibn Mas'ud recited tudhrīhi, from adhrā, in the four-letter form. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Ḥasan, al-Nakha'ī, al-A'mash, Ṭalḥa, Ibn Abī Layla, Ibn Muḥaysin, Khalaf, Ibn 'Īsā and Ibn Jarīr recited "al-rīḥ" (the wind) in the singular. The majority recite "the winds scatter it" (tadhruhu al-riyāḥ).

When Allah mentioned His overwhelming power in changing what was in the utmost freshness and brightness into a state of crumbling and vanishing, until the winds scattered it and played with it, going and coming, He informed of His power over everything, of creation and annihilation and other things related to His power.

When Allah belittled the state of this world with this parable, He mentioned that what the disbeliever (ʿUyayna and his like) took pride in, namely wealth and sons, is only the adornment of this belittled "life of this world," and that its fate is only to perish. Therefore one should not be concerned with it. Allah informed of the adornment of wealth and children by a deletion of the modifier: that is, the place of the adornment, or He placed "wealth and children" in the position of meaning and abundance, so He informed about it by saying "adornment" (zīna). "And better in hope" (wa-khayrun amalan): that is, better as a object of hope, because its possessor hopes in this world for Allah's reward and his share in the Hereafter, unlike the owner of wealth and children who is devoid of the enduring good deeds, for he does not hope for any reward.

When Allah mentioned the fate of the life of this world, which is passing away, He followed this with the early conditions of the Day of Resurrection, saying: "And the Day We set the mountains moving" (wa-yawma nusayyiru al-jibāla), like His words: "The Day the sky shall sway with a sway, and the mountains shall move with a movement" [52:9]. And He said: "And you see the mountains, you think them solid, but they pass as clouds pass" [27:88]. And He said: "Say: My Lord will blow them away with a blowing, then He will leave it a level flat plain" [20:105]. And He said: "And when the mountains are set moving" [81:3]. The meaning is that the order of this worldly world is dissolved, and the otherworldly world is brought forth. "The Day" (yawma) is in the accusative, by implying "remember" (udhkur), or by the verb implied at His words "You have come to Us" [18:48], that is: We said on a day such-and-such, you have come. 

Nāfi', Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī, al-A'raj, Shayba, 'Āṣim, Ibn Muṣarrif and Abū 'Abd al-Raḥmān recited nusayyiru with the plural of majesty (nūn al-'aẓama), with al-jibāla in the accusative. Ibn 'Āmir, Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr, al-Ḥasan, Shibl, Qatāda, 'Īsā, al-Zuhrī, Ḥumayd, Ṭalḥa, al-Yazīdī and al-Zubayrī from his men from Ya'qūb recited with a dammah on the tā' and a fatḥah on the shaddah yā', in the passive, with al-jibālu in the nominative. From al-Ḥasan likewise, except that it is with a ḍammah on the yā' with two dots below it. Ibn Muḥaysin and Maḥbūb from Abū 'Amr recited tasīru (the mountains move), from "sāratu al-jibāl." Ubayy recited suyyirat al-jibālu.

"And you see the earth laid bare" (wa-tarā al-arḍa bāriza): that is, uncovered and exposed, due to the going of the mountains, hills, trees and buildings. Or it means you see the people of the earth coming forth from its belly. 'Īsā recited wa-turā al-arḍu in the passive.

"And We gather them" (wa-ḥasharnāhum): that is, We raised them from their graves and gathered them to the plain of the Resurrection.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you say, why is "We gathered them" put in the past tense after "We set in motion" and "you see"? I say: to indicate that their gathering is before the setting in motion and before the appearing, so that they may witness those terrors and great events, as if it was said: "And We gathered them" before that. Concluded. The better view is that the "wa" is the wa of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl), not the wa of conjunction, and the meaning is "while We have gathered them," that is, the setting in motion occurs in the state of their gathering. It was also said: "And We gathered them" (wa-ḥasharnāhum), and "And they were presented" [18:48], and "And the Book was placed" [18:49], are of the kind in which the past tense is placed in the position of the future, for certainty of its occurrence.

The majority recited "nughādir" with the plural of majesty. Qatāda recited tughādir, attributing it to the power or to the earth. Abān ibn Yazīd from 'Āṣim likewise, or with a fatḥah on the dāl in the passive with one agent in the nominative; 'Iṣma likewise. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk recited nughdir with a ḍammah on the nūn, a sukūn on the ghayn, and a kasrah on the dāl.

"In rows" (ṣaffan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and it is a singular noun treated as a plural, that is, in rows (ṣufūfan). In the authentic hadith: "Allah gathers the first and the last in one plain, in rows, the caller makes them hear, and the sight penetrates them," the hadith in full. In another hadith: "The people of Paradise on the Day of Resurrection are a hundred and twenty rows, you are eighty of them." Or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun placed in the position of a state, that is, lining up. It was also said: the meaning is "rows, rows," so "rows" was deleted while meant. This repetition indicates the completion of the rows to their end. Their state is likened to that of soldiers presented before the sultan, lined up, visible, so that one sees their whole group just as one sees each individual, none hiding another.

ۧ "You have come to Us [bare and alone], just as We created you the first time" — this is a verb object governed by an omitted verb of saying, meaning "And We will say." And "as We created you" is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a coming like the coming of your creation, i.e., "barefoot, naked, uncircumcised," as is stated in the hadith, and free of wealth and children. The (an) here is a lightened form of the heavy (anna). It is separated from the verb by the negative particle (lan), as it is separated in His saying, "Does man think that We will not gather his bones?" The (bal) is for transition (idrab), meaning a move from one statement to another, not meaning nullification. The meaning is that We will not make for your resurrection and gathering a (mawʿid), i.e., a place or time of promise for fulfilling what you were promised through the tongues of the prophets regarding resurrection and raising. The address in "You have come to Us" is to the disbelievers who deny resurrection, by way of rebuke and reproach.

﴿And the Book will be placed﴾ Zayd ibn ʿAli read (wa-waḍaʿa), in the active voice, with (al-kitāb) in the accusative. Al-kitāb is a collective noun (ism jins), i.e., the books of the deeds of creation. It is possible that all the pages were made into one book, which the angels placed for the reckoning of creation. Ishfaq (apprehension) means their fear of their evil deeds being exposed and them being disgraced, and what follows from that of everlasting punishment. They will call out for their destruction, by which they were ruined specifically among all destructions, and say, "Woe to us!" The intended meaning is those present with them, as if they said, "O you who are present with us, look at our destruction." Likewise is the calling of what does not reason, as in His saying, "O our sorrow over Joseph" [Yusuf: 84], "O our regret over what we neglected" [al-Zumar: 56], "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?" [Ya-Sin: 52], and the saying of the poet:

"O wonder at this she-camel, and O wonder at her burdened saddle"

It is only intended to alert the one who reasons, through amazement at what has befallen the one calling out. And ﴿does not leave﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl). From Ibn ʿAbbas: the minor (ṣaghīra) is smiling, and the major (kabīra) is loud laughter. From Ibn Jubayr: the kiss and fornication; and from others: forgetfulness and intention. From al-Fudayl: "By God, they wept over minor sins before major ones." The minor is mentioned first out of concern for it, and when it is counted, the major is more deserving. ﴿Except that it has counted them﴾ means it recorded and preserved them. ﴿And they will find what they did present﴾ in the pages, ready; or the recompense for what they did.

﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾ by recording against him what he did not do, or by increasing his punishment beyond what he deserves, or by punishing him without sin. Al-Zamakhshari said: "as is claimed of God's injustice in punishing the children of polytheists," end of quote. It is not said that this is an injustice from Him, the Exalted; because He, the Exalted, is the owner of all who are owned by Him, so He may dispose of His possessions as He wills, and He is not questioned about what He does. The correct view regarding the children of polytheists is that they will be in Paradise as servants to its people, as stated in al-Bukhari from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).
