Commentary on the verses 50–53 of Surah al-Kahf, by Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit):

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord. Will you then take him and his offspring as allies besides Me, while they are your enemy? Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿I did not make them witnesses to the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor to the creation of themselves, and I would not take misleaders as helpers.﴾ ﴿And on the Day He says, "Call upon My partners whom you claimed," they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them, and We will place between them a barrier of destruction (mawbiq).﴾ ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will be certain (fa-zannu) that they are about to fall into it, and they will find no escape from it.﴾

They mentioned, regarding the connection (irtibat) of this verse with what precedes it, that when Allah commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to sit with the poor, and those arrogant ones had disdained sitting with them, and had asked the Messenger ﷺ to drive them away, because of what they were disposed to of arrogance, of boasting with wealth and children, and of nobility of origin and lineage, while those poor ones were the opposite of them in that, the mention of the story of Iblis was fitting, due to the common ground they shared in arrogance and in boasting of the origin from which he was created. This which they mentioned about the connection is evident with respect to the verses preceding the two parables (mathalayn), but as for what follows the two parables, it is not clear. What appears to me regarding the connection of this verse with the one before it is that when He mentioned the Day of Resurrection and the gathering, and mentioned the fear of the polytheists of what was inscribed in that Book, and since Iblis was the one who drove the criminals to their sins and to taking partners with Allah, it was fitting to mention Iblis and the prohibition of taking his offspring as allies besides Allah, as a distancing from sins and from obeying what he whispers.

The discussion has preceded (p-136) concerning the exception of Iblis: whether it is a contiguous exception (istithna' muttasil) or a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), and whether he was of the angels or not, at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, so it suffices and there is no need to repeat it. The apparent meaning of this verse is that he was not of the angels, but was of the jinn. Qatadah said: "The jinn are a kind of the angels, created from the fire of the samum wind." Shahr ibn Hawshab said: "He was one of the jinn whom the angels had overcome; one of the angels took him captive and carried him off to the heaven." Al-Hasan and others said: "He was the first of the jinn, and their origin is like that of Adam among mankind." A group said: "Iblis and his kind were jinn, but the devils today are his offspring, so he is like Noah among mankind." Al-Zamakhshari said: "'He was of the jinn' is a new sentence (kalam mustaʼnaf) functioning as a causal explanation after the exception of Iblis from those who prostrated, as if someone said: 'What is wrong with him, that he did not prostrate?' So it was said, '[He] was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord.' The fa' here is also for causation (tasbib). He made his being of the jinn the cause of his defiance, meaning: if he had been an angel like all who prostrated to Adam, he would not have defied the command of Allah, because the angels are absolutely infallible (ma'sumun), and what is permissible for the jinn and mankind is not permissible for them, as He said: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya': 27]. This interjected statement is a deliberate act by Allah, exalted and high, to protect the angels from any doubt arising concerning their infallibility. How far apart is what Allah intended from the statement of one who opposed Him, who claimed that he was an angel and a chief over the angels, who disobeyed and was cursed and transformed into a devil, and then attributed that to Ibn Abbas." End of quotation.

The apparent meaning of ﴿fa-fasaqa 'an amri rabbihi﴾ is: he went out from what his Lord had commanded him, namely prostration. Ru'bah said:

"They sink into the highland and the deep lowland, deviating from their course, bewildered."

It was also said: "fa-fasaqa" means he became a fasiq, a disbelieving one, because of the command of his Lord, which is His saying ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾, in that he did not comply with it. It was said: It may also be that the meaning is ﴿fa-fasaqa﴾ by the command of his Lord, that is, by His will and decree, because will is also called a command, as you say: "I did that by your command," meaning according to your desire. The interrogative hamzah in ﴿Will you then take him﴾ is for reproach, denial and wonder: that is, after what manifested from him of defiance and disobedience, do you take him and his offspring as allies besides Me, while his enmity toward you is established? Do you take him as a friend?

'Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad recited from the pulpit while he was delivering a sermon: (afa-tattakhidhunahu wa-dhurriyyatahu) with a fatha on the dhal. Evidently Iblis has offspring, and this was said by a group including Qatadah, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak and al-A'mash.

Qatadah said: "He marries and begets, as the children of Adam beget." Al-Sha'bi said: "There is no offspring except from a wife." Ibn Zayd said: "Allah said to Iblis: 'I do not create for Adam any offspring except that I create for you the like of it,' so no child of Adam is born except that a devil is born with him, joined to him." It was said to the Messenger: "Do you have a devil?" He said: "Yes, but Allah has helped me against him, so he submitted." Al-Dahhak and others named a group of the offspring of Iblis; Allah knows best the correctness of that. Likewise they mentioned modes of his intercourse and begetting; Allah knows best about that. A group went to the view that Iblis has no offspring, and that the devils are those who assist him in reaching his aims. The one singled out for censure is omitted, meaning: ﴿evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾, the substitute for Allah is Iblis and his offspring. He said "for the wrongdoers" because they exchanged the truth for falsehood and put Iblis and his offspring in the place of their allegiance (wilayah) to Allah. This is the very essence of wrongdoing (zulm), because it is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

The majority read ﴿mā ashhadtuhum﴾ with the first person singular (ta' of the speaker). Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-Sakhtiyani, 'Awn al-'Uqayli and Ibn Miqsam read: mā ashhadnāhum with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah). The apparent reference of the object pronoun in ﴿ashhadtuhum﴾ is to Iblis and his offspring, meaning: I did not consult them in the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor in the creation of themselves, but I created them as I willed. For this reason He said ﴿and I would not take misleaders as helpers﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It means that you took partners for Me in worship, and they would only be partners in it if they were partners in divinity. So He denied their sharing in divinity by His saying ﴿I did not make them witnesses to the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, I do not rely on them in its creation, ﴿nor the creation of themselves﴾, that is, nor did I make some of them witness the creation of others, like His saying ﴿and do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29], and I would not take them as assistants. So He placed ﴿the misleaders﴾ in the position of the pronoun, as a censure of them for misleading (p-137). If they were not a helper to Me in creation, then why do you take them as partners in worship?" End of quotation.

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the angels, and the meaning is that He did not make them witness to that, nor did He seek their help in creating it, but He created them to obey Me and worship Me, so how could they worship them?

It was said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers. It was said: it refers to all creation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the pronoun in ﴿ashhadtuhum﴾ refers to the disbelievers and to humanity in general, so the verse contains a refutation of groups of astrologers (munajjimun), those of the natural philosophies (ahl al-tabaʼi'), those who claim to control affairs (al-mutahakkimun), physicians, and others of every kind who speculate about these matters. 'Abd al-Haqq al-Saqalli said this, interpreted it in this way, and said that this verse is a refutation of these groups, and some of the usuli scholars mentioned this. End of quotation.

Abu Ja'far, al-Jahdari, al-Hasan and Shaybah read ﴿wa-mā kunta﴾ with a fatha on the ta', addressing the Messenger ﷺ.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: it was not proper for you to rely upon them, nor should you take pride in them. End of quotation. What I say is that the meaning is a report from Allah about His Prophet, and an address from Him, exalted, to him concerning the negation of his being one who takes as a helper any of the misleaders. Rather, from the time he came into existence, peace be upon him, he was in the utmost disavowal of them and distance from them, so that his community would know that he had always been protected from the beginning of his upbringing; he never relied upon a misleader nor inclined toward him, ﷺ. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib read: muttakhidhan al-mudilliyn, using the active participle as the operative form. 'Isa read ('adadan) with a sukun on the dad, lightening the pattern (fa'l) as they said rajl and sab' for rajul and sabu', and this is a dialect of Tamim; and from him also with two fathas. Shaybah and Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of Harun, Kharijah and al-Khaffaf, read ('ududan) with two dammas. From al-Hasan (ʻadadan) with two fathas, and from him also with two dammas. Al-Dahhak read ('idadan) with a kasra on the ʻayn and a fatha on the dad.

The majority read ﴿wa-yawma yaqulu﴾ with the ya', meaning Allah. Al-A'mash, Talhah, Yahya, Ibn Abi Layla, Hamzah and Ibn Miqsam read (naqulu) with the nun of majesty, meaning: to those who associated others with Him in this world, ﴿call upon My partners﴾. The meaning is not that He informed that they are His partners, but that it is according to your claim, and the attribution (idafah) may be by the slightest connection. The two objects of ﴿zaʻamtum﴾ are omitted, being indicated by the meaning, since the sense is "you claimed them to be My partners." The calling (nida') here means seeking help, that is: call for help from your partners, and what is meant is: call upon them to remove the punishment from you or to intercede for you. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (baynahum) refers to the callers and those called, namely the polytheists and the partners. It was said: it refers to the people of guidance and the people of error. The apparent reading is that the calling actually occurs, and that the answer is absent. It was said: it may be a metaphor, as if the thought of the disbeliever and his consideration that those lifeless things can neither benefit nor harm is equivalent to calling and to not answering.

The majority read (shurakaʼiya) as a lengthened form with the pronoun suffix ya'; Ibn Kathir and the people of Makkah read it shortened with the same suffix. The apparent reading is that (baynahum) is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf). Al-Farra' said: "al-bayn" here means the connection, that is: "and We made their connection in this world a destruction on the Day of Resurrection." On this reading, it is the first object of (ja'alna); and on the adverbial reading, it is in the position of the second object. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: al-mawbiq is the place of destruction. Al-Zajjaj said: We placed between them of the punishment that which destroys them. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, Anas and Mujahid said: it is a valley in Hell which flows with blood and pus. al-Hasan said: enmity. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it is the gathering-place. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is the appointed place.

﴿And the criminals will see the Fire﴾: it is the seeing of the eye, that is, they will witness it directly. The word (zann) here is said by some to be in its original sense, of inclining toward one of two sides. Their not being certain that they would enter it is due to hope and desire for the mercy of Allah. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿fa-zannu﴾ is "they were certain," as most people said, and the meaning of ﴿muwaqi'uha﴾ is "those who mix with it, falling into it," like His saying ﴿and they thought there was no refuge from Allah except in Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 118], and ﴿those who think that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: People have said without restriction that the zann here means certainty, and if he had said "certain" (ayqanu) instead of "thought" (zannu), the statement would be consistent, with an intensification in it. But the expression of zann never comes in a place of complete certainty that has been reached by the senses; at its highest level it comes in a place of verified knowledge, but that which is thought did not occur. Otherwise, whoever has experienced it and perceived it is hardly ever expressed with zann in the speech of the Arabs. End of quotation.

Consider this verse, and consider the verse of Duraid:

"I said to them: 'Consider it, against two thousand armored men.'"

End of quotation. In the codex of 'Abd Allah, "mulaquha" stands in place of ﴿muwaqi'uha﴾, and al-A'mash and Ibn Ghazwan from Talhah read it thus; but the better course is to take it as an explanation of the variant from the consonantal text. From 'Alqamah, he read "mullaffuha" with fa' and a shaddah, from lafaftu. In a hadith: "The disbeliever sees Hell and thinks that it will fall upon him from a distance of forty years." The meaning of ﴿masrifan﴾ is a way of escape (ma'dilan) and a place of refuge (mara'an). From it is the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

"O Zuhayr, is there any escape for Shaybah? Or is there no eternity for the one who spends and strives?"

Abu Mu'adh permitted (masrafan) with a fatha on the ra'; this is the reading of Zayd ibn 'Ali, and he made it a verbal noun (masdar), like al-madrab, because its present form yasrifu follows the pattern yaf'ilu like yadribu.

The apparent meaning of this verse is that he was not of the angels, but was of the jinn. Qatadah said: "The jinn are a kind of the angels, created from the fire of the samum wind." Shahr ibn Hawshab said: "He was one of the jinn whom the angels had overcome; one of the angels took him captive and carried him off to the heaven." Al-Hasan and others said: "He was the first of the jinn, and their origin is like that of Adam among mankind." A group said: "Iblis and his kind were jinn, but the devils today are his offspring, so he is like Noah among mankind." Al-Zamakhshari said: "'He was of the jinn' is a new sentence (kalam mustaʼnaf) functioning as a causal explanation after the exception of Iblis from those who prostrated, as if someone said: 'What is wrong with him, that he did not prostrate?' So it was said, '[He] was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord.' The fa' here is also for causation (tasbib). He made his being of the jinn the cause of his defiance, meaning: if he had been an angel like all who prostrated to Adam, he would not have defied the command of Allah, because the angels are absolutely infallible (ma'sumun), and what is permissible for the jinn and mankind is not permissible for them, as He said: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya': 27]. This interjected statement is a deliberate act by Allah, exalted and high, to protect the angels from any doubt arising concerning their infallibility. How far apart is what Allah intended from the statement of one who opposed Him, who claimed that he was an angel and a chief over the angels, who disobeyed and was cursed and transformed into a devil, and then attributed that to Ibn Abbas." End of quotation.

The apparent meaning of ﴿fa-fasaqa 'an amri rabbihi﴾ is: he went out from what his Lord had commanded him, namely prostration. Ru'bah said:

"They sink into the highland and the deep lowland, deviating from their course, bewildered."

It was also said: "fa-fasaqa" means he became a fasiq, a disbelieving one, because of the command of his Lord, which is His saying ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾, in that he did not comply with it. It was said: It may also be that the meaning is ﴿fa-fasaqa﴾ by the command of his Lord, that is, by His will and decree, because will is also called a command, as you say: "I did that by your command," meaning according to your desire. The interrogative hamzah in ﴿Will you then take him﴾ is for reproach, denial and wonder: that is, after what manifested from him of defiance and disobedience, do you take him and his offspring as allies besides Me, while his enmity toward you is established? Do you take him as a friend?

'Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad recited from the pulpit while he was delivering a sermon: (afa-tattakhidhunahu wa-dhurriyyatahu) with a fatha on the dhal. Evidently Iblis has offspring, and this was said by a group including Qatadah, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak and al-A'mash.

Qatadah said: "He marries and begets, as the children of Adam beget." Al-Sha'bi said: "There is no offspring except from a wife." Ibn Zayd said: "Allah said to Iblis: 'I do not create for Adam any offspring except that I create for you the like of it,' so no child of Adam is born except that a devil is born with him, joined to him." It was said to the Messenger: "Do you have a devil?" He said: "Yes, but Allah has helped me against him, so he submitted." Al-Dahhak and others named a group of the offspring of Iblis; Allah knows best the correctness of that. Likewise they mentioned modes of his intercourse and begetting; Allah knows best about that. A group went to the view that Iblis has no offspring, and that the devils are those who assist him in reaching his aims. The one singled out for censure is omitted, meaning: ﴿evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾, the substitute for Allah is Iblis and his offspring. He said "for the wrongdoers" because they exchanged the truth for falsehood and put Iblis and his offspring in the place of their allegiance (wilayah) to Allah. This is the very essence of wrongdoing (zulm), because it is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

The majority read ﴿mā ashhadtuhum﴾ with the first person singular (ta' of the speaker). Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-Sakhtiyani, 'Awn al-'Uqayli and Ibn Miqsam read: mā ashhadnāhum with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah). The apparent reference of the object pronoun in ﴿ashhadtuhum﴾ is to Iblis and his offspring, meaning: I did not consult them in the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor in the creation of themselves, but I created them as I willed. For this reason He said ﴿and I would not take misleaders as helpers﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It means that you took partners for Me in worship, and they would only be partners in it if they were partners in divinity. So He denied their sharing in divinity by His saying ﴿I did not make them witnesses to the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, I do not rely on them in its creation, ﴿nor the creation of themselves﴾, that is, nor did I make some of them witness the creation of others, like His saying ﴿and do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29], and I would not take them as assistants. So He placed ﴿the misleaders﴾ in the position of the pronoun, as a censure of them for misleading (p-137). If they were not a helper to Me in creation, then why do you take them as partners in worship?" End of quotation.

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the angels, and the meaning is that He did not make them witness to that, nor did He seek their help in creating it, but He created them to obey Me and worship Me, so how could they worship them?

It was said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers. It was said: it refers to all creation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the pronoun in ﴿ashhadtuhum﴾ refers to the disbelievers and to humanity in general, so the verse contains a refutation of groups of astrologers (munajjimun), those of the natural philosophies (ahl al-tabaʼi'), those who claim to control affairs (al-mutahakkimun), physicians, and others of every kind who speculate about these matters. 'Abd al-Haqq al-Saqalli said this, interpreted it in this way, and said that this verse is a refutation of these groups, and some of the usuli scholars mentioned this. End of quotation.

Abu Ja'far, al-Jahdari, al-Hasan and Shaybah read ﴿wa-mā kunta﴾ with a fatha on the ta', addressing the Messenger ﷺ.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: it was not proper for you to rely upon them, nor should you take pride in them. End of quotation. What I say is that the meaning is a report from Allah about His Prophet, and an address from Him, exalted, to him concerning the negation of his being one who takes as a helper any of the misleaders. Rather, from the time he came into existence, peace be upon him, he was in the utmost disavowal of them and distance from them, so that his community would know that he had always been protected from the beginning of his upbringing; he never relied upon a misleader nor inclined toward him, ﷺ. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib read: muttakhidhan al-mudilliyn, using the active participle as the operative form. 'Isa read ('adadan) with a sukun on the dad, lightening the pattern (fa'l) as they said rajl and sab' for rajul and sabu', and this is a dialect of Tamim; and from him also with two fathas. Shaybah and Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of Harun, Kharijah and al-Khaffaf, read ('ududan) with two dammas. From al-Hasan (ʻadadan) with two fathas, and from him also with two dammas. Al-Dahhak read ('idadan) with a kasra on the ʻayn and a fatha on the dad.

The majority read ﴿wa-yawma yaqulu﴾ with the ya', meaning Allah. Al-A'mash, Talhah, Yahya, Ibn Abi Layla, Hamzah and Ibn Miqsam read (naqulu) with the nun of majesty, meaning: to those who associated others with Him in this world, ﴿call upon My partners﴾. The meaning is not that He informed that they are His partners, but that it is according to your claim, and the attribution (idafah) may be by the slightest connection. The two objects of ﴿zaʻamtum﴾ are omitted, being indicated by the meaning, since the sense is "you claimed them to be My partners." The calling (nida') here means seeking help, that is: call for help from your partners, and what is meant is: call upon them to remove the punishment from you or to intercede for you. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (baynahum) refers to the callers and those called, namely the polytheists and the partners. It was said: it refers to the people of guidance and the people of error. The apparent reading is that the calling actually occurs, and that the answer is absent. It was said: it may be a metaphor, as if the thought of the disbeliever and his consideration that those lifeless things can neither benefit nor harm is equivalent to calling and to not answering.

The majority read (shurakaʼiya) as a lengthened form with the pronoun suffix ya'; Ibn Kathir and the people of Makkah read it shortened with the same suffix. The apparent reading is that (baynahum) is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarf). Al-Farra' said: "al-bayn" here means the connection, that is: "and We made their connection in this world a destruction on the Day of Resurrection." On this reading, it is the first object of (ja'alna); and on the adverbial reading, it is in the position of the second object. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: al-mawbiq is the place of destruction. Al-Zajjaj said: We placed between them of the punishment that which destroys them. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, Anas and Mujahid said: it is a valley in Hell which flows with blood and pus. al-Hasan said: enmity. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it is the gathering-place. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is the appointed place.

﴿And the criminals will see the Fire﴾: it is the seeing of the eye, that is, they will witness it directly. The word (zann) here is said by some to be in its original sense, of inclining toward one of two sides. Their not being certain that they would enter it is due to hope and desire for the mercy of Allah. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿fa-zannu﴾ is "they were certain," as most people said, and the meaning of ﴿muwaqi'uha﴾ is "those who mix with it, falling into it," like His saying ﴿and they thought there was no refuge from Allah except in Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 118], and ﴿those who think that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: People have said without restriction that the zann here means certainty, and if he had said "certain" (ayqanu) instead of "thought" (zannu), the statement would be consistent, with an intensification in it. But the expression of zann never comes in a place of complete certainty that has been reached by the senses; at its highest level it comes in a place of verified knowledge, but that which is thought did not occur. Otherwise, whoever has experienced it and perceived it is hardly ever expressed with zann in the speech of the Arabs. End of quotation.

Consider this verse, and consider the verse of Duraid:

"I said to them: 'Consider it, against two thousand armored men.'"

End of quotation. In the codex of 'Abd Allah, "mulaquha" stands in place of ﴿muwaqi'uha﴾, and al-A'mash and Ibn Ghazwan from Talhah read it thus; but the better course is to take it as an explanation of the variant from the consonantal text. From 'Alqamah, he read "mullaffuha" with fa' and a shaddah, from lafaftu. In a hadith: "The disbeliever sees Hell and thinks that it will fall upon him from a distance of forty years." The meaning of ﴿masrifan﴾ is a way of escape (ma'dilan) and a place of refuge (mara'an). From it is the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

"O Zuhayr, is there any escape for Shaybah? Or is there no eternity for the one who spends and strives?"

Abu Mu'adh permitted (masrafan) with a fatha on the ra'; this is the reading of Zayd ibn 'Ali, and he made it a verbal noun (masdar), like al-madrab, because its present form yasrifu follows the pattern yaf'ilu like yadribu.

And indeed We have explained in this Qur'an, for the people, every kind of example, and man is ever the most contentious of things. ﴾54﴿

And nothing prevented the people from believing when the guidance came to them, and from seeking forgiveness from their Lord, except that the way of the earlier peoples should come upon them, or that the punishment should come upon them face to face. ﴾55﴿

And We send the messengers only as bearers of good news and warners. Yet those who disbelieve dispute with falsehood, so that they may refute the truth thereby, and they take My signs and what they were warned of in mockery. ﴾56﴿

And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turns away from them and forgets what his hands have sent forward? Indeed, We have placed coverings over their hearts lest they understand it, and deafness in their ears. And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever. ﴾57﴿

And your Lord is the Most Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy. Were He to take them to account for what they have earned, He would hasten their punishment for them. But for them there is an appointed time, from which they will find no refuge other than it. ﴾58﴿

And those towns — We destroyed them when they did wrong, and We appointed for their destruction a set time. ﴾59﴿

The commentary on the like of the beginning of this verse has already passed. Here (شيء, shay') is singular in form but has the meaning of the plural, i.e., "the most of the things from which argument can arise, if you detail them one after another." (جدلا, jadalan) means contention and disputation. The meaning is that the argument of man is greater than the argument of (p-139) every thing. Its like is the verse ﴿then he is an open adversary﴾ [An-Nahl: 4]. (جدلا, jadalan) is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification of a noun). It has been said: (الإنسان, al-insan) here refers to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. It has been said: Ibn al-Za'ba'ra. It has been said: Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and his argument was about the resurrection when he brought a bone, crumbled it, and said: "Will God be able to restore this?" This was related by Ibn al-Sa'ib. It has been said: every one who has intellect, from angels and jinn, argues, and man is the most of these things in argument. End.

The human being is often mentioned in the context of blame. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited His saying: ﴿And man is ever the most contentious of things﴾ when he rebuked 'Ali, may God honour his face, for sleeping through the voluntary night prayer. 'Ali said to him: "Indeed, our souls are in the hand of God." So (الإنسان, al-insan) was used in a general sense. In His saying ﴿And nothing prevented the people﴾ up to the end of the verse, there is a expression of regret over them and an alert to the corruption of their condition, because this prevention was not with their intention to refrain so that the punishment would come to them. Rather they refrained while believing that they were correct, but the matter in itself drove them to this, so their state required regret over them. (النّاس, al-nas) is intended to mean the disbelievers of the era of the Messenger (ﷺ) who took it upon themselves to repel and deny the Sharia. This is what Ibn 'Atiyya said.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the first (أن يؤمنوا, an yu'minu, "that they believe") is in the accusative and the second is in the nominative, and before them there is an omitted genitive (mudaf, a noun governed by an omitted noun) whose estimate is ﴿nothing prevented the people﴾ from faith, "except" the expectation of ﴿that the way of the earlier peoples should come upon them﴾, which is destruction, "or" the expectation of (أن يأتيهم العذاب, an ya'tiyahumu al-'adhab), meaning the punishment of the Hereafter. End. This is taken from the words of al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj said: its estimate is: what prevented them from faith "except" the request of ﴿that the way of the earlier peoples should come upon them﴾. Al-Wahidi said: the meaning is: what prevented them except that I had decreed the punishment upon them. This verse concerns those of the polytheists who were killed at Badr and Uhud. This statement is similar to the statement of one who said: the estimate is ﴿and nothing prevented the people from believing﴾ except what had preceded in Our knowledge and Our decree, that there would befall them ﴿the way of the earlier peoples﴾ of the punishment of uprooting, such as transformation into animals, the Cry, the sinking into the earth, drowning, the punishment of the cloud, and the like. By "the earlier peoples" he meant the nations of the past who were destroyed. The author of al-Ghuniyan said: "except" the intention or expectation that Our way among the earlier peoples would come upon them. Whoever estimates the omitted genitive as this, or as the request, does so only because they believed the prophets were not truthful in what they promised of punishment, as He said relating about some of them: ﴿If this is indeed the truth from You﴾ [Al-Anfal: 32]. It has been said: (ما, ma) here is interrogative, not negative, and the estimate is: "And what thing prevented the people from believing?" And (الهدى, al-huda) means the Messenger or the Qur'an; these are two views.

Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Layla, Khalaf, Ayyub, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani, Ibn Jarir and the Kufans read (قُبُلًا, qubulan) with a damma on the qaf and the ba'. It may mean the same as (قبلا, qiblan, "face to face"), because Abu 'Ubayda related both with one meaning in opposition. It may also be the plural of (قبيل, qabil), meaning: the punishment will come to them in kinds and types. The rest of the seven, and Mujahid and 'Isa ibn 'Umar, read (قِبَلًا, qibalan) with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', and its meaning is "face to face" (عيانا, 'iyanan). Abu Raja' and al-Hasan also read it with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the ba', which is a lightening of (قُبُلٍ, qubul) according to the dialect of Tamim. Ibn Qutayba mentioned that it was read with two fathas, and al-Zamakhshari related it and said: "coming in the future" (مستقبلا, mustaqbalan). Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Ghazwan from Talha read (قَبِيلًا, qabilan) with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the ba' followed by a ya', on the pattern of (فَعِيلٌ, fa'il).

﴿And We send the messengers only as bearers of good news﴾, meaning of the everlasting bliss for whoever believes, "and warners", meaning of the painful punishment for whoever disbelieves, not so that they may be disputed with, nor so that proposals be dictated to them. "So that they may refute" (ليدحضوا, liyudhidu), meaning to remove, "and they take My signs" gathers the signs of the Qur'an and the signs of the Messenger, in speech and in action. "And what they were warned of" (وما أنذروا, wa ma unthirū), meaning the punishment of the Hereafter. The (ما, ma) may be relative, meaning "what" (الذي, alladhi), with a omitted returning pronoun, i.e., what they were warned of; or it may be verbal-noun (مصدرية, masdariyya), i.e., their warning, and then it needs no returning pronoun according to the most correct view. "In mockery" (هزؤا, huzuan), meaning ridicule and scorn, in response to their saying: "fables of the earlier peoples," and "If we willed, we would say the like of this." Their disputation with the messengers, may God's blessings and peace be upon them, was their saying ﴿You are but a human like us﴾ [Ya-Sin: 15] and ﴿If God had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 24], and what is similar to that. And "the signs" which are attributed to the Lord is the Qur'an, and for this reason the pronoun returned singular in His saying "that they understand it" (أن يفقهوه, an yafqahuhu). Their turning away from them is that they do not remember when they are reminded and do not reflect, and they forget the outcome of what their hands have sent forward of disbelief and sins, without contemplating it, nor considering that the one who does good and the one who does evil are each recompensed for what they did.

The commentary on the like of His saying (p-140) ﴿Indeed, We have placed coverings over their hearts lest they understand it, and deafness in their ears﴾ has already passed. Then the Exalted informed that these will never be guided, ever. This is a general statement, and what is meant by it is particular: those whom God has sealed upon their hearts and decreed for them to die upon disbelief, since many of the disbelievers were guided and believed. It is possible that this is a judgment upon all of them, i.e., ﴿And if you call them﴾, i.e., "to guidance", all of them, ﴿then they will not be guided﴾, all of them, "ever." He first took the wording of (من, man, "whoever") in the singular, then the meaning in the plural, in His saying ﴿Indeed, We have placed over their hearts﴾, so He made plural. They made the Messenger's calling to guidance, which is the thing that would be a cause for the existence of guidance, a cause for the absence of their guidance. This conditional sentence is as if it were an answer to the Messenger, in response to an estimated statement of his: "Why do I not call them to guidance?" out of his eagerness, peace be upon him, for their faith to be realized. So it was said: ﴿And if you call them﴾. Restricting it with "ever" is an intensification in the negation of their guidance.

"The Forgiving" (الغفور, al-Ghafur) is an intensive attribute, and "the Possessor of mercy" (ذو الرحمة, dhu al-rahma), i.e., the one described with mercy. Then He mentioned the evidence of His mercy, which is that the Exalted "does not take them to account" immediately, but gives them respite despite their excess in disbelief and enmity towards the Messenger (ﷺ). The appointed time (الموعد, al-maw'id) is either the term of death, or the punishment of the Hereafter, or the day of Badr, or the day of Uhud. Times of victory or punishment, whether in this world or in the Hereafter, are views.

Al-Mawil (المَوْئِل, refuge): Mujahid said: a place of safety. Al-Dahhak said: a means of escape. The pronoun in "other than it" (من دونه, min dunihi) returns to the appointed time. Al-Zuhri read (مَوِّلًا, mawwilan) with a shadda on the waw, without hamza or ya'. Abu Ja'far, from al-Hulwani, from him, read (مَوِلًا, mawilan) with a kasra on the waw lightly, without hamza or ya'. The majority read it with a sukun on the waw and a hamza after it with a kasra.

By His saying ﴿And those towns﴾ the Exalted refers to the towns neighbouring the people of Makkah and the Arabs, such as the towns of Thamud and the people of Lut and others, so that they might take warning from what befell them and beware of what would befall them, as it befell those towns. "And those" (تلك, tilka) is a subject (مبتدأ, mubtada'), and "the towns" (القرى, al-qura) is an adjective or a appositive (عطف بيان, 'atf bayan), and the predicate is "We destroyed them" (أهلكناهم, ahlaknahum). It is permissible that "the towns" is the predicate and "We destroyed them" is a circumstantial clause (جملة حالية, jumla haliyya), like His saying ﴿So those are their houses, empty﴾ [An-Naml: 52]. It is permissible that "those" is in the accusative by an implied verb which the following explains, i.e., "And We destroyed those towns; We destroyed them." And ﴿those towns﴾ [Al-A'raf: 101] is with an implied genitive, i.e., "and the people of those towns," and for this reason the pronoun returned to that implied noun in His saying "We destroyed them."

His saying "when they did wrong" (لما ظلموا, lamma zalamu) indicates the cause of the destruction, which is wrongdoing. With this, the teacher Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Usfur argued that (لما, lamma) is a particle and not in the sense of "when" (حين, hina), because the time adverb does not indicate causation. In His saying "when they did wrong" there is a warning against wrongdoing, since its outcome is destruction. "And We appointed for their destruction a set time," which is the appointed time, and it is possible that it is a verbal noun or a time. The majority read (مَهْلِك, mahlik) with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the lam, and it is possible that it is a verbal noun added to its object, and that it is a time. Hafs and Harun from Abu Bakr read it with two fathas, which is the time of destruction. Hafs read it with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam, the verbal noun of halaka yahliku, and it is added to the subject. It has been said: halaka is both intransitive and transitive, so on its transitive use it is added to the object. Abu 'Ali recited on this:

"And a desert, one who perishes, whoever crosses it..."

What Abu 'Ali said about this line is not necessarily fixed; rather some grammarians held that "hālik" in it is intransitive and that it is of the type of the attributive adjective (الصفة المشبهة, al-sifa al-mushabbaha), its original form being "hālikin man ta'arraja." So "man" is the subject, then the pronoun in "hālik" refers to "mahh," and "man" is in the accusative by analogy to the object, then the one who puts it in the accusative adds it to it. There is disagreement about whether the relative pronoun can be of the type of the attributive adjective. The correct view is that this is permissible, and it is attested in Arabic poetry. The poet, who is 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a, said:

"Delicate of bodies, slender of waists, / and full-bodied, those upon whom the wrappers cling."

Another said: "So I turned her toward the good, a dwelling, / and the good ones of every garment that the waistwraps have clung to."

And indeed We have explained in this Qur'an, for the people, every kind of example, and man is ever the most contentious of things. ﴾54﴿

And nothing prevented the people from believing when the guidance came to them, and from seeking forgiveness from their Lord, except that the way of the earlier peoples should come upon them, or that the punishment should come upon them face to face. ﴾55﴿

And We send the messengers only as bearers of good news and warners. Yet those who disbelieve dispute with falsehood, so that they may refute the truth thereby, and they take My signs and what they were warned of in mockery. ﴾56﴿

And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turns away from them and forgets what his hands have sent forward? Indeed, We have placed coverings over their hearts lest they understand it, and deafness in their ears. And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever. ﴾57﴿

And your Lord is the Most Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy. Were He to take them to account for what they have earned, He would hasten their punishment for them. But for them there is an appointed time, from which they will find no refuge other than it. ﴾58﴿

And those towns — We destroyed them when they did wrong, and We appointed for their destruction a set time. ﴾59﴿

The commentary on the like of the beginning of this verse has already passed. Here (شيء, shay') is singular in form but has the meaning of the plural, i.e., "the most of the things from which argument can arise, if you detail them one after another." (جدلا, jadalan) means contention and disputation. The meaning is that the argument of man is greater than the argument of (p-139) every thing. Its like is the verse ﴿then he is an open adversary﴾ [An-Nahl: 4]. (جدلا, jadalan) is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification of a noun). It has been said: (الإنسان, al-insan) here refers to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. It has been said: Ibn al-Za'ba'ra. In His saying ﴿And nothing prevented the people﴾ up to the end of the verse, there is a expression of regret over them and an alert to the corruption of their condition, because this prevention was not with their intention to refrain so that the punishment would come to them. Rather they refrained while believing that they were correct, but the matter in itself drove them to this, so their state required regret over them. (النّاس, al-nas) is intended to mean the disbelievers of the era of the Messenger (ﷺ) who took it upon themselves to repel and deny the Sharia. This is what Ibn 'Atiyya said.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the first (أن يؤمنوا, an yu'minu, "that they believe") is in the accusative and the second is in the nominative, and before them there is an omitted genitive (mudaf, a noun governed by an omitted noun) whose estimate is ﴿nothing prevented the people﴾ from faith, "except" the expectation of ﴿that the way of the earlier peoples should come upon them﴾, which is destruction, "or" the expectation of (أن يأتيهم العذاب, an ya'tiyahumu al-'adhab), meaning the punishment of the Hereafter. End. This is taken from the words of al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj said: its estimate is: what prevented them from faith "except" the request of ﴿that the way of the earlier peoples should come upon them﴾. Al-Wahidi said: the meaning is: what prevented them except that I had decreed the punishment upon them. This verse concerns those of the polytheists who were killed at Badr and Uhud. This statement is similar to the statement of one who said: the estimate is ﴿and nothing prevented the people from believing﴾ except what had preceded in Our knowledge and Our decree, that there would befall them ﴿the way of the earlier peoples﴾ of the punishment of uprooting, such as transformation into animals, the Cry, the sinking into the earth, drowning, the punishment of the cloud, and the like. By "the earlier peoples" he meant the nations of the past who were destroyed. The author of al-Ghuniyan said: "except" the intention or expectation that Our way among the earlier peoples would come upon them. Whoever estimates the omitted genitive as this, or as the request, does so only because they believed the prophets were not truthful in what they promised of punishment, as He said relating about some of them: ﴿If this is indeed the truth from You﴾ [Al-Anfal: 32]. It has been said: (ما, ma) here is interrogative, not negative, and the estimate is: "And what thing prevented the people from believing?" And (الهدى, al-huda) means the Messenger or the Qur'an; these are two views.

Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Layla, Khalaf, Ayyub, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani, Ibn Jarir and the Kufans read (قُبُلًا, qubulan) with a damma on the qaf and the ba'. It may mean the same as (قبلا, qiblan, "face to face"), because Abu 'Ubayda related both with one meaning in opposition. It may also be the plural of (قبيل, qabil), meaning: the punishment will come to them in kinds and types. The rest of the seven, and Mujahid and 'Isa ibn 'Umar, read (قِبَلًا, qibalan) with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', and its meaning is "face to face" (عيانا, 'iyanan). Abu Raja' and al-Hasan also read it with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the ba', which is a lightening of (قُبُلٍ, qubul) according to the dialect of Tamim. Ibn Qutayba mentioned that it was read with two fathas, and al-Zamakhshari related it and said: "coming in the future" (مستقبلا, mustaqbalan). Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Ghazwan from Talha read (قَبِيلًا, qabilan) with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the ba' followed by a ya', on the pattern of (فَعِيلٌ, fa'il).

﴿And We send the messengers only as bearers of good news﴾, meaning of the everlasting bliss for whoever believes, "and warners", meaning of the painful punishment for whoever disbelieves, not so that they may be disputed with, nor so that proposals be dictated to them. "So that they may refute" (ليدحضوا, liyudhidu), meaning to remove, "and they take My signs" gathers the signs of the Qur'an and the signs of the Messenger, in speech and in action. "And what they were warned of" (وما أنذروا, wa ma unthirū), meaning the punishment of the Hereafter. The (ما, ma) may be relative, meaning "what" (الذي, alladhi), with a omitted returning pronoun, i.e., what they were warned of; or it may be verbal-noun (مصدرية, masdariyya), i.e., their warning, and then it needs no returning pronoun according to the most correct view. "In mockery" (هزؤا, huzuan), meaning ridicule and scorn, in response to their saying: "fables of the earlier peoples," and "If we willed, we would say the like of this." Their disputation with the messengers, may God's blessings and peace be upon them, was their saying ﴿You are but a human like us﴾ [Ya-Sin: 15] and ﴿If God had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 24], and what is similar to that. And "the signs" which are attributed to the Lord is the Qur'an, and for this reason the pronoun returned singular in His saying "that they understand it" (أن يفقهوه, an yafqahuhu). Their turning away from them is that they do not remember when they are reminded and do not reflect, and they forget the outcome of what their hands have sent forward of disbelief and sins, without contemplating it, nor considering that the one who does good and the one who does evil are each recompensed for what they did.

The commentary on the like of His saying (p-140) ﴿Indeed, We have placed coverings over their hearts lest they understand it, and deafness in their ears﴾ has already passed. Then the Exalted informed that these will never be guided, ever. This is a general statement, and what is meant by it is particular: those whom God has sealed upon their hearts and decreed for them to die upon disbelief, since many of the disbelievers were guided and believed. It is possible that this is a judgment upon all of them, i.e., ﴿And if you call them﴾, i.e., "to guidance", all of them, ﴿then they will not be guided﴾, all of them, "ever." He first took the wording of (من, man, "whoever") in the singular, then the meaning in the plural, in His saying ﴿Indeed, We have placed over their hearts﴾, so He made plural. They made the Messenger's calling to guidance, which is the thing that would be a cause for the existence of guidance, a cause for the absence of their guidance. This conditional sentence is as if it were an answer to the Messenger, in response to an estimated statement of his: "Why do I not call them to guidance?" out of his eagerness, peace be upon him, for their faith to be realized. So it was said: ﴿And if you call them﴾. Restricting it with "ever" is an intensification in the negation of their guidance.

"The Forgiving" (الغفور, al-Ghafur) is an intensive attribute, and "the Possessor of mercy" (ذو الرحمة, dhu al-rahma), i.e., the one described with mercy. Then He mentioned the evidence of His mercy, which is that the Exalted "does not take them to account" immediately, but gives them respite despite their excess in disbelief and enmity towards the Messenger (ﷺ). The appointed time (الموعد, al-maw'id) is either the term of death, or the punishment of the Hereafter, or the day of Badr, or the day of Uhud. Times of victory or punishment, whether in this world or in the Hereafter, are views.

Al-Mawil (المَوْئِل, refuge): Mujahid said: a place of safety. Al-Dahhak said: a means of escape. The pronoun in "other than it" (من دونه, min dunihi) returns to the appointed time. Al-Zuhri read (مَوِّلًا, mawwilan) with a shadda on the waw, without hamza or ya'. Abu Ja'far, from al-Hulwani, from him, read (مَوِلًا, mawilan) with a kasra on the waw lightly, without hamza or ya'. The majority read it with a sukun on the waw and a hamza after it with a kasra.

By His saying ﴿And those towns﴾ the Exalted refers to the towns neighbouring the people of Makkah and the Arabs, such as the towns of Thamud and the people of Lut and others, so that they might take warning from what befell them and beware of what would befall them, as it befell those towns. "And those" (تلك, tilka) is a subject (مبتدأ, mubtada'), and "the towns" (القرى, al-qura) is an adjective or a appositive (عطف بيان, 'atf bayan), and the predicate is "We destroyed them" (أهلكناهم, ahlaknahum). It is permissible that "the towns" is the predicate and "We destroyed them" is a circumstantial clause (جملة حالية, jumla haliyya), like His saying ﴿So those are their houses, empty﴾ [An-Naml: 52]. It is permissible that "those" is in the accusative by an implied verb which the following explains, i.e., "And We destroyed those towns; We destroyed them." And ﴿those towns﴾ [Al-A'raf: 101] is with an implied genitive, i.e., "and the people of those towns," and for this reason the pronoun returned to that implied noun in His saying "We destroyed them."

His saying "when they did wrong" (لما ظلموا, lamma zalamu) indicates the cause of the destruction, which is wrongdoing. With this, the teacher Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Usfur argued that (لما, lamma) is a particle and not in the sense of "when" (حين, hina), because the time adverb does not indicate causation. In His saying "when they did wrong" there is a warning against wrongdoing, since its outcome is destruction. "And We appointed for their destruction a set time," which is the appointed time, and it is possible that it is a verbal noun or a time. The majority read (مَهْلِك, mahlik) with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the lam, and it is possible that it is a verbal noun added to its object, and that it is a time. Hafs and Harun from Abu Bakr read it with two fathas, which is the time of destruction. Hafs read it with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam, the verbal noun of halaka yahliku, and it is added to the subject. It has been said: halaka is both intransitive and transitive, so on its transitive use it is added to the object. Abu 'Ali recited on this:

"And a desert, one who perishes, whoever crosses it..."

What Abu 'Ali said about this line is not necessarily fixed; rather some grammarians held that "hālik" in it is intransitive and that it is of the type of the attributive adjective (الصفة المشبهة, al-sifa al-mushabbaha), its original form being "hālikin man ta'arraja." So "man" is the subject, then the pronoun in "hālik" refers to "mahh," and "man" is in the accusative by analogy to the object, then the one who puts it in the accusative adds it to it. There is disagreement about whether the relative pronoun can be of the type of the attributive adjective. The correct view is that this is permissible, and it is attested in Arabic poetry. The poet, who is 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a, said:

"Delicate of bodies, slender of waists, / and full-bodied, those upon whom the wrappers cling."

Another said: "So I turned her toward the good, a dwelling, / and the good ones of every garment that the waistwraps have clung to."

(p-142)﴿And when Moses said to his servant, "I will not stop until I reach the meeting place of the two seas, or I will journey for a long age."﴾ ﴿But when they reached the meeting place of the two of them, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, freely.﴾ ﴿Then when they had passed on, he said to his servant, "Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed met with fatigue from this journey of ours."﴾ ﴿He said, "Did you see? When we took refuge at the rock, I forgot the fish, and none but Satan made me forget it, so that I did not remember it. It took its way into the sea in a wondrous manner."﴾ ﴿He said, "That is what we were seeking." So they went back, retracing their footsteps.﴾ ﴿Then they found a servant from Our servants, whom We had given mercy from Us and taught knowledge from Our own presence.﴾ ﴿Moses said to him, "May I follow you, on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, as right guidance?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed you will not be able to have patience with me."﴾ ﴿"And how can you have patience with what you have not encompassed in knowledge?"﴾ ﴿He said, "You will find me, God willing, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter."﴾ ﴿He said, "If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you."﴾ .
(p-143)Moses mentioned in this verse is Moses son of Imran (peace be upon him). Allah has not mentioned any Moses in His Book other than him. As for the one who holds that he is another, namely Moses son of Mishya son of Yusuf, or Moses son of Ifraithim son of Yusuf, that view is not sound. Rather, what is established in the authentic hadith and in the histories is that he is Moses son of Imran, the prophet of the Children of Israel, and the one sent, together with his brother Aaron, to Pharaoh. His servant (fata) was Joshua son of Nun son of Ifraithim son of Yusuf son of Ya'qub (peace be upon them). A fata is a young man. Since servants are most often young men, a servant was called a fata as a matter of good manners, and the Shari'a encouraged this. In the hadith: "Let none of you say 'my slave' or 'my maidservant'; let him say 'my young man' (fataya) and 'my young woman' (fataty)." He said "his servant" because he served him and followed him. It was also said that he took knowledge from him. It is said that Joshua was the son of Moses' sister. The cause of this story is that Moses (peace be upon him) sat one day in an assembly of the Children of Israel and delivered a sermon with eloquence. He was asked, "Do you know anyone more knowledgeable than you?" He said, "No." So Allah revealed to him that he should travel along the shore of the sea until he reached "the meeting place of the two seas," and that when he lost the fish, it would be there. Moses did this, and to his servant, in the manner of firmly resolving, he said, "I will not stop travelling," meaning, "I will not cease." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He only said this statement while he was travelling." From this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:
"They did not cease until their women were carried along in litters, in the valley of Dhu Qar, bearing perfumed garments."
End of quotation. What he mentioned here involves omitting the predicate of "I will not stop" (la abrah), and these are among the sisters of kana (verbs of state). Our scholars stated that omitting the predicate of kana and its sisters is not permitted, even if it is indicated, except in what has come in poetry, such as the saying:
"Alas for you, the distress of one who is afraid, who seeks your protection when there is no protector."
That is, when there is no one in the world. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "la abrah," if it means "I will not depart" from "barih al-makan" (to leave a place), then it indicates staying put during a journey; if it means "I will not cease," then the predicate must be present. I say: It means "I will not cease," and the predicate has been omitted, because the situation and the speech together both indicate it. As for the situation, it was a situation of travel. As for the speech, "until I reach the meeting place of the two seas" is a fixed limit that calls for a point to which it is a limit. So the meaning must be: "My journey will not cease until I reach..." The predicate is "until I reach," and when the governing noun was omitted, the pronoun of the speaker replaced the governed noun, so the verb shifted from the third-person pronoun to the first-person form. This is a subtle point. End of quotation. These are two possibilities which al-Zamakhshari conflated. As for the first: he made the verb predicated of the speaker, both in form and in implication, and made the predicate omitted, as Ibn 'Atiyya estimated, with "until I reach" being a complement attached to the omitted predicate and a limit for it. The second possibility: he made "la abrah" predicated, in form, of the speaker, and in meaning, of that omitted estimate, and made it so that "la abrah" is "until I reach." Thus it is a principal element, since its origin is the predicate of the subject, because it is the predicate of (abrah).
Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is possible that the meaning is: "I will not cease" in what I am doing, meaning "I will keep to the journey and the search, and I will not leave it or part from it, until I reach," as you say, "I will not leave the place." End of quotation. He means that "barih" can mean "to part from," and then it takes an object, and this requires a sound transmission.
Al-Tabari mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Moses and his people prevailed over Egypt, he settled his people in Egypt. When the situation was stable, he delivered a sermon one day, reminding them of the favors of Allah and His days among the Children of Israel. Then he mentioned that he knew of no one more knowledgeable than himself.
Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is not seen at all that Moses (peace be upon him) settled his people in Egypt except in this statement, and I do not think it is sound. Rather, what is apparent is that Moses died in the wilderness of the Wandering (al-Tih), before the conquest of the lands of the tyrants. This report from Ibn 'Abbas was also mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, who said: It is reported that when Moses prevailed over Egypt with the Children of Israel and they settled after the destruction of the Copts, Allah commanded him to remind his people of the blessing. So he stood among them as a preacher and mentioned the blessing of Allah, and said: "Allah has chosen your prophet and spoke to him." They said to him, "We already know this; who among the people is the most knowledgeable?" He said, "I am." So Allah rebuked him because he did not refer knowledge to Allah. Then Allah revealed to him: "Rather, someone more knowledgeable than you is a servant of Mine at the meeting place of the two seas, and he is al-Khadir." Al-Khadir was in the days of Afridun, before Moses, and was in the vanguard of Dhu al-Qarnayn the Great, and he remained until the days of Moses. It is also mentioned in the questions of Moses that he said: "If there is among Your servants someone more knowledgeable than me, guide me to him." He said: "More knowledgeable than you is al-Khadir." End of quotation. This contradicts what is established in the Sahih, that he was asked, "Is there anyone more knowledgeable than you?" and he said, "No."
As for "the meeting place of the two seas": Mujahid and Qatada said it is the confluence of the Persian Sea and the Roman Sea. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is an arm that extends from the Encircling Ocean from north to south, in the land of Persia behind Adharbayjan. So the corner where the two seas meet, on the side near the land of al-Sham, is the meeting place of the two seas according to this view. A group, among them Muhammad son of Ka'b al-Qurazi, said: It is at Tangier, where the Encircling Ocean meets the sea that flows out of it, from the west wind to the east wind. It is also reported from Ubayy (may Allah be pleased with him) that it is in Ifriqiya. It was said: It is the Sea of Andalus, and the town which refused to host them is al-Jazira al-Khadra. It was said: "The meeting place of the two seas" is a salt sea and a sweet sea, so al-Khadir would be, by this view, at the point where a great river enters the sea. A group said: The two seas are a metaphor for Moses and al-Khadir, because they were two seas of knowledge. This resembles the interpretation of the Batiniyya (esoteric sect) and the extreme Sufis, whereas the hadiths indicate that they are two bodies of water.
Al-Zamakhshari said: Among the strange interpretations is that the two seas are Moses and al-Khadir, because they were two seas in knowledge. End of quotation. It was also said: the Sea of al-Qulzum (the Red Sea). It was said: the Sea of al-Azraq.
Al-Dahhak and 'Abdullah son of Muslim son of Yasar read "majma'" (with a kasra on the second mim), and al-Nadr reported from Ibn Muslim in both places. This is anomalous; by analogy, from the pattern yaf'alu, the mim should be fatha, as in the reading of the majority. The apparent meaning is that "majma' al-bahrayn" is the name of the place where the two seas meet. It was also said to be a verbal noun.
Ibn 'Abbas said: "Huqub" means an age (dahr). 'Abdullah son of 'Amr and Abu Hurayra said: eighty years. Al-Hasan said: seventy. It was said: a year in the dialect of Quraysh, mentioned by al-Farra'. It was said: an unlimited period of time, said by Abu (p-145) 'Ubayda. The apparent meaning is that His statement "or I will journey" is conjoined to "I reach," so it sets a limit by one of two matters: either by reaching the meeting place or by journeying "a long age." It was said: it is a limit for his statement "I will not cease," as when you say, "I will not leave you, or you pay me my right," meaning: "I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas," or until I journey for a period of time in which I am certain of missing the meeting place of the two seas. Al-Dahhak read "huqban" with the qaf sukun, while the majority read it with a damma.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 60–70 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Then, when they reached the meeting place of the two seas﴾. Then (thumma) introduces an omitted clause; the implied meaning is "so they set out, and when they reached". That is, Musa (Moses) and his young companion reached ﴿the meeting place of the two seas﴾, that is, between the two seas. ﴿They forgot their fish﴾. The account of the fish and its story is that when Musa (peace be upon him) was told by revelation that there was a servant of Ours at the meeting place of the two seas who was more knowledgeable than you, Musa said: "My Lord, how can I reach him?" He said: "Take a fish with you and put it in a mikhtal (basket). Wherever you lose the fish, he is there." So he took a fish and put it in a basket, then set out, and his young companion Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua son of Nun) set out with him, until they came to the rock, and they laid down their heads. Musa slept, and the fish stirred in the basket, came out of it, and fell into the sea ﴿making its way in the sea, tunnelling﴾. Allah held back the flow of water from the fish, so that over it there became something like an arch (tāq). It was said: the fish was salted. It was said: it was roasted. It was said: it was fresh. It was said: Yusha' had gathered the fish and the bread in a basket, and they stopped for a night by the bank of a spring called the Spring of Life, and Musa slept. When the breeze and coolness of the water reached the fish, it came back to life. It is also reported that they both ate from it. It was also said: Yusha' performed ablution with water from that spring, and the water splashed onto the fish, so it came to life and fell into the water. The apparent meaning is that the forgetting is attributed to Musa and his companion.

It was also said: the forgetting was on the part of only one of them, namely Musa's young companion, who forgot to inform Musa about the matter of the fish while Musa was sleeping. Yusha' had perceived its coming out of the basket into the sea and saw that it had made its way (sarab), so he was reluctant to wake Musa. He said: "I will delay until he wakes," but then he forgot to inform him, until they set off and ﴿passed on﴾. It is possible for a thing to be attributed to a group even if only one of them did it. It was also said: this is by omission of a word, meaning "one of them forgot". Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, they both forgot to examine the matter and what would come of it, which had been made a sign of success in attaining the goal. It was also said: Yusha' forgot to bring it forward, and Musa forgot to give an instruction about it. End of quotation.

The path the fish took in the water is likened to a sarab, since the water did not close again behind it but remained like an arch. This is what is found in the hadith. The majority said: the place where it passed remained empty. Qatada said: it was solid water. Ibn Abbas said: a smooth rock. Ibn Zayd said: it only made its way as a sarab on land until it reached the sea, and then it swam as usual. It seems he meant by the words ﴿sarab﴾ free movement and roaming, from the expression fahlun sārib, meaning a stallion left unrestrained, grazing wherever it wishes. From this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and one who moves freely by day﴾ [al-Ra'd: 10], meaning one who moves about freely. Some said: he made a sarab in the earth from the basket, and on his path he came upon a rock and bored through it. The apparent meaning is that the sarab was in the water, and it cannot be interpreted except by what is found in the authentic hadith, that the water became over it like an arch. This is a miracle for Musa (peace be upon him), or for al-Khadir if we say he is a prophet, and otherwise it is a karama (a marvel granted to a righteous person).

It was said: the place where the fish had passed turned back into a dry path of stone, and Musa walked along it following the fish, until that led him to an island in the sea, where he found al-Khadir. ﴿So when they had passed on﴾, that is, the meeting place of the two seas. Al-Zamakhshari said: the appointed place is the rock. It was said: they travelled after passing the rock through the night and the next day until noon, and fatigue and hunger came upon Musa when he passed the appointed place, and he had not been tired or hungry before that, so he remembered the fish and asked for it. His words ﴿from this journey of ours﴾ refer to their travelling beyond the rock. The majority read ﴿nasaban﴾ (fatigue) with two fathas, and Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr read it with two dammas. The author of al-Lawami' said: this is one of the four dialects in which it occurs.

Al-Zamakhshari said: if you ask, how could Yusha' forget that, when such a thing is not forgotten, since it was a sign for them of the goal for which they were striving, and since it was two clear miracles: the living of the salted fish that was eaten from, and it was also said it was only half a fish; the standing up of the water and its rising like an arch; and its passage in the manner of a sarab? Then how did forgetfulness persist with him until they left the appointed place and travelled a night's journey until midday the next day, and until Musa asked for the fish? I say: Satan had occupied him with his whisperings, and his thoughts went in every direction until forgetfulness overtook him. Added to that is that he had become accustomed to seeing such wonders with Musa, and he had become comfortable with his own kind, so familiarity overcame his lack of concern. End of quotation.

Abu Bakr Ghalib ibn Atiyya and the exegete Abd al-Haqq al-Dani said: I heard Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari say in his preaching: Musa walked to the private conversation with Allah and remained forty days without needing food, but when he walked to a human being, hunger reached him in part of a day.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ara'ayta﴾ (have you seen?) here means "inform me". If you ask, what is the connection of this speech, since each of ﴿ara'ayta﴾, ﴿when we took refuge at the rock﴾ and ﴿I forgot the fish﴾ has no connection? I say: when Musa asked for the fish, Yusha' mentioned what he had seen of it and how forgetfulness had overcome him to that extent, and he was bewildered and began to ask Musa about the cause of this. It was as if he said: "Have you seen what has afflicted me, ﴿when we took refuge at the rock, for I forgot the fish﴾", so the answer was omitted. End of quotation.

That ﴿ara'ayta﴾ means "inform me" was mentioned by Sibawayh. We have explained this at length in the surah of al-An'am and in our commentary on the book al-Tashil.

As for what is specific to ﴿ara'ayta﴾ in this place, al-Akhfash (Abu al-Hasan) said: the Arabs removed it entirely from its original meaning, so they say ara'ayta-ka and ara-yta-ka with the hamza dropped when it means "inform me". When it means "I saw", its hamza is not dropped. He said: it is also irregular in that it requires the second-person address with this meaning, and one never says in it "arani Zayd 'Amran ma sana'a" (Zayd showed me what Amr did); but one says it with the meaning "I know". It is also irregular in that it has been removed entirely from its place, as shown by the entry of the fa' (then), for you see the words ﴿ara'ayta idh awaynā ila al-sakhrati fa-innī nasītu al-ḥūta﴾. The fa' only enters when the word has been moved to mean amma (as for) or tanabbah (take note), and the meaning is: as for ﴿when we took refuge at the rock﴾, then the matter is such-and-such. It has also been moved to the meaning "inform me", as we have said. When it means "inform me", there must follow it a noun about which information is sought, and the clause after it must be a question. It may also come out with the meaning amma, and after it there always comes a conditional or a time adverb. So His words ﴿fa-innī nasītu al-ḥūta﴾ mean "as for ﴿when we took refuge﴾, ﴿for I forgot the fish﴾", or "take note, ﴿when we took refuge﴾". The fa' is only a response to ara'ayta, because idh cannot be used as a conditional particle except when accompanied by mā, without any disagreement. End of al-Akhfash's words.

In this there is a point: when ara'ayta means "inform me", there must follow it a noun about which information is sought, and the clause after it must be a question; and these two are absent in al-Zamakhshari's interpretation of ara'ayta here as "inform me". The meaning of ﴿I forgot the fish﴾ is: I forgot the mention of what happened concerning it to you.

In His words ﴿and none made me forget it but Satan﴾ there is a beautiful courtesy, in that he attributed the forgetting to the one who caused it by his whispering. ﴿That I mention it﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the pronoun referring back to the fish. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿and it took its way into the sea, wondrously﴾ refers back to the fish, as it did in His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea as a sarab﴾, and this is part of Yusha's speech. It was also said: the pronoun refers to Musa, meaning Musa took it. The meaning of ʿajaban is: a wonder at that, or taking it as a wonder, namely that its trace remained wherever it went. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: its way was wondrous, that is, it was like the sarab. He said: or it was said ʿajaban at the end of the speech, as an expression of wonder at his state in seeing that marvel and forgetting it, or at the two miracles he had seen. His words ﴿and none made me forget it but Satan, that I mention it﴾ are a parenthetical insertion between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. It was also said that ʿajaban is a report of Musa's wonder, but this is not the case. End of quotation.

Ibn Atiyya said: ﴿and it took its way into the sea, wondrously﴾ may be the words of Yusha' to Musa, meaning: the fish took a wondrous way for the people. It may also be that His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea﴾ are the completion of the report, and then He resumed with wonder, saying from Himself ʿajaban (wondrously) at this matter. The point of wonder is that a fish should die, and half of it be eaten, and then come back to life after that. End of quotation.

Abu Shuja' said in the book of al-Tabari: "I saw it. I came with it, and behold, it was half a fish, one eye, and another half in which there was nothing." Ibn Atiyya said: I too have seen it, and the half which had something on it had a thin skin under which there was no bone. It may be that ﴿and it took its way﴾ and the rest of the verse are a report from Allah the Exalted. This may be in two ways: either He reports about Musa that he took the fish's path from the sea as a wonder, that is, he was amazed by it; or He reports about the fish that it took its path as a wonder for the people. End of quotation.

Hafs read ﴿wa-mā ansānīhu﴾ with a dammah on the ha' (hu), and with fath (a) in the pause (when reciting continuously, the vowel is as stated). Al-Kisa'i inclined the fatha of the sin. In the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and his recitation, the reading is ﴿an adhkurahu﴾ and ﴿illa al-shaytana﴾ (with an accusative on al-shaytan). Abu Haywa read ﴿wa-ittikhādha sabīlihi﴾ as a conjunction with the verbal noun (maṣdar) in the pronoun object of ﴿adhkurahu﴾. The reference of ﴿dhālika﴾ (that) is to the matter of the fish, its loss, and its taking its way in the sea, because it was a sign of success in attaining the goal, namely meeting that righteous servant. The word ﴿mā﴾ (what) is a relative pronoun and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: ﴿nabghī﴾ (we seek). It was read ﴿nabghi﴾ without a yā' in continuous recitation, and including the yā' is better. This is the reading of Abu Amr, al-Kisa'i and Nafi'. In pause, most people omit the yā', following the orthography of the codex, while Ibn Kathir includes it in both states.

﴿Then they both returned﴾: they went back by the same tracks by which they had come.

﴿Retracing (qasasan)﴾: that is, they followed their own trail back, retracing it. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun with an implied verb meaning "they retraced", or it may be in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning "tracing back", and it is governed by the word ﴿returned﴾.

﴿And they found a servant from among Our servants﴾: this is an idafa of honour and distinction. They found him near the rock where the fish had been lost, and he was lying on his back on the ground, covered in his garment. So Musa said: "Peace be upon you." He lifted his head and said: "How is there peace in your land?" Then he said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "I am Musa." He said: "Musa of the Children of Israel?" He said: "Yes." He said to him: "Did you not have among the Children of Israel what occupied you from travelling here?" He said: "Yes, but I wanted to meet you and to learn from you." He said to him: "I have knowledge from the knowledge of Allah which He taught me, which you do not know, and you have knowledge from the knowledge of Allah which Allah taught you, which I do not know."

The majority hold that he is al-Khadir, and one whose dissent is not considered disagreed, claiming that he is another scholar. It was said: he was al-Yasa' (Elisha). It was said: he was Ilyas (Elias). It was said: he was Khadirun ibn Qabil ibn Adam (peace be upon him). It was said: the name of al-Khadir was Balya ibn Malkan. The majority hold that al-Khadir was a prophet, and that his knowledge was knowledge of inner realities that had been revealed to him, while the knowledge of Musa was of legal rulings and fatwas concerning the outward. It is reported that he was found sitting on the crest of the sea. In a hadith, he was called al-Khadir because he sat on a dry tuft of land which then turned green (akhdar) beneath him. It was said: whenever he prayed, the area around him turned green. It was said: he sat on a white tuft (fawwah), that is, a raised land, or a hard one, and it turned green beneath him. It was said: his mother was Roman and his father Persian. It was said: he was the son of a king among the kings, whose father wished to make him his successor after him, but he did not accept this, and he joined the islands of the sea, and his father sought him but could not find him. The majority hold that he died.

Sharaf al-Din Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi said: as for al-Khadir of Musa son of Imran, he is not alive, because if he were alive it would be incumbent upon him to come to the Prophet ﷺ, to believe in him, and to follow him. It has been reported from him that he said: "If Musa and Isa were alive, they would have no choice but to follow me." End of quotation. This is how the hadith is cited. The doctrine of the Muslims is that Isa is alive, and that he will descend from heaven. Perhaps the hadith is: "If Musa were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verse 60–70 (part 3 of 3):

The mercy that Allah gave him (raḥmah) is revelation and prophethood. It was also said: it is provision (rizq). (And We taught him from Our presence a knowledge) — meaning, from Our side, that is, of the knowledge that is specific to Us, which is informing about the unseen. Abu Zayd, from Abu 'Amr, read "min ladunā" with a lightened nun, and it is a dialect form of ladun, which is the original form.

It has been said: Many of those who ascribe themselves to righteousness have become fond of claiming this knowledge and calling it "ladunni knowledge" (al-'ilm al-ladunni), and that something of it is cast into the heart of the righteous among them, to the point that he informs that whoever among his companions is among the people of Paradise is certain, and that some of them see al-Khidr. Abu al-Fath Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mutī' al-Qushayri, known as Ibn Daqiq al-'Id, the chief judge, used to report about a shaykh of his that he saw al-Khidr and spoke with him. It was said to him: "Who informed him that he was al-Khidr? And from where did he know that?" So he fell silent. Some of them claim that al-Khidriyyah is a rank held by some of the righteous on the footing of al-Khidr. We heard the hadith from a shaykh called 'Abd al-Wahid al-'Abbasi al-Hanbali, and his companions, the Hanbalis, believed about him that he meets al-Khidr.

(He said to him, Musa) There is an omitted element in the speech; its estimate is: "So when they met and exchanged words," and this is what is related in the authentic hadith: ﴿Musa said to him, May I follow you?﴾ In this there is evidence of humility before the scholar. In this story there is evidence of encouragement to travel in seeking knowledge, and of good gentleness, coaxing, and good manners in seeking knowledge, by his saying ﴿May I follow you?﴾. In it is also the accompanying of the scholar in order to acquire his benefits. The meaning is: "Will it be light for you and will it suit you?"
