He said: it is also irregular in that it requires the second-person address with this meaning, and one never says in it "arani Zayd 'Amran ma sana'a" (Zayd showed me what Amr did); but one says it with the meaning "I know". It is also irregular in that it has been removed entirely from its place, as shown by the entry of the fa' (then), for you see the words ﴿ara'ayta idh awaynā ila al-sakhrati fa-innī nasītu al-ḥūta﴾. The fa' only enters when the word has been moved to mean amma (as for) or tanabbah (take note), and the meaning is: as for ﴿when we took refuge at the rock﴾, then the matter is such-and-such. It has also been moved to the meaning "inform me", as we have said. When it means "inform me", there must follow it a noun about which information is sought, and the clause after it must be a question. It may also come out with the meaning amma, and after it there always comes a conditional or a time adverb. So His words ﴿fa-innī nasītu al-ḥūta﴾ mean "as for ﴿when we took refuge﴾, ﴿for I forgot the fish﴾", or "take note, ﴿when we took refuge﴾". The fa' is only a response to ara'ayta, because idh cannot be used as a conditional particle except when accompanied by mā, without any disagreement. End of al-Akhfash's words.

In this there is a point: when ara'ayta means "inform me", there must follow it a noun about which information is sought, and the clause after it must be a question; and these two are absent in al-Zamakhshari's interpretation of ara'ayta here as "inform me". The meaning of ﴿I forgot the fish﴾ is: I forgot the mention of what happened concerning it to you.

In His words ﴿and none made me forget it but Satan﴾ there is a beautiful courtesy, in that he attributed the forgetting to the one who caused it by his whispering. ﴿That I mention it﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the pronoun referring back to the fish. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿and it took its way into the sea, wondrously﴾ refers back to the fish, as it did in His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea as a sarab﴾, and this is part of Yusha's speech. It was also said: the pronoun refers to Musa, meaning Musa took it. The meaning of ʿajaban is: a wonder at that, or taking it as a wonder, namely that its trace remained wherever it went. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: its way was wondrous, that is, it was like the sarab. He said: or it was said ʿajaban at the end of the speech, as an expression of wonder at his state in seeing that marvel and forgetting it, or at the two miracles he had seen. His words ﴿and none made me forget it but Satan, that I mention it﴾ are a parenthetical insertion between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. It was also said that ʿajaban is a report of Musa's wonder, but this is not the case. End of quotation.

Ibn Atiyya said: ﴿and it took its way into the sea, wondrously﴾ may be the words of Yusha' to Musa, meaning: the fish took a wondrous way for the people. It may also be that His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea﴾ are the completion of the report, and then He resumed with wonder, saying from Himself ʿajaban (wondrously) at this matter. The point of wonder is that a fish should die, and half of it be eaten, and then come back to life after that. End of quotation.

Abu Shuja' said in the book of al-Tabari: "I saw it. I came with it, and behold, it was half a fish, one eye, and another half in which there was nothing." Ibn Atiyya said: I too have seen it, and the half which had something on it had a thin skin under which there was no bone. It may be that ﴿and it took its way﴾ and the rest of the verse are a report from Allah the Exalted. This may be in two ways: either He reports about Musa that he took the fish's path from the sea as a wonder, that is, he was amazed by it; or He reports about the fish that it took its path as a wonder for the people. End of quotation.

Hafs read ﴿wa-mā ansānīhu﴾ with a dammah on the ha' (hu), and with fath (a) in the pause (when reciting continuously, the vowel is as stated). Al-Kisa'i inclined the fatha of the sin. In the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and his recitation, the reading is ﴿an adhkurahu﴾ and ﴿illa al-shaytana﴾ (with an accusative on al-shaytan). Abu Haywa read ﴿wa-ittikhādha sabīlihi﴾ as a conjunction with the verbal noun (maṣdar) in the pronoun object of ﴿adhkurahu﴾. The reference of ﴿dhālika﴾ (that) is to the matter of the fish, its loss, and its taking its way in the sea, because it was a sign of success in attaining the goal, namely meeting that righteous servant. The word ﴿mā﴾ (what) is a relative pronoun and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: ﴿nabghī﴾ (we seek). It was read ﴿nabghi﴾ without a yā' in continuous recitation, and including the yā' is better. This is the reading of Abu Amr, al-Kisa'i and Nafi'. In pause, most people omit the yā', following the orthography of the codex, while Ibn Kathir includes it in both states.

﴿Then they both returned﴾: they went back by the same tracks by which they had come.

﴿Retracing (qasasan)﴾: that is, they followed their own trail back, retracing it. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun with an implied verb meaning "they retraced", or it may be in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning "tracing back", and it is governed by the word ﴿returned﴾.

﴿And they found a servant from among Our servants﴾: this is an idafa of honour and distinction. They found him near the rock where the fish had been lost, and he was lying on his back on the ground, covered in his garment. So Musa said: "Peace be upon you." He lifted his head and said: "How is there peace in your land?" Then he said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "I am Musa." He said: "Musa of the Children of Israel?" He said: "Yes." He said to him: "Did you not have among the Children of Israel what occupied you from travelling here?" He said: "Yes, but I wanted to meet you and to learn from you." He said to him: "I have knowledge from the knowledge of Allah which He taught me, which you do not know, and you have knowledge from the knowledge of Allah which Allah taught you, which I do not know."

The majority hold that he is al-Khadir, and one whose dissent is not considered disagreed, claiming that he is another scholar. It was said: he was al-Yasa' (Elisha). It was said: he was Ilyas (Elias). It was said: he was Khadirun ibn Qabil ibn Adam (peace be upon him). It was said: the name of al-Khadir was Balya ibn Malkan. The majority hold that al-Khadir was a prophet, and that his knowledge was knowledge of inner realities that had been revealed to him, while the knowledge of Musa was of legal rulings and fatwas concerning the outward. It is reported that he was found sitting on the crest of the sea. In a hadith, he was called al-Khadir because he sat on a dry tuft of land which then turned green (akhdar) beneath him. It was said: whenever he prayed, the area around him turned green. It was said: he sat on a white tuft (fawwah), that is, a raised land, or a hard one, and it turned green beneath him. It was said: his mother was Roman and his father Persian. It was said: he was the son of a king among the kings, whose father wished to make him his successor after him, but he did not accept this, and he joined the islands of the sea, and his father sought him but could not find him. The majority hold that he died.

Sharaf al-Din Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi said: as for al-Khadir of Musa son of Imran, he is not alive, because if he were alive it would be incumbent upon him to come to the Prophet ﷺ, to believe in him, and to follow him. It has been reported from him that he said: "If Musa and Isa were alive, they would have no choice but to follow me." End of quotation. This is how the hadith is cited. The doctrine of the Muslims is that Isa is alive, and that he will descend from heaven. Perhaps the hadith is: "If Musa were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verse 60–70 (part 3 of 3):

The mercy that Allah gave him (raḥmah) is revelation and prophethood. It was also said: it is provision (rizq). (And We taught him from Our presence a knowledge) — meaning, from Our side, that is, of the knowledge that is specific to Us, which is informing about the unseen. Abu Zayd, from Abu 'Amr, read "min ladunā" with a lightened nun, and it is a dialect form of ladun, which is the original form.

It has been said: Many of those who ascribe themselves to righteousness have become fond of claiming this knowledge and calling it "ladunni knowledge" (al-'ilm al-ladunni), and that something of it is cast into the heart of the righteous among them, to the point that he informs that whoever among his companions is among the people of Paradise is certain, and that some of them see al-Khidr. Abu al-Fath Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mutī' al-Qushayri, known as Ibn Daqiq al-'Id, the chief judge, used to report about a shaykh of his that he saw al-Khidr and spoke with him. It was said to him: "Who informed him that he was al-Khidr? And from where did he know that?" So he fell silent. Some of them claim that al-Khidriyyah is a rank held by some of the righteous on the footing of al-Khidr. We heard the hadith from a shaykh called 'Abd al-Wahid al-'Abbasi al-Hanbali, and his companions, the Hanbalis, believed about him that he meets al-Khidr.

(He said to him, Musa) There is an omitted element in the speech; its estimate is: "So when they met and exchanged words," and this is what is related in the authentic hadith: ﴿Musa said to him, May I follow you?﴾ In this there is evidence of humility before the scholar. In this story there is evidence of encouragement to travel in seeking knowledge, and of good gentleness, coaxing, and good manners in seeking knowledge, by his saying ﴿May I follow you?﴾. In it is also the accompanying of the scholar in order to acquire his benefits. The meaning is: "Will it be light for you and will it suit you?" And (rushdan) is in the accusative either as a second object of his saying ﴿you teach me﴾, or as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), whose ṣāḥib al-ḥāl is the pronoun in ﴿I follow you﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (knowledge) with rectitude (rushd), by which I am guided in my religion. He said: If you say, does his need to learn from another in his time not show that he was, as has been said, Musa ibn Mīshā and not Musa ibn 'Imran? For a prophet must be the most knowledgeable of the people of his time and their imam to whom recourse is had in matters of religion? I say: There is no shame for a prophet in taking knowledge from a prophet before him; what diminishes him is only that he take from one lower than himself.

From Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Nawf, the son of Ka'b's wife, claims that al-Khidr is not the companion of Musa, and that Musa is Musa ibn Mīshā." He said: "The enemy of Allah has lied." End.

Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Abu Bahriyyah, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Munadhir, Ya'qub, Abu 'Ubayd, and al-Yazidi read (rashadan) with two fathas, and this is the reading of Abu 'Amr from the Seven. The rest of the Seven read with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the shin.

Al-Khidr negated the ability to be patient with him, by way of emphasis, as though it were something that is not sound and not proper. He justified that by saying that he undertakes matters which, outwardly, a righteous man would disapprove of, so how much more a prophet; he would not be able to restrain himself from recoiling at that and hastening to object: ﴿And how can you be patient?﴾, that is: your patience regarding what you have no experience of is far-fetched. In this there is an expression of excuse for him, since he cannot be patient seeing what contradicts what he is upon of his own law. (Khubran) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), meaning: "about what your knowledge does not encompass," so it is transferred from the subject, or it is a verbal noun not of the same root, because the meaning of ﴿what you do not encompass with knowledge﴾ [al-Naml: 22] is "you are not informed of it." Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz read (khubura) with a damma on the ba'.

﴿He said: You will find me, if Allah wills, patient﴾. He promised him that he would find him (ṣābiran) patient, and he joined that with the will of Allah, knowing from himself the severity and difficulty of the matter, since one is only patient regarding what contradicts what he is upon when he sees it. ﴿And I will not disobey you﴾ may be conjoined to (ṣābiran), meaning: patient and not disobeying, in which case it is in the accusative position, the verb being coordinated with a noun when it has the same meaning, as in His saying ﴿lining up and seizing﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], meaning: and seizing. It may also be conjoined to (satajidunī), in which case it has no place in the grammatical structure and is not restricted by the will in wording.

Al-Qushayri said: Musa promised of himself two things: patience, which he tied to the exception of the will; so he was patient when he saw, at the hands of al-Khidr, what he did; and that he would not disobey him, which he stated without tying it to the exception, so he disobeyed him when he said to him ﴿then do not ask me﴾, and he kept asking him. What he tied to the exception he did not contravene, and what he stated without condition, dispute arose concerning it. End. This is from him on the assumption that ﴿and I will not disobey﴾ is conjoined to (satajidunī), so it does not fall under the will.

﴿He said: If you follow me﴾, that is: if you see from me something whose correctness is hidden from you and you disapprove of it in yourself, then do not open up to me with questions until I am the one who opens to you. This is among the manners of the student with the scholar he follows. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read (fa-la tas'alnī). From Abu Ja'far, with a fatha on the sin and the lam without hamza, with a shadda on the nun. The rest of the Seven read with hamza, sukun on the lam, and light nun. Abu 'Ali said: "All of them with a ya' in both states." End. And regarding Ibn 'Amir's omission of the ya' there is a strange disagreement.

(p-142)﴿And when Moses said to his servant, "I will not stop until I reach the meeting place of the two seas, or I will journey for a long age."﴾ ﴿But when they reached the meeting place of the two of them, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, freely.﴾ ﴿Then when they had passed on, he said to his servant, "Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed met with fatigue from this journey of ours."﴾ ﴿He said, "Did you see? When we took refuge at the rock, I forgot the fish, and none but Satan made me forget it, so that I did not remember it. It took its way into the sea in a wondrous manner."﴾ ﴿He said, "That is what we were seeking." So they went back, retracing their footsteps.﴾ ﴿Then they found a servant from Our servants, whom We had given mercy from Us and taught knowledge from Our own presence.﴾ ﴿Moses said to him, "May I follow you, on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, as right guidance?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed you will not be able to have patience with me."﴾ ﴿"And how can you have patience with what you have not encompassed in knowledge?"﴾ ﴿He said, "You will find me, God willing, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter."﴾ ﴿He said, "If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you."﴾ .
(p-143)Moses mentioned in this verse is Moses son of Imran (peace be upon him). Allah has not mentioned any Moses in His Book other than him. As for the one who holds that he is another, namely Moses son of Mishya son of Yusuf, or Moses son of Ifraithim son of Yusuf, that view is not sound. Rather, what is established in the authentic hadith and in the histories is that he is Moses son of Imran, the prophet of the Children of Israel, and the one sent, together with his brother Aaron, to Pharaoh. His servant (fata) was Joshua son of Nun son of Ifraithim son of Yusuf son of Ya'qub (peace be upon them). A fata is a young man. Since servants are most often young men, a servant was called a fata as a matter of good manners, and the Shari'a encouraged this. In the hadith: "Let none of you say 'my slave' or 'my maidservant'; let him say 'my young man' (fataya) and 'my young woman' (fataty)." He said "his servant" because he served him and followed him. It was also said that he took knowledge from him. It is said that Joshua was the son of Moses' sister. The cause of this story is that Moses (peace be upon him) sat one day in an assembly of the Children of Israel and delivered a sermon with eloquence. He was asked, "Do you know anyone more knowledgeable than you?" He said, "No." So Allah revealed to him that he should travel along the shore of the sea until he reached "the meeting place of the two seas," and that when he lost the fish, it would be there. Moses did this, and to his servant, in the manner of firmly resolving, he said, "I will not stop travelling," meaning, "I will not cease." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He only said this statement while he was travelling." From this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:
"They did not cease until their women were carried along in litters, in the valley of Dhu Qar, bearing perfumed garments."
End of quotation. What he mentioned here involves omitting the predicate of "I will not stop" (la abrah), and these are among the sisters of kana (verbs of state). Our scholars stated that omitting the predicate of kana and its sisters is not permitted, even if it is indicated, except in what has come in poetry, such as the saying:
"Alas for you, the distress of one who is afraid, who seeks your protection when there is no protector."
That is, when there is no one in the world. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "la abrah," if it means "I will not depart" from "barih al-makan" (to leave a place), then it indicates staying put during a journey; if it means "I will not cease," then the predicate must be present. I say: It means "I will not cease," and the predicate has been omitted, because the situation and the speech together both indicate it. As for the situation, it was a situation of travel. As for the speech, "until I reach the meeting place of the two seas" is a fixed limit that calls for a point to which it is a limit. So the meaning must be: "My journey will not cease until I reach..." The predicate is "until I reach," and when the governing noun was omitted, the pronoun of the speaker replaced the governed noun, so the verb shifted from the third-person pronoun to the first-person form. This is a subtle point. End of quotation. These are two possibilities which al-Zamakhshari conflated. As for the first: he made the verb predicated of the speaker, both in form and in implication, and made the predicate omitted, as Ibn 'Atiyya estimated, with "until I reach" being a complement attached to the omitted predicate and a limit for it. The second possibility: he made "la abrah" predicated, in form, of the speaker, and in meaning, of that omitted estimate, and made it so that "la abrah" is "until I reach." Thus it is a principal element, since its origin is the predicate of the subject, because it is the predicate of (abrah).
Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is possible that the meaning is: "I will not cease" in what I am doing, meaning "I will keep to the journey and the search, and I will not leave it or part from it, until I reach," as you say, "I will not leave the place." End of quotation. He means that "barih" can mean "to part from," and then it takes an object, and this requires a sound transmission.
Al-Tabari mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Moses and his people prevailed over Egypt, he settled his people in Egypt. When the situation was stable, he delivered a sermon one day, reminding them of the favors of Allah and His days among the Children of Israel. Then he mentioned that he knew of no one more knowledgeable than himself.
Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is not seen at all that Moses (peace be upon him) settled his people in Egypt except in this statement, and I do not think it is sound. Rather, what is apparent is that Moses died in the wilderness of the Wandering (al-Tih), before the conquest of the lands of the tyrants. This report from Ibn 'Abbas was also mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, who said: It is reported that when Moses prevailed over Egypt with the Children of Israel and they settled after the destruction of the Copts, Allah commanded him to remind his people of the blessing. So he stood among them as a preacher and mentioned the blessing of Allah, and said: "Allah has chosen your prophet and spoke to him." They said to him, "We already know this; who among the people is the most knowledgeable?" He said, "I am." So Allah rebuked him because he did not refer knowledge to Allah. Then Allah revealed to him: "Rather, someone more knowledgeable than you is a servant of Mine at the meeting place of the two seas, and he is al-Khadir." Al-Khadir was in the days of Afridun, before Moses, and was in the vanguard of Dhu al-Qarnayn the Great, and he remained until the days of Moses. It is also mentioned in the questions of Moses that he said: "If there is among Your servants someone more knowledgeable than me, guide me to him." He said: "More knowledgeable than you is al-Khadir." End of quotation. This contradicts what is established in the Sahih, that he was asked, "Is there anyone more knowledgeable than you?" and he said, "No."
As for "the meeting place of the two seas": Mujahid and Qatada said it is the confluence of the Persian Sea and the Roman Sea. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is an arm that extends from the Encircling Ocean from north to south, in the land of Persia behind Adharbayjan. So the corner where the two seas meet, on the side near the land of al-Sham, is the meeting place of the two seas according to this view. A group, among them Muhammad son of Ka'b al-Qurazi, said: It is at Tangier, where the Encircling Ocean meets the sea that flows out of it, from the west wind to the east wind. It is also reported from Ubayy (may Allah be pleased with him) that it is in Ifriqiya. It was said: It is the Sea of Andalus, and the town which refused to host them is al-Jazira al-Khadra. It was said: "The meeting place of the two seas" is a salt sea and a sweet sea, so al-Khadir would be, by this view, at the point where a great river enters the sea. A group said: The two seas are a metaphor for Moses and al-Khadir, because they were two seas of knowledge. This resembles the interpretation of the Batiniyya (esoteric sect) and the extreme Sufis, whereas the hadiths indicate that they are two bodies of water.
Al-Zamakhshari said: Among the strange interpretations is that the two seas are Moses and al-Khadir, because they were two seas in knowledge. End of quotation. It was also said: the Sea of al-Qulzum (the Red Sea). It was said: the Sea of al-Azraq.
Al-Dahhak and 'Abdullah son of Muslim son of Yasar read "majma'" (with a kasra on the second mim), and al-Nadr reported from Ibn Muslim in both places. This is anomalous; by analogy, from the pattern yaf'alu, the mim should be fatha, as in the reading of the majority. The apparent meaning is that "majma' al-bahrayn" is the name of the place where the two seas meet. It was also said to be a verbal noun.
Ibn 'Abbas said: "Huqub" means an age (dahr). 'Abdullah son of 'Amr and Abu Hurayra said: eighty years. Al-Hasan said: seventy. It was said: a year in the dialect of Quraysh, mentioned by al-Farra'. It was said: an unlimited period of time, said by Abu (p-145) 'Ubayda. The apparent meaning is that His statement "or I will journey" is conjoined to "I reach," so it sets a limit by one of two matters: either by reaching the meeting place or by journeying "a long age." It was said: it is a limit for his statement "I will not cease," as when you say, "I will not leave you, or you pay me my right," meaning: "I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas," or until I journey for a period of time in which I am certain of missing the meeting place of the two seas. Al-Dahhak read "huqban" with the qaf sukun, while the majority read it with a damma.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 60–70 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Then, when they reached the meeting place of the two seas﴾. Then (thumma) introduces an omitted clause; the implied meaning is "so they set out, and when they reached". That is, Musa (Moses) and his young companion reached ﴿the meeting place of the two seas﴾, that is, between the two seas. ﴿They forgot their fish﴾. The account of the fish and its story is that when Musa (peace be upon him) was told by revelation that there was a servant of Ours at the meeting place of the two seas who was more knowledgeable than you, Musa said: "My Lord, how can I reach him?" He said: "Take a fish with you and put it in a mikhtal (basket). Wherever you lose the fish, he is there." So he took a fish and put it in a basket, then set out, and his young companion Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua son of Nun) set out with him, until they came to the rock, and they laid down their heads. Musa slept, and the fish stirred in the basket, came out of it, and fell into the sea ﴿making its way in the sea, tunnelling﴾. Allah held back the flow of water from the fish, so that over it there became something like an arch (tāq). It was said: the fish was salted. It was said: it was roasted. It was said: it was fresh. It was said: Yusha' had gathered the fish and the bread in a basket, and they stopped for a night by the bank of a spring called the Spring of Life, and Musa slept. When the breeze and coolness of the water reached the fish, it came back to life. It is also reported that they both ate from it. It was also said: Yusha' performed ablution with water from that spring, and the water splashed onto the fish, so it came to life and fell into the water. The apparent meaning is that the forgetting is attributed to Musa and his companion.

It was also said: the forgetting was on the part of only one of them, namely Musa's young companion, who forgot to inform Musa about the matter of the fish while Musa was sleeping. Yusha' had perceived its coming out of the basket into the sea and saw that it had made its way (sarab), so he was reluctant to wake Musa. He said: "I will delay until he wakes," but then he forgot to inform him, until they set off and ﴿passed on﴾. It is possible for a thing to be attributed to a group even if only one of them did it. It was also said: this is by omission of a word, meaning "one of them forgot". Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, they both forgot to examine the matter and what would come of it, which had been made a sign of success in attaining the goal. It was also said: Yusha' forgot to bring it forward, and Musa forgot to give an instruction about it. End of quotation.

The path the fish took in the water is likened to a sarab, since the water did not close again behind it but remained like an arch. This is what is found in the hadith. The majority said: the place where it passed remained empty. Qatada said: it was solid water. Ibn Abbas said: a smooth rock. Ibn Zayd said: it only made its way as a sarab on land until it reached the sea, and then it swam as usual. It seems he meant by the words ﴿sarab﴾ free movement and roaming, from the expression fahlun sārib, meaning a stallion left unrestrained, grazing wherever it wishes. From this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and one who moves freely by day﴾ [al-Ra'd: 10], meaning one who moves about freely. Some said: he made a sarab in the earth from the basket, and on his path he came upon a rock and bored through it. The apparent meaning is that the sarab was in the water, and it cannot be interpreted except by what is found in the authentic hadith, that the water became over it like an arch. This is a miracle for Musa (peace be upon him), or for al-Khadir if we say he is a prophet, and otherwise it is a karama (a marvel granted to a righteous person).

It was said: the place where the fish had passed turned back into a dry path of stone, and Musa walked along it following the fish, until that led him to an island in the sea, where he found al-Khadir. ﴿So when they had passed on﴾, that is, the meeting place of the two seas. Al-Zamakhshari said: the appointed place is the rock. It was said: they travelled after passing the rock through the night and the next day until noon, and fatigue and hunger came upon Musa when he passed the appointed place, and he had not been tired or hungry before that, so he remembered the fish and asked for it. His words ﴿from this journey of ours﴾ refer to their travelling beyond the rock. The majority read ﴿nasaban﴾ (fatigue) with two fathas, and Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr read it with two dammas. The author of al-Lawami' said: this is one of the four dialects in which it occurs.

Al-Zamakhshari said: if you ask, how could Yusha' forget that, when such a thing is not forgotten, since it was a sign for them of the goal for which they were striving, and since it was two clear miracles: the living of the salted fish that was eaten from, and it was also said it was only half a fish; the standing up of the water and its rising like an arch; and its passage in the manner of a sarab? Then how did forgetfulness persist with him until they left the appointed place and travelled a night's journey until midday the next day, and until Musa asked for the fish? I say: Satan had occupied him with his whisperings, and his thoughts went in every direction until forgetfulness overtook him. Added to that is that he had become accustomed to seeing such wonders with Musa, and he had become comfortable with his own kind, so familiarity overcame his lack of concern. End of quotation.

Abu Bakr Ghalib ibn Atiyya and the exegete Abd al-Haqq al-Dani said: I heard Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari say in his preaching: Musa walked to the private conversation with Allah and remained forty days without needing food, but when he walked to a human being, hunger reached him in part of a day.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ara'ayta﴾ (have you seen?) here means "inform me". If you ask, what is the connection of this speech, since each of ﴿ara'ayta﴾, ﴿when we took refuge at the rock﴾ and ﴿I forgot the fish﴾ has no connection? I say: when Musa asked for the fish, Yusha' mentioned what he had seen of it and how forgetfulness had overcome him to that extent, and he was bewildered and began to ask Musa about the cause of this. It was as if he said: "Have you seen what has afflicted me, ﴿when we took refuge at the rock, for I forgot the fish﴾", so the answer was omitted. End of quotation.

That ﴿ara'ayta﴾ means "inform me" was mentioned by Sibawayh. We have explained this at length in the surah of al-An'am and in our commentary on the book al-Tashil.

As for what is specific to ﴿ara'ayta﴾ in this place, al-Akhfash (Abu al-Hasan) said: the Arabs removed it entirely from its original meaning, so they say ara'ayta-ka and ara-yta-ka with the hamza dropped when it means "inform me". When it means "I saw", its hamza is not dropped. He said: it is also irregular in that it requires the second-person address with this meaning, and one never says in it "arani Zayd 'Amran ma sana'a" (Zayd showed me what Amr did); but one says it with the meaning "I know". It is also irregular in that it has been removed entirely from its place, as shown by the entry of the fa' (then), for you see the words ﴿ara'ayta idh awaynā ila al-sakhrati fa-innī nasītu al-ḥūta﴾. The fa' only enters when the word has been moved to mean amma (as for) or tanabbah (take note), and the meaning is: as for ﴿when we took refuge at the rock﴾, then the matter is such-and-such. It has also been moved to the meaning "inform me", as we have said. When it means "inform me", there must follow it a noun about which information is sought, and the clause after it must be a question. It may also come out with the meaning amma, and after it there always comes a conditional or a time adverb. So His words ﴿fa-innī nasītu al-ḥūta﴾ mean "as for ﴿when we took refuge﴾, ﴿for I forgot the fish﴾", or "take note, ﴿when we took refuge﴾". The fa' is only a response to ara'ayta, because idh cannot be used as a conditional particle except when accompanied by mā, without any disagreement. End of al-Akhfash's words.

In this there is a point: when ara'ayta means "inform me", there must follow it a noun about which information is sought, and the clause after it must be a question; and these two are absent in al-Zamakhshari's interpretation of ara'ayta here as "inform me". The meaning of ﴿I forgot the fish﴾ is: I forgot the mention of what happened concerning it to you.

In His words ﴿and none made me forget it but Satan﴾ there is a beautiful courtesy, in that he attributed the forgetting to the one who caused it by his whispering. ﴿That I mention it﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the pronoun referring back to the fish. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿and it took its way into the sea, wondrously﴾ refers back to the fish, as it did in His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea as a sarab﴾, and this is part of Yusha's speech. It was also said: the pronoun refers to Musa, meaning Musa took it. The meaning of ʿajaban is: a wonder at that, or taking it as a wonder, namely that its trace remained wherever it went. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: its way was wondrous, that is, it was like the sarab. He said: or it was said ʿajaban at the end of the speech, as an expression of wonder at his state in seeing that marvel and forgetting it, or at the two miracles he had seen. His words ﴿and none made me forget it but Satan, that I mention it﴾ are a parenthetical insertion between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. It was also said that ʿajaban is a report of Musa's wonder, but this is not the case. End of quotation.

Ibn Atiyya said: ﴿and it took its way into the sea, wondrously﴾ may be the words of Yusha' to Musa, meaning: the fish took a wondrous way for the people. It may also be that His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea﴾ are the completion of the report, and then He resumed with wonder, saying from Himself ʿajaban (wondrously) at this matter. The point of wonder is that a fish should die, and half of it be eaten, and then come back to life after that. End of quotation.

Abu Shuja' said in the book of al-Tabari: "I saw it. I came with it, and behold, it was half a fish, one eye, and another half in which there was nothing." Ibn Atiyya said: I too have seen it, and the half which had something on it had a thin skin under which there was no bone. It may be that ﴿and it took its way﴾ and the rest of the verse are a report from Allah the Exalted. This may be in two ways: either He reports about Musa that he took the fish's path from the sea as a wonder, that is, he was amazed by it; or He reports about the fish that it took its path as a wonder for the people. End of quotation.

Hafs read ﴿wa-mā ansānīhu﴾ with a dammah on the ha' (hu), and with fath (a) in the pause (when reciting continuously, the vowel is as stated). Al-Kisa'i inclined the fatha of the sin. In the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and his recitation, the reading is ﴿an adhkurahu﴾ and ﴿illa al-shaytana﴾ (with an accusative on al-shaytan). Abu Haywa read ﴿wa-ittikhādha sabīlihi﴾ as a conjunction with the verbal noun (maṣdar) in the pronoun object of ﴿adhkurahu﴾. The reference of ﴿dhālika﴾ (that) is to the matter of the fish, its loss, and its taking its way in the sea, because it was a sign of success in attaining the goal, namely meeting that righteous servant. The word ﴿mā﴾ (what) is a relative pronoun and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: ﴿nabghī﴾ (we seek). It was read ﴿nabghi﴾ without a yā' in continuous recitation, and including the yā' is better. This is the reading of Abu Amr, al-Kisa'i and Nafi'. In pause, most people omit the yā', following the orthography of the codex, while Ibn Kathir includes it in both states.

﴿Then they both returned﴾: they went back by the same tracks by which they had come.

﴿Retracing (qasasan)﴾: that is, they followed their own trail back, retracing it. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun with an implied verb meaning "they retraced", or it may be in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning "tracing back", and it is governed by the word ﴿returned﴾.

﴿And they found a servant from among Our servants﴾: this is an idafa of honour and distinction. They found him near the rock where the fish had been lost, and he was lying on his back on the ground, covered in his garment. So Musa said: "Peace be upon you." He lifted his head and said: "How is there peace in your land?" Then he said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "I am Musa." He said: "Musa of the Children of Israel?" He said: "Yes." He said to him: "Did you not have among the Children of Israel what occupied you from travelling here?" He said: "Yes, but I wanted to meet you and to learn from you." He said to him: "I have knowledge from the knowledge of Allah which He taught me, which you do not know, and you have knowledge from the knowledge of Allah which Allah taught you, which I do not know."

The majority hold that he is al-Khadir, and one whose dissent is not considered disagreed, claiming that he is another scholar. It was said: he was al-Yasa' (Elisha). It was said: he was Ilyas (Elias). It was said: he was Khadirun ibn Qabil ibn Adam (peace be upon him). It was said: the name of al-Khadir was Balya ibn Malkan. The majority hold that al-Khadir was a prophet, and that his knowledge was knowledge of inner realities that had been revealed to him, while the knowledge of Musa was of legal rulings and fatwas concerning the outward. It is reported that he was found sitting on the crest of the sea. In a hadith, he was called al-Khadir because he sat on a dry tuft of land which then turned green (akhdar) beneath him. It was said: whenever he prayed, the area around him turned green. It was said: he sat on a white tuft (fawwah), that is, a raised land, or a hard one, and it turned green beneath him. It was said: his mother was Roman and his father Persian. It was said: he was the son of a king among the kings, whose father wished to make him his successor after him, but he did not accept this, and he joined the islands of the sea, and his father sought him but could not find him. The majority hold that he died.

Sharaf al-Din Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi said: as for al-Khadir of Musa son of Imran, he is not alive, because if he were alive it would be incumbent upon him to come to the Prophet ﷺ, to believe in him, and to follow him. It has been reported from him that he said: "If Musa and Isa were alive, they would have no choice but to follow me." End of quotation. This is how the hadith is cited. The doctrine of the Muslims is that Isa is alive, and that he will descend from heaven. Perhaps the hadith is: "If Musa were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verse 60–70 (part 3 of 3):

The mercy that Allah gave him (raḥmah) is revelation and prophethood. It was also said: it is provision (rizq). (And We taught him from Our presence a knowledge) — meaning, from Our side, that is, of the knowledge that is specific to Us, which is informing about the unseen. Abu Zayd, from Abu 'Amr, read "min ladunā" with a lightened nun, and it is a dialect form of ladun, which is the original form.

It has been said: Many of those who ascribe themselves to righteousness have become fond of claiming this knowledge and calling it "ladunni knowledge" (al-'ilm al-ladunni), and that something of it is cast into the heart of the righteous among them, to the point that he informs that whoever among his companions is among the people of Paradise is certain, and that some of them see al-Khidr. Abu al-Fath Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mutī' al-Qushayri, known as Ibn Daqiq al-'Id, the chief judge, used to report about a shaykh of his that he saw al-Khidr and spoke with him. It was said to him: "Who informed him that he was al-Khidr? And from where did he know that?" So he fell silent. Some of them claim that al-Khidriyyah is a rank held by some of the righteous on the footing of al-Khidr. We heard the hadith from a shaykh called 'Abd al-Wahid al-'Abbasi al-Hanbali, and his companions, the Hanbalis, believed about him that he meets al-Khidr.

(He said to him, Musa) There is an omitted element in the speech; its estimate is: "So when they met and exchanged words," and this is what is related in the authentic hadith: ﴿Musa said to him, May I follow you?﴾ In this there is evidence of humility before the scholar. In this story there is evidence of encouragement to travel in seeking knowledge, and of good gentleness, coaxing, and good manners in seeking knowledge, by his saying ﴿May I follow you?﴾. In it is also the accompanying of the scholar in order to acquire his benefits. The meaning is: "Will it be light for you and will it suit you?" And (rushdan) is in the accusative either as a second object of his saying ﴿you teach me﴾, or as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), whose ṣāḥib al-ḥāl is the pronoun in ﴿I follow you﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (knowledge) with rectitude (rushd), by which I am guided in my religion. He said: If you say, does his need to learn from another in his time not show that he was, as has been said, Musa ibn Mīshā and not Musa ibn 'Imran? For a prophet must be the most knowledgeable of the people of his time and their imam to whom recourse is had in matters of religion? I say: There is no shame for a prophet in taking knowledge from a prophet before him; what diminishes him is only that he take from one lower than himself.

From Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Nawf, the son of Ka'b's wife, claims that al-Khidr is not the companion of Musa, and that Musa is Musa ibn Mīshā." He said: "The enemy of Allah has lied." End.

Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Abu Bahriyyah, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Munadhir, Ya'qub, Abu 'Ubayd, and al-Yazidi read (rashadan) with two fathas, and this is the reading of Abu 'Amr from the Seven. The rest of the Seven read with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the shin.

Al-Khidr negated the ability to be patient with him, by way of emphasis, as though it were something that is not sound and not proper. He justified that by saying that he undertakes matters which, outwardly, a righteous man would disapprove of, so how much more a prophet; he would not be able to restrain himself from recoiling at that and hastening to object: ﴿And how can you be patient?﴾, that is: your patience regarding what you have no experience of is far-fetched. In this there is an expression of excuse for him, since he cannot be patient seeing what contradicts what he is upon of his own law. (Khubran) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), meaning: "about what your knowledge does not encompass," so it is transferred from the subject, or it is a verbal noun not of the same root, because the meaning of ﴿what you do not encompass with knowledge﴾ [al-Naml: 22] is "you are not informed of it." Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz read (khubura) with a damma on the ba'.

﴿He said: You will find me, if Allah wills, patient﴾. He promised him that he would find him (ṣābiran) patient, and he joined that with the will of Allah, knowing from himself the severity and difficulty of the matter, since one is only patient regarding what contradicts what he is upon when he sees it. ﴿And I will not disobey you﴾ may be conjoined to (ṣābiran), meaning: patient and not disobeying, in which case it is in the accusative position, the verb being coordinated with a noun when it has the same meaning, as in His saying ﴿lining up and seizing﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], meaning: and seizing. It may also be conjoined to (satajidunī), in which case it has no place in the grammatical structure and is not restricted by the will in wording.

Al-Qushayri said: Musa promised of himself two things: patience, which he tied to the exception of the will; so he was patient when he saw, at the hands of al-Khidr, what he did; and that he would not disobey him, which he stated without tying it to the exception, so he disobeyed him when he said to him ﴿then do not ask me﴾, and he kept asking him. What he tied to the exception he did not contravene, and what he stated without condition, dispute arose concerning it. End. This is from him on the assumption that ﴿and I will not disobey﴾ is conjoined to (satajidunī), so it does not fall under the will.

﴿He said: If you follow me﴾, that is: if you see from me something whose correctness is hidden from you and you disapprove of it in yourself, then do not open up to me with questions until I am the one who opens to you. This is among the manners of the student with the scholar he follows. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read (fa-la tas'alnī). From Abu Ja'far, with a fatha on the sin and the lam without hamza, with a shadda on the nun. The rest of the Seven read with hamza, sukun on the lam, and light nun. Abu 'Ali said: "All of them with a ya' in both states." End. And regarding Ibn 'Amir's omission of the ya' there is a strange disagreement.

(p-142)﴿And when Moses said to his servant, "I will not stop until I reach the meeting place of the two seas, or I will journey for a long age."﴾ ﴿But when they reached the meeting place of the two of them, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, freely.﴾ ﴿Then when they had passed on, he said to his servant, "Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed met with fatigue from this journey of ours."﴾ ﴿He said, "Did you see? When we took refuge at the rock, I forgot the fish, and none but Satan made me forget it, so that I did not remember it. It took its way into the sea in a wondrous manner."﴾ ﴿He said, "That is what we were seeking." So they went back, retracing their footsteps.﴾ ﴿Then they found a servant from Our servants, whom We had given mercy from Us and taught knowledge from Our own presence.﴾ ﴿Moses said to him, "May I follow you, on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, as right guidance?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed you will not be able to have patience with me."﴾ ﴿"And how can you have patience with what you have not encompassed in knowledge?"﴾ ﴿He said, "You will find me, God willing, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter."﴾ ﴿He said, "If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you."﴾ .
(p-143)Moses mentioned in this verse is Moses son of Imran (peace be upon him). Allah has not mentioned any Moses in His Book other than him. As for the one who holds that he is another, namely Moses son of Mishya son of Yusuf, or Moses son of Ifraithim son of Yusuf, that view is not sound. Rather, what is established in the authentic hadith and in the histories is that he is Moses son of Imran, the prophet of the Children of Israel, and the one sent, together with his brother Aaron, to Pharaoh. His servant (fata) was Joshua son of Nun son of Ifraithim son of Yusuf son of Ya'qub (peace be upon them). A fata is a young man. Since servants are most often young men, a servant was called a fata as a matter of good manners, and the Shari'a encouraged this. In the hadith: "Let none of you say 'my slave' or 'my maidservant'; let him say 'my young man' (fataya) and 'my young woman' (fataty)." He said "his servant" because he served him and followed him. It was also said that he took knowledge from him. It is said that Joshua was the son of Moses' sister. The cause of this story is that Moses (peace be upon him) sat one day in an assembly of the Children of Israel and delivered a sermon with eloquence. He was asked, "Do you know anyone more knowledgeable than you?" He said, "No." So Allah revealed to him that he should travel along the shore of the sea until he reached "the meeting place of the two seas," and that when he lost the fish, it would be there. Moses did this, and to his servant, in the manner of firmly resolving, he said, "I will not stop travelling," meaning, "I will not cease." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He only said this statement while he was travelling." From this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:
"They did not cease until their women were carried along in litters, in the valley of Dhu Qar, bearing perfumed garments."
End of quotation. What he mentioned here involves omitting the predicate of "I will not stop" (la abrah), and these are among the sisters of kana (verbs of state). Our scholars stated that omitting the predicate of kana and its sisters is not permitted, even if it is indicated, except in what has come in poetry, such as the saying:
"Alas for you, the distress of one who is afraid, who seeks your protection when there is no protector."
That is, when there is no one in the world. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "la abrah," if it means "I will not depart" from "barih al-makan" (to leave a place), then it indicates staying put during a journey; if it means "I will not cease," then the predicate must be present. I say: It means "I will not cease," and the predicate has been omitted, because the situation and the speech together both indicate it. As for the situation, it was a situation of travel. As for the speech, "until I reach the meeting place of the two seas" is a fixed limit that calls for a point to which it is a limit. So the meaning must be: "My journey will not cease until I reach..." The predicate is "until I reach," and when the governing noun was omitted, the pronoun of the speaker replaced the governed noun, so the verb shifted from the third-person pronoun to the first-person form. This is a subtle point. End of quotation. These are two possibilities which al-Zamakhshari conflated. As for the first: he made the verb predicated of the speaker, both in form and in implication, and made the predicate omitted, as Ibn 'Atiyya estimated, with "until I reach" being a complement attached to the omitted predicate and a limit for it. The second possibility: he made "la abrah" predicated, in form, of the speaker, and in meaning, of that omitted estimate, and made it so that "la abrah" is "until I reach." Thus it is a principal element, since its origin is the predicate of the subject, because it is the predicate of (abrah).
Al-Zamakhshari also said: It is possible that the meaning is: "I will not cease" in what I am doing, meaning "I will keep to the journey and the search, and I will not leave it or part from it, until I reach," as you say, "I will not leave the place." End of quotation. He means that "barih" can mean "to part from," and then it takes an object, and this requires a sound transmission.
Al-Tabari mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Moses and his people prevailed over Egypt, he settled his people in Egypt. When the situation was stable, he delivered a sermon one day, reminding them of the favors of Allah and His days among the Children of Israel. Then he mentioned that he knew of no one more knowledgeable than himself.
Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is not seen at all that Moses (peace be upon him) settled his people in Egypt except in this statement, and I do not think it is sound. Rather, what is apparent is that Moses died in the wilderness of the Wandering (al-Tih), before the conquest of the lands of the tyrants. This report from Ibn 'Abbas was also mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, who said: It is reported that when Moses prevailed over Egypt with the Children of Israel and they settled after the destruction of the Copts, Allah commanded him to remind his people of the blessing. So he stood among them as a preacher and mentioned the blessing of Allah, and said: "Allah has chosen your prophet and spoke to him." They said to him, "We already know this; who among the people is the most knowledgeable?" He said, "I am." So Allah rebuked him because he did not refer knowledge to Allah. Then Allah revealed to him: "Rather, someone more knowledgeable than you is a servant of Mine at the meeting place of the two seas, and he is al-Khadir." Al-Khadir was in the days of Afridun, before Moses, and was in the vanguard of Dhu al-Qarnayn the Great, and he remained until the days of Moses. It is also mentioned in the questions of Moses that he said: "If there is among Your servants someone more knowledgeable than me, guide me to him." He said: "More knowledgeable than you is al-Khadir." End of quotation. This contradicts what is established in the Sahih, that he was asked, "Is there anyone more knowledgeable than you?" and he said, "No."
As for "the meeting place of the two seas": Mujahid and Qatada said it is the confluence of the Persian Sea and the Roman Sea. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is an arm that extends from the Encircling Ocean from north to south, in the land of Persia behind Adharbayjan. So the corner where the two seas meet, on the side near the land of al-Sham, is the meeting place of the two seas according to this view. A group, among them Muhammad son of Ka'b al-Qurazi, said: It is at Tangier, where the Encircling Ocean meets the sea that flows out of it, from the west wind to the east wind. It is also reported from Ubayy (may Allah be pleased with him) that it is in Ifriqiya. It was said: It is the Sea of Andalus, and the town which refused to host them is al-Jazira al-Khadra. It was said: "The meeting place of the two seas" is a salt sea and a sweet sea, so al-Khadir would be, by this view, at the point where a great river enters the sea. A group said: The two seas are a metaphor for Moses and al-Khadir, because they were two seas of knowledge. This resembles the interpretation of the Batiniyya (esoteric sect) and the extreme Sufis, whereas the hadiths indicate that they are two bodies of water.
Al-Zamakhshari said: Among the strange interpretations is that the two seas are Moses and al-Khadir, because they were two seas in knowledge. End of quotation. It was also said: the Sea of al-Qulzum (the Red Sea). It was said: the Sea of al-Azraq.
Al-Dahhak and 'Abdullah son of Muslim son of Yasar read "majma'" (with a kasra on the second mim), and al-Nadr reported from Ibn Muslim in both places. This is anomalous; by analogy, from the pattern yaf'alu, the mim should be fatha, as in the reading of the majority. The apparent meaning is that "majma' al-bahrayn" is the name of the place where the two seas meet. It was also said to be a verbal noun.
Ibn 'Abbas said: "Huqub" means an age (dahr). 'Abdullah son of 'Amr and Abu Hurayra said: eighty years. Al-Hasan said: seventy. It was said: a year in the dialect of Quraysh, mentioned by al-Farra'. It was said: an unlimited period of time, said by Abu (p-145) 'Ubayda. The apparent meaning is that His statement "or I will journey" is conjoined to "I reach," so it sets a limit by one of two matters: either by reaching the meeting place or by journeying "a long age." It was said: it is a limit for his statement "I will not cease," as when you say, "I will not leave you, or you pay me my right," meaning: "I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas," or until I journey for a period of time in which I am certain of missing the meeting place of the two seas. Al-Dahhak read "huqban" with the qaf sukun, while the majority read it with a damma.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 60–70 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Then, when they reached the meeting place of the two seas﴾. Then (thumma) introduces an omitted clause; the implied meaning is "so they set out, and when they reached". That is, Musa (Moses) and his young companion reached ﴿the meeting place of the two seas﴾, that is, between the two seas. ﴿They forgot their fish﴾. The account of the fish and its story is that when Musa (peace be upon him) was told by revelation that there was a servant of Ours at the meeting place of the two seas who was more knowledgeable than you, Musa said: "My Lord, how can I reach him?" He said: "Take a fish with you and put it in a mikhtal (basket). Wherever you lose the fish, he is there." So he took a fish and put it in a basket, then set out, and his young companion Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua son of Nun) set out with him, until they came to the rock, and they laid down their heads. Musa slept, and the fish stirred in the basket, came out of it, and fell into the sea ﴿making its way in the sea, tunnelling﴾. Allah held back the flow of water from the fish, so that over it there became something like an arch (tāq). It was said: the fish was salted. It was said: it was roasted. It was said: it was fresh. It was said: Yusha' had gathered the fish and the bread in a basket, and they stopped for a night by the bank of a spring called the Spring of Life, and Musa slept. When the breeze and coolness of the water reached the fish, it came back to life. It is also reported that they both ate from it. It was also said: Yusha' performed ablution with water from that spring, and the water splashed onto the fish, so it came to life and fell into the water. The apparent meaning is that the forgetting is attributed to Musa and his companion.

It was also said: the forgetting was on the part of only one of them, namely Musa's young companion, who forgot to inform Musa about the matter of the fish while Musa was sleeping. Yusha' had perceived its coming out of the basket into the sea and saw that it had made its way (sarab), so he was reluctant to wake Musa. He said: "I will delay until he wakes," but then he forgot to inform him, until they set off and ﴿passed on﴾. It is possible for a thing to be attributed to a group even if only one of them did it. It was also said: this is by omission of a word, meaning "one of them forgot". Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, they both forgot to examine the matter and what would come of it, which had been made a sign of success in attaining the goal. It was also said: Yusha' forgot to bring it forward, and Musa forgot to give an instruction about it. End of quotation.

The path the fish took in the water is likened to a sarab, since the water did not close again behind it but remained like an arch. This is what is found in the hadith. The majority said: the place where it passed remained empty. Qatada said: it was solid water. Ibn Abbas said: a smooth rock. Ibn Zayd said: it only made its way as a sarab on land until it reached the sea, and then it swam as usual. It seems he meant by the words ﴿sarab﴾ free movement and roaming, from the expression fahlun sārib, meaning a stallion left unrestrained, grazing wherever it wishes. From this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and one who moves freely by day﴾ [al-Ra'd: 10], meaning one who moves about freely. Some said: he made a sarab in the earth from the basket, and on his path he came upon a rock and bored through it. The apparent meaning is that the sarab was in the water, and it cannot be interpreted except by what is found in the authentic hadith, that the water became over it like an arch. This is a miracle for Musa (peace be upon him), or for al-Khadir if we say he is a prophet, and otherwise it is a karama (a marvel granted to a righteous person).

It was said: the place where the fish had passed turned back into a dry path of stone, and Musa walked along it following the fish, until that led him to an island in the sea, where he found al-Khadir. ﴿So when they had passed on﴾, that is, the meeting place of the two seas. Al-Zamakhshari said: the appointed place is the rock. It was said: they travelled after passing the rock through the night and the next day until noon, and fatigue and hunger came upon Musa when he passed the appointed place, and he had not been tired or hungry before that, so he remembered the fish and asked for it. His words ﴿from this journey of ours﴾ refer to their travelling beyond the rock. The majority read ﴿nasaban﴾ (fatigue) with two fathas, and Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr read it with two dammas. The author of al-Lawami' said: this is one of the four dialects in which it occurs.

Al-Zamakhshari said: if you ask, how could Yusha' forget that, when such a thing is not forgotten, since it was a sign for them of the goal for which they were striving, and since it was two clear miracles: the living of the salted fish that was eaten from, and it was also said it was only half a fish; the standing up of the water and its rising like an arch; and its passage in the manner of a sarab? Then how did forgetfulness persist with him until they left the appointed place and travelled a night's journey until midday the next day, and until Musa asked for the fish? I say: Satan had occupied him with his whisperings, and his thoughts went in every direction until forgetfulness overtook him. Added to that is that he had become accustomed to seeing such wonders with Musa, and he had become comfortable with his own kind, so familiarity overcame his lack of concern. End of quotation.

Abu Bakr Ghalib ibn Atiyya and the exegete Abd al-Haqq al-Dani said: I heard Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari say in his preaching: Musa walked to the private conversation with Allah and remained forty days without needing food, but when he walked to a human being, hunger reached him in part of a day.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ara'ayta﴾ (have you seen?) here means "inform me". If you ask, what is the connection of this speech, since each of ﴿ara'ayta﴾, ﴿when we took refuge at the rock﴾ and ﴿I forgot the fish﴾ has no connection? I say: when Musa asked for the fish, Yusha' mentioned what he had seen of it and how forgetfulness had overcome him to that extent, and he was bewildered and began to ask Musa about the cause of this. It was as if he said: "Have you seen what has afflicted me, ﴿when we took refuge at the rock, for I forgot the fish﴾", so the answer was omitted. End of quotation.

That ﴿ara'ayta﴾ means "inform me" was mentioned by Sibawayh. We have explained this at length in the surah of al-An'am and in our commentary on the book al-Tashil.

As for what is specific to ﴿ara'ayta﴾ in this place, al-Akhfash (Abu al-Hasan) said: the Arabs removed it entirely from its original meaning, so they say ara'ayta-ka and ara-yta-ka with the hamza dropped when it means "inform me". When it means "I saw", its hamza is not dropped. He said: it is also irregular in that it requires the second-person address with this meaning, and one never says in it "arani Zayd 'Amran ma sana'a" (Zayd showed me what Amr did); but one says it with the meaning "I know". It is also irregular in that it has been removed entirely from its place, as shown by the entry of the fa' (then), for you see the words ﴿ara'ayta idh awaynā ila al-sakhrati fa-innī nasītu al-ḥūta﴾. The fa' only enters when the word has been moved to mean amma (as for) or tanabbah (take note), and the meaning is: as for ﴿when we took refuge at the rock﴾, then the matter is such-and-such. It has also been moved to the meaning "inform me", as we have said. When it means "inform me", there must follow it a noun about which information is sought, and the clause after it must be a question. It may also come out with the meaning amma, and after it there always comes a conditional or a time adverb. So His words ﴿fa-innī nasītu al-ḥūta﴾ mean "as for ﴿when we took refuge﴾, ﴿for I forgot the fish﴾", or "take note, ﴿when we took refuge﴾". The fa' is only a response to ara'ayta, because idh cannot be used as a conditional particle except when accompanied by mā, without any disagreement. End of al-Akhfash's words.

In this there is a point: when ara'ayta means "inform me", there must follow it a noun about which information is sought, and the clause after it must be a question; and these two are absent in al-Zamakhshari's interpretation of ara'ayta here as "inform me". The meaning of ﴿I forgot the fish﴾ is: I forgot the mention of what happened concerning it to you.

In His words ﴿and none made me forget it but Satan﴾ there is a beautiful courtesy, in that he attributed the forgetting to the one who caused it by his whispering. ﴿That I mention it﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the pronoun referring back to the fish. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿and it took its way into the sea, wondrously﴾ refers back to the fish, as it did in His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea as a sarab﴾, and this is part of Yusha's speech. It was also said: the pronoun refers to Musa, meaning Musa took it. The meaning of ʿajaban is: a wonder at that, or taking it as a wonder, namely that its trace remained wherever it went. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: its way was wondrous, that is, it was like the sarab. He said: or it was said ʿajaban at the end of the speech, as an expression of wonder at his state in seeing that marvel and forgetting it, or at the two miracles he had seen. His words ﴿and none made me forget it but Satan, that I mention it﴾ are a parenthetical insertion between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. It was also said that ʿajaban is a report of Musa's wonder, but this is not the case. End of quotation.

Ibn Atiyya said: ﴿and it took its way into the sea, wondrously﴾ may be the words of Yusha' to Musa, meaning: the fish took a wondrous way for the people. It may also be that His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea﴾ are the completion of the report, and then He resumed with wonder, saying from Himself ʿajaban (wondrously) at this matter. The point of wonder is that a fish should die, and half of it be eaten, and then come back to life after that. End of quotation.

Abu Shuja' said in the book of al-Tabari: "I saw it. I came with it, and behold, it was half a fish, one eye, and another half in which there was nothing." Ibn Atiyya said: I too have seen it, and the half which had something on it had a thin skin under which there was no bone. It may be that ﴿and it took its way﴾ and the rest of the verse are a report from Allah the Exalted. This may be in two ways: either He reports about Musa that he took the fish's path from the sea as a wonder, that is, he was amazed by it; or He reports about the fish that it took its path as a wonder for the people. End of quotation.

Hafs read ﴿wa-mā ansānīhu﴾ with a dammah on the ha' (hu), and with fath (a) in the pause (when reciting continuously, the vowel is as stated). Al-Kisa'i inclined the fatha of the sin. In the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and his recitation, the reading is ﴿an adhkurahu﴾ and ﴿illa al-shaytana﴾ (with an accusative on al-shaytan). Abu Haywa read ﴿wa-ittikhādha sabīlihi﴾ as a conjunction with the verbal noun (maṣdar) in the pronoun object of ﴿adhkurahu﴾. The reference of ﴿dhālika﴾ (that) is to the matter of the fish, its loss, and its taking its way in the sea, because it was a sign of success in attaining the goal, namely meeting that righteous servant. The word ﴿mā﴾ (what) is a relative pronoun and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: ﴿nabghī﴾ (we seek). It was read ﴿nabghi﴾ without a yā' in continuous recitation, and including the yā' is better. This is the reading of Abu Amr, al-Kisa'i and Nafi'. In pause, most people omit the yā', following the orthography of the codex, while Ibn Kathir includes it in both states.

﴿Then they both returned﴾: they went back by the same tracks by which they had come.

﴿Retracing (qasasan)﴾: that is, they followed their own trail back, retracing it. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun with an implied verb meaning "they retraced", or it may be in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning "tracing back", and it is governed by the word ﴿returned﴾.

﴿And they found a servant from among Our servants﴾: this is an idafa of honour and distinction. They found him near the rock where the fish had been lost, and he was lying on his back on the ground, covered in his garment. So Musa said: "Peace be upon you." He lifted his head and said: "How is there peace in your land?" Then he said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "I am Musa." He said: "Musa of the Children of Israel?" He said: "Yes." He said to him: "Did you not have among the Children of Israel what occupied you from travelling here?" He said: "Yes, but I wanted to meet you and to learn from you." He said to him: "I have knowledge from the knowledge of Allah which He taught me, which you do not know, and you have knowledge from the knowledge of Allah which Allah taught you, which I do not know."

The majority hold that he is al-Khadir, and one whose dissent is not considered disagreed, claiming that he is another scholar. It was said: he was al-Yasa' (Elisha). It was said: he was Ilyas (Elias). It was said: he was Khadirun ibn Qabil ibn Adam (peace be upon him). It was said: the name of al-Khadir was Balya ibn Malkan. The majority hold that al-Khadir was a prophet, and that his knowledge was knowledge of inner realities that had been revealed to him, while the knowledge of Musa was of legal rulings and fatwas concerning the outward. It is reported that he was found sitting on the crest of the sea. In a hadith, he was called al-Khadir because he sat on a dry tuft of land which then turned green (akhdar) beneath him. It was said: whenever he prayed, the area around him turned green. It was said: he sat on a white tuft (fawwah), that is, a raised land, or a hard one, and it turned green beneath him. It was said: his mother was Roman and his father Persian. It was said: he was the son of a king among the kings, whose father wished to make him his successor after him, but he did not accept this, and he joined the islands of the sea, and his father sought him but could not find him. The majority hold that he died.

Sharaf al-Din Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi said: as for al-Khadir of Musa son of Imran, he is not alive, because if he were alive it would be incumbent upon him to come to the Prophet ﷺ, to believe in him, and to follow him. It has been reported from him that he said: "If Musa and Isa were alive, they would have no choice but to follow me." End of quotation. This is how the hadith is cited. The doctrine of the Muslims is that Isa is alive, and that he will descend from heaven. Perhaps the hadith is: "If Musa were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verse 60–70 (part 3 of 3):

The mercy that Allah gave him (raḥmah) is revelation and prophethood. It was also said: it is provision (rizq). (And We taught him from Our presence a knowledge) — meaning, from Our side, that is, of the knowledge that is specific to Us, which is informing about the unseen. Abu Zayd, from Abu 'Amr, read "min ladunā" with a lightened nun, and it is a dialect form of ladun, which is the original form.

It has been said: Many of those who ascribe themselves to righteousness have become fond of claiming this knowledge and calling it "ladunni knowledge" (al-'ilm al-ladunni), and that something of it is cast into the heart of the righteous among them, to the point that he informs that whoever among his companions is among the people of Paradise is certain, and that some of them see al-Khidr. Abu al-Fath Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mutī' al-Qushayri, known as Ibn Daqiq al-'Id, the chief judge, used to report about a shaykh of his that he saw al-Khidr and spoke with him. It was said to him: "Who informed him that he was al-Khidr? And from where did he know that?" So he fell silent. Some of them claim that al-Khidriyyah is a rank held by some of the righteous on the footing of al-Khidr. We heard the hadith from a shaykh called 'Abd al-Wahid al-'Abbasi al-Hanbali, and his companions, the Hanbalis, believed about him that he meets al-Khidr.

(He said to him, Musa) There is an omitted element in the speech; its estimate is: "So when they met and exchanged words," and this is what is related in the authentic hadith: ﴿Musa said to him, May I follow you?﴾ In this there is evidence of humility before the scholar. In this story there is evidence of encouragement to travel in seeking knowledge, and of good gentleness, coaxing, and good manners in seeking knowledge, by his saying ﴿May I follow you?﴾. In it is also the accompanying of the scholar in order to acquire his benefits. The meaning is: "Will it be light for you and will it suit you?" And (rushdan) is in the accusative either as a second object of his saying ﴿you teach me﴾, or as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), whose ṣāḥib al-ḥāl is the pronoun in ﴿I follow you﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (knowledge) with rectitude (rushd), by which I am guided in my religion. He said: If you say, does his need to learn from another in his time not show that he was, as has been said, Musa ibn Mīshā and not Musa ibn 'Imran? For a prophet must be the most knowledgeable of the people of his time and their imam to whom recourse is had in matters of religion? I say: There is no shame for a prophet in taking knowledge from a prophet before him; what diminishes him is only that he take from one lower than himself.

From Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Nawf, the son of Ka'b's wife, claims that al-Khidr is not the companion of Musa, and that Musa is Musa ibn Mīshā." He said: "The enemy of Allah has lied." End.

Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Abu Bahriyyah, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Munadhir, Ya'qub, Abu 'Ubayd, and al-Yazidi read (rashadan) with two fathas, and this is the reading of Abu 'Amr from the Seven. The rest of the Seven read with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the shin.

Al-Khidr negated the ability to be patient with him, by way of emphasis, as though it were something that is not sound and not proper. He justified that by saying that he undertakes matters which, outwardly, a righteous man would disapprove of, so how much more a prophet; he would not be able to restrain himself from recoiling at that and hastening to object: ﴿And how can you be patient?﴾, that is: your patience regarding what you have no experience of is far-fetched. In this there is an expression of excuse for him, since he cannot be patient seeing what contradicts what he is upon of his own law. (Khubran) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), meaning: "about what your knowledge does not encompass," so it is transferred from the subject, or it is a verbal noun not of the same root, because the meaning of ﴿what you do not encompass with knowledge﴾ [al-Naml: 22] is "you are not informed of it." Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz read (khubura) with a damma on the ba'.

﴿He said: You will find me, if Allah wills, patient﴾. He promised him that he would find him (ṣābiran) patient, and he joined that with the will of Allah, knowing from himself the severity and difficulty of the matter, since one is only patient regarding what contradicts what he is upon when he sees it. ﴿And I will not disobey you﴾ may be conjoined to (ṣābiran), meaning: patient and not disobeying, in which case it is in the accusative position, the verb being coordinated with a noun when it has the same meaning, as in His saying ﴿lining up and seizing﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], meaning: and seizing. It may also be conjoined to (satajidunī), in which case it has no place in the grammatical structure and is not restricted by the will in wording.

Al-Qushayri said: Musa promised of himself two things: patience, which he tied to the exception of the will; so he was patient when he saw, at the hands of al-Khidr, what he did; and that he would not disobey him, which he stated without tying it to the exception, so he disobeyed him when he said to him ﴿then do not ask me﴾, and he kept asking him. What he tied to the exception he did not contravene, and what he stated without condition, dispute arose concerning it. End. This is from him on the assumption that ﴿and I will not disobey﴾ is conjoined to (satajidunī), so it does not fall under the will.

﴿He said: If you follow me﴾, that is: if you see from me something whose correctness is hidden from you and you disapprove of it in yourself, then do not open up to me with questions until I am the one who opens to you. This is among the manners of the student with the scholar he follows. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read (fa-la tas'alnī). From Abu Ja'far, with a fatha on the sin and the lam without hamza, with a shadda on the nun. The rest of the Seven read with hamza, sukun on the lam, and light nun. Abu 'Ali said: "All of them with a ya' in both states." End. And regarding Ibn 'Amir's omission of the ya' there is a strange disagreement.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verse 71–75:

(p-149) ﴿So they set out, until when they boarded the ship, he made a hole in it. [Moses] said: "Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a grave thing."﴾ ﴿He said: "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to bear patience with me?"﴾ ﴿He said: "Do not take me to task for what I forgot, and do not burden me with difficulty in my affair."﴾ ﴿So they set out, until when they met a boy and he killed him. [Moses] said: "Have you killed a pure soul without a soul [to justify it]? You have certainly done an abominable thing."﴾ ﴿He said: "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to bear patience with me?"﴾ ﴿He said: "If I ask you about anything after this, do not keep me as your companion; you will have received an excuse from me."﴾ [al-Kahf: 76] ﴿So they set out, until when they came to the people of a town and asked its people for food, but they refused to host them. And they found in it a wall about to collapse, so he set it upright. [Moses] said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾ [al-Kahf: 77] ﴿He said: "This is the parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience."﴾ [al-Kahf: 78].

(So they set out): that is, Moses and al-Khidr, and Yusha' was with them, but he is not mentioned explicitly because he was in the position of a follower. It was also said that Moses had sent him back and returned him to the Children of Israel. The alif and lam in (al-safina, the ship) are for generic definition (ta'rif al-jins), since no prior reference to a specific ship had been made. Various accounts were narrated about the manner of their boarding the ship, its breaching and its sealing, but the relied-upon account is what al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated in their Sahihs. They said: "So they set out walking along the seashore, and a ship passed by, and they asked the people [of the ship] to carry them. They recognised al-Khidr and carried him without a fare. When they boarded the ship, suddenly al-Khidr had pulled out a plank from the planks of the ship with an adze. Moses said to him: 'These people carried us without a fare, and you deliberately went to their ship and breached it, [in order] to drown its people,' until his words, 'difficulty.'" He said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The first [act] from Moses was forgetfulness.'" He said: "A sparrow came and landed on the edge of the ship and pecked, and al-Khidr said to him: 'My knowledge and your knowledge, in comparison with the knowledge of Allah, are no more than what this sparrow has taken from this sea.'"

The lam in ﴿li-tughriqa ahlaha﴾ (in order that he drown its people): it is said to be the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), and it is said to be the lam of causation (lam al-'illah). Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Abi Layla, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Sa'dan and Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani read (liyaghraqa) with a fatha on the ya' and the ra', a sukun on the ghayn, and (ahluha) in the nominative. The rest of the seven read with a damma on the ta' of address, a sukun on the ghayn, a kasra on the ra', and a fatha on the lam of (ahlaha). Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read likewise, except that they put a fatha on the ghayn and a shadda on the ra'.
