Then al-Khidr reminded him of what had preceded from him, namely the denial of his ability to bear patience in the face of what he sees, and so he said: ﴿Do not take me to task for what I forgot﴾ (p-150). The apparent meaning is to take forgetfulness in its literal sense. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The first [act] from Moses was forgetfulness." The meaning is that he forgot the covenant that was between them, of not asking until he himself would inform him first. This is the view of the majority. From Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is reported that he did not actually forget, but that his statement was one of the indirect expressions of speech (ma'arid al-kalam). Al-Zamakhshari said: He meant that he forgot his charge, and there is no blame upon one who forgets; or he expressed the words in the form of a prohibition against taking to task for forgetfulness, imagining that he had forgotten, in order to extend his excuse in denial; and this is among the indirect expressions by which a lie is negated while achieving the purpose, like the statement of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): "This is my sister," and "I am sick." Or he meant by forgetfulness "leaving": that is, ﴿do not take me to task﴾ for what I left of your charge the first time. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyyah explained Ubayy's words at length in a passage that may be consulted in his book, but only the statement of the Messenger is relied upon: "The first [act] from Moses was forgetfulness."

﴿Do not burden me﴾: do not cover me and impose upon me ﴿in my affair﴾, which is following you, ﴿difficulty﴾, that is, something hard; rather, make it easy for me in following you by leaving off objection. Abu Ja'far read ﴿'usuran﴾ with a damma on the sin wherever it occurs. In the narrative there is an omission: the estimated meaning of "so they set out" is "so they disembarked from the ship, and no drowning befell its people." Then they set out, and while they were walking along the shore, al-Khidr saw a boy (ghulaman) playing with children. In some narrations: he passed by boys playing, and al-Khidr went to a boy of good appearance and bright face and pulled off his head. It was said: he crushed him with a stone. It was said: he slaughtered him. It was said: he twisted his neck. It was said: he struck his head against the wall. It was said: this boy had not reached puberty, and for this reason [Moses] said: ﴿Have you killed a pure soul?﴾ It was said: the boy was adult, a youth, and the Arabs still apply the name "boy" (ghulam) to a young man. From this is the verse of Layla al-Akhyaliyyah concerning al-Hajjaj:

"He healed her of the sickness that had afflicted her, a boy who, when he shakes the spear, gives her drink."

And another said:

"Ward off the edge of the sword from me, for I am a boy when I am provoked, not a poet."

It was said: its origin is from al-ightilam, which is intense sexual desire, and that occurs only in youths who have reached puberty; and the term may be applied to a small child figuratively, naming a thing by what it will become. (It has been disputed concerning the name of this boy, the name of his father, and the name of his mother), but nothing of that has come in a hadith. In a report it is stated that this boy used to corrupt, and would swear to his parents that he had not done it, so they would affirm his oath and protect him from anyone seeking him.

Al-Qurtubi related from the author of al-'Urs wa-l-'Ara'is that when Moses (peace be upon him) said to al-Khidr, ﴿Have you killed a pure soul?﴾, al-Khidr became angry, pulled out the boy's left shoulder, stripped the flesh from it, and there in the bone of his shoulder was written: "An unbeliever who will never believe in Allah."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why is (kharaqaha, he made a hole in it) said without a fa', while (faqatalahu, so he killed him) is said with a fa'? I say: (kharaqaha) was made the response (jaza') to the condition, and (qatalahu) was made part of the condition, coordinated with what precedes it, while the response is (aqatalta, have you killed). If you ask: why was a difference made between them? I say: because the breaching of the ship did not follow the boarding directly, whereas the killing did follow the meeting with the boy. End of quotation.

The meaning of ﴿zakiyyatan﴾ is pure from sins. He described her with this description because he had not seen her commit a sin; it was said, or because she was a small child who had not reached the age of responsibility (hinth). His statement "without a soul" refutes this and indicates the boy's maturity; otherwise, if he had not reached puberty, killing him would not have been obligatory either for a soul or for no soul. Ibn 'Abbas, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Zuhri, Nafi', al-Yazidi, Ibn Muslim, Zayd, Ibn Bukayr from Ya'qub, al-Tammar from Ruways from him, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (zakiyyatan) with an alif. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans read (zakiyyatan) without an alif and with a shadda on the ya', and it is more emphatic than (zakiyyatin), because the form fa'il converted from fa'il indicates intensification (al-mubalaghah).

The majority read (nukran) with a sukun on the kaf. Nafi', Abu Bakr, Ibn Dhakwan, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Talhah, Ya'qub and Abu Hatim read it with a damma on the kaf wherever it occurs in the accusative. It was said: nukr is less than imr, because killing one soul is easier than drowning the people of the ship. It was said: (p-151) its meaning is: a thing more reprehensible than the first, because a breach can be repaired, whereas with killing there is no way to reverse the life once taken. In his statement "to you" (laka) there is a rebuke and severity absent from the first, because its context is questioning after having been warned to abandon questioning and after Moses had offered the excuse of forgetfulness; so it is more grievous and more severe in violating what he had undertaken upon himself of patience and of not disobeying.

In the narrative there is an omission: the estimated meaning of "so they set out" is "so they disembarked from the ship, and no drowning befell its people." Then they set out, and while they were walking along the shore, al-Khidr saw a boy (ghulaman) playing with children. In some narrations: he passed by boys playing, and al-Khidr went to a boy of good appearance and bright face and pulled off his head. It was said: he crushed him with a stone. It was said: he slaughtered him. It was said: he twisted his neck. It was said: he struck his head against the wall. It was said: this boy had not reached puberty, and for this reason [Moses] said: ﴿Have you killed a pure soul?﴾ It was said: the boy was adult, a youth, and the Arabs still apply the name "boy" (ghulam) to a young man. From this is the verse of Layla al-Akhyaliyyah concerning al-Hajjaj:

"He healed her of the sickness that had afflicted her, a boy who, when he shakes the spear, gives her drink."

And another said:

"Ward off the edge of the sword from me, for I am a boy when I am provoked, not a poet."

It was said: its origin is from al-ightilam, which is intense sexual desire, and that occurs only in youths who have reached puberty; and the term may be applied to a small child figuratively, naming a thing by what it will become. (It has been disputed concerning the name of this boy, the name of his father, and the name of his mother), but nothing of that has come in a hadith. In a report it is stated that this boy used to corrupt, and would swear to his parents that he had not done it, so they would affirm his oath and protect him from anyone seeking him.

Al-Qurtubi related from the author of al-'Urs wa-l-'Ara'is that when Moses (peace be upon him) said to al-Khidr, ﴿Have you killed a pure soul?﴾, al-Khidr became angry, pulled out the boy's left shoulder, stripped the flesh from it, and there in the bone of his shoulder was written: "An unbeliever who will never believe in Allah."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why is (kharaqaha, he made a hole in it) said without a fa', while (faqatalahu, so he killed him) is said with a fa'? I say: (kharaqaha) was made the response (jaza') to the condition, and (qatalahu) was made part of the condition, coordinated with what precedes it, while the response is (aqatalta, have you killed). If you ask: why was a difference made between them? I say: because the breaching of the ship did not follow the boarding directly, whereas the killing did follow the meeting with the boy. End of quotation.

The meaning of ﴿zakiyyatan﴾ is pure from sins. He described her with this description because he had not seen her commit a sin; it was said, or because she was a small child who had not reached the age of responsibility (hinth). His statement "without a soul" refutes this and indicates the boy's maturity; otherwise, if he had not reached puberty, killing him would not have been obligatory either for a soul or for no soul. Ibn 'Abbas, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Zuhri, Nafi', al-Yazidi, Ibn Muslim, Zayd, Ibn Bukayr from Ya'qub, al-Tammar from Ruways from him, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (zakiyyatan) with an alif. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans read (zakiyyatan) without an alif and with a shadda on the ya', and it is more emphatic than (zakiyyatin), because the form fa'il converted from fa'il indicates intensification (al-mubalaghah).

The majority read (nukran) with a sukun on the kaf. Nafi', Abu Bakr, Ibn Dhakwan, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Talhah, Ya'qub and Abu Hatim read it with a damma on the kaf wherever it occurs in the accusative. It was said: nukr is less than imr, because killing one soul is easier than drowning the people of the ship. It was said: (p-151) its meaning is: a thing more reprehensible than the first, because a breach can be repaired, whereas with killing there is no way to reverse the life once taken. In his statement "to you" (laka) there is a rebuke and severity absent from the first, because its context is questioning after having been warned to abandon questioning and after Moses had offered the excuse of forgetfulness; so it is more grievous and more severe in violating what he had undertaken upon himself of patience and of not disobeying.

﴿He said: "If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep company with me."﴾ That is, after this incident or after this question. ﴿Do not keep company with me﴾: that is, cause separation between me and you. The majority of reciters read ﴿فَلا تُصاحِبْنِي﴾ (fa-la tusahibni) in the form of the verb *mufa'ala* (the third form). ʿIsa and Yaʿqub read فَلا تَصْحَبْنِي (fa-la tasḥabni), the imperfect of *ṣaḥiba*. ʿIsa also read it as تُصْحِبْنِي with a *ḍamma* on the *ta* and a *kasra* on the *ha*, the imperfect of *aṣḥaba*, and Sahl transmitted it from Abu ʿAmr. The meaning would then be: "Do not make me keep your knowledge company." Some commentators supplied the object as "do not make me keep company with you," and others as "with yourself." Al-Aʿraj read it with a *fatha* on the *ta* and the *ba*, and with a shadda on the *nun*. The meaning of ﴿قَدْ بَلَغْتَ مِن لَدُنِّي عُذْرًا﴾ ("you have indeed reached an excuse from my side") is: you have offered me an excuse and reached the point of excuse. The majority read ﴿مِن لَدُنِّي﴾ (min ladunni) with *idgham* (assimilation, merging of identical or similar consonants) of the *nun* of *ladun* into the protective *nun* (nun al-wiqaya, the *nun* inserted before the first-person pronoun suffix) that is attached to the pronoun of the speaker. Nafiʿ and ʿAsim read it with a lightened *nun*, which is the *nun* of *ladun* attached to the first-person pronoun. This is the analogical form, because when nouns are annexed to the first-person pronoun the protective *nun* is not added, as in *ghulamī* ("my boy") and *faraskī* ("my horse"). Shuʿba read the *dal* with a *ḍamma* in a weakened (*ishmam*) form, and it is transmitted from ʿAsim that the *dal* is sukun (unvowelled). Ibn Mujahid said: "This is an error," meaning, as it seems, in terms of transmission. As for the language, it is not an error, because among the dialects of this word is *ladḥ* with a *fatha* on the *lam* and a sukun on the *dal*. ʿIsa read ﴿عُذُرًا﴾ with a *ḍamma* on the *dhal*, and it is transmitted from Abu ʿAmr and from Ubayy as ﴿عُذْرِي﴾ ("my excuse") with a *kasra* on the *ra'*, annexed to the first-person pronoun.

In al-Bukhari, it is related that he said: "May Allah have mercy on Musa. We wished that he had been patient until he related to us their story." Al-Tabari also cited with a chain of narration that he said: "Whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked mercy for someone, he began with himself, saying: 'The mercy of Allah be upon us and upon Musa. Had he been patient with his companion, he would have seen wonders.'" But he said ﴿فَلا تُصاحِبْنِي قَدْ بَلَغْتَ مِن لَدُنِّي عُذْرًا﴾.

As for the town they came to: it is Antioch, or Ubulla, or the Green Island in al-Andalus, or Burqa, or Abu Hawran in the region of Adharbayjan, or Nasira from the land of the Romans, or a village in Armenia. These are conflicting opinions, differing according to where on earth the story of Musa took place, and Allah knows best its reality. In a hadith it is said: "They were walking over the gatherings of those people, asking them for food." This is an explicit lesson on the lowliness of this world in the sight of Allah, the Exalted. The word ﴿أهْل﴾ (ahl, "people") is repeated for emphasis. A benefit of this emphasis may appear: when ﴿أتَيا أهْلَ قَرْيَةٍ﴾ ("they came to the people of a town"), they did not come to all the people of the town, but only to some of them. So when it says ﴿اسْتَطْعَما﴾ ("they asked for food"), it could be understood that they only asked that part they had come to. Therefore the phrase "its people" (ahlaha) was used so that it would include all of them, and so that they would be asked one by one for food. Had the construction been "asked them" (istaṭʿamahum), it would have referred only to the part that had been approached.

The majority read ﴿يُضَيِّفُوهُما﴾ ("would host them") with *tashdid* (gemination) from *dayyafa*. Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Razin, Ibn Muhaysin, ʿAsim in the transmission of al-Mufaddal, and Aban read it with a *kasra* on the *ḍad* and sukun on the *ya'*, from *aḍāfa*, just as one says *mayyala* and *amāla* (both meaning "to incline"). Attributing the act of "wanting" (irada) to a wall is a metaphor of eloquent force and a striking figure of speech. It is very common in Arabic speech to attribute to non-rational beings, to animals that lack reason, and to inanimate objects, things that would be done by rational beings, as if that act had come from them in place of a rational agent. Al-Zamakhshari and others cited many examples of this, and anyone with even slight acquaintance with Arabic speech would not need an example for it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It has reached me that some of those who distort the words of Allah, from among those who lack knowledge, used to make the pronoun refer to al-Khadir, because they saw in it an affliction of ignorance and a sickness of understanding; they thought that the highest speech in rank is lower in position, so they contrived to return it to what they considered more correct and more eloquent. They held that what is further from metaphor is more fitting for inimitability." (The quotation ends here.) What the scholars of the foundations of jurisprudence transmit from Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Dawud al-Isfahani, that he denies metaphor in the Qur'an, may not be authentically reported from him. How could that be, when he was one of the eminent, accomplished poets and literary figures, skilled in verse and prose?

(p-152) The majority read ﴿يَنْقَضُّ﴾ (yanqaḍḍu), meaning it falls, from the "swooping" (inqiḍaḍ) of a bird. Its form is *infaʿala*, like *injarra*. The author of al-Lawami said: it is from *qaḍḍa*, meaning small pebbles, and from it comes *ṭaʿām qaḍaḍ*, food containing pebbles. On this view ﴿يُرِيدُ أنْ يَنْقَضَّ﴾ means that it was about to crumble and become a pebble. It was also said that its form is *if'alla* from *naqḍ* (breaking down), like *iḥmarra*. Ubayy read يُنْقَضَّ (yunqaḍḍa) with a *ḍamma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *qaf* and the *ḍad*, in the passive voice, from *naqaḍtu*. This is transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ). In the reading of ʿAbd Allah and the reading of al-Aʿmash it is (لِيَنْقَضَّ) with the same vowels, except that it is in the subjunctive after the *lam* with the hidden *an*. ʿAli, ʿIkrima, Abu Shaykh Khayawan ibn Khalid al-Hunai, Khulayd ibn Saʿd and Yahya ibn Yaʿmur read يَنْقاصُ (yanqaṣu) with an unpointed *ṣad* and an *alif*. Its form is *yanfaʿilu*, intransitive, from *qaṣa yaqīṣu*. When you break it, you say *qayytuhu*, then *infāṣa*. Ibn Khalawayh said: the Arabs say *infāṣati al-sinn* when the tooth splits lengthwise. Dhu al-Rumma said: "*munqāṣ* and *munkathib*." It was also said that it means whenever it cracks in any way. From this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Separation like the cracking of a tooth; so be patient, for surely for every person there is a stumble and a mending."

Al-Zuhri read يَنْقاضُ (yanqāḍu) with an *alif* and a pointed *ḍad*, which comes from their saying *quḍtuhu* (with a pointed *ḍad*), then *infāḍa*, meaning: I demolished it, so it collapsed. Abu ʿAli said: the well-known reading from al-Zuhri has an unpointed *ṣad*.

﴿فَأقامَهُ﴾ ("then he set it up"): the apparent meaning is that he did not demolish it and then rebuild it, as some of them held, that he demolished it and sat building it. This occurs in the codex of ʿAbd Allah and is supported by his words, "you would have taken a wage for it," because rebuilding it after demolishing it would deserve a wage. Ibn Jubayr said: he wiped it with his hand and it set up and stood. It was also said: he set it up with a pole he used as a prop. Muqatil said: he plastered it with *shid* (plaster), meaning he coated it with it, and that is *al-jayyar* (mortar). From Ibn ʿAbbas: he pushed it with his hand and it stood straight, and this is more fitting to the condition of the prophets. Al-Zamakhshari said: the situation was one of compulsion and need for food, and they were bound by the need for the last means of livelihood, which is asking. They found no one to console them. When he set up the wall, Musa could not contain himself, seeing the deprivation and the pressure of need, and said ﴿لَوْ شِئْتَ لاتَّخَذْتَ عَلَيْهِ أجْرًا﴾ ("If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it"), and asked a payment for your work, so that you might be revived by it and ward off dire necessity. (End of quotation.) Ibn ʿAtiyya said: his words ﴿لَوْ شِئْتَ لاتَّخَذْتَ عَلَيْهِ أجْرًا﴾, even if they are not a question, contain within them a denial of his act, and an assertion that taking a wage was correct, and in that there is a judgment of error against leaving the wage. ʿAbd Allah, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Bahriyya read لَتَخِذْتَ (lataḵidhta) with an open *ta'* and a *kasra* on the *kha'*. It is said *takhidha* and *ittakhadha*, like *tabiʿa* and *ittabaʿa*: *iftaʿala* from *takhidha*, with the *ta'* assimilated into the *ta'*. The poet said:

"And my leg has taken a stand beside its stirrup, a shaking, like the crouching hollow of a sandgrouse, flattened."

The *ta'* is original according to the Basran grammarians and is not from *akhdh* (taking). Some claimed that *ittikhadh* is *iftiʿal* from *akhdh*, and that they supposed the *ta'* was original, so they said in the triliteral *takhidha*, just as they said *taqiya* from *ittaqā*. The apparent meaning is that this refers to his words ﴿لَوْ شِئْتَ﴾ ("if you had wished"), meaning this objection is the cause of separation ﴿بَيْنِي وبَيْنِكَ﴾ ("between me and you"), according to the appointed agreement mentioned earlier. He said ﴿إنْ سَألْتُكَ﴾ ("if I ask you"), and this sentence, though it is not a question, contains one, since the meaning is: "Were you not taking a wage for it, since we needed it?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: a separation between them is imagined when the appointed time arrives, according to what Musa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿إنْ سَألْتُكَ عَنْ شَيْءٍ بَعْدَهُ فَلا تُصاحِبْنِي﴾. He pointed to it and made it a subject, and reported about it, just as you say "this is your brother," so this "this" cannot refer to anything other than the brother. (End of quotation.) There is scrutiny in what he said.

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿فِراقٌ بَيْنِي﴾ with tanwin, while the majority read it as an annexed construction. Al-Bayn: Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is the connection that exists between two companions and the like, and it is figuratively derived from the adverbial sense, used as a noun. Its repetition in ﴿بَيْنِي وبَيْنِكَ﴾ and his deviation from "between us" (baynina) serve the sense of emphasis. ﴿سَأُنَبِّئُكَ﴾ ("I will inform you"): that is, I will tell you about the *ta'wil* (interpretation, final meaning) of what you saw of the breaking of the boat, the killing of the boy, and the setting up of the wall. That is, the outcome of matters where the apparent meaning was that it should not have been so. Ibn Wththab read سَأُنْبِيكَ (sa-unbīka) with a pure *ya'* without *hamza*. From Ibn ʿAbbas: Musa's words about the boat and about the boy were for Allah, while his words about the wall were for himself, seeking something of this world, and so this became the cause of separation. The scholars of meanings said: these examples that befell Musa with al-Khadir are a proof against Musa and his haste. When he denied the breaking of the boat, he was addressed: "O Musa, where was this planning of yours when you were cast in the ark on the river?" When he denied the killing of the boy, it was said to him: "Where is your denial of this from your striking of the Copt and your judgment against him?" When he denied the setting up of the wall, he was addressed: "Where is this from your lifting the stone for the daughters of Shuʿayb without a wage?" ﴿سَأُنَبِّئُكَ﴾ ("I will inform you") means: in the meanings of this I am with you, and I will not part from you until I clarify for you what was obscure to you.

Muqatil said: he plastered it with *shid* (plaster), meaning he coated it with it, and that is *al-jayyar* (mortar). From Ibn ʿAbbas: he pushed it with his hand and it stood straight, and this is more fitting to the condition of the prophets. Al-Zamakhshari said: the situation was one of compulsion and need for food, and they were bound by the need for the last means of livelihood, which is asking. They found no one to console them. When he set up the wall, Musa could not contain himself, seeing the deprivation and the pressure of need, and said ﴿لَوْ شِئْتَ لاتَّخَذْتَ عَلَيْهِ أجْرًا﴾ ("If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it"), and asked a payment for your work, so that you might be revived by it and ward off dire necessity. (End of quotation.) Ibn ʿAtiyya said: his words ﴿لَوْ شِئْتَ لاتَّخَذْتَ عَلَيْهِ أجْرًا﴾, even if they are not a question, contain within them a denial of his act, and an assertion that taking a wage was correct, and in that there is a judgment of error against leaving the wage. ʿAbd Allah, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Bahriyya read لَتَخِذْتَ (lataḵidhta) with an open *ta'* and a *kasra* on the *kha'*. It is said *takhidha* and *ittakhadha*, like *tabiʿa* and *ittabaʿa*: *iftaʿala* from *takhidha*, with the *ta'* assimilated into the *ta'*. The poet said:

"And my leg has taken a stand beside its stirrup, a shaking, like the crouching hollow of a sandgrouse, flattened."

The *ta'* is original according to the Basran grammarians and is not from *akhdh* (taking). Some claimed that *ittikhadh* is *iftiʿal* from *akhdh*, and that they supposed the *ta'* was original, so they said in the triliteral *takhidha*, just as they said *taqiya* from *ittaqā*. The apparent meaning is that this refers to his words ﴿لَوْ شِئْتَ﴾ ("if you had wished"), meaning this objection is the cause of separation ﴿بَيْنِي وبَيْنِكَ﴾ ("between me and you"), according to the appointed agreement mentioned earlier. He said ﴿إنْ سَألْتُكَ﴾ ("if I ask you"), and this sentence, though it is not a question, contains one, since the meaning is: "Were you not taking a wage for it, since we needed it?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: a separation between them is imagined when the appointed time arrives, according to what Musa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿إنْ سَألْتُكَ عَنْ شَيْءٍ بَعْدَهُ فَلا تُصاحِبْنِي﴾. He pointed to it and made it a subject, and reported about it, just as you say "this is your brother," so this "this" cannot refer to anything other than the brother. (End of quotation.) There is scrutiny in what he said.

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿فِراقٌ بَيْنِي﴾ with tanwin, while the majority read it as an annexed construction. Al-Bayn: Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is the connection that exists between two companions and the like, and it is figuratively derived from the adverbial sense, used as a noun. Its repetition in ﴿بَيْنِي وبَيْنِكَ﴾ and his deviation from "between us" (baynina) serve the sense of emphasis. ﴿سَأُنَبِّئُكَ﴾ ("I will inform you"): that is, I will tell you about the *ta'wil* (interpretation, final meaning) of what you saw of the breaking of the boat, the killing of the boy, and the setting up of the wall. That is, the outcome of matters where the apparent meaning was that it should not have been so. Ibn Wththab read سَأُنْبِيكَ (sa-unbīka) with a pure *ya'* without *hamza*. From Ibn ʿAbbas: Musa's words about the boat and about the boy were for Allah, while his words about the wall were for himself, seeking something of this world, and so this became the cause of separation. The scholars of meanings said: these examples that befell Musa with al-Khadir are a proof against Musa and his haste. When he denied the breaking of the boat, he was addressed: "O Musa, where was this planning of yours when you were cast in the ark on the river?" When he denied the killing of the boy, it was said to him: "Where is your denial of this from your striking of the Copt and your judgment against him?" When he denied the setting up of the wall, he was addressed: "Where is this from your lifting the stone for the daughters of Shuʿayb without a wage?" ﴿سَأُنَبِّئُكَ﴾ ("I will inform you") means: in the meanings of this I am with you, and I will not part from you until I clarify for you what was obscure to you.

﴿He said: "If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep company with me."﴾ That is, after this incident or after this question. ﴿Do not keep company with me﴾: that is, cause separation between me and you. The majority of reciters read ﴿فَلا تُصاحِبْنِي﴾ (fa-la tusahibni) in the form of the verb *mufa'ala* (the third form). ʿIsa and Yaʿqub read فَلا تَصْحَبْنِي (fa-la tasḥabni), the imperfect of *ṣaḥiba*. ʿIsa also read it as تُصْحِبْنِي with a *ḍamma* on the *ta* and a *kasra* on the *ha*, the imperfect of *aṣḥaba*, and Sahl transmitted it from Abu ʿAmr. The meaning would then be: "Do not make me keep your knowledge company." Some commentators supplied the object as "do not make me keep company with you," and others as "with yourself." Al-Aʿraj read it with a *fatha* on the *ta* and the *ba*, and with a shadda on the *nun*. The meaning of ﴿قَدْ بَلَغْتَ مِن لَدُنِّي عُذْرًا﴾ ("you have indeed reached an excuse from my side") is: you have offered me an excuse and reached the point of excuse. The majority read ﴿مِن لَدُنِّي﴾ (min ladunni) with *idgham* (assimilation, merging of identical or similar consonants) of the *nun* of *ladun* into the protective *nun* (nun al-wiqaya, the *nun* inserted before the first-person pronoun suffix) that is attached to the pronoun of the speaker. Nafiʿ and ʿAsim read it with a lightened *nun*, which is the *nun* of *ladun* attached to the first-person pronoun. This is the analogical form, because when nouns are annexed to the first-person pronoun the protective *nun* is not added, as in *ghulamī* ("my boy") and *faraskī* ("my horse"). Shuʿba read the *dal* with a *ḍamma* in a weakened (*ishmam*) form, and it is transmitted from ʿAsim that the *dal* is sukun (unvowelled). Ibn Mujahid said: "This is an error," meaning, as it seems, in terms of transmission. As for the language, it is not an error, because among the dialects of this word is *ladḥ* with a *fatha* on the *lam* and a sukun on the *dal*. ʿIsa read ﴿عُذُرًا﴾ with a *ḍamma* on the *dhal*, and it is transmitted from Abu ʿAmr and from Ubayy as ﴿عُذْرِي﴾ ("my excuse") with a *kasra* on the *ra'*, annexed to the first-person pronoun.

In al-Bukhari, it is related that he said: "May Allah have mercy on Musa. We wished that he had been patient until he related to us their story." Al-Tabari also cited with a chain of narration that he said: "Whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked mercy for someone, he began with himself, saying: 'The mercy of Allah be upon us and upon Musa. Had he been patient with his companion, he would have seen wonders.'" But he said ﴿فَلا تُصاحِبْنِي قَدْ بَلَغْتَ مِن لَدُنِّي عُذْرًا﴾.

As for the town they came to: it is Antioch, or Ubulla, or the Green Island in al-Andalus, or Burqa, or Abu Hawran in the region of Adharbayjan, or Nasira from the land of the Romans, or a village in Armenia. These are conflicting opinions, differing according to where on earth the story of Musa took place, and Allah knows best its reality. In a hadith it is said: "They were walking over the gatherings of those people, asking them for food." This is an explicit lesson on the lowliness of this world in the sight of Allah, the Exalted. The word ﴿أهْل﴾ (ahl, "people") is repeated for emphasis. A benefit of this emphasis may appear: when ﴿أتَيا أهْلَ قَرْيَةٍ﴾ ("they came to the people of a town"), they did not come to all the people of the town, but only to some of them. So when it says ﴿اسْتَطْعَما﴾ ("they asked for food"), it could be understood that they only asked that part they had come to. Therefore the phrase "its people" (ahlaha) was used so that it would include all of them, and so that they would be asked one by one for food. Had the construction been "asked them" (istaṭʿamahum), it would have referred only to the part that had been approached.

The majority read ﴿يُضَيِّفُوهُما﴾ ("would host them") with *tashdid* (gemination) from *dayyafa*. Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Razin, Ibn Muhaysin, ʿAsim in the transmission of al-Mufaddal, and Aban read it with a *kasra* on the *ḍad* and sukun on the *ya'*, from *aḍāfa*, just as one says *mayyala* and *amāla* (both meaning "to incline"). Attributing the act of "wanting" (irada) to a wall is a metaphor of eloquent force and a striking figure of speech. It is very common in Arabic speech to attribute to non-rational beings, to animals that lack reason, and to inanimate objects, things that would be done by rational beings, as if that act had come from them in place of a rational agent. Al-Zamakhshari and others cited many examples of this, and anyone with even slight acquaintance with Arabic speech would not need an example for it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It has reached me that some of those who distort the words of Allah, from among those who lack knowledge, used to make the pronoun refer to al-Khadir, because they saw in it an affliction of ignorance and a sickness of understanding; they thought that the highest speech in rank is lower in position, so they contrived to return it to what they considered more correct and more eloquent. They held that what is further from metaphor is more fitting for inimitability." (The quotation ends here.) What the scholars of the foundations of jurisprudence transmit from Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Dawud al-Isfahani, that he denies metaphor in the Qur'an, may not be authentically reported from him. How could that be, when he was one of the eminent, accomplished poets and literary figures, skilled in verse and prose?

(p-152) The majority read ﴿يَنْقَضُّ﴾ (yanqaḍḍu), meaning it falls, from the "swooping" (inqiḍaḍ) of a bird. Its form is *infaʿala*, like *injarra*. The author of al-Lawami said: it is from *qaḍḍa*, meaning small pebbles, and from it comes *ṭaʿām qaḍaḍ*, food containing pebbles. On this view ﴿يُرِيدُ أنْ يَنْقَضَّ﴾ means that it was about to crumble and become a pebble. It was also said that its form is *if'alla* from *naqḍ* (breaking down), like *iḥmarra*. Ubayy read يُنْقَضَّ (yunqaḍḍa) with a *ḍamma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *qaf* and the *ḍad*, in the passive voice, from *naqaḍtu*. This is transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ). In the reading of ʿAbd Allah and the reading of al-Aʿmash it is (لِيَنْقَضَّ) with the same vowels, except that it is in the subjunctive after the *lam* with the hidden *an*. ʿAli, ʿIkrima, Abu Shaykh Khayawan ibn Khalid al-Hunai, Khulayd ibn Saʿd and Yahya ibn Yaʿmur read يَنْقاصُ (yanqaṣu) with an unpointed *ṣad* and an *alif*. Its form is *yanfaʿilu*, intransitive, from *qaṣa yaqīṣu*. When you break it, you say *qayytuhu*, then *infāṣa*. Ibn Khalawayh said: the Arabs say *infāṣati al-sinn* when the tooth splits lengthwise. Dhu al-Rumma said: "*munqāṣ* and *munkathib*." It was also said that it means whenever it cracks in any way. From this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Separation like the cracking of a tooth; so be patient, for surely for every person there is a stumble and a mending."

Al-Zuhri read يَنْقاضُ (yanqāḍu) with an *alif* and a pointed *ḍad*, which comes from their saying *quḍtuhu* (with a pointed *ḍad*), then *infāḍa*, meaning: I demolished it, so it collapsed. Abu ʿAli said: the well-known reading from al-Zuhri has an unpointed *ṣad*.

This occurs in the codex of ʿAbd Allah and is supported by his words, "you would have taken a wage for it," because rebuilding it after demolishing it would deserve a wage. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 79–82 (part 1 of 2):

﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea, so I wished to damage it, for behind them was a king who seized every boat by force.﴾ ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with tyranny and disbelief.﴾ ﴿So we wished that their Lord would replace him for them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion.﴾ ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them. Their father had been righteous. So your Lord wished that they reach their maturity and extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord. I did not do it on my own accord. That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience.﴾

It is narrated that when al-Khidr (ع) resolved to part from Musa (ع), Musa took hold of his garments and said: "I will not leave you until you tell me what permitted you to do what you did." When he asked him for this, al-Khidr began to explain and detail, saying: ﴿As for the boat﴾, beginning with the story of what happened to him first.

It was said: the boat belonged to ten brothers, five of them disabled and five of them working on the sea. It was also said: they were hired workers, and the boat was attributed to them because of their particular association with it.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (مساكين) with a light sīn, the plural of (مِسْكين, miskīn, "poor"). ʿAlī (may Allah honour his face) read it with a heavy sīn, as (مَسَّاك, massāk), in the sound plural form (جمع تصحيح, jam' taṣḥīḥ, the regular masculine plural). It was said the meaning is "sailors," for the (مَسَّاك, massāk) is the one who holds the helm of the boat, and each of them is fit for that. It was also said that the (مَسَّاكون, massākūn) are the tanners of hides (مُسُوك, musūk, sing. مَسْك, mask), which are skins. The first reading indicates that the boat belonged to weak people who deserve compassion. From this verse it was argued that the miskīn is the one who has a means of livelihood, like the boat for these people, and that he is in a better condition than the faqīr (the one in greater need).

His saying ﴿so I wished﴾ attributes the wish to damage the boat to himself. In His saying "so your Lord wished that they reach..." (فأراد ربك أن يبلغا), there is the following: because of the mention of damage, which is included in it, he did not attribute it to Allah, and because of the good in that, he attributed it to Allah, exalted is He.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: His saying ﴿so I wished to damage it﴾ is caused by fear of seizure of the boat, so its rightful place is to come after the cause. Why was it placed before it? I say: the intention behind it is delay, and it was placed first for emphasis, and because fear of seizure was not the sole cause, but rather together with the fact that the boat belonged to poor people. So it is like your saying: "Zayd, my opinion is that he is staying."

It was said regarding the reading of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allah: (كل سفينة صالحة, "every good boat"). End of quotation. The meaning of ﴿to damage it﴾ is by breaking it (بخرقها, bi-kharqihā). The majority read (وراءهم, warāʾahum), and this is a word that is used for both what is behind and what is in front. Its meaning here is "in front of them." Likewise Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr read it. That (وراءهم) means "in front of them" is the view of Qatadah, Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Zajjaj. There is no disagreement among the lexicographers that (وراء, warāʾ) may mean "in front of" (قدام, qudām). It occurs in the Revelation and in poetry. Allah, exalted is He, says ﴿Behind him is Hell﴾ [Ibrahim: 16], and ﴿Behind him is a severe punishment﴾ [Ibrahim: 17], and ﴿And behind them is a barrier﴾ [al-Muminun: 100]. Labid said:

Is it not that behind me, if my death is delayed, is the leaning on a staff, its fingers bent around it?

Sawwar ibn al-Mudarrib al-Saʿdi said:

Do the Banu Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while my people are Tamim and the wilderness is behind me?

Another said:

Is it not that behind me is to shuffle along on a staff, so that enemies feel safe and my family grows weary of me?

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: In my view, His saying (وراءهم) is on its proper usage, for these words are used in relation to time, and what comes after is the (وراء), which is what was left behind. That is in contrast to what appears first in opinion. Reflect on these words in their contexts wherever they occur, and you will find them consistent. The meaning of this verse is that these people, their work and their effort, come after the seizure by this king in time. Whoever reads (أمامهم, amāmahum, "in front of them") intends place, meaning that they were traveling toward his city. His saying, exalted is He, in the Torah and the Gospel, "they are before the Qur'an" (بين يدي القرآن), is consistent with what we have said regarding time. His saying ﴿behind them is Hell﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10] is consistent with what we said about observing time. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Prayer is in front of you" means place, otherwise their being at that time was before prayer in time. Reflect on this statement, for it relieves one of the confusion of words.

It occurred to Qatadah in the books of al-Tabari: ﴿And behind them was a king﴾. Qatadah said: "In front of them. Do you not see that He says ﴿behind them is Hell﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10], and it is before them?" This view is not sound, and this is the non-Arabic (عجمة, ʿujmah) error that al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan used to complain about, as al-Zajjaj reported. It is possible, if their return on their way was past the usurper, that it would be (وراءهم) in the literal sense. End of quotation. It is a statement with excessive elaboration, and it seems that he has in mind what al-Farra' said. Al-Farra' said: It is not permissible to say of a man "he is before you" (بين يديك) while saying "he is behind you" (وراءك). This usage is permissible only regarding periods of nights, days and time. You say: "Behind you is severe cold" and "Before you is severe cold"; both expressions are permissible, because when the cold reaches you it becomes behind you, and when you reach it, it becomes before you. He said: This is permissible in the language because what is before you and in front of you, when it is hidden from you, has become behind you.

Abu ʿAli said: The use of (وراء) to mean (أمام) is permitted by extension, because it is a direction opposite to another direction, so each of the two directions is behind the other when the sense of facing is not intended. This is permissible with bodies that have no front, such as two opposing stones, each one of which is behind the other. Most lexicographers hold that (وراء, warāʾ) is one of the words with opposite meanings (من الأضداد, min al-ḍiddād). End of quotation.

It was said: the name of this king was Hudad ibn Budad, and he was an unbeliever. It was also said: he was al-Julandi, king of Ghassan.

His saying ﴿and his parents were believers﴾ contains an ellipsis, meaning: "and he was an unbeliever," and so it is found in the codex of Ubayy. Ibn ʿAbbas read: (As for the boy, he was an unbeliever, and his parents were believers). The hadith explicitly states that he was an unbeliever, naturally disposed to disbelief. By "his two parents" is meant his father and his mother, expressed in the dual by way of prevalence (تغليب, taghlib), as in the example of the two moons for the moon and the sun. It is a dual form that is not analogically productive. Abu Saʿid al-Khudri and al-Jahdari read: (فكان أبواهما مؤمنان, "and his parents were two believers"). Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn ʿAtiyyah and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi analysed this as the pronoun of the matter (ضمير الشأن, ḍamīr al-shaʾn) in (كان), with the clause in the position of the predicate of (كان). Abu al-Fadl al-Razi also permitted that (مؤمنان) be in the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Kaʿb, in which case it would be in the accusative, and he also permitted that the pronoun in (كان) refer to the boy, with the clause being the predicate of (كان).

﴿So we feared﴾, that is: we were afraid that he would overwhelm his two believing parents ﴿with tyranny﴾ against them ﴿and disbelief﴾ in their blessing, through his disobedience and his evil conduct, and would bring upon them evil and affliction. Or his tyranny and disbelief would be joined to their faith, so that two believers and a tyrant unbeliever would be gathered in one house. Or he would infect them with his disease and mislead them with his error, so that they would apostatize because of him, become tyrants, and disbelieve after faith. al-Khidr feared this from him because Allah, mighty and exalted, informed him of his state, made him aware of the secrets of his affair, and commanded him to kill him, like one who takes him away because of a corruption He knew of in his life. In the reading of Ubayy: (فخاف ربك, "so your Lord feared"), and the meaning is: your Lord disliked it, with the dislike of one who fears the bad outcome of a matter, and so changed it. It is also possible that His saying ﴿so we feared﴾ is a report of the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic, meaning "so we disliked," like His saying ﴿that I may give you﴾ [Maryam: 19]. This was said by al-Zamakhshari.

In his saying "like one who takes him away because of a corruption He knew of in his life," is the position of the Mu'tazila in their doctrine of the two terms (القول بالأجلين, al-qawl bi-l-ajalayn, the view that a person has two appointed terms). The apparent sense is that the verb of fear in ﴿we feared﴾ is attributed to the pronoun of al-Khidr and his righteous companions, whom the matter concerned and who spoke about it. It was said: it refers to the side of Allah, and al-Khidr expressed it that way. This is the view for which al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that..." to the end of his statement. al-Tabari said: its meaning is "so we knew," and he said: its meaning is "so we disliked." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The more evident view to me in explaining this interpretation, though the wording resists it, is that it is a metaphor (استعارة, isti'arah), i.e., according to the assumption of created beings, and the addressee, if they had known his state, would have feared the burdening of the two parents.

Ibn Masʿud read: ﴿so your Lord feared﴾. This is a clear metaphor in the Qur'an regarding Allah, exalted is He, from (لعل, la'alla, "perhaps") and (عسى, 'asā, "perhaps"), for all of that expresses hope, expectation, fear and apprehension, which are only according to your measure, O addressees.

"﴿Burden them﴾" (يرهقهما) means to weigh them down and impose upon them with severity. The meaning is that his love would throw them into following him.

Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, Humayd, al-Aʿmash and Ibn Jarir read (أن يبدلهما) with the heavy form here and in al-Tahrim and al-Qalam. The rest of the seven readers, along with al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin, read it with the light form.

Here, (زكاة, zakāh) means purity and freedom from sins, and what is contained in it of noble character and tranquillity. (الرُّحْم, al-ruḥm) and (الرَّحْمة, al-raḥmah, "mercy") meaning compassion are two verbal nouns, like (الكُثْر, al-kuthr) and (الكَثْرة, al-kathrah, "abundance"). The form (أفعل, afʿal) here is not comparative, because that boy had no purity or mercy. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾ is: the compassion of his parents. Ibn Jurayj said: "They would have mercy on him." Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj said:

O you who bestow compassion upon Idris, and bestow the curse upon Iblis.

Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Jaʿfar in one transmission, Yaʿqub and Abu Hatim read (رُحُمًا, ruḥuman) with a damma on the ḥāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbas read (رَحِمًا, raḥiman) with a fatḥa on the rāʾ and a kasra on the ḥāʾ. It is said that (الرُّحْم, al-ruḥm) is from (الرَّحِم, al-raḥim, "kinship") and close relationship, meaning: more joining of kinship. It was said: she gave birth to a Muslim boy. It was said: she was a girl whom a prophet married, and she bore a prophet through whom Allah guided a nation of the nations. It was also said: she bore seventy prophets. This was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: This is far-fetched, and the multitude of prophets is only known among the Children of Israel, and this woman was not from them. End of quotation.

The description of the two boys as orphans indicates that they were young. In a hadith: "There is no orphanhood after puberty" (لا يتم بعد بلوغ), meaning: they were ﴿orphans﴾ in the sense of compassion for them. It is said that their names were Asram and Suraym, the name of their father was Kashih, and the name of their mother was Dahna. Regarding the treasure, the apparent meaning is that it was a large hidden wealth of gold and silver, as said by ʿIkrimah and Qatadah. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr said it was knowledge in hidden scrolls. It was said: it was a tablet of gold containing words of wisdom and remembrance. The commentators have mentioned it in their books, and we will not lengthen by mentioning it. The apparent meaning is that their father was the nearest to them, the one who begot them when he was far advanced. It was said: he was the seventh. It was said: the tenth. These two boys were protected because of the righteousness of their father. In a hadith: "Indeed Allah protects the righteous man in his offspring."

(رحمة, raḥmah, "mercy") is in the accusative as an object of purpose (مفعول له, maf'ūl lahu). al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be in the accusative as an absolute object (مصدر, maṣdar) with (أراد, arāda), saying: because it has the sense of "He had mercy on them." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (حال, ḥāl). Both are strained.

﴿And I did not do it﴾, that is: I did not do what you saw, the breaking of the boat, the killing of the boy and the setting up of the wall, out of my own effort and opinion. I did it only by the command of Allah, and this indicates that he was a prophet to whom revelation was sent.

(تسطع, tasṭaʿ) is the imperfect of (اسطاع, istaṭāʿa) with a hamzat al-waṣl. Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is said: (ما أستطيع, mā astaṭīʿu), (ما أسطيع, mā asṭīʿu), (ما أستتيع, mā astatīʿu), and (أستيع, astīʿ): four dialects. The original of (اسطاع) is (استطاع) on the pattern of (استفعل). The element deleted in (اسطاع) is the (ت) of the (افتعال) form, since the (ط) that is the root is present, and there is no need to hold that the deleted element is the (ط) which is the first root letter of the verb. Then they changed the (ت) of the (افتعال) form into (ط). As for (أستتيع), it has the (ط) changed into (ت). In (تستيع) it should be that the deleted element is the (ت) of the (افتعال) form, as in (تسطيع).

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 79-82 (part 2 of 2):

In the book *Al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir* there is the following text: Some ignorant people have relied on what happened between Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both, to argue that al-Khidr is superior to Musa. They extended this ruling and said: "It may be that some of the awliya' (saints, friends of God) are superior to some individual prophets." They also cited the saying of Abu Yazid: "I plunged into an ocean on whose shore the prophets stood." All of this is among the fruits of foolishness and of conceit in oneself. End of quote. Thus we have heard someone relate this view from one of the misguided and misleading, namely Ibn al-Arabi al-Ta'i al-Hatimi, author of *Al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya*. He should rather be named for the disastrous ugly deeds (al-qubuh al-halakiyya). He used to claim that the wali (saint) is better than the prophet, saying: "Because the wali takes from God without an intermediary, while the prophet takes from God through an intermediary; and because the wali sits in the divine presence (al-hadra al-ilahiyya, the presence of God), while the prophet is sent to a people. Whoever is in the presence is better than the one whom the Lord of the presence sends to things of this kind of unbelief and heresy." The admirers of this man have multiplied in this age among the extremist heretics who hold the doctrine of unity (al-wahda, the doctrine of the unity of existence). We ask God for safety in our religion and our bodies.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 79–82 (part 1 of 2):

﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea, so I wished to damage it, for behind them was a king who seized every boat by force.﴾ ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with tyranny and disbelief.﴾ ﴿So we wished that their Lord would replace him for them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion.﴾ ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them. Their father had been righteous. So your Lord wished that they reach their maturity and extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord. I did not do it on my own accord. That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience.﴾

It is narrated that when al-Khidr (ع) resolved to part from Musa (ع), Musa took hold of his garments and said: "I will not leave you until you tell me what permitted you to do what you did." When he asked him for this, al-Khidr began to explain and detail, saying: ﴿As for the boat﴾, beginning with the story of what happened to him first.

It was said: the boat belonged to ten brothers, five of them disabled and five of them working on the sea. It was also said: they were hired workers, and the boat was attributed to them because of their particular association with it.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (مساكين) with a light sīn, the plural of (مِسْكين, miskīn, "poor"). ʿAlī (may Allah honour his face) read it with a heavy sīn, as (مَسَّاك, massāk), in the sound plural form (جمع تصحيح, jam' taṣḥīḥ, the regular masculine plural). It was said the meaning is "sailors," for the (مَسَّاك, massāk) is the one who holds the helm of the boat, and each of them is fit for that. It was also said that the (مَسَّاكون, massākūn) are the tanners of hides (مُسُوك, musūk, sing. مَسْك, mask), which are skins. The first reading indicates that the boat belonged to weak people who deserve compassion. From this verse it was argued that the miskīn is the one who has a means of livelihood, like the boat for these people, and that he is in a better condition than the faqīr (the one in greater need).

His saying ﴿so I wished﴾ attributes the wish to damage the boat to himself. In His saying "so your Lord wished that they reach..." (فأراد ربك أن يبلغا), there is the following: because of the mention of damage, which is included in it, he did not attribute it to Allah, and because of the good in that, he attributed it to Allah, exalted is He.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: His saying ﴿so I wished to damage it﴾ is caused by fear of seizure of the boat, so its rightful place is to come after the cause. Why was it placed before it? I say: the intention behind it is delay, and it was placed first for emphasis, and because fear of seizure was not the sole cause, but rather together with the fact that the boat belonged to poor people. So it is like your saying: "Zayd, my opinion is that he is staying."

It was said regarding the reading of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allah: (كل سفينة صالحة, "every good boat"). End of quotation. The meaning of ﴿to damage it﴾ is by breaking it (بخرقها, bi-kharqihā). The majority read (وراءهم, warāʾahum), and this is a word that is used for both what is behind and what is in front. Its meaning here is "in front of them." Likewise Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr read it. That (وراءهم) means "in front of them" is the view of Qatadah, Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Zajjaj. There is no disagreement among the lexicographers that (وراء, warāʾ) may mean "in front of" (قدام, qudām). It occurs in the Revelation and in poetry. Allah, exalted is He, says ﴿Behind him is Hell﴾ [Ibrahim: 16], and ﴿Behind him is a severe punishment﴾ [Ibrahim: 17], and ﴿And behind them is a barrier﴾ [al-Muminun: 100]. Labid said:

Is it not that behind me, if my death is delayed, is the leaning on a staff, its fingers bent around it?

Sawwar ibn al-Mudarrib al-Saʿdi said:

Do the Banu Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while my people are Tamim and the wilderness is behind me?

Another said:

Is it not that behind me is to shuffle along on a staff, so that enemies feel safe and my family grows weary of me?

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: In my view, His saying (وراءهم) is on its proper usage, for these words are used in relation to time, and what comes after is the (وراء), which is what was left behind. That is in contrast to what appears first in opinion. Reflect on these words in their contexts wherever they occur, and you will find them consistent. The meaning of this verse is that these people, their work and their effort, come after the seizure by this king in time. Whoever reads (أمامهم, amāmahum, "in front of them") intends place, meaning that they were traveling toward his city. His saying, exalted is He, in the Torah and the Gospel, "they are before the Qur'an" (بين يدي القرآن), is consistent with what we have said regarding time. His saying ﴿behind them is Hell﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10] is consistent with what we said about observing time. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Prayer is in front of you" means place, otherwise their being at that time was before prayer in time. Reflect on this statement, for it relieves one of the confusion of words.

It occurred to Qatadah in the books of al-Tabari: ﴿And behind them was a king﴾. Qatadah said: "In front of them. Do you not see that He says ﴿behind them is Hell﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10], and it is before them?" This view is not sound, and this is the non-Arabic (عجمة, ʿujmah) error that al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan used to complain about, as al-Zajjaj reported. It is possible, if their return on their way was past the usurper, that it would be (وراءهم) in the literal sense. End of quotation. It is a statement with excessive elaboration, and it seems that he has in mind what al-Farra' said. Al-Farra' said: It is not permissible to say of a man "he is before you" (بين يديك) while saying "he is behind you" (وراءك). This usage is permissible only regarding periods of nights, days and time. You say: "Behind you is severe cold" and "Before you is severe cold"; both expressions are permissible, because when the cold reaches you it becomes behind you, and when you reach it, it becomes before you. He said: This is permissible in the language because what is before you and in front of you, when it is hidden from you, has become behind you.

Abu ʿAli said: The use of (وراء) to mean (أمام) is permitted by extension, because it is a direction opposite to another direction, so each of the two directions is behind the other when the sense of facing is not intended. This is permissible with bodies that have no front, such as two opposing stones, each one of which is behind the other. Most lexicographers hold that (وراء, warāʾ) is one of the words with opposite meanings (من الأضداد, min al-ḍiddād). End of quotation.

It was said: the name of this king was Hudad ibn Budad, and he was an unbeliever. It was also said: he was al-Julandi, king of Ghassan.

His saying ﴿and his parents were believers﴾ contains an ellipsis, meaning: "and he was an unbeliever," and so it is found in the codex of Ubayy. Ibn ʿAbbas read: (As for the boy, he was an unbeliever, and his parents were believers). The hadith explicitly states that he was an unbeliever, naturally disposed to disbelief. By "his two parents" is meant his father and his mother, expressed in the dual by way of prevalence (تغليب, taghlib), as in the example of the two moons for the moon and the sun. It is a dual form that is not analogically productive. Abu Saʿid al-Khudri and al-Jahdari read: (فكان أبواهما مؤمنان, "and his parents were two believers"). Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn ʿAtiyyah and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi analysed this as the pronoun of the matter (ضمير الشأن, ḍamīr al-shaʾn) in (كان), with the clause in the position of the predicate of (كان). ﴿So we feared﴾, that is: we were afraid that he would overwhelm his two believing parents ﴿with tyranny﴾ against them ﴿and disbelief﴾ in their blessing, through his disobedience and his evil conduct, and would bring upon them evil and affliction. It is also possible that His saying ﴿so we feared﴾ is a report of the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic, meaning "so we disliked," like His saying ﴿that I may give you﴾ [Maryam: 19]. It was said: it refers to the side of Allah, and al-Khidr expressed it that way. This is the view for which al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that..." to the end of his statement. al-Tabari said: its meaning is "so we knew," and he said: its meaning is "so we disliked." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The more evident view to me in explaining this interpretation, though the wording resists it, is that it is a metaphor (استعارة, isti'arah), i.e., according to the assumption of created beings, and the addressee, if they had known his state, would have feared the burdening of the two parents.

Ibn Masʿud read: ﴿so your Lord feared﴾. This is a clear metaphor in the Qur'an regarding Allah, exalted is He, from (لعل, la'alla, "perhaps") and (عسى, 'asā, "perhaps"), for all of that expresses hope, expectation, fear and apprehension, which are only according to your measure, O addressees.

"﴿Burden them﴾" (يرهقهما) means to weigh them down and impose upon them with severity. The meaning is that his love would throw them into following him.

It was said: she was a girl whom a prophet married, and she bore a prophet through whom Allah guided a nation of the nations. It was also said: she bore seventy prophets. This was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: This is far-fetched, and the multitude of prophets is only known among the Children of Israel, and this woman was not from them. End of quotation.

The description of the two boys as orphans indicates that they were young. In a hadith: "There is no orphanhood after puberty" (لا يتم بعد بلوغ), meaning: they were ﴿orphans﴾ in the sense of compassion for them. ﴿And I did not do it﴾, that is: I did not do what you saw, the breaking of the boat, the killing of the boy and the setting up of the wall, out of my own effort and opinion. I did it only by the command of Allah, and this indicates that he was a prophet to whom revelation was sent.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 79–82 (part 1 of 2):

﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea, so I wished to damage it, for behind them was a king who seized every boat by force.﴾ ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with tyranny and disbelief.﴾ ﴿So we wished that their Lord would replace him for them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion.﴾ ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them. Their father had been righteous. So your Lord wished that they reach their maturity and extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord. I did not do it on my own accord. That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience.﴾

It is narrated that when al-Khidr (ع) resolved to part from Musa (ع), Musa took hold of his garments and said: "I will not leave you until you tell me what permitted you to do what you did." When he asked him for this, al-Khidr began to explain and detail, saying: ﴿As for the boat﴾, beginning with the story of what happened to him first.

It was said: the boat belonged to ten brothers, five of them disabled and five of them working on the sea. It was also said: they were hired workers, and the boat was attributed to them because of their particular association with it.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (مساكين) with a light sīn, the plural of (مِسْكين, miskīn, "poor"). ʿAlī (may Allah honour his face) read it with a heavy sīn, as (مَسَّاك, massāk), in the sound plural form (جمع تصحيح, jam' taṣḥīḥ, the regular masculine plural). It was said the meaning is "sailors," for the (مَسَّاك, massāk) is the one who holds the helm of the boat, and each of them is fit for that. It was also said that the (مَسَّاكون, massākūn) are the tanners of hides (مُسُوك, musūk, sing. مَسْك, mask), which are skins. The first reading indicates that the boat belonged to weak people who deserve compassion. From this verse it was argued that the miskīn is the one who has a means of livelihood, like the boat for these people, and that he is in a better condition than the faqīr (the one in greater need).

His saying ﴿so I wished﴾ attributes the wish to damage the boat to himself. In His saying "so your Lord wished that they reach..." (فأراد ربك أن يبلغا), there is the following: because of the mention of damage, which is included in it, he did not attribute it to Allah, and because of the good in that, he attributed it to Allah, exalted is He.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: His saying ﴿so I wished to damage it﴾ is caused by fear of seizure of the boat, so its rightful place is to come after the cause. Why was it placed before it? I say: the intention behind it is delay, and it was placed first for emphasis, and because fear of seizure was not the sole cause, but rather together with the fact that the boat belonged to poor people. So it is like your saying: "Zayd, my opinion is that he is staying."

It was said regarding the reading of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allah: (كل سفينة صالحة, "every good boat"). End of quotation. The meaning of ﴿to damage it﴾ is by breaking it (بخرقها, bi-kharqihā). The majority read (وراءهم, warāʾahum), and this is a word that is used for both what is behind and what is in front. Its meaning here is "in front of them." Likewise Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr read it. That (وراءهم) means "in front of them" is the view of Qatadah, Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Zajjaj. There is no disagreement among the lexicographers that (وراء, warāʾ) may mean "in front of" (قدام, qudām). It occurs in the Revelation and in poetry. Allah, exalted is He, says ﴿Behind him is Hell﴾ [Ibrahim: 16], and ﴿Behind him is a severe punishment﴾ [Ibrahim: 17], and ﴿And behind them is a barrier﴾ [al-Muminun: 100]. Labid said:

Is it not that behind me, if my death is delayed, is the leaning on a staff, its fingers bent around it?

Sawwar ibn al-Mudarrib al-Saʿdi said:

Do the Banu Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while my people are Tamim and the wilderness is behind me?

Another said:

Is it not that behind me is to shuffle along on a staff, so that enemies feel safe and my family grows weary of me?

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: In my view, His saying (وراءهم) is on its proper usage, for these words are used in relation to time, and what comes after is the (وراء), which is what was left behind. That is in contrast to what appears first in opinion. Reflect on these words in their contexts wherever they occur, and you will find them consistent. The meaning of this verse is that these people, their work and their effort, come after the seizure by this king in time. Whoever reads (أمامهم, amāmahum, "in front of them") intends place, meaning that they were traveling toward his city. His saying, exalted is He, in the Torah and the Gospel, "they are before the Qur'an" (بين يدي القرآن), is consistent with what we have said regarding time. His saying ﴿behind them is Hell﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10] is consistent with what we said about observing time. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Prayer is in front of you" means place, otherwise their being at that time was before prayer in time. Reflect on this statement, for it relieves one of the confusion of words.

It occurred to Qatadah in the books of al-Tabari: ﴿And behind them was a king﴾. Qatadah said: "In front of them. Do you not see that He says ﴿behind them is Hell﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10], and it is before them?" This view is not sound, and this is the non-Arabic (عجمة, ʿujmah) error that al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan used to complain about, as al-Zajjaj reported. It is possible, if their return on their way was past the usurper, that it would be (وراءهم) in the literal sense. End of quotation. It is a statement with excessive elaboration, and it seems that he has in mind what al-Farra' said. Al-Farra' said: It is not permissible to say of a man "he is before you" (بين يديك) while saying "he is behind you" (وراءك). This usage is permissible only regarding periods of nights, days and time. You say: "Behind you is severe cold" and "Before you is severe cold"; both expressions are permissible, because when the cold reaches you it becomes behind you, and when you reach it, it becomes before you. He said: This is permissible in the language because what is before you and in front of you, when it is hidden from you, has become behind you.

Abu ʿAli said: The use of (وراء) to mean (أمام) is permitted by extension, because it is a direction opposite to another direction, so each of the two directions is behind the other when the sense of facing is not intended. This is permissible with bodies that have no front, such as two opposing stones, each one of which is behind the other. Most lexicographers hold that (وراء, warāʾ) is one of the words with opposite meanings (من الأضداد, min al-ḍiddād). End of quotation.

It was said: the name of this king was Hudad ibn Budad, and he was an unbeliever. It was also said: he was al-Julandi, king of Ghassan.

His saying ﴿and his parents were believers﴾ contains an ellipsis, meaning: "and he was an unbeliever," and so it is found in the codex of Ubayy. Ibn ʿAbbas read: (As for the boy, he was an unbeliever, and his parents were believers). The hadith explicitly states that he was an unbeliever, naturally disposed to disbelief. By "his two parents" is meant his father and his mother, expressed in the dual by way of prevalence (تغليب, taghlib), as in the example of the two moons for the moon and the sun. It is a dual form that is not analogically productive. Abu Saʿid al-Khudri and al-Jahdari read: (فكان أبواهما مؤمنان, "and his parents were two believers"). Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn ʿAtiyyah and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi analysed this as the pronoun of the matter (ضمير الشأن, ḍamīr al-shaʾn) in (كان), with the clause in the position of the predicate of (كان). Abu al-Fadl al-Razi also permitted that (مؤمنان) be in the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Kaʿb, in which case it would be in the accusative, and he also permitted that the pronoun in (كان) refer to the boy, with the clause being the predicate of (كان).

﴿So we feared﴾, that is: we were afraid that he would overwhelm his two believing parents ﴿with tyranny﴾ against them ﴿and disbelief﴾ in their blessing, through his disobedience and his evil conduct, and would bring upon them evil and affliction. Or his tyranny and disbelief would be joined to their faith, so that two believers and a tyrant unbeliever would be gathered in one house. Or he would infect them with his disease and mislead them with his error, so that they would apostatize because of him, become tyrants, and disbelieve after faith. al-Khidr feared this from him because Allah, mighty and exalted, informed him of his state, made him aware of the secrets of his affair, and commanded him to kill him, like one who takes him away because of a corruption He knew of in his life. In the reading of Ubayy: (فخاف ربك, "so your Lord feared"), and the meaning is: your Lord disliked it, with the dislike of one who fears the bad outcome of a matter, and so changed it. It is also possible that His saying ﴿so we feared﴾ is a report of the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic, meaning "so we disliked," like His saying ﴿that I may give you﴾ [Maryam: 19]. This was said by al-Zamakhshari.

In his saying "like one who takes him away because of a corruption He knew of in his life," is the position of the Mu'tazila in their doctrine of the two terms (القول بالأجلين, al-qawl bi-l-ajalayn, the view that a person has two appointed terms). The apparent sense is that the verb of fear in ﴿we feared﴾ is attributed to the pronoun of al-Khidr and his righteous companions, whom the matter concerned and who spoke about it. It was said: it refers to the side of Allah, and al-Khidr expressed it that way. This is the view for which al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that..." to the end of his statement. al-Tabari said: its meaning is "so we knew," and he said: its meaning is "so we disliked." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The more evident view to me in explaining this interpretation, though the wording resists it, is that it is a metaphor (استعارة, isti'arah), i.e., according to the assumption of created beings, and the addressee, if they had known his state, would have feared the burdening of the two parents.

Ibn Masʿud read: ﴿so your Lord feared﴾. This is a clear metaphor in the Qur'an regarding Allah, exalted is He, from (لعل, la'alla, "perhaps") and (عسى, 'asā, "perhaps"), for all of that expresses hope, expectation, fear and apprehension, which are only according to your measure, O addressees.

"﴿Burden them﴾" (يرهقهما) means to weigh them down and impose upon them with severity. The meaning is that his love would throw them into following him.

Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, Humayd, al-Aʿmash and Ibn Jarir read (أن يبدلهما) with the heavy form here and in al-Tahrim and al-Qalam. The rest of the seven readers, along with al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin, read it with the light form.

Here, (زكاة, zakāh) means purity and freedom from sins, and what is contained in it of noble character and tranquillity. (الرُّحْم, al-ruḥm) and (الرَّحْمة, al-raḥmah, "mercy") meaning compassion are two verbal nouns, like (الكُثْر, al-kuthr) and (الكَثْرة, al-kathrah, "abundance"). The form (أفعل, afʿal) here is not comparative, because that boy had no purity or mercy. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾ is: the compassion of his parents. Ibn Jurayj said: "They would have mercy on him." Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj said:

O you who bestow compassion upon Idris, and bestow the curse upon Iblis.

Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Jaʿfar in one transmission, Yaʿqub and Abu Hatim read (رُحُمًا, ruḥuman) with a damma on the ḥāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbas read (رَحِمًا, raḥiman) with a fatḥa on the rāʾ and a kasra on the ḥāʾ. It is said that (الرُّحْم, al-ruḥm) is from (الرَّحِم, al-raḥim, "kinship") and close relationship, meaning: more joining of kinship. It was said: she gave birth to a Muslim boy. It was said: she was a girl whom a prophet married, and she bore a prophet through whom Allah guided a nation of the nations. It was also said: she bore seventy prophets. This was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: This is far-fetched, and the multitude of prophets is only known among the Children of Israel, and this woman was not from them. End of quotation.

The description of the two boys as orphans indicates that they were young. In a hadith: "There is no orphanhood after puberty" (لا يتم بعد بلوغ), meaning: they were ﴿orphans﴾ in the sense of compassion for them. It is said that their names were Asram and Suraym, the name of their father was Kashih, and the name of their mother was Dahna. Regarding the treasure, the apparent meaning is that it was a large hidden wealth of gold and silver, as said by ʿIkrimah and Qatadah. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr said it was knowledge in hidden scrolls. It was said: it was a tablet of gold containing words of wisdom and remembrance. The commentators have mentioned it in their books, and we will not lengthen by mentioning it. The apparent meaning is that their father was the nearest to them, the one who begot them when he was far advanced. It was said: he was the seventh. It was said: the tenth. These two boys were protected because of the righteousness of their father. In a hadith: "Indeed Allah protects the righteous man in his offspring."

(رحمة, raḥmah, "mercy") is in the accusative as an object of purpose (مفعول له, maf'ūl lahu). al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be in the accusative as an absolute object (مصدر, maṣdar) with (أراد, arāda), saying: because it has the sense of "He had mercy on them." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (حال, ḥāl). Both are strained.

﴿And I did not do it﴾, that is: I did not do what you saw, the breaking of the boat, the killing of the boy and the setting up of the wall, out of my own effort and opinion. I did it only by the command of Allah, and this indicates that he was a prophet to whom revelation was sent.

(تسطع, tasṭaʿ) is the imperfect of (اسطاع, istaṭāʿa) with a hamzat al-waṣl. Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is said: (ما أستطيع, mā astaṭīʿu), (ما أسطيع, mā asṭīʿu), (ما أستتيع, mā astatīʿu), and (أستيع, astīʿ): four dialects. The original of (اسطاع) is (استطاع) on the pattern of (استفعل). The element deleted in (اسطاع) is the (ت) of the (افتعال) form, since the (ط) that is the root is present, and there is no need to hold that the deleted element is the (ط) which is the first root letter of the verb. Then they changed the (ت) of the (افتعال) form into (ط). As for (أستتيع), it has the (ط) changed into (ت). In (تستيع) it should be that the deleted element is the (ت) of the (افتعال) form, as in (تسطيع).

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 79-82 (part 2 of 2):

In the book *Al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir* there is the following text: Some ignorant people have relied on what happened between Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both, to argue that al-Khidr is superior to Musa. They extended this ruling and said: "It may be that some of the awliya' (saints, friends of God) are superior to some individual prophets." They also cited the saying of Abu Yazid: "I plunged into an ocean on whose shore the prophets stood." All of this is among the fruits of foolishness and of conceit in oneself. End of quote. Thus we have heard someone relate this view from one of the misguided and misleading, namely Ibn al-Arabi al-Ta'i al-Hatimi, author of *Al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya*. He should rather be named for the disastrous ugly deeds (al-qubuh al-halakiyya). He used to claim that the wali (saint) is better than the prophet, saying: "Because the wali takes from God without an intermediary, while the prophet takes from God through an intermediary; and because the wali sits in the divine presence (al-hadra al-ilahiyya, the presence of God), while the prophet is sent to a people. Whoever is in the presence is better than the one whom the Lord of the presence sends to things of this kind of unbelief and heresy." The admirers of this man have multiplied in this age among the extremist heretics who hold the doctrine of unity (al-wahda, the doctrine of the unity of existence). We ask God for safety in our religion and our bodies.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 79–82 (part 1 of 2):

﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea, so I wished to damage it, for behind them was a king who seized every boat by force.﴾ ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with tyranny and disbelief.﴾ ﴿So we wished that their Lord would replace him for them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion.﴾ ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them. Their father had been righteous. So your Lord wished that they reach their maturity and extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord. I did not do it on my own accord. That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience.﴾

It is narrated that when al-Khidr (ع) resolved to part from Musa (ع), Musa took hold of his garments and said: "I will not leave you until you tell me what permitted you to do what you did." When he asked him for this, al-Khidr began to explain and detail, saying: ﴿As for the boat﴾, beginning with the story of what happened to him first.

It was said: the boat belonged to ten brothers, five of them disabled and five of them working on the sea. It was also said: they were hired workers, and the boat was attributed to them because of their particular association with it.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (مساكين) with a light sīn, the plural of (مِسْكين, miskīn, "poor"). ʿAlī (may Allah honour his face) read it with a heavy sīn, as (مَسَّاك, massāk), in the sound plural form (جمع تصحيح, jam' taṣḥīḥ, the regular masculine plural). It was said the meaning is "sailors," for the (مَسَّاك, massāk) is the one who holds the helm of the boat, and each of them is fit for that. It was also said that the (مَسَّاكون, massākūn) are the tanners of hides (مُسُوك, musūk, sing. مَسْك, mask), which are skins. The first reading indicates that the boat belonged to weak people who deserve compassion. From this verse it was argued that the miskīn is the one who has a means of livelihood, like the boat for these people, and that he is in a better condition than the faqīr (the one in greater need).

His saying ﴿so I wished﴾ attributes the wish to damage the boat to himself. In His saying "so your Lord wished that they reach..." (فأراد ربك أن يبلغا), there is the following: because of the mention of damage, which is included in it, he did not attribute it to Allah, and because of the good in that, he attributed it to Allah, exalted is He.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: His saying ﴿so I wished to damage it﴾ is caused by fear of seizure of the boat, so its rightful place is to come after the cause. Why was it placed before it?
