I say: the intention behind it is delay, and it was placed first for emphasis, and because fear of seizure was not the sole cause, but rather together with the fact that the boat belonged to poor people. So it is like your saying: "Zayd, my opinion is that he is staying."

It was said regarding the reading of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allah: (كل سفينة صالحة, "every good boat"). End of quotation. The meaning of ﴿to damage it﴾ is by breaking it (بخرقها, bi-kharqihā). The majority read (وراءهم, warāʾahum), and this is a word that is used for both what is behind and what is in front. Its meaning here is "in front of them." Likewise Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr read it. That (وراءهم) means "in front of them" is the view of Qatadah, Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Zajjaj. There is no disagreement among the lexicographers that (وراء, warāʾ) may mean "in front of" (قدام, qudām). It occurs in the Revelation and in poetry. Allah, exalted is He, says ﴿Behind him is Hell﴾ [Ibrahim: 16], and ﴿Behind him is a severe punishment﴾ [Ibrahim: 17], and ﴿And behind them is a barrier﴾ [al-Muminun: 100]. Labid said:

Is it not that behind me, if my death is delayed, is the leaning on a staff, its fingers bent around it?

Sawwar ibn al-Mudarrib al-Saʿdi said:

Do the Banu Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while my people are Tamim and the wilderness is behind me?

Another said:

Is it not that behind me is to shuffle along on a staff, so that enemies feel safe and my family grows weary of me?

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: In my view, His saying (وراءهم) is on its proper usage, for these words are used in relation to time, and what comes after is the (وراء), which is what was left behind. That is in contrast to what appears first in opinion. Reflect on these words in their contexts wherever they occur, and you will find them consistent. The meaning of this verse is that these people, their work and their effort, come after the seizure by this king in time. Whoever reads (أمامهم, amāmahum, "in front of them") intends place, meaning that they were traveling toward his city. His saying, exalted is He, in the Torah and the Gospel, "they are before the Qur'an" (بين يدي القرآن), is consistent with what we have said regarding time. His saying ﴿behind them is Hell﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10] is consistent with what we said about observing time. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Prayer is in front of you" means place, otherwise their being at that time was before prayer in time. Reflect on this statement, for it relieves one of the confusion of words.

It occurred to Qatadah in the books of al-Tabari: ﴿And behind them was a king﴾. Qatadah said: "In front of them. Do you not see that He says ﴿behind them is Hell﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 10], and it is before them?" This view is not sound, and this is the non-Arabic (عجمة, ʿujmah) error that al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan used to complain about, as al-Zajjaj reported. It is possible, if their return on their way was past the usurper, that it would be (وراءهم) in the literal sense. End of quotation. It is a statement with excessive elaboration, and it seems that he has in mind what al-Farra' said. Al-Farra' said: It is not permissible to say of a man "he is before you" (بين يديك) while saying "he is behind you" (وراءك). This usage is permissible only regarding periods of nights, days and time. You say: "Behind you is severe cold" and "Before you is severe cold"; both expressions are permissible, because when the cold reaches you it becomes behind you, and when you reach it, it becomes before you. He said: This is permissible in the language because what is before you and in front of you, when it is hidden from you, has become behind you.

Abu ʿAli said: The use of (وراء) to mean (أمام) is permitted by extension, because it is a direction opposite to another direction, so each of the two directions is behind the other when the sense of facing is not intended. This is permissible with bodies that have no front, such as two opposing stones, each one of which is behind the other. Most lexicographers hold that (وراء, warāʾ) is one of the words with opposite meanings (من الأضداد, min al-ḍiddād). End of quotation.

It was said: the name of this king was Hudad ibn Budad, and he was an unbeliever. It was also said: he was al-Julandi, king of Ghassan.

His saying ﴿and his parents were believers﴾ contains an ellipsis, meaning: "and he was an unbeliever," and so it is found in the codex of Ubayy. Ibn ʿAbbas read: (As for the boy, he was an unbeliever, and his parents were believers). The hadith explicitly states that he was an unbeliever, naturally disposed to disbelief. By "his two parents" is meant his father and his mother, expressed in the dual by way of prevalence (تغليب, taghlib), as in the example of the two moons for the moon and the sun. It is a dual form that is not analogically productive. Abu Saʿid al-Khudri and al-Jahdari read: (فكان أبواهما مؤمنان, "and his parents were two believers"). Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn ʿAtiyyah and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi analysed this as the pronoun of the matter (ضمير الشأن, ḍamīr al-shaʾn) in (كان), with the clause in the position of the predicate of (كان). Abu al-Fadl al-Razi also permitted that (مؤمنان) be in the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Kaʿb, in which case it would be in the accusative, and he also permitted that the pronoun in (كان) refer to the boy, with the clause being the predicate of (كان).

﴿So we feared﴾, that is: we were afraid that he would overwhelm his two believing parents ﴿with tyranny﴾ against them ﴿and disbelief﴾ in their blessing, through his disobedience and his evil conduct, and would bring upon them evil and affliction. Or his tyranny and disbelief would be joined to their faith, so that two believers and a tyrant unbeliever would be gathered in one house. Or he would infect them with his disease and mislead them with his error, so that they would apostatize because of him, become tyrants, and disbelieve after faith. al-Khidr feared this from him because Allah, mighty and exalted, informed him of his state, made him aware of the secrets of his affair, and commanded him to kill him, like one who takes him away because of a corruption He knew of in his life. In the reading of Ubayy: (فخاف ربك, "so your Lord feared"), and the meaning is: your Lord disliked it, with the dislike of one who fears the bad outcome of a matter, and so changed it. It is also possible that His saying ﴿so we feared﴾ is a report of the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic, meaning "so we disliked," like His saying ﴿that I may give you﴾ [Maryam: 19]. This was said by al-Zamakhshari.

In his saying "like one who takes him away because of a corruption He knew of in his life," is the position of the Mu'tazila in their doctrine of the two terms (القول بالأجلين, al-qawl bi-l-ajalayn, the view that a person has two appointed terms). The apparent sense is that the verb of fear in ﴿we feared﴾ is attributed to the pronoun of al-Khidr and his righteous companions, whom the matter concerned and who spoke about it. It was said: it refers to the side of Allah, and al-Khidr expressed it that way. This is the view for which al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that..." to the end of his statement. al-Tabari said: its meaning is "so we knew," and he said: its meaning is "so we disliked." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The more evident view to me in explaining this interpretation, though the wording resists it, is that it is a metaphor (استعارة, isti'arah), i.e., according to the assumption of created beings, and the addressee, if they had known his state, would have feared the burdening of the two parents.

Ibn Masʿud read: ﴿so your Lord feared﴾. This is a clear metaphor in the Qur'an regarding Allah, exalted is He, from (لعل, la'alla, "perhaps") and (عسى, 'asā, "perhaps"), for all of that expresses hope, expectation, fear and apprehension, which are only according to your measure, O addressees.

"﴿Burden them﴾" (يرهقهما) means to weigh them down and impose upon them with severity. The meaning is that his love would throw them into following him.

Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, Humayd, al-Aʿmash and Ibn Jarir read (أن يبدلهما) with the heavy form here and in al-Tahrim and al-Qalam. The rest of the seven readers, along with al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin, read it with the light form.

Here, (زكاة, zakāh) means purity and freedom from sins, and what is contained in it of noble character and tranquillity. (الرُّحْم, al-ruḥm) and (الرَّحْمة, al-raḥmah, "mercy") meaning compassion are two verbal nouns, like (الكُثْر, al-kuthr) and (الكَثْرة, al-kathrah, "abundance"). The form (أفعل, afʿal) here is not comparative, because that boy had no purity or mercy. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾ is: the compassion of his parents. Ibn Jurayj said: "They would have mercy on him." Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj said:

O you who bestow compassion upon Idris, and bestow the curse upon Iblis.

Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Jaʿfar in one transmission, Yaʿqub and Abu Hatim read (رُحُمًا, ruḥuman) with a damma on the ḥāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbas read (رَحِمًا, raḥiman) with a fatḥa on the rāʾ and a kasra on the ḥāʾ. It is said that (الرُّحْم, al-ruḥm) is from (الرَّحِم, al-raḥim, "kinship") and close relationship, meaning: more joining of kinship. It was said: she gave birth to a Muslim boy. It was said: she was a girl whom a prophet married, and she bore a prophet through whom Allah guided a nation of the nations. It was also said: she bore seventy prophets. This was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: This is far-fetched, and the multitude of prophets is only known among the Children of Israel, and this woman was not from them. End of quotation.

The description of the two boys as orphans indicates that they were young. In a hadith: "There is no orphanhood after puberty" (لا يتم بعد بلوغ), meaning: they were ﴿orphans﴾ in the sense of compassion for them. It is said that their names were Asram and Suraym, the name of their father was Kashih, and the name of their mother was Dahna. Regarding the treasure, the apparent meaning is that it was a large hidden wealth of gold and silver, as said by ʿIkrimah and Qatadah. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr said it was knowledge in hidden scrolls. It was said: it was a tablet of gold containing words of wisdom and remembrance. The commentators have mentioned it in their books, and we will not lengthen by mentioning it. The apparent meaning is that their father was the nearest to them, the one who begot them when he was far advanced. It was said: he was the seventh. It was said: the tenth. These two boys were protected because of the righteousness of their father. In a hadith: "Indeed Allah protects the righteous man in his offspring."

(رحمة, raḥmah, "mercy") is in the accusative as an object of purpose (مفعول له, maf'ūl lahu). al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be in the accusative as an absolute object (مصدر, maṣdar) with (أراد, arāda), saying: because it has the sense of "He had mercy on them." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (حال, ḥāl). Both are strained.

﴿And I did not do it﴾, that is: I did not do what you saw, the breaking of the boat, the killing of the boy and the setting up of the wall, out of my own effort and opinion. I did it only by the command of Allah, and this indicates that he was a prophet to whom revelation was sent.

(تسطع, tasṭaʿ) is the imperfect of (اسطاع, istaṭāʿa) with a hamzat al-waṣl. Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is said: (ما أستطيع, mā astaṭīʿu), (ما أسطيع, mā asṭīʿu), (ما أستتيع, mā astatīʿu), and (أستيع, astīʿ): four dialects. The original of (اسطاع) is (استطاع) on the pattern of (استفعل). The element deleted in (اسطاع) is the (ت) of the (افتعال) form, since the (ط) that is the root is present, and there is no need to hold that the deleted element is the (ط) which is the first root letter of the verb. Then they changed the (ت) of the (افتعال) form into (ط). As for (أستتيع), it has the (ط) changed into (ت). In (تستيع) it should be that the deleted element is the (ت) of the (افتعال) form, as in (تسطيع).

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 18, verses 79-82 (part 2 of 2):

In the book *Al-Tahrir wa'l-Tahbir* there is the following text: Some ignorant people have relied on what happened between Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both, to argue that al-Khidr is superior to Musa. They extended this ruling and said: "It may be that some of the awliya' (saints, friends of God) are superior to some individual prophets." They also cited the saying of Abu Yazid: "I plunged into an ocean on whose shore the prophets stood." All of this is among the fruits of foolishness and of conceit in oneself. End of quote. Thus we have heard someone relate this view from one of the misguided and misleading, namely Ibn al-Arabi al-Ta'i al-Hatimi, author of *Al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya*. He should rather be named for the disastrous ugly deeds (al-qubuh al-halakiyya). He used to claim that the wali (saint) is better than the prophet, saying: "Because the wali takes from God without an intermediary, while the prophet takes from God through an intermediary; and because the wali sits in the divine presence (al-hadra al-ilahiyya, the presence of God), while the prophet is sent to a people. Whoever is in the presence is better than the one whom the Lord of the presence sends to things of this kind of unbelief and heresy." The admirers of this man have multiplied in this age among the extremist heretics who hold the doctrine of unity (al-wahda, the doctrine of the unity of existence). We ask God for safety in our religion and our bodies.

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah al-Kahf, verses 83–88 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿They ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn. Say: "I will recite to you a remembrance of him."﴾ ﴿Indeed, We established him in the land and gave him a means to every thing.﴾ ﴿So he followed a means.﴾ ﴿until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun, he found it setting in a spring of black mud, and found near it a people. We said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish them or you take a good course with them."﴾ ﴿He said: "As for one who wrongs, we will punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment.﴾ ﴿But as for one who believes and does righteous deeds, he will have a reward of the best, and we will speak to him of Our command with ease."﴾ ﴿Then he followed a means.﴾ ﴿until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun, he found it rising upon a people for whom We had made no shelter against it.﴾ ﴿So it was. And We had full knowledge of what was with him.﴾ ﴿Then he followed a means.﴾ ﴿until, when he reached between the two barriers, he found beside them a people who could hardly understand any speech.﴾ ﴿They said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are corrupters in the land. So shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set up a barrier between us and them?"﴾ ﴿He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better. So help me with strength, and I will set up between you and them a rampart.﴾ ﴿Bring me sheets of iron." Until, when he had leveled [them] between the two cliffs, he said: "Blow," until, when he had made it fire, he said: "Bring me molten copper to pour over it."﴾ ﴿So they could not scale it, nor could they pierce it.﴾ ﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level, and the promise of my Lord is true."﴾ ﴿And We will leave some of them that day surging against one another, and the Horn will be blown, and We will gather them in a gathering.﴾ ﴿And We will present Hell that day to the disbelievers, displayed.﴾ ﴿Those whose eyes were under a covering from My remembrance, and who could not hear.﴾ ﴿Do those who disbelieve think that they may take My servants as protectors instead of Me? Indeed, We have prepared Hell as a lodging for the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Say: "Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in deeds?﴾ ﴿Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world while they think they are doing well in work."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in meeting Him, so their deeds are rendered void, and We will assign them no weight on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ ﴿That is their recompense: Hell, because they disbelieved and took My signs and My messengers in mockery.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds will have the Gardens of Paradise as a lodging,﴾ ﴿abiding therein, not desiring any removal from it.﴾ ﴿Say: "If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as an addition."﴾ ﴿Say: "I am only a human like you. It is revealed to me that your God is one God. So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and associate no one in the worship of his Lord."﴾

**al-Sadd** (the barrier, the obstacle) is that which stands between two things, and it may be pronounced with a *ḍamma* or a *fatḥa*. **al-Radm** is a barrier. It is said that al-radm is greater than al-sadd, because al-radm is what has been placed one part upon another. One says: "a garment *muraddam*" when a patch has been put over a patch. It is also said that al-radm means filling a gap. ʿAntara said:

> Have the poets left any *mutaraddam*?

That is, a gap in meanings, which one fills in as a *radm*. **al-Zubra** is a piece, and its root meaning is gathering; from it comes *zubrat al-asad*, the mane of the lion, because the hair gathers on its shoulder. *Zabartu al-kitāb* means I gathered its letters. **al-Ṣadafān** are the two sides of a mountain when they face each other, either because they are close or because they meet; this is what al-Azhari said. It is also said *ṣudufun*, with *ḍamma* or *fatḥa* on both letters, or with *ḍamma* on the *ṣād* and sukun on the *dāl*, or the reverse. Some philologists said: the *fatḥa* on both is the dialect of Tamim, and the *ḍamma* on both is the dialect of Himyar. Abu ʿUbayda said: *al-ṣadaf* is any great, high building. **al-Qiṭr** is molten copper according to most scholars. It is also said to be molten iron, and it is also said to be molten lead. **al-Naqb** is the verbal noun of *naqaba*, meaning he dug or cut through. **al-Ghiṭāʾ** is well known, its plural is *aghiyah*, and it derives from *ghaṭṭā*, meaning he covered. **al-Firdaws**: al-Farraʾ said it is the orchard containing vines, and Thaʿlab said it is every orchard enclosed by a wall.

﴿They ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn...﴾ up to ﴿...and We had full knowledge of what was with him﴾ [al-Kahf: 89–91]. (Commentary continues.)

The pronoun in ﴿They ask you﴾ refers to the Quraysh or to the Jews. The well-known view is that the questioners were the Quraysh, after the Jews had put them up to asking him about the Spirit, the wandering man, and the youths who went away in ancient times, so that he would be tested by this. Dhul-Qarnayn is Alexander the Greek (al-Iskandar al-Yunani), as Ibn Ishaq mentioned. Wahb said he was Roman. Was he a prophet or a righteous servant? He was not a prophet; there are two opinions. It is also said he was an angel, but this view is strange. It is said that two believers ruled the whole world, Solomon and Dhul-Qarnayn, and two disbelievers, Nimrod and Bukhtnasar, who came after Nimrod. From ʿAli: he was a righteous servant, neither an angel nor a prophet. He was struck on his right horn and died in obedience to God; then God raised him, and he was struck on his left horn and died; then God raised him, and he was called Dhul-Qarnayn (the Two-Horned). It is said he traveled the two horns of the world, meaning its two sides, east and west. It is said he had two horns, that is, two braids. It is said that two generations of people died out in his time. From Wahb: he was called this because he ruled the Romans and the Persians; it is also narrated: the Romans and the Turks. From him also: the two plates of his head were of copper. It is said his crown had two horns. It is said there was on his head something resembling two horns. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that he was named so for his bravery, just as a brave man is called a ram, as if he butts his rivals. He was from the Romans, a child of an old woman who had no other child, end of quote. Other explanations have been given for his name, but the well-known view is that he is Alexander.

Abu al-Rayhan al-Biruni, the astrologer, author of *al-Athar al-Baqiya ʿan al-Qurun al-Khaliya* (The Remaining Traces of Past Generations), said: he is Abu Bakr ibn Sumayy ibn ʿUmayr ibn Ifriqis al-Himyari. His rule reached the easts and wests of the earth, and it is this that one of the poets of Himyar boasted about when he said:

> Dhul-Qarnayn before me was a Muslim,
> a king who rose in the land, not dispersed.
> He reached the easts and the wests, seeking
> the means of kingship from a noble lord.

Abu al-Rayhan said: This view seems closer, because the *Adhwaʾ* (the lords with *dhū* in their names) were from Yemen, and their names are never without *dhū*, like Dhu al-Manar and Dhu Yazan. End of quote. The poem he recited is also attributed to Tubbaʿ al-Himyari:

> Dhul-Qarnayn was my grandfather, a Muslim.

From ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas: his name was ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Dahhak. From Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn al-Husayn: ʿAyyash. From Abu Khaythama: he was al-Saʿb ibn Jabir ibn al-Qalammas. It is also said he was Marzuban ibn Marzabah the Greek, of the descendants of Yunan ibn Yafith. From ʿAli: he was of the first generation of the descendants of Yafith ibn Nuh. From al-Hasan: he was after Thamud, and his lifespan was one thousand six hundred years. From Wahb: he was in the interval between ʿIsa and Muhammad, may God bless them both and grant them peace.

The address in ﴿upon you﴾ is to the questioners, either the Jews or the Quraysh, according to the disagreement that preceded about the questioners. His saying ﴿a remembrance﴾ may mean a Qur'an, or a narrative and good news. The establishment that he had ﴿in the land﴾ is his being the ruler of the world, and all kings submitted to him. Some exegetes said: The proof that he is Alexander is that the Qur'an indicates that the man called Dhul-Qarnayn reached, in his rule, the farthest west, the farthest east, and the farthest north. This is shown by the fact that Gog and Magog are a people of the Turks living in the farthest north. The extent of this man's rule is the limit of the inhabited earth, and such a vast kingdom is without doubt contrary to custom. What is so must have its memory preserved forever and must not be hidden. The king whose name in the books of history reached this extent is none other than Alexander. When his father died, he gathered the kingdom of the Romans, after it had been divided among groups. Then he marched against the kings of the Arabs and conquered them, and went on until he reached the Green Sea. Then he returned to Egypt and built Alexandria and named it after himself. Then he entered al-Sham and went against the Children of Israel and came to Jerusalem and sacrificed on its altar. Then he turned to Armenia, and the Iraqis, the Copts and the Berbers submitted to him. Then he went toward the house of Ibn Dara, and defeated him several times until his own commander killed him. Alexander took control of the realms of the Persians, went to India and China, invaded distant nations, returned to Khurasan and built many cities, returned to Iraq, fell ill at Shahrazur, and died there.

It is related in a hadith: "The ones who ruled the earth were four, two of them believers: Solomon son of David, and Dhul-Qarnayn." This has been mentioned before. It is established in the science of history that the one of this rank was none other than Alexander, so it is certain that the one meant by Dhul-Qarnayn is Alexander son of Philip the Greek. It is also said that his establishment in the land was through prophethood and the performance of miracles. It is said his establishment was that the clouds were subjected to him, he was carried upon them, and light was spread for him, so that night and day were alike for him. It is said it was through the abundance of his helpers and armies, through awe and dignity, through the casting of terror into his enemies, through making travel easy for him, through acquainting him with the paths of the earth, and through his dominion over its land and sea.

﴿And We gave him from every thing﴾, that is, what he needed to reach his aims, ﴿a means﴾, that is, a route leading to it. A means is whatever one reaches the desired goal by, whether knowledge, power, or equipment. He wanted to reach the west, ﴿so he followed a means﴾ leading him to it until he arrived. Likewise he wanted the east, ﴿so he followed a means﴾; and he wanted to reach the two barriers, ﴿so he followed a means﴾. The root meaning of *sabab* is a rope, then it was extended until it came to mean whatever one reaches the goal by. al-Hasan said: a means of arrival to wherever he intended. Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Zuhri, al-Aʿmash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, the Kufans, and Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿fa-atbaʿa﴾ in all three places with a light pronunciation of the *tāʾ* (with a *hamza* for the *ʿayn* in the first verb form, it is read *atbaʿa*). The remaining seven read it with *tashdid* (doubled *tāʾ*, *ittabaʿa*). The apparent meaning is that both have the same sense. From Yunus ibn Habib and Abu Zayd: that with a cut *hamza* it expresses one who is diligent, quick and eager in pursuit, while with a connected *hamza* it only implies following, without these qualities.

ʿAbd Allah, Talha ibn ʿUbayd Allah, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, Muʿawiya, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza and al-Kisai read ﴿ḥāmiyatin﴾ with a *yāʾ*, meaning hot. Ibn ʿAbbas and the remaining seven, along with Shayba, Humayd, Ibn Abi Layla, Yaʿqub, Abu Hatim, and Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki read ﴿ḥamiʾatin﴾ with a *hamza* and a *fatḥa*. al-Zuhri softened the *hamza*. It is said *ḥamiʾat al-bi'r taḥmaʾu ḥamaʾan*, "the well became muddy," fa-hiya ḥamiʾa (it is muddy). *Ḥamaʾtuhā* means I drew out its mud, and *aḥmaʾtuhā* means I left the mud in it. There is no contradiction between *ḥāmiya* (hot) and *ḥamiʾa* (muddy), since the spring may combine both qualities. Abu Hatim said: It is possible that *ḥāmiya* with *hamza* means possessing mud, so the two readings have one meaning, meaning that the *hamza* was made easier by changing it into a *yāʾ*, because of the *kasra* before it. In the Torah it says he set in water and mud. Tubbaʿ said:

> He saw the setting of the sun at its return,
> in the spring of a wet and dark mire.

in a spring of murky water, black and muddy. In the hadith of Abu Dharr: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the sun as it set and said: "Do you know where it sets, Abu Dharr?" I said: "No." He said: "It sets in a hot spring." This hadith and the apparent sense of the text are evidence that His words ﴿in a spring﴾ are connected to His words ﴿it set﴾, not to what some over-strained interpreters said: that His words "in a spring of black mud" mean that Dhul-Qarnayn was in it, i.e. that it is the end of the earth, and the meaning of ﴿it set in a spring﴾ is "as far as the eye can see," not that this is literally so, as we observe on a smooth plain, as if it enters the earth. It is also possible that this spring is part of the sea, and it is possible that the sun sets behind it. Some of the Baghdadi grammarians claimed that (fi) here means (ʿinda), i.e. "it sets near a spring."

﴿And he found near it a people﴾, i.e. near that spring. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: they were believers and disbelievers. Others said: they were unbelievers, their clothing was the skins of beasts, and their food was what the sun had burned of creatures, and what the spring cast out of fish when the sun set. Wahb said: he set out heading west until he reached Basak, where he found a multitude that none could count but Allah. He placed three armies around them until he gathered them in one place, then he entered upon them in the light and called them to the worship of Allah. Some of them believed and some turned away from him. Abu Zayd al-Suhayli said: they were the people of Hābūs (and in Syriac it is called Jirjīsā), inhabited by a people descended from Thamud, the remnant of those who believed in Salih, peace be upon him.

The apparent sense of His words (We said) is that Allah revealed to him through an angel. It was said: He spoke to him directly without a messenger, as He spoke to Musa, peace be upon him. According to these two views he would be a prophet. What some interpreters said, that it was inspiration cast into his heart, is unlikely, because such a choice can only come through revelation, since obligations and the taking of lives are not established by inspiration except through information. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: the meaning is "We said, O Muhammad, they said: ﴿O Dhul-Qarnayn﴾," and then the first saying was omitted, because it is not established that Dhul-Qarnayn was a prophet who would be addressed by Allah. On this view, the pronoun in the omitted "they said" refers to his troops and army who were with him.

His words ﴿Either you punish﴾ by killing for disbelief, ﴿or you take among them goodness﴾, i.e. by leading them to faith and guidance. Either you disbelieve and are punished, or you believe and do good, so the choice is expressed through the effect in place of the cause. Al-Tabari said: taking goodness is their capture along with their disbelief, meaning that he was given the choice, while they remained disbelievers, between killing them and capturing them. The detail of Dhul-Qarnayn's words ﴿As for the one who does wrong﴾ and (As for the one who believes) refutes this view. When Allah gave him the choice between punishing them and calling them to Islam, he chose the call and striving to win them over. He said: as for the one whose call he rejected, refusing to remain on wrong, which here is disbelief without dispute, he is the one punished in both abodes. As for the one who believes and does what faith requires, ﴿he will have the best reward﴾. He used the particle of futurity in ﴿we will punish him﴾ because of what intervenes between his showing his disbelief and his punishment: his calling him to faith and his refusal of it. He does not hasten to kill them for their wrong, but calls them and reminds them; if they return, well, otherwise there is killing.

His words ﴿Then he will be returned to his Lord﴾, i.e. on the Day of Resurrection. He used the plural of majesty in ﴿we will punish him﴾, following the custom of kings in saying "we did." His words (to his Lord) imply that the choice given to Dhul-Qarnayn was not from Allah, for if it were, the wording would be: "then he will be returned to You, and You will punish him." It is not unlikely that the choice was from Allah and that Dhul-Qarnayn informed his followers of it, then he elaborated, addressing his followers and not his Lord. How excellent is the coming of these sentences: when he mentioned what he deserves of wrong, he began with what is nearest to them and perceptible to them, which is His words ﴿we will punish him﴾, then he informed of what befalls him last, on the Day of Resurrection, which is Allah's punishment of him with a dreadful punishment. And because the order of occurrence is so; when he mentioned what he deserves, ﴿and whoever believes and does righteousness﴾, he mentioned Allah's reward for him in the Hereafter, which is (the best), i.e. Paradise, because the believer's hope and expectation of the Hereafter is what moved him to believe for the sake of his reward in the Hereafter, and it is great compared with the goodness of this world. Then he followed this with His goodness to him in this world, in His words ﴿And We will speak to him of Our command with ease﴾, i.e. We will not say to him what is burdensome for him to bear, meaning words that are easy and smooth, as He said "a gentle word." When He mentioned what He prepared for him of the best reward, it was not fitting to mention his reward in deed, but He confined Himself to speech, out of courtesy toward Allah, even though He knows that He benefits him in deed and in speech.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, Abu Bahriyya, al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Munadhir, Ya'qub, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, and Muhammad ibn Jarir read ﴿fa-lahu jazaʾan﴾ with the accusative and tanwin. (Jazaʾan) is in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state, i.e. "rewarded," like your saying: "in the house, standing, is Zayd." Abu ʿAli said: Abu al-Hasan said: the Arabs hardly speak this way with it placed first except in poetry. It was also said that it is accusative as a verbal noun, i.e. "he will recompense (a reward)." Al-Farra' said: it is accusative by way of explanation, and the meaning of al-husna in the accusative reading is Paradise. The rest of the Seven read (jazaʾu al-husna) with (jazaʾ) in the nominative, construed with (al-husna). Abu ʿAli said: the reward of the good qualities which he did and performed, or al-husna is meant as the good deed, and Paradise is the reward; the construction is as one says "the abode of the Hereafter," and (jazaʾ) is the subject whose predicate is (lahu).

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ishaq read (fa-lahu jazaʾun) with the nominative, a subject and predicate, and (al-husna) is an apposition to (jazaʾun). Ibn ʿAbbas and Masruq read (jazaʾa) in the accusative without tanwin, (al-husna) construed with it, and this is explained as the omission of the subject, indicated by the meaning, i.e. "for him is the reward," (jazaʾa al-husna). Al-Mahdawi explained it as dropping the tanwin because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters. Abu Jaʿfar read (yusran) with a damma on the sin wherever it occurs.

﴿Then he followed a way﴾ [al-Kahf: 89], i.e. a road to his destination which was made easy for him. Al-Hasan, ʿIsa and Ibn Muhaysin read (matlaʿa) with a fatha on the lam, and it is reported from Ibn Kathir and the people of Mecca, and it is the analogical form. The majority read it with a kasra, and this is a transmitted form in a number of words; its analogical kasra would require the imperfect to be (tatlaʿu) with a kasra on the lam. Al-Kisa'i used to say: this is a dialect that died out in many of the dialects of the Arabs, meaning that those among the Arabs who said (tatlu') with a kasra on the lam have gone, and (matli') with a kasra remained in the noun of place and time according to that analogy. The people here are the Zanj. Qatadah said they are the Indians and those beyond them. "The screen" is a building, or garments, or trees and mountains, these are the views, and the meaning is that they have nothing to shield them from the heat of the sun. It was said: the sun penetrates their roofs and garments and reaches their bodies. It was said: when it rises they go down into the water until its heat breaks, as said al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj. It was said: they enter caves. Mujahid said: the Sudanese at the place of the sunrise are more numerous than all the people of the earth. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the apparent sense of the wording is that it is an eloquent expression for the sun's nearness to them, its action upon them by Allah's power, and its reaching them; and if they had caves, there would be a dense screen. Then ended. Some of the rajaz poets said:

"By the Zanj a heat has changed the bodies, until it clothed their skins in blackness."

This is only from the intensity and persistence of the sun's heat among them. Likewise, the indication is to reaching: just as he reached the sun's setting, he reached its rising. It was said: ﴿he followed a way﴾ [al-Kahf: 89] like ﴿he followed a way﴾ [al-Kahf: 89]. It was said: just as he found those at the sun's setting and judged among them, so he found these at the sun's rising and judged among them. It was said: thus he commanded them, as we have related to you. It was said: (it rises) its rising is like its setting. It was said: ﴿We had not made for them against it any screen﴾ [al-Kahf: 90], i.e. like those whom he found at the sun's setting, disbelievers like them, and their judgment like their judgment: punishment for whoever remains on disbelief, and goodness for whoever believes.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (thus), i.e. the matter of Dhul-Qarnayn is thus, i.e. as we described it, magnifying his affair. It was said: ﴿We had not made for them against it any screen﴾ [al-Kahf: 90], like that screen which we made for you from mountains, fortresses, buildings and shelters of every kind, and garments of every sort. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: (thus) means he dealt with them as he dealt with the first people of the west, and He informed with His words (thus), then He informed about His encompassing of all that was with Dhul-Qarnayn and of what he did in his actions. It is possible that (thus) is a resumption of speech, not referring back to the first group, so consider it; the first is more correct. And if it is a resumption with no connection to what precedes, it requires an added phrase to complete the sentence.

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah al-Kahf, verses 83–88 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿They ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn. Say: "I will recite to you a remembrance of him."﴾ ﴿Indeed, We established him in the land and gave him a means to every thing.﴾ ﴿So he followed a means.﴾ ﴿until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun, he found it setting in a spring of black mud, and found near it a people. We said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish them or you take a good course with them."﴾ ﴿He said: "As for one who wrongs, we will punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment.﴾ ﴿But as for one who believes and does righteous deeds, he will have a reward of the best, and we will speak to him of Our command with ease."﴾ ﴿Then he followed a means.﴾ ﴿until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun, he found it rising upon a people for whom We had made no shelter against it.﴾ ﴿So it was. And We had full knowledge of what was with him.﴾ ﴿Then he followed a means.﴾ ﴿until, when he reached between the two barriers, he found beside them a people who could hardly understand any speech.﴾ ﴿They said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are corrupters in the land. So shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set up a barrier between us and them?"﴾ ﴿He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better. So help me with strength, and I will set up between you and them a rampart.﴾ ﴿Bring me sheets of iron." Until, when he had leveled [them] between the two cliffs, he said: "Blow," until, when he had made it fire, he said: "Bring me molten copper to pour over it."﴾ ﴿So they could not scale it, nor could they pierce it.﴾ ﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level, and the promise of my Lord is true."﴾ ﴿And We will leave some of them that day surging against one another, and the Horn will be blown, and We will gather them in a gathering.﴾ ﴿And We will present Hell that day to the disbelievers, displayed.﴾ ﴿Those whose eyes were under a covering from My remembrance, and who could not hear.﴾ ﴿Do those who disbelieve think that they may take My servants as protectors instead of Me? Indeed, We have prepared Hell as a lodging for the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Say: "Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in deeds?﴾ ﴿Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world while they think they are doing well in work."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in meeting Him, so their deeds are rendered void, and We will assign them no weight on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ ﴿That is their recompense: Hell, because they disbelieved and took My signs and My messengers in mockery.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds will have the Gardens of Paradise as a lodging,﴾ ﴿abiding therein, not desiring any removal from it.﴾ ﴿Say: "If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as an addition."﴾ ﴿Say: "I am only a human like you. It is revealed to me that your God is one God. So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and associate no one in the worship of his Lord."﴾

**al-Sadd** (the barrier, the obstacle) is that which stands between two things, and it may be pronounced with a *ḍamma* or a *fatḥa*. **al-Radm** is a barrier. It is said that al-radm is greater than al-sadd, because al-radm is what has been placed one part upon another. One says: "a garment *muraddam*" when a patch has been put over a patch. It is also said that al-radm means filling a gap. ʿAntara said:

> Have the poets left any *mutaraddam*?

That is, a gap in meanings, which one fills in as a *radm*. **al-Zubra** is a piece, and its root meaning is gathering; from it comes *zubrat al-asad*, the mane of the lion, because the hair gathers on its shoulder. *Zabartu al-kitāb* means I gathered its letters. **al-Ṣadafān** are the two sides of a mountain when they face each other, either because they are close or because they meet; this is what al-Azhari said. It is also said *ṣudufun*, with *ḍamma* or *fatḥa* on both letters, or with *ḍamma* on the *ṣād* and sukun on the *dāl*, or the reverse. Some philologists said: the *fatḥa* on both is the dialect of Tamim, and the *ḍamma* on both is the dialect of Himyar. Abu ʿUbayda said: *al-ṣadaf* is any great, high building. **al-Qiṭr** is molten copper according to most scholars. It is also said to be molten iron, and it is also said to be molten lead. **al-Naqb** is the verbal noun of *naqaba*, meaning he dug or cut through. **al-Ghiṭāʾ** is well known, its plural is *aghiyah*, and it derives from *ghaṭṭā*, meaning he covered. **al-Firdaws**: al-Farraʾ said it is the orchard containing vines, and Thaʿlab said it is every orchard enclosed by a wall.

﴿They ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn...﴾ up to ﴿...and We had full knowledge of what was with him﴾ [al-Kahf: 89–91]. (Commentary continues.)

The pronoun in ﴿They ask you﴾ refers to the Quraysh or to the Jews. The well-known view is that the questioners were the Quraysh, after the Jews had put them up to asking him about the Spirit, the wandering man, and the youths who went away in ancient times, so that he would be tested by this. Dhul-Qarnayn is Alexander the Greek (al-Iskandar al-Yunani), as Ibn Ishaq mentioned. Wahb said he was Roman. Was he a prophet or a righteous servant? He was not a prophet; there are two opinions. It is also said he was an angel, but this view is strange. It is said that two believers ruled the whole world, Solomon and Dhul-Qarnayn, and two disbelievers, Nimrod and Bukhtnasar, who came after Nimrod. From ʿAli: he was a righteous servant, neither an angel nor a prophet. He was struck on his right horn and died in obedience to God; then God raised him, and he was struck on his left horn and died; then God raised him, and he was called Dhul-Qarnayn (the Two-Horned). It is said he traveled the two horns of the world, meaning its two sides, east and west. It is said he had two horns, that is, two braids. It is said that two generations of people died out in his time. From Wahb: he was called this because he ruled the Romans and the Persians; it is also narrated: the Romans and the Turks. From him also: the two plates of his head were of copper. It is said his crown had two horns. It is said there was on his head something resembling two horns. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that he was named so for his bravery, just as a brave man is called a ram, as if he butts his rivals. He was from the Romans, a child of an old woman who had no other child, end of quote. Other explanations have been given for his name, but the well-known view is that he is Alexander.

Abu al-Rayhan al-Biruni, the astrologer, author of *al-Athar al-Baqiya ʿan al-Qurun al-Khaliya* (The Remaining Traces of Past Generations), said: he is Abu Bakr ibn Sumayy ibn ʿUmayr ibn Ifriqis al-Himyari. His rule reached the easts and wests of the earth, and it is this that one of the poets of Himyar boasted about when he said:

> Dhul-Qarnayn before me was a Muslim,
> a king who rose in the land, not dispersed.
> He reached the easts and the wests, seeking
> the means of kingship from a noble lord.

Abu al-Rayhan said: This view seems closer, because the *Adhwaʾ* (the lords with *dhū* in their names) were from Yemen, and their names are never without *dhū*, like Dhu al-Manar and Dhu Yazan. End of quote. The poem he recited is also attributed to Tubbaʿ al-Himyari:

> Dhul-Qarnayn was my grandfather, a Muslim.

From ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas: his name was ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Dahhak. From Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn al-Husayn: ʿAyyash. From Abu Khaythama: he was al-Saʿb ibn Jabir ibn al-Qalammas. It is also said he was Marzuban ibn Marzabah the Greek, of the descendants of Yunan ibn Yafith. From ʿAli: he was of the first generation of the descendants of Yafith ibn Nuh. From al-Hasan: he was after Thamud, and his lifespan was one thousand six hundred years. From Wahb: he was in the interval between ʿIsa and Muhammad, may God bless them both and grant them peace.

The address in ﴿upon you﴾ is to the questioners, either the Jews or the Quraysh, according to the disagreement that preceded about the questioners. His saying ﴿a remembrance﴾ may mean a Qur'an, or a narrative and good news. The establishment that he had ﴿in the land﴾ is his being the ruler of the world, and all kings submitted to him. Some exegetes said: The proof that he is Alexander is that the Qur'an indicates that the man called Dhul-Qarnayn reached, in his rule, the farthest west, the farthest east, and the farthest north. This is shown by the fact that Gog and Magog are a people of the Turks living in the farthest north. The extent of this man's rule is the limit of the inhabited earth, and such a vast kingdom is without doubt contrary to custom. What is so must have its memory preserved forever and must not be hidden. The king whose name in the books of history reached this extent is none other than Alexander. When his father died, he gathered the kingdom of the Romans, after it had been divided among groups. Then he marched against the kings of the Arabs and conquered them, and went on until he reached the Green Sea. Then he returned to Egypt and built Alexandria and named it after himself. Then he entered al-Sham and went against the Children of Israel and came to Jerusalem and sacrificed on its altar. Then he turned to Armenia, and the Iraqis, the Copts and the Berbers submitted to him. Then he went toward the house of Ibn Dara, and defeated him several times until his own commander killed him. Alexander took control of the realms of the Persians, went to India and China, invaded distant nations, returned to Khurasan and built many cities, returned to Iraq, fell ill at Shahrazur, and died there.

It is related in a hadith: "The ones who ruled the earth were four, two of them believers: Solomon son of David, and Dhul-Qarnayn." This has been mentioned before. It is established in the science of history that the one of this rank was none other than Alexander, so it is certain that the one meant by Dhul-Qarnayn is Alexander son of Philip the Greek. It is also said that his establishment in the land was through prophethood and the performance of miracles. It is said his establishment was that the clouds were subjected to him, he was carried upon them, and light was spread for him, so that night and day were alike for him. It is said it was through the abundance of his helpers and armies, through awe and dignity, through the casting of terror into his enemies, through making travel easy for him, through acquainting him with the paths of the earth, and through his dominion over its land and sea.

﴿And We gave him from every thing﴾, that is, what he needed to reach his aims, ﴿a means﴾, that is, a route leading to it. A means is whatever one reaches the desired goal by, whether knowledge, power, or equipment. He wanted to reach the west, ﴿so he followed a means﴾ leading him to it until he arrived. Likewise he wanted the east, ﴿so he followed a means﴾; and he wanted to reach the two barriers, ﴿so he followed a means﴾. The root meaning of *sabab* is a rope, then it was extended until it came to mean whatever one reaches the goal by. al-Hasan said: a means of arrival to wherever he intended. Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Zuhri, al-Aʿmash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, the Kufans, and Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿fa-atbaʿa﴾ in all three places with a light pronunciation of the *tāʾ* (with a *hamza* for the *ʿayn* in the first verb form, it is read *atbaʿa*). The remaining seven read it with *tashdid* (doubled *tāʾ*, *ittabaʿa*). The apparent meaning is that both have the same sense. From Yunus ibn Habib and Abu Zayd: that with a cut *hamza* it expresses one who is diligent, quick and eager in pursuit, while with a connected *hamza* it only implies following, without these qualities.

ʿAbd Allah, Talha ibn ʿUbayd Allah, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, Muʿawiya, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza and al-Kisai read ﴿ḥāmiyatin﴾ with a *yāʾ*, meaning hot. Ibn ʿAbbas and the remaining seven, along with Shayba, Humayd, Ibn Abi Layla, Yaʿqub, Abu Hatim, and Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki read ﴿ḥamiʾatin﴾ with a *hamza* and a *fatḥa*. al-Zuhri softened the *hamza*. It is said *ḥamiʾat al-bi'r taḥmaʾu ḥamaʾan*, "the well became muddy," fa-hiya ḥamiʾa (it is muddy). *Ḥamaʾtuhā* means I drew out its mud, and *aḥmaʾtuhā* means I left the mud in it. There is no contradiction between *ḥāmiya* (hot) and *ḥamiʾa* (muddy), since the spring may combine both qualities. Abu Hatim said: It is possible that *ḥāmiya* with *hamza* means possessing mud, so the two readings have one meaning, meaning that the *hamza* was made easier by changing it into a *yāʾ*, because of the *kasra* before it. In the Torah it says he set in water and mud. Tubbaʿ said:

> He saw the setting of the sun at its return,
> in the spring of a wet and dark mire.

in a spring of murky water, black and muddy. In the hadith of Abu Dharr: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the sun as it set and said: "Do you know where it sets, Abu Dharr?" I said: "No." He said: "It sets in a hot spring." This hadith and the apparent sense of the text are evidence that His words ﴿in a spring﴾ are connected to His words ﴿it set﴾, not to what some over-strained interpreters said: that His words "in a spring of black mud" mean that Dhul-Qarnayn was in it, i.e. that it is the end of the earth, and the meaning of ﴿it set in a spring﴾ is "as far as the eye can see," not that this is literally so, as we observe on a smooth plain, as if it enters the earth. It is also possible that this spring is part of the sea, and it is possible that the sun sets behind it. Some of the Baghdadi grammarians claimed that (fi) here means (ʿinda), i.e. "it sets near a spring."

﴿And he found near it a people﴾, i.e. near that spring. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: they were believers and disbelievers. Others said: they were unbelievers, their clothing was the skins of beasts, and their food was what the sun had burned of creatures, and what the spring cast out of fish when the sun set. Wahb said: he set out heading west until he reached Basak, where he found a multitude that none could count but Allah. He placed three armies around them until he gathered them in one place, then he entered upon them in the light and called them to the worship of Allah. Some of them believed and some turned away from him. Abu Zayd al-Suhayli said: they were the people of Hābūs (and in Syriac it is called Jirjīsā), inhabited by a people descended from Thamud, the remnant of those who believed in Salih, peace be upon him.

The apparent sense of His words (We said) is that Allah revealed to him through an angel. It was said: He spoke to him directly without a messenger, as He spoke to Musa, peace be upon him. According to these two views he would be a prophet. What some interpreters said, that it was inspiration cast into his heart, is unlikely, because such a choice can only come through revelation, since obligations and the taking of lives are not established by inspiration except through information. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: the meaning is "We said, O Muhammad, they said: ﴿O Dhul-Qarnayn﴾," and then the first saying was omitted, because it is not established that Dhul-Qarnayn was a prophet who would be addressed by Allah. On this view, the pronoun in the omitted "they said" refers to his troops and army who were with him.

His words ﴿Either you punish﴾ by killing for disbelief, ﴿or you take among them goodness﴾, i.e. by leading them to faith and guidance. Either you disbelieve and are punished, or you believe and do good, so the choice is expressed through the effect in place of the cause. Al-Tabari said: taking goodness is their capture along with their disbelief, meaning that he was given the choice, while they remained disbelievers, between killing them and capturing them. The detail of Dhul-Qarnayn's words ﴿As for the one who does wrong﴾ and (As for the one who believes) refutes this view. When Allah gave him the choice between punishing them and calling them to Islam, he chose the call and striving to win them over. He said: as for the one whose call he rejected, refusing to remain on wrong, which here is disbelief without dispute, he is the one punished in both abodes. As for the one who believes and does what faith requires, ﴿he will have the best reward﴾. He used the particle of futurity in ﴿we will punish him﴾ because of what intervenes between his showing his disbelief and his punishment: his calling him to faith and his refusal of it. He does not hasten to kill them for their wrong, but calls them and reminds them; if they return, well, otherwise there is killing.

His words ﴿Then he will be returned to his Lord﴾, i.e. on the Day of Resurrection. He used the plural of majesty in ﴿we will punish him﴾, following the custom of kings in saying "we did." His words (to his Lord) imply that the choice given to Dhul-Qarnayn was not from Allah, for if it were, the wording would be: "then he will be returned to You, and You will punish him." It is not unlikely that the choice was from Allah and that Dhul-Qarnayn informed his followers of it, then he elaborated, addressing his followers and not his Lord. How excellent is the coming of these sentences: when he mentioned what he deserves of wrong, he began with what is nearest to them and perceptible to them, which is His words ﴿we will punish him﴾, then he informed of what befalls him last, on the Day of Resurrection, which is Allah's punishment of him with a dreadful punishment. And because the order of occurrence is so; when he mentioned what he deserves, ﴿and whoever believes and does righteousness﴾, he mentioned Allah's reward for him in the Hereafter, which is (the best), i.e. Paradise, because the believer's hope and expectation of the Hereafter is what moved him to believe for the sake of his reward in the Hereafter, and it is great compared with the goodness of this world. Then he followed this with His goodness to him in this world, in His words ﴿And We will speak to him of Our command with ease﴾, i.e. We will not say to him what is burdensome for him to bear, meaning words that are easy and smooth, as He said "a gentle word." When He mentioned what He prepared for him of the best reward, it was not fitting to mention his reward in deed, but He confined Himself to speech, out of courtesy toward Allah, even though He knows that He benefits him in deed and in speech.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, Abu Bahriyya, al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Munadhir, Ya'qub, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, and Muhammad ibn Jarir read ﴿fa-lahu jazaʾan﴾ with the accusative and tanwin. (Jazaʾan) is in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state, i.e. "rewarded," like your saying: "in the house, standing, is Zayd." Abu ʿAli said: Abu al-Hasan said: the Arabs hardly speak this way with it placed first except in poetry. It was also said that it is accusative as a verbal noun, i.e. "he will recompense (a reward)." Al-Farra' said: it is accusative by way of explanation, and the meaning of al-husna in the accusative reading is Paradise. The rest of the Seven read (jazaʾu al-husna) with (jazaʾ) in the nominative, construed with (al-husna). Abu ʿAli said: the reward of the good qualities which he did and performed, or al-husna is meant as the good deed, and Paradise is the reward; the construction is as one says "the abode of the Hereafter," and (jazaʾ) is the subject whose predicate is (lahu).

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ishaq read (fa-lahu jazaʾun) with the nominative, a subject and predicate, and (al-husna) is an apposition to (jazaʾun). Ibn ʿAbbas and Masruq read (jazaʾa) in the accusative without tanwin, (al-husna) construed with it, and this is explained as the omission of the subject, indicated by the meaning, i.e. "for him is the reward," (jazaʾa al-husna). Al-Mahdawi explained it as dropping the tanwin because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters. Abu Jaʿfar read (yusran) with a damma on the sin wherever it occurs.

﴿Then he followed a way﴾ [al-Kahf: 89], i.e. a road to his destination which was made easy for him. Al-Hasan, ʿIsa and Ibn Muhaysin read (matlaʿa) with a fatha on the lam, and it is reported from Ibn Kathir and the people of Mecca, and it is the analogical form. The majority read it with a kasra, and this is a transmitted form in a number of words; its analogical kasra would require the imperfect to be (tatlaʿu) with a kasra on the lam. Al-Kisa'i used to say: this is a dialect that died out in many of the dialects of the Arabs, meaning that those among the Arabs who said (tatlu') with a kasra on the lam have gone, and (matli') with a kasra remained in the noun of place and time according to that analogy. The people here are the Zanj. Qatadah said they are the Indians and those beyond them. "The screen" is a building, or garments, or trees and mountains, these are the views, and the meaning is that they have nothing to shield them from the heat of the sun. It was said: the sun penetrates their roofs and garments and reaches their bodies. It was said: when it rises they go down into the water until its heat breaks, as said al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj. It was said: they enter caves. Mujahid said: the Sudanese at the place of the sunrise are more numerous than all the people of the earth. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the apparent sense of the wording is that it is an eloquent expression for the sun's nearness to them, its action upon them by Allah's power, and its reaching them; and if they had caves, there would be a dense screen. Then ended. Some of the rajaz poets said:

"By the Zanj a heat has changed the bodies, until it clothed their skins in blackness."

This is only from the intensity and persistence of the sun's heat among them. Likewise, the indication is to reaching: just as he reached the sun's setting, he reached its rising. It was said: ﴿he followed a way﴾ [al-Kahf: 89] like ﴿he followed a way﴾ [al-Kahf: 89]. It was said: just as he found those at the sun's setting and judged among them, so he found these at the sun's rising and judged among them. It was said: thus he commanded them, as we have related to you. It was said: (it rises) its rising is like its setting. It was said: ﴿We had not made for them against it any screen﴾ [al-Kahf: 90], i.e. like those whom he found at the sun's setting, disbelievers like them, and their judgment like their judgment: punishment for whoever remains on disbelief, and goodness for whoever believes.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (thus), i.e. the matter of Dhul-Qarnayn is thus, i.e. as we described it, magnifying his affair. It was said: ﴿We had not made for them against it any screen﴾ [al-Kahf: 90], like that screen which we made for you from mountains, fortresses, buildings and shelters of every kind, and garments of every sort. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: (thus) means he dealt with them as he dealt with the first people of the west, and He informed with His words (thus), then He informed about His encompassing of all that was with Dhul-Qarnayn and of what he did in his actions. It is possible that (thus) is a resumption of speech, not referring back to the first group, so consider it; the first is more correct. And if it is a resumption with no connection to what precedes, it requires an added phrase to complete the sentence.

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah al-Kahf, verses 83–88 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿They ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn. Say: "I will recite to you a remembrance of him."﴾ ﴿Indeed, We established him in the land and gave him a means to every thing.﴾ ﴿So he followed a means.﴾ ﴿until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun, he found it setting in a spring of black mud, and found near it a people. We said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish them or you take a good course with them."﴾ ﴿He said: "As for one who wrongs, we will punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment.﴾ ﴿But as for one who believes and does righteous deeds, he will have a reward of the best, and we will speak to him of Our command with ease."﴾ ﴿Then he followed a means.﴾ ﴿until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun, he found it rising upon a people for whom We had made no shelter against it.﴾ ﴿So it was. And We had full knowledge of what was with him.﴾ ﴿Then he followed a means.﴾ ﴿until, when he reached between the two barriers, he found beside them a people who could hardly understand any speech.﴾ ﴿They said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are corrupters in the land. So shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set up a barrier between us and them?"﴾ ﴿He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better. So help me with strength, and I will set up between you and them a rampart.﴾ ﴿Bring me sheets of iron." Until, when he had leveled [them] between the two cliffs, he said: "Blow," until, when he had made it fire, he said: "Bring me molten copper to pour over it."﴾ ﴿So they could not scale it, nor could they pierce it.﴾ ﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level, and the promise of my Lord is true."﴾ ﴿And We will leave some of them that day surging against one another, and the Horn will be blown, and We will gather them in a gathering.﴾ ﴿And We will present Hell that day to the disbelievers, displayed.﴾ ﴿Those whose eyes were under a covering from My remembrance, and who could not hear.﴾ ﴿Do those who disbelieve think that they may take My servants as protectors instead of Me? Indeed, We have prepared Hell as a lodging for the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Say: "Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in deeds?﴾ ﴿Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world while they think they are doing well in work."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in meeting Him, so their deeds are rendered void, and We will assign them no weight on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ ﴿That is their recompense: Hell, because they disbelieved and took My signs and My messengers in mockery.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds will have the Gardens of Paradise as a lodging,﴾ ﴿abiding therein, not desiring any removal from it.﴾ ﴿Say: "If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as an addition."﴾ ﴿Say: "I am only a human like you. It is revealed to me that your God is one God. So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and associate no one in the worship of his Lord."﴾

**al-Sadd** (the barrier, the obstacle) is that which stands between two things, and it may be pronounced with a *ḍamma* or a *fatḥa*. **al-Radm** is a barrier. It is said that al-radm is greater than al-sadd, because al-radm is what has been placed one part upon another. One says: "a garment *muraddam*" when a patch has been put over a patch. It is also said that al-radm means filling a gap. ʿAntara said:

> Have the poets left any *mutaraddam*?

That is, a gap in meanings, which one fills in as a *radm*. **al-Zubra** is a piece, and its root meaning is gathering; from it comes *zubrat al-asad*, the mane of the lion, because the hair gathers on its shoulder. *Zabartu al-kitāb* means I gathered its letters. **al-Ṣadafān** are the two sides of a mountain when they face each other, either because they are close or because they meet; this is what al-Azhari said. It is also said *ṣudufun*, with *ḍamma* or *fatḥa* on both letters, or with *ḍamma* on the *ṣād* and sukun on the *dāl*, or the reverse. Some philologists said: the *fatḥa* on both is the dialect of Tamim, and the *ḍamma* on both is the dialect of Himyar. Abu ʿUbayda said: *al-ṣadaf* is any great, high building. **al-Qiṭr** is molten copper according to most scholars. It is also said to be molten iron, and it is also said to be molten lead. **al-Naqb** is the verbal noun of *naqaba*, meaning he dug or cut through. **al-Ghiṭāʾ** is well known, its plural is *aghiyah*, and it derives from *ghaṭṭā*, meaning he covered. **al-Firdaws**: al-Farraʾ said it is the orchard containing vines, and Thaʿlab said it is every orchard enclosed by a wall.

﴿They ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn...﴾ up to ﴿...and We had full knowledge of what was with him﴾ [al-Kahf: 89–91]. (Commentary continues.)

The pronoun in ﴿They ask you﴾ refers to the Quraysh or to the Jews. The well-known view is that the questioners were the Quraysh, after the Jews had put them up to asking him about the Spirit, the wandering man, and the youths who went away in ancient times, so that he would be tested by this. Dhul-Qarnayn is Alexander the Greek (al-Iskandar al-Yunani), as Ibn Ishaq mentioned. Wahb said he was Roman. Was he a prophet or a righteous servant? He was not a prophet; there are two opinions. It is also said he was an angel, but this view is strange. It is said that two believers ruled the whole world, Solomon and Dhul-Qarnayn, and two disbelievers, Nimrod and Bukhtnasar, who came after Nimrod. From ʿAli: he was a righteous servant, neither an angel nor a prophet. He was struck on his right horn and died in obedience to God; then God raised him, and he was struck on his left horn and died; then God raised him, and he was called Dhul-Qarnayn (the Two-Horned). It is said he traveled the two horns of the world, meaning its two sides, east and west. It is said he had two horns, that is, two braids. It is said that two generations of people died out in his time. From Wahb: he was called this because he ruled the Romans and the Persians; it is also narrated: the Romans and the Turks. From him also: the two plates of his head were of copper. It is said his crown had two horns. It is said there was on his head something resembling two horns. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that he was named so for his bravery, just as a brave man is called a ram, as if he butts his rivals. He was from the Romans, a child of an old woman who had no other child, end of quote. Other explanations have been given for his name, but the well-known view is that he is Alexander.

Abu al-Rayhan al-Biruni, the astrologer, author of *al-Athar al-Baqiya ʿan al-Qurun al-Khaliya* (The Remaining Traces of Past Generations), said: he is Abu Bakr ibn Sumayy ibn ʿUmayr ibn Ifriqis al-Himyari. His rule reached the easts and wests of the earth, and it is this that one of the poets of Himyar boasted about when he said:

> Dhul-Qarnayn before me was a Muslim,
> a king who rose in the land, not dispersed.
> He reached the easts and the wests, seeking
> the means of kingship from a noble lord.

Abu al-Rayhan said: This view seems closer, because the *Adhwaʾ* (the lords with *dhū* in their names) were from Yemen, and their names are never without *dhū*, like Dhu al-Manar and Dhu Yazan. End of quote. The poem he recited is also attributed to Tubbaʿ al-Himyari:

> Dhul-Qarnayn was my grandfather, a Muslim.

From ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas: his name was ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Dahhak. From Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn al-Husayn: ʿAyyash. From Abu Khaythama: he was al-Saʿb ibn Jabir ibn al-Qalammas. It is also said he was Marzuban ibn Marzabah the Greek, of the descendants of Yunan ibn Yafith. From ʿAli: he was of the first generation of the descendants of Yafith ibn Nuh. From al-Hasan: he was after Thamud, and his lifespan was one thousand six hundred years. From Wahb: he was in the interval between ʿIsa and Muhammad, may God bless them both and grant them peace.

The address in ﴿upon you﴾ is to the questioners, either the Jews or the Quraysh, according to the disagreement that preceded about the questioners. His saying ﴿a remembrance﴾ may mean a Qur'an, or a narrative and good news. The establishment that he had ﴿in the land﴾ is his being the ruler of the world, and all kings submitted to him. Some exegetes said: The proof that he is Alexander is that the Qur'an indicates that the man called Dhul-Qarnayn reached, in his rule, the farthest west, the farthest east, and the farthest north. This is shown by the fact that Gog and Magog are a people of the Turks living in the farthest north. The extent of this man's rule is the limit of the inhabited earth, and such a vast kingdom is without doubt contrary to custom. What is so must have its memory preserved forever and must not be hidden. The king whose name in the books of history reached this extent is none other than Alexander. When his father died, he gathered the kingdom of the Romans, after it had been divided among groups. Then he marched against the kings of the Arabs and conquered them, and went on until he reached the Green Sea. Then he returned to Egypt and built Alexandria and named it after himself. Then he entered al-Sham and went against the Children of Israel and came to Jerusalem and sacrificed on its altar. Then he turned to Armenia, and the Iraqis, the Copts and the Berbers submitted to him. Then he went toward the house of Ibn Dara, and defeated him several times until his own commander killed him. Alexander took control of the realms of the Persians, went to India and China, invaded distant nations, returned to Khurasan and built many cities, returned to Iraq, fell ill at Shahrazur, and died there.

It is related in a hadith: "The ones who ruled the earth were four, two of them believers: Solomon son of David, and Dhul-Qarnayn." This has been mentioned before. It is established in the science of history that the one of this rank was none other than Alexander, so it is certain that the one meant by Dhul-Qarnayn is Alexander son of Philip the Greek. It is also said that his establishment in the land was through prophethood and the performance of miracles. It is said his establishment was that the clouds were subjected to him, he was carried upon them, and light was spread for him, so that night and day were alike for him. It is said it was through the abundance of his helpers and armies, through awe and dignity, through the casting of terror into his enemies, through making travel easy for him, through acquainting him with the paths of the earth, and through his dominion over its land and sea.

﴿And We gave him from every thing﴾, that is, what he needed to reach his aims, ﴿a means﴾, that is, a route leading to it. A means is whatever one reaches the desired goal by, whether knowledge, power, or equipment. He wanted to reach the west, ﴿so he followed a means﴾ leading him to it until he arrived. Likewise he wanted the east, ﴿so he followed a means﴾; and he wanted to reach the two barriers, ﴿so he followed a means﴾. The root meaning of *sabab* is a rope, then it was extended until it came to mean whatever one reaches the goal by. al-Hasan said: a means of arrival to wherever he intended. Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Zuhri, al-Aʿmash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, the Kufans, and Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿fa-atbaʿa﴾ in all three places with a light pronunciation of the *tāʾ* (with a *hamza* for the *ʿayn* in the first verb form, it is read *atbaʿa*). The remaining seven read it with *tashdid* (doubled *tāʾ*, *ittabaʿa*). The apparent meaning is that both have the same sense. From Yunus ibn Habib and Abu Zayd: that with a cut *hamza* it expresses one who is diligent, quick and eager in pursuit, while with a connected *hamza* it only implies following, without these qualities.

ʿAbd Allah, Talha ibn ʿUbayd Allah, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, Muʿawiya, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza and al-Kisai read ﴿ḥāmiyatin﴾ with a *yāʾ*, meaning hot. Ibn ʿAbbas and the remaining seven, along with Shayba, Humayd, Ibn Abi Layla, Yaʿqub, Abu Hatim, and Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki read ﴿ḥamiʾatin﴾ with a *hamza* and a *fatḥa*. al-Zuhri softened the *hamza*. It is said *ḥamiʾat al-bi'r taḥmaʾu ḥamaʾan*, "the well became muddy," fa-hiya ḥamiʾa (it is muddy). *Ḥamaʾtuhā* means I drew out its mud, and *aḥmaʾtuhā* means I left the mud in it. There is no contradiction between *ḥāmiya* (hot) and *ḥamiʾa* (muddy), since the spring may combine both qualities. Abu Hatim said: It is possible that *ḥāmiya* with *hamza* means possessing mud, so the two readings have one meaning, meaning that the *hamza* was made easier by changing it into a *yāʾ*, because of the *kasra* before it. In the Torah it says he set in water and mud. Tubbaʿ said:

> He saw the setting of the sun at its return,
> in the spring of a wet and dark mire.

in a spring of murky water, black and muddy. In the hadith of Abu Dharr: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the sun as it set and said: "Do you know where it sets, Abu Dharr?" I said: "No." He said: "It sets in a hot spring." This hadith and the apparent sense of the text are evidence that His words ﴿in a spring﴾ are connected to His words ﴿it set﴾, not to what some over-strained interpreters said: that His words "in a spring of black mud" mean that Dhul-Qarnayn was in it, i.e. that it is the end of the earth, and the meaning of ﴿it set in a spring﴾ is "as far as the eye can see," not that this is literally so, as we observe on a smooth plain, as if it enters the earth. It is also possible that this spring is part of the sea, and it is possible that the sun sets behind it. Some of the Baghdadi grammarians claimed that (fi) here means (ʿinda), i.e. "it sets near a spring."

﴿And he found near it a people﴾, i.e. near that spring. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: they were believers and disbelievers. Others said: they were unbelievers, their clothing was the skins of beasts, and their food was what the sun had burned of creatures, and what the spring cast out of fish when the sun set. Wahb said: he set out heading west until he reached Basak, where he found a multitude that none could count but Allah. He placed three armies around them until he gathered them in one place, then he entered upon them in the light and called them to the worship of Allah. Some of them believed and some turned away from him. Abu Zayd al-Suhayli said: they were the people of Hābūs (and in Syriac it is called Jirjīsā), inhabited by a people descended from Thamud, the remnant of those who believed in Salih, peace be upon him.

The apparent sense of His words (We said) is that Allah revealed to him through an angel. It was said: He spoke to him directly without a messenger, as He spoke to Musa, peace be upon him. According to these two views he would be a prophet. What some interpreters said, that it was inspiration cast into his heart, is unlikely, because such a choice can only come through revelation, since obligations and the taking of lives are not established by inspiration except through information. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: the meaning is "We said, O Muhammad, they said: ﴿O Dhul-Qarnayn﴾," and then the first saying was omitted, because it is not established that Dhul-Qarnayn was a prophet who would be addressed by Allah. On this view, the pronoun in the omitted "they said" refers to his troops and army who were with him.

His words ﴿Either you punish﴾ by killing for disbelief, ﴿or you take among them goodness﴾, i.e. by leading them to faith and guidance. Either you disbelieve and are punished, or you believe and do good, so the choice is expressed through the effect in place of the cause. Al-Tabari said: taking goodness is their capture along with their disbelief, meaning that he was given the choice, while they remained disbelievers, between killing them and capturing them. The detail of Dhul-Qarnayn's words ﴿As for the one who does wrong﴾ and (As for the one who believes) refutes this view. When Allah gave him the choice between punishing them and calling them to Islam, he chose the call and striving to win them over. He said: as for the one whose call he rejected, refusing to remain on wrong, which here is disbelief without dispute, he is the one punished in both abodes. As for the one who believes and does what faith requires, ﴿he will have the best reward﴾. He used the particle of futurity in ﴿we will punish him﴾ because of what intervenes between his showing his disbelief and his punishment: his calling him to faith and his refusal of it. He does not hasten to kill them for their wrong, but calls them and reminds them; if they return, well, otherwise there is killing.

His words ﴿Then he will be returned to his Lord﴾, i.e. on the Day of Resurrection. He used the plural of majesty in ﴿we will punish him﴾, following the custom of kings in saying "we did." His words (to his Lord) imply that the choice given to Dhul-Qarnayn was not from Allah, for if it were, the wording would be: "then he will be returned to You, and You will punish him." It is not unlikely that the choice was from Allah and that Dhul-Qarnayn informed his followers of it, then he elaborated, addressing his followers and not his Lord. How excellent is the coming of these sentences: when he mentioned what he deserves of wrong, he began with what is nearest to them and perceptible to them, which is His words ﴿we will punish him﴾, then he informed of what befalls him last, on the Day of Resurrection, which is Allah's punishment of him with a dreadful punishment. And because the order of occurrence is so; when he mentioned what he deserves, ﴿and whoever believes and does righteousness﴾, he mentioned Allah's reward for him in the Hereafter, which is (the best), i.e. Paradise, because the believer's hope and expectation of the Hereafter is what moved him to believe for the sake of his reward in the Hereafter, and it is great compared with the goodness of this world. Then he followed this with His goodness to him in this world, in His words ﴿And We will speak to him of Our command with ease﴾, i.e. We will not say to him what is burdensome for him to bear, meaning words that are easy and smooth, as He said "a gentle word." When He mentioned what He prepared for him of the best reward, it was not fitting to mention his reward in deed, but He confined Himself to speech, out of courtesy toward Allah, even though He knows that He benefits him in deed and in speech.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, Abu Bahriyya, al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Munadhir, Ya'qub, Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, and Muhammad ibn Jarir read ﴿fa-lahu jazaʾan﴾ with the accusative and tanwin. (Jazaʾan) is in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state, i.e. "rewarded," like your saying: "in the house, standing, is Zayd."
