Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is a request for handing over, not a request for a gift or grant, since it was linked to his saying that he would not take tribute from them, so only a request for handing over remains. He concluded. The majority read ﴿bring me﴾ (ataunī). Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (i'tuni), meaning "come to me." (Zubar) is in the accusative with (i'tuni) with the preposition dropped, meaning: come to me with blocks of (al-hadid) iron. The majority read (zubar) with a fatha on the ba', and al-Hasan with a damma. There is an ellipsis in the speech; its implied sense is: they brought them, and he ordered some of them to be piled on top of others. ﴿Until, when he had leveled﴾.

The majority read ﴿leveled﴾ (sawa), Qatada read ﴿made level﴾ [Ta-Ha: 58] (sawwa), and Ibn Abi Umayya from Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (suwwiya) in the passive. It is related regarding the manner that Dhul-Qarnayn measured the space between the two cliffs, digging the foundation until he reached water, then he made its filling of rock and its mortar of copper, which was melted and poured over it. The building was of blocks of iron with wood and charcoal between them, until he closed the gap between the two mountains up to their tops. Then he set the bellows, until it became like fire, and he poured the molten copper over the heated iron, so it mixed and its parts adhered to one another and became a solid mountain. It has also been said: the length between the two barriers was a hundred farsakhs and their width fifty. In a hadith: a man informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "How did you see it?" He said: like striped cloth, a black stripe and a red stripe. He said: "You have seen it."

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Zuhri, Mujahid and al-Hasan read ﴿the two cliffs (al-Sudufayn)﴾ with damma on the sad and dal. Abu Bakr, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Raja' and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman did likewise, except that they made the dal quiescent. The rest of the seven, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Humayd, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, a group from Ya'qub, Khalaf in his choice, Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn Sa'dan read both with fatha; Ibn Jundub read with fatha and sukun on the dal; and this is reported from Qatada. al-Majshun read with fatha and damma on the dal. Qatada and Aban from 'Asim read with a damma on the sad and a fatha on the dal.

﴿Until, when he made it fire﴾: there is an ellipsis in the speech, its implied sense being: then they blew, until. The majority read: He said ﴿bring me﴾, that is: give me. Al-A'mash, Talha, Hamza and Abu Bakr, in a variant from him, read: he said (i'tuni), that is: come to me. And ﴿molten copper﴾ is in the accusative with ufrigh, by the rule of the second verb being the governor, and the object of ﴿bring me﴾ is omitted as indicated by the second verb.

﴿So they were unable﴾, that is: Gog and Magog, ﴿to scale it﴾, that is: to reach its top, because of its height, its steepness and its smoothness, ﴿nor could they pierce it﴾ because of its hardness and thickness. Thus there is no way to pass beyond it to other nations except by one of these two: either climbing or piercing. And He removed their power to do either.

The majority read ﴿so they were unable﴾ with the deletion of the ta' for lightness, because it is close to the ta'. Hamza and Talha read with its assimilation into the ta', which is an assimilation contrary to its rule. Abu 'Ali said it is not permissible. Al-A'sha from Abu Bakr read (fama istaṭa'u) with the substitution of sad for sin because of the ta'. Al-A'mash read (fama istatā'u) with the ta' and without deletion.

﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾, that is: Dhul-Qarnayn said it. The reference of "this" is: to the rampart, the strength to build it, and the benefit of it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it refers to the rampart and the power over it and the benefit from it. Al-Zamakhshari said: it refers to the barrier, that is: this barrier is a blessing from God and a mercy upon His servants, or this empowerment and enabling to level it. It is said that in the speech there is an ellipsis, its implied sense being: when he completed the building of the barrier, made it level and strengthened it, ﴿he said: "This is a mercy from my Lord."﴾

Ibn Abi 'Abla recited (هَذِهِ رَحْمَةٌ مِن رَبِّي, "This is a mercy from my Lord") with the feminine form of the demonstrative. The "promise" (al-wa'd) may be understood as referring to the Day of Resurrection, or to the time of the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. Al-Zamakhshari said: When the coming of the Day of Resurrection draws near and is about to arrive, He will make the barrier (al-sadd) into dakk, that is, levelled, flattened and made even with the ground; and whatever is flattened after being elevated has been "undakka" (crushed). End of quotation. The Kufans read (دَكّاءَ, "dakka'," with the long vowel and without tanwin, as a diptote), while the rest of the seven readers read dakkan with tanwin, as a verbal noun (masdar) of dakaktuhu. The apparent reading is that (ja'alahu) means "made it," so dakkan is the second object. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that ja'ala means "created," and dakkan is then in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Abu Hayyan said: This is very far-fetched, because the barrier at that time already exists as a created thing, and what is created is not created again; rather, it passes from one of its states to another state. The word wa'd here means "that which is promised" (mawud), not a verbal noun, and the meaning is: "When the promise of my Lord comes," not intending the verbal noun, because the verbal noun has already been mentioned. The pronoun in (تَرَكْنا, "We left," Al-'Ankabut: 35) refers to God Most High. The more apparent view is that the pronoun in (بَعْضِهِمْ, "some of them") refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj. The omitted clause after (إذِ, "when"), for which the tanwin is the substitute, is to be estimated as "when the promise came," which is their emergence and their spreading over the earth; or it is estimated as "when the barrier stood between them and the people who used to be corrupting among them, while they were amazed at the barrier," so that some of them surged over others.

It has been said: The pronoun in (بَعْضِهِمْ) refers to the creatures, meaning: on the day when the promise of God came, which is the Day of Resurrection. This is strengthened by His saying (﴿ونُفِخَ في الصُّورِ﴾, "and the Trumpet is blown"). Thus it is evident that this is the Day of Resurrection, and likewise what comes after it, namely the gathering and the presentation of Hell. The discussion of the blowing of the Trumpet has already occurred in Surat al-An'am. (جَمْعًا, "a gathering") is a verbal noun like (مَوْعِدٍ). (﴿وعَرَضْنا﴾, "And We presented") means: We made manifest (abrazna) (﴿جَهَنَّمَ يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾, "Hell that Day"), that is, on the day when We gathered them. It has been said that the lam means "upon," as in the verse: "So he fell prone upon his hands and his mouth." He who claimed that it is inverted (maqlub) is too far off. The estimated meaning is: "And We presented the disbelievers before Hell (arda)." Restricting it to the disbelievers is good news for the believers. (﴿الَّذِينَ كانَتْ أعْيُنُهُمْ﴾, "Those whose eyes were") is a description of blame, in (﴿غِطاءٍ﴾, "a covering"); the covering is a metaphor for their eyes. The meaning is that they do not see My signs which are looked at so that one may take lesson from them; and (واذْكُرْ بِالتَّعْظِيمِ, "remembrance" with reverence) is in this case with an omitted modifier, that is: from the signs of (ذِكْرِي, "My remembrance"). It has been said that (﴿عَنْ ذِكْرِي﴾, "from My remembrance") means from the Qur'an and reflection upon its meanings, and in this case "eyes" here means insights, not the bodily organs, because the bodily organs have no relation to the remembrance. (﴿وكانُوا لا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ سَمْعًا﴾, "and they could not hear") is an intensification in negating hearing, since the ability is negated; and although they are deaf, a deaf person may still be able to hear when shouted at, whereas these people's hearing has been stopped up, so they have no ability to hear.

(﴿أفَحَسِبَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾, "Do those who disbelieve think"): these are those who worshipped the angels, 'Uzayr and the Messiah, and took them as protectors apart from God; they include some of the Arabs, the Jews and the Christians. This is an interrogative with the sense of denial and rebuke, and the meaning is (p-166) that these have no share in the guardianship of those whom they took as protectors, and they find no benefit from them. It is apparent that there is an omission in the speech, and the estimated meaning is: (﴿أنْ يَتَّخِذُوا عِبادِي مِن دُونِي أوْلِياءَ﴾, "that they may take My servants apart from Me as protectors"), so that this would benefit them and they would profit from that taking. It has been said: "servants" here means the devils, related from Ibn 'Abbas; Muqatil said: it means the idols, because they are His creation and His possession. The more apparent interpretation of "servants" is what we have stated, because of their being attributed to Him, and most often in this kind of expression the attribution is an attribution of honour.

Here (حَسِبَ, "thought") means (ظَنَّ, "supposed"), and 'Abdullah read with it (أفَظَنَّ, "Do they suppose"). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, Qatada, Nu'aym ibn Maysara, al-Dahhak, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Kathir, Ya'qub (with a variant from them), Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Haywa, al-Shafi'i and Mas'ud ibn Salih read (﴿أفَحَسْبُ﴾, "Is the sufficiency") with a sukun on the sin and a damma on the ba', as a construct phrase with (الَّذِينَ, "those who"), meaning: "Is it sufficient for them, their reckoning, and the limit of their concern?" The meaning is that this does not suffice them and does not benefit them with God, as they supposed. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: Sahl, meaning Abu Hatim, said: its meaning is "Is their sufficiency and portion" except that (أفَحَسِبَ) is more forceful in blame, because it makes it the ultimate of their aim. End of quotation.

(حَسْبُ, "sufficiency") is in the nominative as a subject, and the predicate is (﴿أنْ يَتَّخِذُوا﴾, "that they take"). Al-Zamakhshari said: Or it is on the basis of a verb and its agent, because when the active participle relies on the interrogative hamza, it equals the verb in governing, as in your saying: "Is standing Zayd and 'Amr?" and this is a sound and good reading. End of quotation. What appears is that this parsing is not permissible, because hasb is not an active participle, so that it would govern, and it does not follow that when one thing is explained by another, all its rulings apply to it. Sibawayh mentioned several of the descriptive words that function like nouns, and that the preferred form for them is the nominative. He then said: "Such as: I passed by a man, better than his father," "I passed by a man, the good and the bad are alike to him," "I passed by a man, a father to him is his companion," "I passed by a man, enough of a man for you," and "I passed by a man, what a man he is." End of quotation. It is not far-fetched that an apparent noun may be raised by it, for they permitted in "I passed by a man, father of ten, his father" that "his father" is raised by "father of ten," because it has the meaning of "parent of ten."

(﴿إنّا أعْتَدْنا﴾, "Indeed We have prepared") means: We have made ready and facilitated. (النُّزُلُ, "nuzul") is the place of descending, and nuzul also means what is set forth for a guest and prepared for him and for the arriving one of food. Here nuzul may bear both interpretations; that it is the place of descending was said by al-Zajjaj here, and that it is what is prepared of food for the guest is the statement of al-Qutabi. It has been said: it is the plural of nazil, and its accusative is as a circumstantial state, like sharif and sharaf. If it is what is set forth for the guest and the arriving one, it would be like His saying: (﴿فَبَشِّرْهم بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾, "so give them tidings of a painful punishment," Al 'Imran: 21), and like the poet's words: "Their greeting among them is a painful blow." Abu Haywa and Abu 'Amr, with a variant from him, read (نُزْلًا, "nuzlan") with a sukun on the zay.

[p. 162]﴿Then he followed a course﴾ ﴿until, when he reached the rising place of the sun, he found it rising over a people for whom We had made no shelter against it﴾ ﴿Thus. And We had full knowledge of what was with him﴾ ﴿Then he followed a course﴾ ﴿until, when he reached between the two barriers, he found beside them a people who could hardly understand any speech﴾ ﴿They said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, Gog and Magog are spreading corruption in the land. Shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set a barrier between us and them?"﴾ ﴿He said: "What my Lord has established me in is better. So help me with strength, and I will set a rampart between you and them﴾ ﴿Bring me blocks of iron," until, when he had filled the gap between the two cliffs, he said: "Blow," until, when he had made it fire, he said: "Bring me molten copper to pour over it."﴾ ﴿So they were unable to scale it, nor could they pierce it﴾ ﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will level it to dust, and the promise of my Lord is true."﴾ ﴿On that day We will leave them surging against one another, and the Trumpet will be blown, and We will gather them all together﴾ ﴿And We will present Hell on that day to the disbelievers, displayed﴾ ﴿those whose eyes were veiled from My reminder and who could not bear to hear﴾ ﴿Do those who disbelieve think they may take My servants as protectors besides Me? Indeed, We have prepared Hell as a lodging for the disbelievers﴾.

[p. 163] (A course) means a way or a route leading to the north, for the two barriers are there. Wahb said: the two barriers are two lofty mountains in the sky, with lands behind them and in front of them, and they lie at the farthest edge of the land of the Turks, on the side adjoining Armenia and Adharbayjan. Al-Harawi mentioned that they are two mountains beyond the land of the Turks. It has also been said: they are two smooth, slippery mountains to the north, on which everything slides. The two mountains were called two barriers (saddayn) because each of them blocked the passes of the land, and between them was a gap through which Gog and Magog would enter.

Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Nakha'i, Hafs, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿between the two barriers﴾ with a fatha on the sin (saddayn with fath). The rest of the seven readers read it with a damma. Al-Kisa'i said: both are dialectal forms with one meaning. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: with damma it is the noun, and with fatha it is the verbal noun (masdar). Ikrimah, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Abu 'Ubayda said: what is part of God's creation, in which no human has a share, takes the damma; what is the work of humans takes the fatha. Ibn Abi Ishaq said: what your eyes see takes the damma, and what is not seen takes the fatha.

Bayn (between) is in the accusative as the direct object of balagha (reached), just as it is in the nominative in ﴿your bond has been severed﴾ [al-An'am: 94], and in the genitive by being in construct in ﴿this is the parting between me and you﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. Bayn is one of the flexible adverbs, unless it is combined with another like it, as in the expression "a hamza between between" (hamza bayn bayn).

﴿Beside them﴾ means beside the two barriers. And "a people" refers to humans. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are the Turks. He concluded. He who held that they were jinn is far from the truth. Al-Zamakhshari said: this place is at the farthest edge of the land of the Turks, on the eastern side. The verse denies that they could comprehend speech (qawlan), and this implies a denial of their understanding. Al-Zamakhshari said: they can hardly understand it except with effort and hardship, as if the understanding were a kind of negation that almost occurs, meaning that understanding comes from them only after difficulty. This is the view of some who say that a negation with "they almost" is an affirmation, and an affirmation is a negation; but this is not the preferred view.

Al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Layla, Khalaf, Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (yafqahuna) with a damma on the ya and a kasra on the qaf, meaning: they make their speech unintelligible to the listener, not that they explain it, because their language is strange and unknown.

The pronoun in (qalu) refers to these people, who complained of what they suffered from Gog and Magog, since they hoped for something beneficial from him, because he had possessed the earth, subdued the kings, and reached them, while no king before him had reached their land. Gog and Magog are two tribes descended from Adam. It has also been said that they are descended from Yafith son of Noah. It has been said that Gog are of the Turks and Magog of the Gil and the Daylam. Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: the Turks are a remnant of them who came out to raid, so Dhul-Qarnayn came and built the barrier, and they remained on this side. Qatada and al-Suddi said: the barrier was built against twenty-one tribes, and one tribe remained outside the barrier, and they are the Turks. Their number and attributes differ, and nothing authentic is transmitted about this. Both names are diptotes (non-declinable). Whoever claims that both are foreign has the reasons of foreignness and definiteness; whoever claims they are Arabic has the reasons of feminine form and definiteness, since they are the names of two tribes.

Al-Akhfash said: if we take their alif as original, then Ya'juj is on the pattern of yaf'ul and Ma'juj on the pattern of maf'ul, as if derived from ajij al-nar (the crackling of fire). Whoever does not pronounce the hamza takes the alif as additional: Ya'juj is from yajjat, and Ma'juj from majjat. Qutrub said regarding the unhamzated form: Ma'juj is fa'ul from al-majj, and Ya'juj is fa'ul from yajj. Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Samad al-Sakhawi, one of our teachers, said: the apparent view is that it is Arabic, and its origin is with hamza, and omitting the hamza is a lightening. It is either from al-aj'ja, which is disagreement, as He said: ﴿We will leave them surging against one another﴾; or from al-ajj, which is rapid running, as He said: ﴿and they will swarm down from every slope﴾ [al-Anbiya': 96], and a poet said:

"He rushes as the fleeing ostrich rushes."

Or it is from al-ajja, which is intense heat; or from ajja al-ma' ya'iju uj'uju, when water is salty and bitter. He concluded.

'Asim, al-A'mash and Ya'qub in one transmission read with a hamza both in (Ya'juj wa Ma'juj) and similarly in al-Anbiya'. This is in the dialect of Banu Asad, as al-Farra' mentioned. It is said: there is no justification for it except the strange dialect attributed to al-'Ajjaj, that he used to hamz al-'alam and al-khatam. The rest of the seven read with an unhamzated alif, which is the dialect of all Arabs except Banu Asad. Al-'Ajjaj and his son Ru'ba read Ajuj with a hamza in place of the ya.

[p. 164] Their corruption: the apparent meaning is that the corruption from them is certain, not merely expected, since the people complained of harm that had reached them. Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: their corruption is eating the children of Adam. It has also been said: it is oppression and killing and the known forms of corruption from humans. It has been said: they used to come out in the spring and leave nothing green without eating it, and nothing dry without carrying it away. It is also reported that none of them would die until he saw a thousand males of his offspring, each bearing arms.

﴿So shall we pay you a tribute?﴾ is a request from them that he accept what they offer, which would help him in what they sought, and it was in courteous manner, since they asked him this, like Musa's words to al-Khidr: ﴿May I follow you on condition that you teach me?﴾ [al-Kahf: 66]. Al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Talha, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, and among the seven, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (kharajan) with an alif here, and in the two places in "qad aflaha" (the chapter of al-Mu'minun). Ibn 'Amir read the ra' in these places with sukun. The rest of the seven read (kharjan) in both places with a sukun on the ra'. So kharaj with the alif and kharj have the same meaning, like nawl and nawal (gift). The meaning is a payment that we bring out from our wealth. Whatever is extracted by way of tax, poll tax, or yield is kharaj or kharj. It has been said: kharj is the verbal noun applied to kharaj, while kharaj is the name for what is paid out. Ibn al-A'rabi said: kharj is levied on heads (per person), as one says "pay the kharj of your head," while kharaj is levied on land. Tha'lab said: kharj is more specific and kharaj is more general. It has been said: kharj is wealth paid out once, while kharaj is repeated revenue collected. They offered him that they would gather wealth for him, by which he would maintain the work of the barrier. Ibn 'Abbas said: (kharajan) means a wage.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read (suddan) with a damma on the sin. Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Zuhri, al-A'mash, Talha, Ya'qub in one transmission, Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani, Ibn Jarir, and the rest of the seven read it with a fatha. ﴿He said: "What my Lord has established me in is better"﴾, that is: what God has extended to me of power and kingdom is better than your tribute. ﴿So help me with strength﴾, that is: with what I can use to strengthen myself, of workers and craftsmen who do good work and building. Muqatil said this, and al-Kalbi said: with tools. ﴿A rampart﴾: a strong, firmly bound barrier. Ibn Kathir and Humayd read (ma makkananni) with two moving nuns, and the rest of the seven with the assimilation of the nun of makkana into the protective nun (nun al-wiqaya).

Then the help was explained as strength, so He said: ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾, that is: give them to me. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is a request for handing over, not a request for a gift or grant, since it was linked to his saying that he would not take tribute from them, so only a request for handing over remains. He concluded. The majority read ﴿bring me﴾ (ataunī). Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (i'tuni), meaning "come to me." (Zubar) is in the accusative with (i'tuni) with the preposition dropped, meaning: come to me with blocks of (al-hadid) iron. The majority read (zubar) with a fatha on the ba', and al-Hasan with a damma. There is an ellipsis in the speech; its implied sense is: they brought them, and he ordered some of them to be piled on top of others. ﴿Until, when he had leveled﴾.

The majority read ﴿leveled﴾ (sawa), Qatada read ﴿made level﴾ [Ta-Ha: 58] (sawwa), and Ibn Abi Umayya from Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (suwwiya) in the passive. It is related regarding the manner that Dhul-Qarnayn measured the space between the two cliffs, digging the foundation until he reached water, then he made its filling of rock and its mortar of copper, which was melted and poured over it. The building was of blocks of iron with wood and charcoal between them, until he closed the gap between the two mountains up to their tops. Then he set the bellows, until it became like fire, and he poured the molten copper over the heated iron, so it mixed and its parts adhered to one another and became a solid mountain. It has also been said: the length between the two barriers was a hundred farsakhs and their width fifty. In a hadith: a man informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "How did you see it?" He said: like striped cloth, a black stripe and a red stripe. He said: "You have seen it."

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Zuhri, Mujahid and al-Hasan read ﴿the two cliffs (al-Sudufayn)﴾ with damma on the sad and dal. Abu Bakr, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Raja' and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman did likewise, except that they made the dal quiescent. The rest of the seven, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Humayd, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, a group from Ya'qub, Khalaf in his choice, Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn Sa'dan read both with fatha; Ibn Jundub read with fatha and sukun on the dal; and this is reported from Qatada. al-Majshun read with fatha and damma on the dal. Qatada and Aban from 'Asim read with a damma on the sad and a fatha on the dal.

﴿Until, when he made it fire﴾: there is an ellipsis in the speech, its implied sense being: then they blew, until. The majority read: He said ﴿bring me﴾, that is: give me. Al-A'mash, Talha, Hamza and Abu Bakr, in a variant from him, read: he said (i'tuni), that is: come to me. And ﴿molten copper﴾ is in the accusative with ufrigh, by the rule of the second verb being the governor, and the object of ﴿bring me﴾ is omitted as indicated by the second verb.

﴿So they were unable﴾, that is: Gog and Magog, ﴿to scale it﴾, that is: to reach its top, because of its height, its steepness and its smoothness, ﴿nor could they pierce it﴾ because of its hardness and thickness. Thus there is no way to pass beyond it to other nations except by one of these two: either climbing or piercing. And He removed their power to do either.

The majority read ﴿so they were unable﴾ with the deletion of the ta' for lightness, because it is close to the ta'. Hamza and Talha read with its assimilation into the ta', which is an assimilation contrary to its rule. Abu 'Ali said it is not permissible. Al-A'sha from Abu Bakr read (fama istaṭa'u) with the substitution of sad for sin because of the ta'. Al-A'mash read (fama istatā'u) with the ta' and without deletion.

﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾, that is: Dhul-Qarnayn said it. The reference of "this" is: to the rampart, the strength to build it, and the benefit of it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it refers to the rampart and the power over it and the benefit from it. Al-Zamakhshari said: it refers to the barrier, that is: this barrier is a blessing from God and a mercy upon His servants, or this empowerment and enabling to level it. It is said that in the speech there is an ellipsis, its implied sense being: when he completed the building of the barrier, made it level and strengthened it, ﴿he said: "This is a mercy from my Lord."﴾

Ibn Abi 'Abla recited (هَذِهِ رَحْمَةٌ مِن رَبِّي, "This is a mercy from my Lord") with the feminine form of the demonstrative. The "promise" (al-wa'd) may be understood as referring to the Day of Resurrection, or to the time of the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. Al-Zamakhshari said: When the coming of the Day of Resurrection draws near and is about to arrive, He will make the barrier (al-sadd) into dakk, that is, levelled, flattened and made even with the ground; and whatever is flattened after being elevated has been "undakka" (crushed). End of quotation. The Kufans read (دَكّاءَ, "dakka'," with the long vowel and without tanwin, as a diptote), while the rest of the seven readers read dakkan with tanwin, as a verbal noun (masdar) of dakaktuhu. The apparent reading is that (ja'alahu) means "made it," so dakkan is the second object. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that ja'ala means "created," and dakkan is then in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Abu Hayyan said: This is very far-fetched, because the barrier at that time already exists as a created thing, and what is created is not created again; rather, it passes from one of its states to another state. The word wa'd here means "that which is promised" (mawud), not a verbal noun, and the meaning is: "When the promise of my Lord comes," not intending the verbal noun, because the verbal noun has already been mentioned. The pronoun in (تَرَكْنا, "We left," Al-'Ankabut: 35) refers to God Most High. The more apparent view is that the pronoun in (بَعْضِهِمْ, "some of them") refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj. The omitted clause after (إذِ, "when"), for which the tanwin is the substitute, is to be estimated as "when the promise came," which is their emergence and their spreading over the earth; or it is estimated as "when the barrier stood between them and the people who used to be corrupting among them, while they were amazed at the barrier," so that some of them surged over others.

It has been said: The pronoun in (بَعْضِهِمْ) refers to the creatures, meaning: on the day when the promise of God came, which is the Day of Resurrection. This is strengthened by His saying (﴿ونُفِخَ في الصُّورِ﴾, "and the Trumpet is blown"). Thus it is evident that this is the Day of Resurrection, and likewise what comes after it, namely the gathering and the presentation of Hell. The discussion of the blowing of the Trumpet has already occurred in Surat al-An'am. (جَمْعًا, "a gathering") is a verbal noun like (مَوْعِدٍ). (﴿وعَرَضْنا﴾, "And We presented") means: We made manifest (abrazna) (﴿جَهَنَّمَ يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾, "Hell that Day"), that is, on the day when We gathered them. It has been said that the lam means "upon," as in the verse: "So he fell prone upon his hands and his mouth." He who claimed that it is inverted (maqlub) is too far off. The estimated meaning is: "And We presented the disbelievers before Hell (arda)." Restricting it to the disbelievers is good news for the believers. (﴿الَّذِينَ كانَتْ أعْيُنُهُمْ﴾, "Those whose eyes were") is a description of blame, in (﴿غِطاءٍ﴾, "a covering"); the covering is a metaphor for their eyes. The meaning is that they do not see My signs which are looked at so that one may take lesson from them; and (واذْكُرْ بِالتَّعْظِيمِ, "remembrance" with reverence) is in this case with an omitted modifier, that is: from the signs of (ذِكْرِي, "My remembrance"). It has been said that (﴿عَنْ ذِكْرِي﴾, "from My remembrance") means from the Qur'an and reflection upon its meanings, and in this case "eyes" here means insights, not the bodily organs, because the bodily organs have no relation to the remembrance. (﴿وكانُوا لا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ سَمْعًا﴾, "and they could not hear") is an intensification in negating hearing, since the ability is negated; and although they are deaf, a deaf person may still be able to hear when shouted at, whereas these people's hearing has been stopped up, so they have no ability to hear.

(﴿أفَحَسِبَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾, "Do those who disbelieve think"): these are those who worshipped the angels, 'Uzayr and the Messiah, and took them as protectors apart from God; they include some of the Arabs, the Jews and the Christians. This is an interrogative with the sense of denial and rebuke, and the meaning is (p-166) that these have no share in the guardianship of those whom they took as protectors, and they find no benefit from them. It is apparent that there is an omission in the speech, and the estimated meaning is: (﴿أنْ يَتَّخِذُوا عِبادِي مِن دُونِي أوْلِياءَ﴾, "that they may take My servants apart from Me as protectors"), so that this would benefit them and they would profit from that taking. It has been said: "servants" here means the devils, related from Ibn 'Abbas; Muqatil said: it means the idols, because they are His creation and His possession. The more apparent interpretation of "servants" is what we have stated, because of their being attributed to Him, and most often in this kind of expression the attribution is an attribution of honour.

Here (حَسِبَ, "thought") means (ظَنَّ, "supposed"), and 'Abdullah read with it (أفَظَنَّ, "Do they suppose"). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, Qatada, Nu'aym ibn Maysara, al-Dahhak, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Kathir, Ya'qub (with a variant from them), Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Haywa, al-Shafi'i and Mas'ud ibn Salih read (﴿أفَحَسْبُ﴾, "Is the sufficiency") with a sukun on the sin and a damma on the ba', as a construct phrase with (الَّذِينَ, "those who"), meaning: "Is it sufficient for them, their reckoning, and the limit of their concern?" The meaning is that this does not suffice them and does not benefit them with God, as they supposed. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: Sahl, meaning Abu Hatim, said: its meaning is "Is their sufficiency and portion" except that (أفَحَسِبَ) is more forceful in blame, because it makes it the ultimate of their aim. End of quotation.

(حَسْبُ, "sufficiency") is in the nominative as a subject, and the predicate is (﴿أنْ يَتَّخِذُوا﴾, "that they take"). Al-Zamakhshari said: Or it is on the basis of a verb and its agent, because when the active participle relies on the interrogative hamza, it equals the verb in governing, as in your saying: "Is standing Zayd and 'Amr?" and this is a sound and good reading. End of quotation. What appears is that this parsing is not permissible, because hasb is not an active participle, so that it would govern, and it does not follow that when one thing is explained by another, all its rulings apply to it. Sibawayh mentioned several of the descriptive words that function like nouns, and that the preferred form for them is the nominative. He then said: "Such as: I passed by a man, better than his father," "I passed by a man, the good and the bad are alike to him," "I passed by a man, a father to him is his companion," "I passed by a man, enough of a man for you," and "I passed by a man, what a man he is." End of quotation. It is not far-fetched that an apparent noun may be raised by it, for they permitted in "I passed by a man, father of ten, his father" that "his father" is raised by "father of ten," because it has the meaning of "parent of ten."

(﴿إنّا أعْتَدْنا﴾, "Indeed We have prepared") means: We have made ready and facilitated. (النُّزُلُ, "nuzul") is the place of descending, and nuzul also means what is set forth for a guest and prepared for him and for the arriving one of food. Here nuzul may bear both interpretations; that it is the place of descending was said by al-Zajjaj here, and that it is what is prepared of food for the guest is the statement of al-Qutabi. It has been said: it is the plural of nazil, and its accusative is as a circumstantial state, like sharif and sharaf. If it is what is set forth for the guest and the arriving one, it would be like His saying: (﴿فَبَشِّرْهم بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾, "so give them tidings of a painful punishment," Al 'Imran: 21), and like the poet's words: "Their greeting among them is a painful blow." Abu Haywa and Abu 'Amr, with a variant from him, read (نُزْلًا, "nuzlan") with a sukun on the zay.

[p. 162]﴿Then he followed a course﴾ ﴿until, when he reached the rising place of the sun, he found it rising over a people for whom We had made no shelter against it﴾ ﴿Thus. And We had full knowledge of what was with him﴾ ﴿Then he followed a course﴾ ﴿until, when he reached between the two barriers, he found beside them a people who could hardly understand any speech﴾ ﴿They said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, Gog and Magog are spreading corruption in the land. Shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set a barrier between us and them?"﴾ ﴿He said: "What my Lord has established me in is better. So help me with strength, and I will set a rampart between you and them﴾ ﴿Bring me blocks of iron," until, when he had filled the gap between the two cliffs, he said: "Blow," until, when he had made it fire, he said: "Bring me molten copper to pour over it."﴾ ﴿So they were unable to scale it, nor could they pierce it﴾ ﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will level it to dust, and the promise of my Lord is true."﴾ ﴿On that day We will leave them surging against one another, and the Trumpet will be blown, and We will gather them all together﴾ ﴿And We will present Hell on that day to the disbelievers, displayed﴾ ﴿those whose eyes were veiled from My reminder and who could not bear to hear﴾ ﴿Do those who disbelieve think they may take My servants as protectors besides Me? Indeed, We have prepared Hell as a lodging for the disbelievers﴾.

[p. 163] (A course) means a way or a route leading to the north, for the two barriers are there. Wahb said: the two barriers are two lofty mountains in the sky, with lands behind them and in front of them, and they lie at the farthest edge of the land of the Turks, on the side adjoining Armenia and Adharbayjan. Al-Harawi mentioned that they are two mountains beyond the land of the Turks. It has also been said: they are two smooth, slippery mountains to the north, on which everything slides. The two mountains were called two barriers (saddayn) because each of them blocked the passes of the land, and between them was a gap through which Gog and Magog would enter.

Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Nakha'i, Hafs, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿between the two barriers﴾ with a fatha on the sin (saddayn with fath). The rest of the seven readers read it with a damma. Al-Kisa'i said: both are dialectal forms with one meaning. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: with damma it is the noun, and with fatha it is the verbal noun (masdar). Ikrimah, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Abu 'Ubayda said: what is part of God's creation, in which no human has a share, takes the damma; what is the work of humans takes the fatha. Ibn Abi Ishaq said: what your eyes see takes the damma, and what is not seen takes the fatha.

Bayn (between) is in the accusative as the direct object of balagha (reached), just as it is in the nominative in ﴿your bond has been severed﴾ [al-An'am: 94], and in the genitive by being in construct in ﴿this is the parting between me and you﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. Bayn is one of the flexible adverbs, unless it is combined with another like it, as in the expression "a hamza between between" (hamza bayn bayn).

﴿Beside them﴾ means beside the two barriers. And "a people" refers to humans. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are the Turks. He concluded. He who held that they were jinn is far from the truth. Al-Zamakhshari said: this place is at the farthest edge of the land of the Turks, on the eastern side. The verse denies that they could comprehend speech (qawlan), and this implies a denial of their understanding. Al-Zamakhshari said: they can hardly understand it except with effort and hardship, as if the understanding were a kind of negation that almost occurs, meaning that understanding comes from them only after difficulty. This is the view of some who say that a negation with "they almost" is an affirmation, and an affirmation is a negation; but this is not the preferred view.

Al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Layla, Khalaf, Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (yafqahuna) with a damma on the ya and a kasra on the qaf, meaning: they make their speech unintelligible to the listener, not that they explain it, because their language is strange and unknown.

The pronoun in (qalu) refers to these people, who complained of what they suffered from Gog and Magog, since they hoped for something beneficial from him, because he had possessed the earth, subdued the kings, and reached them, while no king before him had reached their land. Gog and Magog are two tribes descended from Adam. It has also been said that they are descended from Yafith son of Noah. It has been said that Gog are of the Turks and Magog of the Gil and the Daylam. Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: the Turks are a remnant of them who came out to raid, so Dhul-Qarnayn came and built the barrier, and they remained on this side. Qatada and al-Suddi said: the barrier was built against twenty-one tribes, and one tribe remained outside the barrier, and they are the Turks. Their number and attributes differ, and nothing authentic is transmitted about this. Both names are diptotes (non-declinable). Whoever claims that both are foreign has the reasons of foreignness and definiteness; whoever claims they are Arabic has the reasons of feminine form and definiteness, since they are the names of two tribes.

Al-Akhfash said: if we take their alif as original, then Ya'juj is on the pattern of yaf'ul and Ma'juj on the pattern of maf'ul, as if derived from ajij al-nar (the crackling of fire). Whoever does not pronounce the hamza takes the alif as additional: Ya'juj is from yajjat, and Ma'juj from majjat. Qutrub said regarding the unhamzated form: Ma'juj is fa'ul from al-majj, and Ya'juj is fa'ul from yajj. Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Samad al-Sakhawi, one of our teachers, said: the apparent view is that it is Arabic, and its origin is with hamza, and omitting the hamza is a lightening. It is either from al-aj'ja, which is disagreement, as He said: ﴿We will leave them surging against one another﴾; or from al-ajj, which is rapid running, as He said: ﴿and they will swarm down from every slope﴾ [al-Anbiya': 96], and a poet said:

"He rushes as the fleeing ostrich rushes."

Or it is from al-ajja, which is intense heat; or from ajja al-ma' ya'iju uj'uju, when water is salty and bitter. He concluded.

'Asim, al-A'mash and Ya'qub in one transmission read with a hamza both in (Ya'juj wa Ma'juj) and similarly in al-Anbiya'. This is in the dialect of Banu Asad, as al-Farra' mentioned. It is said: there is no justification for it except the strange dialect attributed to al-'Ajjaj, that he used to hamz al-'alam and al-khatam. The rest of the seven read with an unhamzated alif, which is the dialect of all Arabs except Banu Asad. Al-'Ajjaj and his son Ru'ba read Ajuj with a hamza in place of the ya.

[p. 164] Their corruption: the apparent meaning is that the corruption from them is certain, not merely expected, since the people complained of harm that had reached them. Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: their corruption is eating the children of Adam. It has also been said: it is oppression and killing and the known forms of corruption from humans. It has been said: they used to come out in the spring and leave nothing green without eating it, and nothing dry without carrying it away. It is also reported that none of them would die until he saw a thousand males of his offspring, each bearing arms.

﴿So shall we pay you a tribute?﴾ is a request from them that he accept what they offer, which would help him in what they sought, and it was in courteous manner, since they asked him this, like Musa's words to al-Khidr: ﴿May I follow you on condition that you teach me?﴾ [al-Kahf: 66]. Al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Talha, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, and among the seven, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (kharajan) with an alif here, and in the two places in "qad aflaha" (the chapter of al-Mu'minun). Ibn 'Amir read the ra' in these places with sukun. The rest of the seven read (kharjan) in both places with a sukun on the ra'. So kharaj with the alif and kharj have the same meaning, like nawl and nawal (gift). The meaning is a payment that we bring out from our wealth. Whatever is extracted by way of tax, poll tax, or yield is kharaj or kharj. It has been said: kharj is the verbal noun applied to kharaj, while kharaj is the name for what is paid out. Ibn al-A'rabi said: kharj is levied on heads (per person), as one says "pay the kharj of your head," while kharaj is levied on land. Tha'lab said: kharj is more specific and kharaj is more general. It has been said: kharj is wealth paid out once, while kharaj is repeated revenue collected. They offered him that they would gather wealth for him, by which he would maintain the work of the barrier. Ibn 'Abbas said: (kharajan) means a wage.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read (suddan) with a damma on the sin. Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Zuhri, al-A'mash, Talha, Ya'qub in one transmission, Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani, Ibn Jarir, and the rest of the seven read it with a fatha. ﴿He said: "What my Lord has established me in is better"﴾, that is: what God has extended to me of power and kingdom is better than your tribute. ﴿So help me with strength﴾, that is: with what I can use to strengthen myself, of workers and craftsmen who do good work and building. Muqatil said this, and al-Kalbi said: with tools. ﴿A rampart﴾: a strong, firmly bound barrier. Ibn Kathir and Humayd read (ma makkananni) with two moving nuns, and the rest of the seven with the assimilation of the nun of makkana into the protective nun (nun al-wiqaya).

Then the help was explained as strength, so He said: ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾, that is: give them to me. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is a request for handing over, not a request for a gift or grant, since it was linked to his saying that he would not take tribute from them, so only a request for handing over remains. He concluded. The majority read ﴿bring me﴾ (ataunī). Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (i'tuni), meaning "come to me." (Zubar) is in the accusative with (i'tuni) with the preposition dropped, meaning: come to me with blocks of (al-hadid) iron. The majority read (zubar) with a fatha on the ba', and al-Hasan with a damma. There is an ellipsis in the speech; its implied sense is: they brought them, and he ordered some of them to be piled on top of others. ﴿Until, when he had leveled﴾.

The majority read ﴿leveled﴾ (sawa), Qatada read ﴿made level﴾ [Ta-Ha: 58] (sawwa), and Ibn Abi Umayya from Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (suwwiya) in the passive. It is related regarding the manner that Dhul-Qarnayn measured the space between the two cliffs, digging the foundation until he reached water, then he made its filling of rock and its mortar of copper, which was melted and poured over it. The building was of blocks of iron with wood and charcoal between them, until he closed the gap between the two mountains up to their tops. Then he set the bellows, until it became like fire, and he poured the molten copper over the heated iron, so it mixed and its parts adhered to one another and became a solid mountain. It has also been said: the length between the two barriers was a hundred farsakhs and their width fifty. In a hadith: a man informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "How did you see it?" He said: like striped cloth, a black stripe and a red stripe. He said: "You have seen it."

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Zuhri, Mujahid and al-Hasan read ﴿the two cliffs (al-Sudufayn)﴾ with damma on the sad and dal. Abu Bakr, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Raja' and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman did likewise, except that they made the dal quiescent. The rest of the seven, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Humayd, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, a group from Ya'qub, Khalaf in his choice, Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn Sa'dan read both with fatha; Ibn Jundub read with fatha and sukun on the dal; and this is reported from Qatada. al-Majshun read with fatha and damma on the dal. Qatada and Aban from 'Asim read with a damma on the sad and a fatha on the dal.

﴿Until, when he made it fire﴾: there is an ellipsis in the speech, its implied sense being: then they blew, until. The majority read: He said ﴿bring me﴾, that is: give me. Al-A'mash, Talha, Hamza and Abu Bakr, in a variant from him, read: he said (i'tuni), that is: come to me. And ﴿molten copper﴾ is in the accusative with ufrigh, by the rule of the second verb being the governor, and the object of ﴿bring me﴾ is omitted as indicated by the second verb.

﴿So they were unable﴾, that is: Gog and Magog, ﴿to scale it﴾, that is: to reach its top, because of its height, its steepness and its smoothness, ﴿nor could they pierce it﴾ because of its hardness and thickness. Thus there is no way to pass beyond it to other nations except by one of these two: either climbing or piercing. And He removed their power to do either.

The majority read ﴿so they were unable﴾ with the deletion of the ta' for lightness, because it is close to the ta'. Hamza and Talha read with its assimilation into the ta', which is an assimilation contrary to its rule. Abu 'Ali said it is not permissible. Al-A'sha from Abu Bakr read (fama istaṭa'u) with the substitution of sad for sin because of the ta'. Al-A'mash read (fama istatā'u) with the ta' and without deletion.

﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾, that is: Dhul-Qarnayn said it. The reference of "this" is: to the rampart, the strength to build it, and the benefit of it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it refers to the rampart and the power over it and the benefit from it. Al-Zamakhshari said: it refers to the barrier, that is: this barrier is a blessing from God and a mercy upon His servants, or this empowerment and enabling to level it. It is said that in the speech there is an ellipsis, its implied sense being: when he completed the building of the barrier, made it level and strengthened it, ﴿he said: "This is a mercy from my Lord."﴾

Ibn Abi 'Abla recited (هَذِهِ رَحْمَةٌ مِن رَبِّي, "This is a mercy from my Lord") with the feminine form of the demonstrative. The "promise" (al-wa'd) may be understood as referring to the Day of Resurrection, or to the time of the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. Al-Zamakhshari said: When the coming of the Day of Resurrection draws near and is about to arrive, He will make the barrier (al-sadd) into dakk, that is, levelled, flattened and made even with the ground; and whatever is flattened after being elevated has been "undakka" (crushed). End of quotation. The Kufans read (دَكّاءَ, "dakka'," with the long vowel and without tanwin, as a diptote), while the rest of the seven readers read dakkan with tanwin, as a verbal noun (masdar) of dakaktuhu. The apparent reading is that (ja'alahu) means "made it," so dakkan is the second object. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that ja'ala means "created," and dakkan is then in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Abu Hayyan said: This is very far-fetched, because the barrier at that time already exists as a created thing, and what is created is not created again; rather, it passes from one of its states to another state. The word wa'd here means "that which is promised" (mawud), not a verbal noun, and the meaning is: "When the promise of my Lord comes," not intending the verbal noun, because the verbal noun has already been mentioned. The pronoun in (تَرَكْنا, "We left," Al-'Ankabut: 35) refers to God Most High. The more apparent view is that the pronoun in (بَعْضِهِمْ, "some of them") refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj. The omitted clause after (إذِ, "when"), for which the tanwin is the substitute, is to be estimated as "when the promise came," which is their emergence and their spreading over the earth; or it is estimated as "when the barrier stood between them and the people who used to be corrupting among them, while they were amazed at the barrier," so that some of them surged over others.

It has been said: The pronoun in (بَعْضِهِمْ) refers to the creatures, meaning: on the day when the promise of God came, which is the Day of Resurrection. This is strengthened by His saying (﴿ونُفِخَ في الصُّورِ﴾, "and the Trumpet is blown"). Thus it is evident that this is the Day of Resurrection, and likewise what comes after it, namely the gathering and the presentation of Hell. The discussion of the blowing of the Trumpet has already occurred in Surat al-An'am. (جَمْعًا, "a gathering") is a verbal noun like (مَوْعِدٍ). (﴿وعَرَضْنا﴾, "And We presented") means: We made manifest (abrazna) (﴿جَهَنَّمَ يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾, "Hell that Day"), that is, on the day when We gathered them. It has been said that the lam means "upon," as in the verse: "So he fell prone upon his hands and his mouth." He who claimed that it is inverted (maqlub) is too far off. The estimated meaning is: "And We presented the disbelievers before Hell (arda)." Restricting it to the disbelievers is good news for the believers. (﴿الَّذِينَ كانَتْ أعْيُنُهُمْ﴾, "Those whose eyes were") is a description of blame, in (﴿غِطاءٍ﴾, "a covering"); the covering is a metaphor for their eyes. The meaning is that they do not see My signs which are looked at so that one may take lesson from them; and (واذْكُرْ بِالتَّعْظِيمِ, "remembrance" with reverence) is in this case with an omitted modifier, that is: from the signs of (ذِكْرِي, "My remembrance"). It has been said that (﴿عَنْ ذِكْرِي﴾, "from My remembrance") means from the Qur'an and reflection upon its meanings, and in this case "eyes" here means insights, not the bodily organs, because the bodily organs have no relation to the remembrance. (﴿وكانُوا لا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ سَمْعًا﴾, "and they could not hear") is an intensification in negating hearing, since the ability is negated; and although they are deaf, a deaf person may still be able to hear when shouted at, whereas these people's hearing has been stopped up, so they have no ability to hear.

(﴿أفَحَسِبَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾, "Do those who disbelieve think"): these are those who worshipped the angels, 'Uzayr and the Messiah, and took them as protectors apart from God; they include some of the Arabs, the Jews and the Christians. This is an interrogative with the sense of denial and rebuke, and the meaning is (p-166) that these have no share in the guardianship of those whom they took as protectors, and they find no benefit from them. It is apparent that there is an omission in the speech, and the estimated meaning is: (﴿أنْ يَتَّخِذُوا عِبادِي مِن دُونِي أوْلِياءَ﴾, "that they may take My servants apart from Me as protectors"), so that this would benefit them and they would profit from that taking. It has been said: "servants" here means the devils, related from Ibn 'Abbas; Muqatil said: it means the idols, because they are His creation and His possession. The more apparent interpretation of "servants" is what we have stated, because of their being attributed to Him, and most often in this kind of expression the attribution is an attribution of honour.

Here (حَسِبَ, "thought") means (ظَنَّ, "supposed"), and 'Abdullah read with it (أفَظَنَّ, "Do they suppose"). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, Qatada, Nu'aym ibn Maysara, al-Dahhak, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Kathir, Ya'qub (with a variant from them), Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Haywa, al-Shafi'i and Mas'ud ibn Salih read (﴿أفَحَسْبُ﴾, "Is the sufficiency") with a sukun on the sin and a damma on the ba', as a construct phrase with (الَّذِينَ, "those who"), meaning: "Is it sufficient for them, their reckoning, and the limit of their concern?" The meaning is that this does not suffice them and does not benefit them with God, as they supposed. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: Sahl, meaning Abu Hatim, said: its meaning is "Is their sufficiency and portion" except that (أفَحَسِبَ) is more forceful in blame, because it makes it the ultimate of their aim. End of quotation.

(حَسْبُ, "sufficiency") is in the nominative as a subject, and the predicate is (﴿أنْ يَتَّخِذُوا﴾, "that they take"). Al-Zamakhshari said: Or it is on the basis of a verb and its agent, because when the active participle relies on the interrogative hamza, it equals the verb in governing, as in your saying: "Is standing Zayd and 'Amr?" and this is a sound and good reading. End of quotation. What appears is that this parsing is not permissible, because hasb is not an active participle, so that it would govern, and it does not follow that when one thing is explained by another, all its rulings apply to it. Sibawayh mentioned several of the descriptive words that function like nouns, and that the preferred form for them is the nominative. He then said: "Such as: I passed by a man, better than his father," "I passed by a man, the good and the bad are alike to him," "I passed by a man, a father to him is his companion," "I passed by a man, enough of a man for you," and "I passed by a man, what a man he is." End of quotation. It is not far-fetched that an apparent noun may be raised by it, for they permitted in "I passed by a man, father of ten, his father" that "his father" is raised by "father of ten," because it has the meaning of "parent of ten."

(﴿إنّا أعْتَدْنا﴾, "Indeed We have prepared") means: We have made ready and facilitated. (النُّزُلُ, "nuzul") is the place of descending, and nuzul also means what is set forth for a guest and prepared for him and for the arriving one of food. Here nuzul may bear both interpretations; that it is the place of descending was said by al-Zajjaj here, and that it is what is prepared of food for the guest is the statement of al-Qutabi. It has been said: it is the plural of nazil, and its accusative is as a circumstantial state, like sharif and sharaf. If it is what is set forth for the guest and the arriving one, it would be like His saying: (﴿فَبَشِّرْهم بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾, "so give them tidings of a painful punishment," Al 'Imran: 21), and like the poet's words: "Their greeting among them is a painful blow." Abu Haywa and Abu 'Amr, with a variant from him, read (نُزْلًا, "nuzlan") with a sukun on the zay.

[p. 162]﴿Then he followed a course﴾ ﴿until, when he reached the rising place of the sun, he found it rising over a people for whom We had made no shelter against it﴾ ﴿Thus. And We had full knowledge of what was with him﴾ ﴿Then he followed a course﴾ ﴿until, when he reached between the two barriers, he found beside them a people who could hardly understand any speech﴾ ﴿They said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, Gog and Magog are spreading corruption in the land. Shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set a barrier between us and them?"﴾ ﴿He said: "What my Lord has established me in is better. So help me with strength, and I will set a rampart between you and them﴾ ﴿Bring me blocks of iron," until, when he had filled the gap between the two cliffs, he said: "Blow," until, when he had made it fire, he said: "Bring me molten copper to pour over it."﴾ ﴿So they were unable to scale it, nor could they pierce it﴾ ﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will level it to dust, and the promise of my Lord is true."﴾ ﴿On that day We will leave them surging against one another, and the Trumpet will be blown, and We will gather them all together﴾ ﴿And We will present Hell on that day to the disbelievers, displayed﴾ ﴿those whose eyes were veiled from My reminder and who could not bear to hear﴾ ﴿Do those who disbelieve think they may take My servants as protectors besides Me? Indeed, We have prepared Hell as a lodging for the disbelievers﴾.

[p. 163] (A course) means a way or a route leading to the north, for the two barriers are there. Wahb said: the two barriers are two lofty mountains in the sky, with lands behind them and in front of them, and they lie at the farthest edge of the land of the Turks, on the side adjoining Armenia and Adharbayjan. Al-Harawi mentioned that they are two mountains beyond the land of the Turks. It has also been said: they are two smooth, slippery mountains to the north, on which everything slides. The two mountains were called two barriers (saddayn) because each of them blocked the passes of the land, and between them was a gap through which Gog and Magog would enter.

Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Nakha'i, Hafs, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿between the two barriers﴾ with a fatha on the sin (saddayn with fath). The rest of the seven readers read it with a damma. Al-Kisa'i said: both are dialectal forms with one meaning. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: with damma it is the noun, and with fatha it is the verbal noun (masdar). Ikrimah, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Abu 'Ubayda said: what is part of God's creation, in which no human has a share, takes the damma; what is the work of humans takes the fatha. Ibn Abi Ishaq said: what your eyes see takes the damma, and what is not seen takes the fatha.

Bayn (between) is in the accusative as the direct object of balagha (reached), just as it is in the nominative in ﴿your bond has been severed﴾ [al-An'am: 94], and in the genitive by being in construct in ﴿this is the parting between me and you﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. Bayn is one of the flexible adverbs, unless it is combined with another like it, as in the expression "a hamza between between" (hamza bayn bayn).

﴿Beside them﴾ means beside the two barriers. And "a people" refers to humans. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are the Turks. He concluded. He who held that they were jinn is far from the truth. Al-Zamakhshari said: this place is at the farthest edge of the land of the Turks, on the eastern side. The verse denies that they could comprehend speech (qawlan), and this implies a denial of their understanding. Al-Zamakhshari said: they can hardly understand it except with effort and hardship, as if the understanding were a kind of negation that almost occurs, meaning that understanding comes from them only after difficulty. This is the view of some who say that a negation with "they almost" is an affirmation, and an affirmation is a negation; but this is not the preferred view.

Al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Layla, Khalaf, Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (yafqahuna) with a damma on the ya and a kasra on the qaf, meaning: they make their speech unintelligible to the listener, not that they explain it, because their language is strange and unknown.

The pronoun in (qalu) refers to these people, who complained of what they suffered from Gog and Magog, since they hoped for something beneficial from him, because he had possessed the earth, subdued the kings, and reached them, while no king before him had reached their land. Gog and Magog are two tribes descended from Adam. It has also been said that they are descended from Yafith son of Noah. It has been said that Gog are of the Turks and Magog of the Gil and the Daylam. Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: the Turks are a remnant of them who came out to raid, so Dhul-Qarnayn came and built the barrier, and they remained on this side. Qatada and al-Suddi said: the barrier was built against twenty-one tribes, and one tribe remained outside the barrier, and they are the Turks. Their number and attributes differ, and nothing authentic is transmitted about this. Both names are diptotes (non-declinable). Whoever claims that both are foreign has the reasons of foreignness and definiteness; whoever claims they are Arabic has the reasons of feminine form and definiteness, since they are the names of two tribes.

Al-Akhfash said: if we take their alif as original, then Ya'juj is on the pattern of yaf'ul and Ma'juj on the pattern of maf'ul, as if derived from ajij al-nar (the crackling of fire). Whoever does not pronounce the hamza takes the alif as additional: Ya'juj is from yajjat, and Ma'juj from majjat. Qutrub said regarding the unhamzated form: Ma'juj is fa'ul from al-majj, and Ya'juj is fa'ul from yajj. Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Samad al-Sakhawi, one of our teachers, said: the apparent view is that it is Arabic, and its origin is with hamza, and omitting the hamza is a lightening. It is either from al-aj'ja, which is disagreement, as He said: ﴿We will leave them surging against one another﴾; or from al-ajj, which is rapid running, as He said: ﴿and they will swarm down from every slope﴾ [al-Anbiya': 96], and a poet said:

"He rushes as the fleeing ostrich rushes."

Or it is from al-ajja, which is intense heat; or from ajja al-ma' ya'iju uj'uju, when water is salty and bitter. He concluded.

'Asim, al-A'mash and Ya'qub in one transmission read with a hamza both in (Ya'juj wa Ma'juj) and similarly in al-Anbiya'. This is in the dialect of Banu Asad, as al-Farra' mentioned. It is said: there is no justification for it except the strange dialect attributed to al-'Ajjaj, that he used to hamz al-'alam and al-khatam. The rest of the seven read with an unhamzated alif, which is the dialect of all Arabs except Banu Asad. Al-'Ajjaj and his son Ru'ba read Ajuj with a hamza in place of the ya.

[p. 164] Their corruption: the apparent meaning is that the corruption from them is certain, not merely expected, since the people complained of harm that had reached them. Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: their corruption is eating the children of Adam. It has also been said: it is oppression and killing and the known forms of corruption from humans. It has been said: they used to come out in the spring and leave nothing green without eating it, and nothing dry without carrying it away. It is also reported that none of them would die until he saw a thousand males of his offspring, each bearing arms.

﴿So shall we pay you a tribute?﴾ is a request from them that he accept what they offer, which would help him in what they sought, and it was in courteous manner, since they asked him this, like Musa's words to al-Khidr: ﴿May I follow you on condition that you teach me?﴾ [al-Kahf: 66]. Al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Talha, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, and among the seven, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (kharajan) with an alif here, and in the two places in "qad aflaha" (the chapter of al-Mu'minun). Ibn 'Amir read the ra' in these places with sukun. The rest of the seven read (kharjan) in both places with a sukun on the ra'. So kharaj with the alif and kharj have the same meaning, like nawl and nawal (gift). The meaning is a payment that we bring out from our wealth. Whatever is extracted by way of tax, poll tax, or yield is kharaj or kharj. It has been said: kharj is the verbal noun applied to kharaj, while kharaj is the name for what is paid out. Ibn al-A'rabi said: kharj is levied on heads (per person), as one says "pay the kharj of your head," while kharaj is levied on land. Tha'lab said: kharj is more specific and kharaj is more general. It has been said: kharj is wealth paid out once, while kharaj is repeated revenue collected. They offered him that they would gather wealth for him, by which he would maintain the work of the barrier. Ibn 'Abbas said: (kharajan) means a wage.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read (suddan) with a damma on the sin. Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Zuhri, al-A'mash, Talha, Ya'qub in one transmission, Ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani, Ibn Jarir, and the rest of the seven read it with a fatha. ﴿He said: "What my Lord has established me in is better"﴾, that is: what God has extended to me of power and kingdom is better than your tribute. ﴿So help me with strength﴾, that is: with what I can use to strengthen myself, of workers and craftsmen who do good work and building. Muqatil said this, and al-Kalbi said: with tools. ﴿A rampart﴾: a strong, firmly bound barrier. Ibn Kathir and Humayd read (ma makkananni) with two moving nuns, and the rest of the seven with the assimilation of the nun of makkana into the protective nun (nun al-wiqaya).

Then the help was explained as strength, so He said: ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾, that is: give them to me. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is a request for handing over, not a request for a gift or grant, since it was linked to his saying that he would not take tribute from them, so only a request for handing over remains. He concluded. The majority read ﴿bring me﴾ (ataunī). Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (i'tuni), meaning "come to me." (Zubar) is in the accusative with (i'tuni) with the preposition dropped, meaning: come to me with blocks of (al-hadid) iron. The majority read (zubar) with a fatha on the ba', and al-Hasan with a damma. There is an ellipsis in the speech; its implied sense is: they brought them, and he ordered some of them to be piled on top of others. ﴿Until, when he had leveled﴾.

The majority read ﴿leveled﴾ (sawa), Qatada read ﴿made level﴾ [Ta-Ha: 58] (sawwa), and Ibn Abi Umayya from Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (suwwiya) in the passive. It is related regarding the manner that Dhul-Qarnayn measured the space between the two cliffs, digging the foundation until he reached water, then he made its filling of rock and its mortar of copper, which was melted and poured over it. The building was of blocks of iron with wood and charcoal between them, until he closed the gap between the two mountains up to their tops. Then he set the bellows, until it became like fire, and he poured the molten copper over the heated iron, so it mixed and its parts adhered to one another and became a solid mountain. It has also been said: the length between the two barriers was a hundred farsakhs and their width fifty. In a hadith: a man informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "How did you see it?" He said: like striped cloth, a black stripe and a red stripe. He said: "You have seen it."

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Zuhri, Mujahid and al-Hasan read ﴿the two cliffs (al-Sudufayn)﴾ with damma on the sad and dal. Abu Bakr, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Raja' and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman did likewise, except that they made the dal quiescent. The rest of the seven, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Humayd, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla, a group from Ya'qub, Khalaf in his choice, Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn Sa'dan read both with fatha; Ibn Jundub read with fatha and sukun on the dal; and this is reported from Qatada. al-Majshun read with fatha and damma on the dal. Qatada and Aban from 'Asim read with a damma on the sad and a fatha on the dal.

﴿Until, when he made it fire﴾: there is an ellipsis in the speech, its implied sense being: then they blew, until. The majority read: He said ﴿bring me﴾, that is: give me. Al-A'mash, Talha, Hamza and Abu Bakr, in a variant from him, read: he said (i'tuni), that is: come to me. And ﴿molten copper﴾ is in the accusative with ufrigh, by the rule of the second verb being the governor, and the object of ﴿bring me﴾ is omitted as indicated by the second verb.

﴿So they were unable﴾, that is: Gog and Magog, ﴿to scale it﴾, that is: to reach its top, because of its height, its steepness and its smoothness, ﴿nor could they pierce it﴾ because of its hardness and thickness. Thus there is no way to pass beyond it to other nations except by one of these two: either climbing or piercing. And He removed their power to do either.

The majority read ﴿so they were unable﴾ with the deletion of the ta' for lightness, because it is close to the ta'. Hamza and Talha read with its assimilation into the ta', which is an assimilation contrary to its rule. Abu 'Ali said it is not permissible. Al-A'sha from Abu Bakr read (fama istaṭa'u) with the substitution of sad for sin because of the ta'. Al-A'mash read (fama istatā'u) with the ta' and without deletion.

﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾, that is: Dhul-Qarnayn said it. The reference of "this" is: to the rampart, the strength to build it, and the benefit of it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it refers to the rampart and the power over it and the benefit from it. Al-Zamakhshari said: it refers to the barrier, that is: this barrier is a blessing from God and a mercy upon His servants, or this empowerment and enabling to level it. It is said that in the speech there is an ellipsis, its implied sense being: when he completed the building of the barrier, made it level and strengthened it, ﴿he said: "This is a mercy from my Lord."﴾

Ibn Abi 'Abla recited (هَذِهِ رَحْمَةٌ مِن رَبِّي, "This is a mercy from my Lord") with the feminine form of the demonstrative. The "promise" (al-wa'd) may be understood as referring to the Day of Resurrection, or to the time of the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. Al-Zamakhshari said: When the coming of the Day of Resurrection draws near and is about to arrive, He will make the barrier (al-sadd) into dakk, that is, levelled, flattened and made even with the ground; and whatever is flattened after being elevated has been "undakka" (crushed). End of quotation. The Kufans read (دَكّاءَ, "dakka'," with the long vowel and without tanwin, as a diptote), while the rest of the seven readers read dakkan with tanwin, as a verbal noun (masdar) of dakaktuhu. The apparent reading is that (ja'alahu) means "made it," so dakkan is the second object. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that ja'ala means "created," and dakkan is then in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Abu Hayyan said: This is very far-fetched, because the barrier at that time already exists as a created thing, and what is created is not created again; rather, it passes from one of its states to another state. The word wa'd here means "that which is promised" (mawud), not a verbal noun, and the meaning is: "When the promise of my Lord comes," not intending the verbal noun, because the verbal noun has already been mentioned. The pronoun in (تَرَكْنا, "We left," Al-'Ankabut: 35) refers to God Most High. The more apparent view is that the pronoun in (بَعْضِهِمْ, "some of them") refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj. The omitted clause after (إذِ, "when"), for which the tanwin is the substitute, is to be estimated as "when the promise came," which is their emergence and their spreading over the earth; or it is estimated as "when the barrier stood between them and the people who used to be corrupting among them, while they were amazed at the barrier," so that some of them surged over others.

It has been said: The pronoun in (بَعْضِهِمْ) refers to the creatures, meaning: on the day when the promise of God came, which is the Day of Resurrection. This is strengthened by His saying (﴿ونُفِخَ في الصُّورِ﴾, "and the Trumpet is blown"). Thus it is evident that this is the Day of Resurrection, and likewise what comes after it, namely the gathering and the presentation of Hell. The discussion of the blowing of the Trumpet has already occurred in Surat al-An'am. (جَمْعًا, "a gathering") is a verbal noun like (مَوْعِدٍ). (﴿وعَرَضْنا﴾, "And We presented") means: We made manifest (abrazna) (﴿جَهَنَّمَ يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾, "Hell that Day"), that is, on the day when We gathered them. It has been said that the lam means "upon," as in the verse: "So he fell prone upon his hands and his mouth." He who claimed that it is inverted (maqlub) is too far off. The estimated meaning is: "And We presented the disbelievers before Hell (arda)." Restricting it to the disbelievers is good news for the believers. (﴿الَّذِينَ كانَتْ أعْيُنُهُمْ﴾, "Those whose eyes were") is a description of blame, in (﴿غِطاءٍ﴾, "a covering"); the covering is a metaphor for their eyes. The meaning is that they do not see My signs which are looked at so that one may take lesson from them; and (واذْكُرْ بِالتَّعْظِيمِ, "remembrance" with reverence) is in this case with an omitted modifier, that is: from the signs of (ذِكْرِي, "My remembrance"). It has been said that (﴿عَنْ ذِكْرِي﴾, "from My remembrance") means from the Qur'an and reflection upon its meanings, and in this case "eyes" here means insights, not the bodily organs, because the bodily organs have no relation to the remembrance. (﴿وكانُوا لا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ سَمْعًا﴾, "and they could not hear") is an intensification in negating hearing, since the ability is negated; and although they are deaf, a deaf person may still be able to hear when shouted at, whereas these people's hearing has been stopped up, so they have no ability to hear.

(﴿أفَحَسِبَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾, "Do those who disbelieve think"): these are those who worshipped the angels, 'Uzayr and the Messiah, and took them as protectors apart from God; they include some of the Arabs, the Jews and the Christians. This is an interrogative with the sense of denial and rebuke, and the meaning is (p-166) that these have no share in the guardianship of those whom they took as protectors, and they find no benefit from them. It is apparent that there is an omission in the speech, and the estimated meaning is: (﴿أنْ يَتَّخِذُوا عِبادِي مِن دُونِي أوْلِياءَ﴾, "that they may take My servants apart from Me as protectors"), so that this would benefit them and they would profit from that taking. It has been said: "servants" here means the devils, related from Ibn 'Abbas; Muqatil said: it means the idols, because they are His creation and His possession. The more apparent interpretation of "servants" is what we have stated, because of their being attributed to Him, and most often in this kind of expression the attribution is an attribution of honour.

Here (حَسِبَ, "thought") means (ظَنَّ, "supposed"), and 'Abdullah read with it (أفَظَنَّ, "Do they suppose"). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, Qatada, Nu'aym ibn Maysara, al-Dahhak, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Kathir, Ya'qub (with a variant from them), Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Haywa, al-Shafi'i and Mas'ud ibn Salih read (﴿أفَحَسْبُ﴾, "Is the sufficiency") with a sukun on the sin and a damma on the ba', as a construct phrase with (الَّذِينَ, "those who"), meaning: "Is it sufficient for them, their reckoning, and the limit of their concern?" The meaning is that this does not suffice them and does not benefit them with God, as they supposed. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: Sahl, meaning Abu Hatim, said: its meaning is "Is their sufficiency and portion" except that (أفَحَسِبَ) is more forceful in blame, because it makes it the ultimate of their aim. End of quotation.

(حَسْبُ, "sufficiency") is in the nominative as a subject, and the predicate is (﴿أنْ يَتَّخِذُوا﴾, "that they take"). Al-Zamakhshari said: Or it is on the basis of a verb and its agent, because when the active participle relies on the interrogative hamza, it equals the verb in governing, as in your saying: "Is standing Zayd and 'Amr?" and this is a sound and good reading. End of quotation. What appears is that this parsing is not permissible, because hasb is not an active participle, so that it would govern, and it does not follow that when one thing is explained by another, all its rulings apply to it. Sibawayh mentioned several of the descriptive words that function like nouns, and that the preferred form for them is the nominative. He then said: "Such as: I passed by a man, better than his father," "I passed by a man, the good and the bad are alike to him," "I passed by a man, a father to him is his companion," "I passed by a man, enough of a man for you," and "I passed by a man, what a man he is." End of quotation. It is not far-fetched that an apparent noun may be raised by it, for they permitted in "I passed by a man, father of ten, his father" that "his father" is raised by "father of ten," because it has the meaning of "parent of ten."

(﴿إنّا أعْتَدْنا﴾, "Indeed We have prepared") means: We have made ready and facilitated. (النُّزُلُ, "nuzul") is the place of descending, and nuzul also means what is set forth for a guest and prepared for him and for the arriving one of food. Here nuzul may bear both interpretations; that it is the place of descending was said by al-Zajjaj here, and that it is what is prepared of food for the guest is the statement of al-Qutabi. It has been said: it is the plural of nazil, and its accusative is as a circumstantial state, like sharif and sharaf. If it is what is set forth for the guest and the arriving one, it would be like His saying: (﴿فَبَشِّرْهم بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾, "so give them tidings of a painful punishment," Al 'Imran: 21), and like the poet's words: "Their greeting among them is a painful blow." Abu Haywa and Abu 'Amr, with a variant from him, read (نُزْلًا, "nuzlan") with a sukun on the zay.

[p. 162]﴿Then he followed a course﴾ ﴿until, when he reached the rising place of the sun, he found it rising over a people for whom We had made no shelter against it﴾ ﴿Thus. And We had full knowledge of what was with him﴾ ﴿Then he followed a course﴾ ﴿until, when he reached between the two barriers, he found beside them a people who could hardly understand any speech﴾ ﴿They said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, Gog and Magog are spreading corruption in the land. Shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set a barrier between us and them?"﴾ ﴿He said: "What my Lord has established me in is better. So help me with strength, and I will set a rampart between you and them﴾ ﴿Bring me blocks of iron," until, when he had filled the gap between the two cliffs, he said: "Blow," until, when he had made it fire, he said: "Bring me molten copper to pour over it."﴾ ﴿So they were unable to scale it, nor could they pierce it﴾ ﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord.
