These statements should be understood as examples rather than as a restriction, since the greatest losers in deeds are everyone who follows a religion other than Islam, or who shows off with his deeds, or who persists in an innovation that leads him to disbelief. The greatest loser is one who exhausts himself, and his exhaustion leads him to the Fire.

﴿Aʿmalan﴾ is in the accusative as a specifier (tamyiz), and it is plural because their deeds in error are diverse, and they do not share one single deed. ﴿Alladhina﴾ may be in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "They are those who..." as though it were an answer to a question. It may also be in the accusative as a dispraise, with its predicate ﴿dalla saʿyuhum﴾ as a description or substitution, meaning: "their effort perished, was nullified and went astray." ﴿Yahsabuna﴾ and ﴿yuhsinuna﴾ are a case of paronomasia by distortion (tajnis al-tasHif), which is when the dots distinguish between the two words. From it is the saying of Abu ʿUbada al-Buhturi:

"The one deceived by God was not, when he traveled by night to escape, and the one made mighty by God is the one who seeks him."

It is a rare example of this type of paronomasia. The poet said:

"My Lord gave me to drink and made me sing; I became drunk with my love when the young women were glad."

It was distorted by his saying:

"You gave me to drink, my Lord, and made me sing with love for Yahya ibn al-Jurrad."

Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu al-Sammal read ﴿fa-habatat﴾ with a fatha on the ba, while the majority read it with a kasra. The majority read ﴿fa-la nuqimu﴾ with the nun, and ﴿waznan﴾ in the accusative. Mujahid and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read ﴿fa-la yuqimu﴾ with the ya, due to the preceding ﴿bi-ayati rabbihim﴾. It is also reported from ʿUbayd that he read ﴿yaqumu﴾ with a fatha on the ya, as though he made qama transitive. It is reported from Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin and Yaʿqub, with a difference of report from them, that ﴿fa-la yaqumu﴾ is the imperfect of qama, with ﴿wazn﴾ in the nominative as its subject. The phrase ﴿fa-la nuqimu﴾ may only mean that they have no good deed that will be weighed in the scales of the Resurrection, and whoever has no good deed is in the Fire. It may also be meant figuratively, as if He said: "Then they will have no standing with Us on that day."

In a hadith: "A glutton and drinker, huge in body, will be brought forth, and he will not weigh the wing of a gnat." Then he recited ﴿fa-la nuqimu﴾ [the verse]. And in another hadith: "People will come with deeds on the Day of Resurrection which they consider as great as the mountains of Tihama, but when they are weighed, they will weigh nothing."

﴿Dhalika jaʾuhum﴾ is a subject and predicate, and ﴿jahannamu﴾ is an apposition. ﴿Dhalika﴾ refers to the abandonment of establishing the weighing. It is also permissible that ﴿dhalika﴾, though singular, refers to the plural, in which case it has the meaning of ﴿ulaʾika﴾, and ﴿jaʾuhum jahannamu﴾ is then a subject and predicate. Abu al-Baqa said: "﴿Dhalika﴾, that is, the matter is that, and what follows it is a subject and predicate. It is also permissible that ﴿dhalika﴾ be a subject, ﴿jaʾuhum﴾ a second subject, and ﴿jahannamu﴾ its predicate. The clause is the predicate of the first, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: its recompense..." end of quote. This explanation requires consideration. He said: It is also permissible that ﴿dhalika﴾ be a subject, ﴿jaʾuhum﴾ an apposition or explanatory apposition, and ﴿jahannamu﴾ the predicate. It is also permissible that ﴿jahannamu﴾ be a substitute for recompense, or a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is Jahannam. ﴿Bima kafaru﴾ is the predicate of ﴿dhalika﴾. The particle "bi" cannot be attached to ﴿jaʾuhum﴾ because of the separation between them. ﴿Ittakhadhu﴾ may be coordinated with ﴿kafaru﴾, or it may be a new independent clause.

The ﴿ayat﴾ (signs) are the manifest miracles upon the hands of the prophets, and the divine scriptures revealed to them.

(p-168) When the Exalted mentioned what He has prepared for the disbelievers, He mentioned what He has prepared for the believers. In the Sahih (of al-Bukhari), ﴿Gardens of Firdaws﴾ are four: two of gold, their adornments and vessels and whatever is in them, and two of silver, their adornments and vessels and whatever is in them. In the hadith of 'Ubadah: "Al-Firdaws is its highest part," meaning the highest part of Paradise. Qatadah said: "And its elevated ground, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth." Abu Hurayrah said: "It is a mountain from which the rivers of Paradise gush forth." In the hadith of Abu Umamah: "Al-Firdaws is the navel of Paradise." Mujahid said: "Al-Firdaws is the orchard, in Roman (Greek) language." Ka'b and al-Dahhak said: ﴿Gardens of Firdaws﴾ means the vines. 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Ka'b said: it means gardens of vineyards, specifically of the fruits. Al-Mubarrad said: "(Al-Firdaws), as I have heard in the speech of the Arabs, is dense trees, and vines predominate over it." Al-Zajjaj related that it is valleys that grow various kinds of plants. Whether it is Arabic or non-Arabic is a matter of two opinions; and if we say it is non-Arabic, is it Persian, Roman or Syriac? There are views. Hassan said:

"Indeed, the reward of Allah for every monotheist
is gardens of Firdaws, in which he will abide forever."

It was said: the word Firdaws was not heard in the speech of the Arabs except in this verse of Hassan's. This is not sound, for Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"Their dwellings were then apparent,
among them the faradis, then the garlic and onions."

Al-Faradis is the plural of firdaws. The apparent meaning of ﴿Gardens of Firdaws﴾ is orchards around the Firdaws, and for this reason the gardens are attributed to it. It is said: "A vine that is firdasa," meaning trellised; likewise the garden that lies beyond Yamamah was named Firdaws because its palms gathered and were trellised on its ground. In Damascus there is the Bab al-Faradis, from which one goes out to the orchards. The word ﴿nuzulan﴾ admits of the same interpretations as its earlier occurrence (nuzulan). The meaning of ﴿hiwalan﴾ is "transferred to something else." Ibn 'Isa said: it is a verbal noun like 'iwaj and sighar. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is said "halа 'an makanihi hiwalan" (he moved from his place), as in the saying of the poet:

"Her love has repeatedly afflicted me."

That is, there is no greater than it, so that their souls would not yearn for anything better than their aims and wishes. This is the utmost description, since a person in this world, whatever bliss he has, is always aspiring to something higher. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is the negation of change and the affirmation of eternity. End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-hiwal has the meaning of al-tahawwul (change). Mujahid said: "transferred." The poet said:

"For every state there is a term, then there comes for it a change."

It seems that it is a collective noun whose singular is hiwalah, but this is open to question. Al-Zajjaj reported about a people: it means the stratagem in moving about, but this is weak and forced.

"﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord﴾". It is said that the occasion of its revelation was that the Jews said to the Messenger (ﷺ): "How can you claim to be the prophet of all nations and sent to them, and that you have been given what people need of knowledge, while you are deficient? You were asked about the Spirit and did not answer about it?" So it was revealed, informing of the vastness of Allah's knowledge, that it is infinite, and that falling short of it is no wonder or strangeness. So this was expressed by an illustration of what they consider great, which is His saying: "﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord﴾". It was also said that Huyayy ibn Akhtab said: "In your book: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]. Then you recite: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra: 85]." So it was revealed, meaning: that is indeed much good, but it is a drop from the sea of the words of Allah. "﴿Say: If the sea﴾", that is, the water of the sea, "﴿were ink﴾": madad is what the inkwell is supplied with of ink, and what the lamp is supplied with of oil. It is said: "the heaven is the madad of the earth." "﴿for the words of my Lord﴾", that is, the material of the books is the words of my Lord, which is His knowledge and wisdom, and they were written with that ink. "﴿the sea would be exhausted﴾", that is, its water, which is the ink, would run out "﴿before the words of my Lord are exhausted﴾", because His words cannot be exhausted, since they are infinite, while the sea is exhausted because it is necessarily finite. And it is no wonder that I should be ignorant of some of His knowledge. "﴿I am only a human like you﴾": I do not know except what has been revealed to me and I have been informed.

Al-Jumhur recited ﴿madadan li-kalimati rabbi﴾. 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, al-A'mash, (p-169) Mujahid, al-A'raj, al-Hasan and al-Min'qari from Abu 'Amr recited "madadan li-kalimati rabbi" (with a different vowelling). Al-Jumhur recited ﴿tanfada﴾ with a ta' on top. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, al-A'mash, Talhah and Ibn Abi Layla recited it with a ya'. Al-Sulami recited ﴿an tanaffada﴾ with shaddah, in the form tafa''ala in the past tense; it is also reported thus from 'Asim and Abu 'Amr. So it is intransitive of naffada (with shaddah), like kassartuhu fa-takassara (I broke it and it broke). In the recitation of the community, it is intransitive of anfada. The response of "law" (if) is omitted, the meaning indicating it; its estimate is "lanafida" (it would be exhausted).

Al-Jumhur recited ﴿bi-mithlihi madadan﴾ with fatha on the mim and dal, without alif. Al-A'raj recited it with kasrah on the mim. "Madadan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of "mithl", like the saying of the poet:

"Indeed desire is sufficient for you with its like of patience."

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-A'mash in a variant, al-Taymi, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Hasan in one narration, Abu 'Amr in one narration, and Hafs in one narration recited "bi-mithlihi midadan" with an alif between the two dals and kasrah on the mim. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: it is permissible that its accusative be as a verbal noun, meaning "and if We had supplied it with its like as a supplying (imdad)", then madad took the place of imdad, like "anbatakum nabatan" (He caused you to grow as a growing). In His saying ﴿a human like you﴾ there is an announcement of humanness and similarity in that; I do not claim that I am an angel. ﴿It is revealed to me﴾, that is, to me; it is only based on the revelation of my Lord. He drew attention to the oneness (of God), because they were disbelievers in worshipping idols. Then He urged what contains salvation. "Yarju" means "hopes". "Liqa'a rabbihi" is with an omitted estimate, that is, the goodness of the meeting with his Lord. It was also said "yarju" means "fears the evil of the meeting with his Lord", that is, the meeting of his Lord's recompense; and taking hope in its proper meaning is better, because it expands the soul toward the beneficence of Allah the Exalted. He forbade associating anyone in the worship of Allah the Exalted. Ibn Jubayr said: he does not show off in his deed, so he seeks only the face of his Lord, sincerely, not mixing with it anything else. It was said that it was revealed concerning Jundub ibn Zuhayr, who said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I do a deed for Allah, but when it is seen, it pleases me." He said: "Indeed Allah does not accept what has been associated with Him in it." It is narrated that he said: "For you are two rewards: the reward of the secret and the reward of the open," and that is when he intends to be followed. Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan said: this is the last verse revealed from the Qur'an.

Al-Jumhur recited ﴿wa-la yushrik﴾ with the ya' of the third person, like the imperative in His saying "fal-ya'mal" (so let him do). Abu 'Amr in the narration of al-Ju'fi from him recited "wa-la tushrik" with ta', addressing the listener, and a shift (iltifat) from the third-person pronoun to the second-person pronoun, the one commanded to do righteous deeds; then he returned to the shift from address to absence in His saying "bi-rabbihi" (in his Lord). The construction did not come as "bi-rabbika" (in your Lord), indicating that the two pronouns refer to one referent, which is "man" in His saying ﴿fa-man kana yarju﴾ (so whoever hopes).

Al-Jumhur recited ﴿tanfada﴾ with a ta' on top. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, al-A'mash, Talhah and Ibn Abi Layla recited it with a ya'. Al-Sulami recited ﴿an tanaffada﴾ with shaddah, in the form tafa''ala in the past tense; it is also reported thus from 'Asim and Abu 'Amr. So it is intransitive of naffada (with shaddah), like kassartuhu fa-takassara (I broke it and it broke). In the recitation of the community, it is intransitive of anfada. The response of "law" (if) is omitted, the meaning indicating it; its estimate is "lanafida" (it would be exhausted).

Al-Jumhur recited ﴿bi-mithlihi madadan﴾ with fatha on the mim and dal, without alif. Al-A'raj recited it with kasrah on the mim. "Madadan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of "mithl", like the saying of the poet:

"Indeed desire is sufficient for you with its like of patience."

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-A'mash in a variant, al-Taymi, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Hasan in one narration, Abu 'Amr in one narration, and Hafs in one narration recited "bi-mithlihi midadan" with an alif between the two dals and kasrah on the mim. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: it is permissible that its accusative be as a verbal noun, meaning "and if We had supplied it with its like as a supplying (imdad)", then madad took the place of imdad, like "anbatakum nabatan" (He caused you to grow as a growing). In His saying ﴿a human like you﴾ there is an announcement of humanness and similarity in that; I do not claim that I am an angel. ﴿It is revealed to me﴾, that is, to me; it is only based on the revelation of my Lord. He drew attention to the oneness (of God), because they were disbelievers in worshipping idols. Then He urged what contains salvation. "Yarju" means "hopes". "Liqa'a rabbihi" is with an omitted estimate, that is, the goodness of the meeting with his Lord. It was also said "yarju" means "fears the evil of the meeting with his Lord", that is, the meeting of his Lord's recompense; and taking hope in its proper meaning is better, because it expands the soul toward the beneficence of Allah the Exalted. He forbade associating anyone in the worship of Allah the Exalted. Ibn Jubayr said: he does not show off in his deed, so he seeks only the face of his Lord, sincerely, not mixing with it anything else. It was said that it was revealed concerning Jundub ibn Zuhayr, who said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I do a deed for Allah, but when it is seen, it pleases me." He said: "Indeed Allah does not accept what has been associated with Him in it." It is narrated that he said: "For you are two rewards: the reward of the secret and the reward of the open," and that is when he intends to be followed. Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan said: this is the last verse revealed from the Qur'an.

Al-Jumhur recited ﴿wa-la yushrik﴾ with the ya' of the third person, like the imperative in His saying "fal-ya'mal" (so let him do). Abu 'Amr in the narration of al-Ju'fi from him recited "wa-la tushrik" with ta', addressing the listener, and a shift (iltifat) from the third-person pronoun to the second-person pronoun, the one commanded to do righteous deeds; then he returned to the shift from address to absence in His saying "bi-rabbihi" (in his Lord). The construction did not come as "bi-rabbika" (in your Lord), indicating that the two pronouns refer to one referent, which is "man" in His saying ﴿fa-man kana yarju﴾ (so whoever hopes).

(p-168) When the Exalted mentioned what He has prepared for the disbelievers, He mentioned what He has prepared for the believers. In the Sahih (of al-Bukhari), ﴿Gardens of Firdaws﴾ are four: two of gold, their adornments and vessels and whatever is in them, and two of silver, their adornments and vessels and whatever is in them. In the hadith of 'Ubadah: "Al-Firdaws is its highest part," meaning the highest part of Paradise. Qatadah said: "And its elevated ground, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth." Abu Hurayrah said: "It is a mountain from which the rivers of Paradise gush forth." In the hadith of Abu Umamah: "Al-Firdaws is the navel of Paradise." Mujahid said: "Al-Firdaws is the orchard, in Roman (Greek) language." Ka'b and al-Dahhak said: ﴿Gardens of Firdaws﴾ means the vines. 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Ka'b said: it means gardens of vineyards, specifically of the fruits. Al-Mubarrad said: "(Al-Firdaws), as I have heard in the speech of the Arabs, is dense trees, and vines predominate over it." Al-Zajjaj related that it is valleys that grow various kinds of plants. Whether it is Arabic or non-Arabic is a matter of two opinions; and if we say it is non-Arabic, is it Persian, Roman or Syriac? There are views. Hassan said:

"Indeed, the reward of Allah for every monotheist
is gardens of Firdaws, in which he will abide forever."

It was said: the word Firdaws was not heard in the speech of the Arabs except in this verse of Hassan's. This is not sound, for Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"Their dwellings were then apparent,
among them the faradis, then the garlic and onions."

Al-Faradis is the plural of firdaws. The apparent meaning of ﴿Gardens of Firdaws﴾ is orchards around the Firdaws, and for this reason the gardens are attributed to it. It is said: "A vine that is firdasa," meaning trellised; likewise the garden that lies beyond Yamamah was named Firdaws because its palms gathered and were trellised on its ground. In Damascus there is the Bab al-Faradis, from which one goes out to the orchards. The word ﴿nuzulan﴾ admits of the same interpretations as its earlier occurrence (nuzulan). The meaning of ﴿hiwalan﴾ is "transferred to something else." Ibn 'Isa said: it is a verbal noun like 'iwaj and sighar. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is said "halа 'an makanihi hiwalan" (he moved from his place), as in the saying of the poet:

"Her love has repeatedly afflicted me."

That is, there is no greater than it, so that their souls would not yearn for anything better than their aims and wishes. This is the utmost description, since a person in this world, whatever bliss he has, is always aspiring to something higher. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is the negation of change and the affirmation of eternity. End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-hiwal has the meaning of al-tahawwul (change). Mujahid said: "transferred." The poet said:

"For every state there is a term, then there comes for it a change."

It seems that it is a collective noun whose singular is hiwalah, but this is open to question. Al-Zajjaj reported about a people: it means the stratagem in moving about, but this is weak and forced.

"﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord﴾". It is said that the occasion of its revelation was that the Jews said to the Messenger (ﷺ): "How can you claim to be the prophet of all nations and sent to them, and that you have been given what people need of knowledge, while you are deficient? You were asked about the Spirit and did not answer about it?" So it was revealed, informing of the vastness of Allah's knowledge, that it is infinite, and that falling short of it is no wonder or strangeness. So this was expressed by an illustration of what they consider great, which is His saying: "﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord﴾". It was also said that Huyayy ibn Akhtab said: "In your book: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]. Then you recite: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra: 85]." So it was revealed, meaning: that is indeed much good, but it is a drop from the sea of the words of Allah. "﴿Say: If the sea﴾", that is, the water of the sea, "﴿were ink﴾": madad is what the inkwell is supplied with of ink, and what the lamp is supplied with of oil. It is said: "the heaven is the madad of the earth." "﴿for the words of my Lord﴾", that is, the material of the books is the words of my Lord, which is His knowledge and wisdom, and they were written with that ink. "﴿the sea would be exhausted﴾", that is, its water, which is the ink, would run out "﴿before the words of my Lord are exhausted﴾", because His words cannot be exhausted, since they are infinite, while the sea is exhausted because it is necessarily finite. And it is no wonder that I should be ignorant of some of His knowledge. "﴿I am only a human like you﴾": I do not know except what has been revealed to me and I have been informed.
